title: October 18, 2026
description:
Google SecOps

Feature

Specify whether to reopen closed cases when the grouping is by Source Grouping Identifier

You can now specify whether Google SecOps reopens closed cases when grouping SOAR alerts by Source Grouping Identifier. When the option is enabled and a new alert is received with a source grouping identifier of a case that was previously closed in Google SecOps, then Google SecOps reopens the case. For more information, see Configure alert grouping.

You can now specify whether Google SecOps reopens closed cases when grouping alerts by Source Grouping Identifier. Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

You can now provision GKE nodes from storage-optimized Z4M machine series:

  • Manually: starting from GKE version 1.36.3-gke.1767000 and later.
  • Using compute classes, cluster autoscaler, node pool auto-creation and in Autopilot clusters: starting from GKE version 1.37.0-gke.4713000 and later.

Z4M machine series are suited for large parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads and for I/O intensive workloads such as databases. GKE does not support Z4M bare metal instances at this time. See Machine support with GKE.

Security Command Center

Feature

You can view issues created by Correlated Threats and security graph rules at the folder or project level. On the Issues page, you can filter all issues by service type, project number, and folder ID. For more information, see Issues overview.

This feature is in Preview.

Virtual Private Cloud

Feature

General Availability: VPC Flow Logs adds the following metadata annotations and packet drop reasons for Cloud NAT:

  • Metadata annotations: connection.nat_ip, connection.nat_port, and nat_gateway_details
  • Drop reasons: NAT_ENDPOINT_INDEPENDENT_CONFLICT, NAT_OUT_OF_CONNECTIONS, and NAT_OUT_OF_PORTS

For more information, see Record format and Packet drop reasons.

title: How our agents build on-brand pages with design.md
description:
Across Vercel, we use coding agents to design and build pages that have to look and feel like Vercel. The typography, color, and composition all need to carry the same judgment that we put into the pages we already ship ourselves.

We recently wrote about product-design, our skill that teaches agents how we design when they work in our codebases. The skill lives in each repository alongside the code that it governs, explaining how agents can find and understand our design system as well as product guidelines for whatever they are building.

This works great when agents are working in our codebases, where everything the skill needs is right there. But what about reports, proposals, and the one-off pages that still have to look like Vercel but get made in tools that can't read any of those files? For us, the answer was design.md, one public file any agent can load.

How we approached building design.md

What made product-design work well was that the design system and product guidelines were sitting right there in the repository for agents to read. We needed a way for agents and tools outside that environment to reach the same knowledge, so that the pages coming out the other end would still look like something we designed ourselves. That set two requirements:

  • A single public URL that anyone can point their agents at, regardless of the environment they run in.

  • Guidance covering everything that made product-design useful in the first place, from brand, layout, and copywriting to the design system, responsiveness, and information architecture.

The naive approach we tried first was to simply port product-design into a public prompt, collapsing the skill's reference files into one file any agent could read from a URL. The problem we found was that while the prompt described our visual language just fine, every model reading it interpreted that description differently, generating vastly different pages from the same guidance.

Part of this comes from the fact that design language is subjective. Phrases like "keep the layout clean" can really mean anything. What is "clean"? Beyond that, the bigger problem was everything else the prompt left behind. Inside our codebases, an agent reads product-design surrounded by real components and shipped examples of the things it describes. But a public prompt includes none of that, leaving every model to rebuild our style from just words alone.

So what we needed to do was distill what that environment provided into a single file, and the only way to know whether we were getting closer was to look at the pages coming out. We set the port aside and started writing a new file from scratch, this time testing every change against a repeatable set of eval prompts.

We wrote seven of them, pulled from real use cases and paired with mock inputs:

  • Usage and performance report

  • Renewal proposal

  • Benchmark report

  • Interactive planning page

  • Build-versus-buy brief

  • Security governance brief

  • Presentation deck

The prompts stayed fixed while the file changed, so any difference in the output traced back to the guidance.

The first comparison

These evals gave us a way to measure both what the file was actually doing and how it was being interpreted by different agents. For our first test, we wanted to know whether design.md would actually change what a model produced at all. We ran the renewal proposal eval twice in the same environment with the same model, once without design.md and once with it loaded, keeping the prompt, data, and viewport identical in both runs.

Without design.md, the model generated a generic SaaS dashboard. But with it, the page led with the renewal recommendation itself, pulled the commercial evidence into one grid, put peer values on a single scale so they could actually be compared, and kept supporting detail available without letting it compete with the summary. This allowed us to conclude that the file changed the page’s structure and hierarchy as well, not just the styling like we originally found, giving us enough signal to keep building the guidance like this, one rule at a time.

The three parts that make the system work

As we tested and rebuilt design.md, the scope evolved into a three-part system that made the entire thing work:

  • design.md supplies guidance that shows agents how to frame the reader's job, structure evidence, and choose a composition.

  • A public stylesheet that defines a bounded, documented vocabulary of classes and tokens.

  • An evaluation loop turns repeated human feedback into better guidance and deterministic checks.

Each of these layers covers a different slice of the work that creates a high-quality, on-brand Vercel page. The judgment that gets encoded in design.md gives agents guidance on:

  • Shaping a page for both a quick executive read and a detailed audit.

  • Writing copy with concrete claims and honest caveats.

  • Composing hierarchy, typography, and color so that evidence and prose support each other.

  • How to publish as Vercel, down to the asset rules for our wordmark and the triangle logo.

design.md also names the recurring generated-design patterns that we never want to see, allowing agents to recognize and avoid them far more reliably by giving the patterns names.

We created a stylesheet because agents kept inventing their own typography, spacing, and layout, so we took those decisions away from the model entirely. The stylesheet packages our design system's primitives, such as headers, tables, stat strips, and chart styles, as CSS that any page can use via a public URL. Then design.md documents the class names and tokens that the stylesheet provides, allowing the agent to build the page with those names in the HTML instead of reinventing them.

Another benefit to this is that the agent never actually reads the stylesheet itself. The stylesheet loads when the page renders in your browser, so none of the code enters the model's context, saving more room for design guidance instead.

Last, the evaluation loop is what helps make the other two pieces work. Deterministic checks are used to help catch mechanical failures, such as a table that ignores the width available to it, while people judge the subjective parts that can't be automated, like hierarchy, composition, and whether the page actually gives the reader what they came for.

How guidance made it into the file

Every line of guidance in design.md earned its place through the eval loop. We generated pages from fixed scenarios, reviewed what came back, encoded the corrections we accepted, and reran the scenarios to see whether each change stuck, since a change that helped one artifact could quietly hurt another. Nothing got in any other way.

Scenarios and rounds

Each of the seven prompts becomes a scenario, meaning the prompt is frozen together with its mock inputs and render settings. The renewal proposal, for example, always runs with the same fake customer data with the same viewport settings, keeping design.md as the only thing that changes between runs. A round means generating a fresh page from every scenario against the current version of the file. Full rounds cover all seven scenarios on both Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex with GPT-5.5.

If we want to investigate something specific, such as a rule change that only affects tables, we can rerun the affected scenarios or a single model, keeping iteration loops tight.

Generating all seven pages together also made them easy to compare side by side, and what stood out was that design.md wasn't pushing every page toward one template. The interactive planning page put its controls front and center, because someone opens a planning page to change the numbers and see what happens. The renewal proposal instead led with the recommendation and the commercial comparison behind it, because its reader is deciding whether to renew. Every page used the same Vercel typography, color, and spacing, but each one was structured around what its reader came to do.

Reviewing every run

To review the pages each round produced, we built a local app that displays full-page renders and runs blind A/B comparisons. This app eventually became our eval harness, running each scenario and storing the results. Each stored run keeps the prompt, inputs, model configuration, the version of design.md it used, the screenshots, and whatever feedback the reviewer left about it. Reviewers record every correction against the exact run that produced it.

Turning corrections into rules and checks

Each correction a reviewer records gets landed in the narrowest place that can consistently enforce it. Judgment changes go into design.md as prose, reusable mechanics go into the stylesheet, and anything that we can check mechanically becomes a deterministic check in code. Problems with the harness itself stay in the harness, and when a single model fails in a way the others don't, we keep it out of the rules until it repeats.

Take one of the early renewal proposals. Its commercial terms table came back squeezed to the same width as the prose, even though the page had room for the table to be twice as wide.

During review, we flagged that evidence tables should use the full width available to them. But when looking through previous outputs, we found this same failure everywhere. So this correction ended up going into two places:

  • A rule in design.md stating the intended behavior.

  • A deterministic check in code that catches the same layout failure the next time it appears.

Once this landed, later renewal proposal prompts resulted in pages with correct full-width tables. To verify changes like this one, we reran the affected scenarios after encoding them. At milestones we went further, running blind A/B rounds that put the updated design.md against an earlier version of the file to decide whether to keep, revise, or revert each change.

Measuring whether it worked

Building the file had taken well over 200 runs, counting full rounds, targeted checks, dry runs, and all of the dead ends. Alongside the human reviewers, a model judge wrote critiques for each round, and every round's feedback went into improving the next run.

After all of those runs, we wanted to know whether the corrections we had encoded were actually preventing the failures they were written for. So we picked three desktop scenarios, and for each one we had Codex with GPT-5.5 generate the page twice, once with design.md loaded and once without. We kept the first attempt from every generation, with no re-rolls. Then we ran our deterministic checks over all six pages and counted how many times a known failure, like a table that ignores its available width, showed up in each set. The pages generated with design.md had 39 of those failures. The pages generated without it had 91, which works out to 57% fewer in this test.

Those numbers come with two caveats. The checks can only catch failures we have already seen and written down, so this test says nothing about whether a page is well designed overall. Six pages is also far too small a sample to make claims about quality or reliability, and every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping. But what the test does well is tell us that once we name a failure and encode it, that failure tends to stay gone.

How design.md stays current

The eval loop got the file shipped, but what keeps it current is real usage. Inside our Slack, that usage comes through @design-agent, an agent built on eve that we use for anything from design critiques and copy alternatives to icon recommendations and report sites built from pasted data. Instead of setting up a prompt or hunting down source files, you just mention the agent in a thread. For website requests, it loads the current design.md, builds the page against the published stylesheet, and posts a full-page screenshot and deployment URL back to the thread. Unlike our fixed scenarios, each of these threads captures a real request, a real output, and whatever feedback or steering followed, showing us how the guidance performs out in the wild.

Every week, we gather all of that feedback in one place, the Slack threads along with comments from GitHub reviews and Figma. Automation groups the comments that keep repeating, and each repeated complaint becomes a proposed change. A person then reviews each proposal, checks whether the system already handles it, and decides where the accepted fix belongs, whether that is @design-agent, the product-design skill, design.md, the stylesheet, or a deterministic check. And if people start asking for a kind of page we have never tested, that request becomes a new eval scenario.

To know whether any of this is working, we count how often each kind of complaint shows up in similar work over time. Once we encode a fix, that count should start falling. When it does not, something about the fix is wrong. The rule might be unclear, it might not be loading when it is needed, the stylesheet might not have a primitive that can express it, or it might need a deterministic check instead of prose.

Build your own

You can build the same loop yourself, starting with one recurring artifact and one manual comparison.

1. Pick one repeated artifact

Use a recent task with a real reader and real inputs, like a proposal, performance report, benchmark, or microsite. Avoid broad goals such as "make it on-brand." Before generating anything, write down a short rubric. A good one checks that the supplied facts survived, that the reader's decision is clear, and that the correction you keep making by hand actually got resolved.

2. Save the baseline first

Generate the page once without any new design context, and save the prompt, inputs, configuration, and a screenshot. Keep that first output even if it looks rough, unless the harness itself failed. You cannot tell whether new context helped without a before.

3. Start from your last ten corrections

Collect the feedback you keep giving in design reviews, pull requests, or Slack, and rewrite each correction as something observable. That means writing Let evidence tables use the full available width instead of Make the table feel less cramped, since only one of those can be checked.

Put the decisions in one file with sections for scope, reader and task, observable decisions, and available primitives. That file is your first design.md.

4. Constrain repeatable mechanics

If your outputs keep inventing their own typography, spacing, or layout, publish a stylesheet and document the exact classes and tokens the agent may use. Keep your judgment in prose, and push the repeatable mechanics into CSS or deterministic checks.

5. Run one matched comparison

Generate the page one more time with the same input, model, and viewport, but now with your file loaded. Shuffle it with the baseline and score both against your rubric without knowing which is which.

You do not need a runner or a model judge to start, a single trial can reveal the large, obvious failures. To measure reliability, run multiple independent first-attempt trials (Anthropic's guide to evals for agents) and report how often the result holds.

6. Encode the correction

Review the output alongside whatever follow-up prompts you have to send, and then ask:

  • What did the user have to repeat or steer manually?

  • Is a rule missing or unclear?

  • Can the stylesheet express the correction?

  • Is the failure mechanical enough to check in code?

  • Does the correction generalize beyond this output?

Update the guidance instead of hand-tuning the generated page. Your next comparison tells you whether first attempts actually improved.

Add tooling after the manual loop starts paying off:

  • Include scenarios where the guidance should and should not apply.

  • Keep a small holdout hidden while editing.

  • Record model and guidance versions.

  • Automate mechanical checks.

  • Use multiple blind reviewers.

However far you take the automation, keep final changes human-reviewed.

Then keep the loop running. Collect feedback on a cadence, and watch whether each kind of complaint actually becomes less common after you change the guidance. A passing evaluation matters less if people keep correcting the same mistake in production.

And if you want working examples, ours are public. We load design.md into tools like v0, Codex, and Claude every day to make artifacts that feel like Vercel, and the eve design agent template will get you a Slack design agent like the one we run.

title: Set per-user budgets on AI Gateway
description:
You can now use AI Gateway budgets to set a dollar spending limit for each user on your team.

The limit covers spend from every API key attributed to the user, along with their app tokens. After it's reached, AI Gateway rejects new requests until the budget resets or is increased.

This is useful for controlling spend from coding agents and other workloads that run without supervision, and prevents one user from consuming all of the team's shared budget.

Set user budgets

Open the Users view on the Budgets page to set two kinds of user budgets:

  • Default budget: If set, applies separately to every person without a custom budget, including users added later. Each user gets their own allowance rather than sharing one limit across the team.

  • Custom budget: Applies to one person and overrides the default. Removing it returns that user to the default budget.

Both default and custom budgets reset monthly by default, but you can change them to reset daily, weekly, or not at all. Budgets also support usage alerting via email to notify when you are at 50%, 75%, and/or 100% of your allocation.

User budgets don't replace API key, project, or team budgets. A request must remain within every budget that applies to it. Reaching any applicable limit blocks new requests.

API keys are attributed to the user who created them by default. If a key belongs to a production application or another shared workload, attribute it to the team from the API Keys page to keep its spend out of the key creator's budget. Keys created prior to the user budget feature release were attributed to the team for backwards-compatibility, so rotate to new keys if you wish to have current usage fall under the user scope.

Set budgets from the CLI

Upgrade to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade. You need Vercel CLI 59.6.2 or newer for user budgets, then set a default or custom user budget:

Identify a member by their email address, username, or user ID.

Team owners can manage user budgets, and can also grant other members AI Gateway Budget Manager permissions from team member settings. Spend using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) credentials doesn't count toward user budgets.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade to get started, and learn more in the AI Gateway budgets documentation.

title: AWS PrivateLink is now available on Pro and Enterprise
description:
AWS PrivateLink is now available for Pro and Enterprise teams as part of Advanced Networking. It allows Vercel Functions and builds to connect to AWS-hosted services without sending traffic over the public internet.

Use it to reach AWS-hosted databases such as RDS, Aurora, and Neon; SaaS services such as Snowflake and MongoDB Atlas; internal services behind an AWS Network Load Balancer; and S3 or DynamoDB through gateway endpoints.

To configure PrivateLink, open your project's Networking settings and enable Advanced Networking. Select New Connection, then enter the service name and region.

The service must accept connections from all AWS principals or allowlist the IAM role Vercel provides for your team.

Vercel creates the connection and provides a stable hostname. Use this hostname from your Functions and builds to reach the service privately.

Pricing:

  • The first AWS PrivateLink connection is included with Advanced Networking. Each additional connection costs $30 per month.

  • PrivateLink data transfer costs $0.04 per GB.

Learn more in the AWS PrivateLink documentation.

title: Claude Fable 5.1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Fable 5.1 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.1 improvements compared to previous Claude models are concentrated in long, multi-stage work like agentic coding, knowledge work, and research that takes several rounds of searching and following up.

Anthropic ships Fable 5.1 with cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Finding vulnerabilities in source code is allowed, but some routine coding and debugging may still be refused. To ensure requests are still serviced when the safety classifiers are triggered, use model fallbacks.

Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway listing the models to try. AI Gateway sends the request to Fable 5.1 first, and if Anthropic refuses it, works down the array in order and returns the response from the first model that succeeds:

This request falls back to Opus 5, then Sonnet 5, if a safety classifier is triggered. The same models option works on every AI Gateway API format, including Chat Completions, Messages, and OpenAI Responses.

Try Fable 5.1 in the model playground.

To use it in a coding agent, see the coding agents guide, then run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Pi, and more and select anthropic/claude-fable-5.1 inside the agent.

Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for Fable 5.1. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: Compute that takes any shape
description:
Workloads differ in how long they run, how much memory they take, and how much of the environment they control. That previously meant a different compute primitive for each job, so product iterations required provisioning infrastructure, not just working on a feature.

We built Vercel so that none of this has to be your problem. The compute layer is a single system with a simple job. Take any workload, assemble the machine it needs, swap configuration on the fly, and absorb burst capacity in real time.

We call this Fluid.

Builds ran on it first, then sandboxes, and now functions. If you've shipped on Vercel, you've been on Fluid without knowing it.

Fluid compute now runs over 15 million builds a day, 25 million sandboxes a week, and a trillion requests a month.

A history of compute

Changing a machine used to mean changing it by hand. You went down to the computer store, bought a hard drive or a stick of RAM, and swapped it in yourself.

Then you could rent bare metal when you needed it, and use it to serve a website, host a database, or send email.

Then the cloud let you request a machine in any configuration you wanted, choose its operating system, use it, and throw it away when you were done.

For agents, even the cloud is too slow. A standard VM can't provision fast enough to keep up with how they work, but this is where Fluid excels.

How a workload runs on Fluid

When a workload comes in, Fluid assembles a machine to fit its shape. If an agent needs to run code, Hive provides an isolated VM, usually one already warm, so it's ready instantly. Your own image boots on top as the environment. A Drive connects, and your files are right where you left them, because storage was never tied to the machine.

Each workload needs something different. A build is compute-bound, so it wants a beefy machine, heavy on CPU and memory. A function is IO-bound, loading specific code to run the instant a request lands, usually on a small VM. A sandbox is flexibility-bound, taking whatever configuration the work calls for with a Drive attached for user data.

Fluid compute is the execution model that all of this leans on. Many requests run on one instance, instead of each spinning up its own. Work starts immediately, and with Active CPU pricing, you pay for CPU only while your code is working, not while it waits on a database or a model.

Hive

Hive is the "hardware." We built it to control our own compute. It provisions the isolated machines every workload runs on. It picks the right machine for the job, keeps each one isolated in our multitenant environment, and does it at global scale. Hive gives every product one control-plane API, so our teams build on the same foundation instead of each maintaining their own.

Fluid images

Fluid images is the environment. Until now the OS was fixed. You ran the one the cloud gave you, not the one you chose. Now you push your own image to Vercel Container Registry, and run it across sandboxes and functions. In the background, Vercel converts images into a Fluid image in a format we call VHS (Vercel Hive Snapshot), the optimized boot format behind Dockerfile deploys and sandbox custom images, so it can resume rather than boot and a custom machine is ready in milliseconds. It uses the same technology behind Sandbox Snapshots, so optimizations in one product carry to the rest. v0 already uses it to build and run its own development environments.

Vercel Drives

Vercel Drives is the storage. Your files live in portable, durable storage that travels with the workload instead of being stranded on one machine's disk. Storage that outlives the compute attached to it is what makes the rest of the system work. Drives aren't bound to a single machine, you can swap the compute underneath it and pick up exactly where you left off in the next session. Drives attach to sandboxes today, in private beta, and extend to the rest of Fluid from there.

One system underneath

These are different shapes of the same system, not separate platforms. Because it's one compute layer underneath every product, a gain in boot time, isolation, scheduling, or caching lands across functions, sandboxes, and builds at once, instead of being rebuilt three times. New shapes of compute can be added without rebuilding the foundation. You don't end up with separate primitives that drift apart.

And it's real, not a diagram: Hive provisions a full VM in milliseconds and brings your filesystem state along with it, so you get isolation stronger than an isolate or a container, without paying for it in startup time.

The agent workload

For an agent to move fast, it needs the right machine, and it needs it immediately. The faster the machine assembles, the faster the agent works.

An agent runs untrusted code, so the machine needs a secure boundary. It brings its own tools, so the machine needs its own environment. And because an agent spins up and tears down constantly, its state has to outlive the compute. Fluid assembles that machine immediately, and then a fresh one for the next task.

For years, the machine was a fixed thing, and you fit your work to it.

In Fluid you describe the work, and the machine forms around it.

With this architecture, you get:

title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

How it works

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default, and existing Pro teams can opt in. Usage is tracked at the team level and covers all projects, so you no longer need to manage capacity for them individually.

What’s included

On Flat Rate CDN, one fixed monthly fee covers:

  • CDN Requests

  • Fast Data Transfer

  • Blob Data Transfer

  • Observability events generated by CDN requests

The default tier is included with Pro. You can upgrade to a higher tier for increased request and data transfer capacity.

Your tier is fixed throughout any given billing period, so you never have to worry about charges from temporary traffic spikes.

What happens during a spike

The following team had a relatively normal usage profile that would fit comfortably in our $20/month Flat Rate CDN tier:

Only days after the above period, they experienced a viral product launch that generated a significant surge in traffic:

If the team had been on usage-based pricing, their CDN bill would have reached tens of thousands of dollars. On Flat Rate CDN, it stayed at $20 for the month.

No caps and no performance hit

Flat rate pricing from other infrastructure providers often places caps on usage when you reach your capacity, resulting in rapid performance degradation and request rejection. Flat Rate CDN is different in two ways:

  1. We recognize usage spikes and remove them when evaluating your CDN usage against capacity.

  2. We rightsize your Flat Rate CDN tier every month based on sustained usage.

This means we’ll never bring down your site when you’re going viral, and you don’t have to actively manage your tier when you’re growing quickly.

You can still monitor every covered resource on the Usage page or in the CLI, including traffic spikes absorbed by Vercel:

What we heard from customers during beta

Even though surprise bills are rare across our entire customer base, we’ve seen numerous stories from Pro customers about unexpected bills, many of which famously blew up on X. One team we interviewed was running hundreds of client sites and told us that CDN costs were “by far our largest line item, and the hardest to forecast,” especially when traffic spiked “from a client’s listing going viral, seasonal traffic, or bot traffic.”

In May, we released Flat Rate CDN to a small set of teams in limited beta. Over the last several months, it has changed how they operate on Vercel.

They worried less:

Flat Rate CDN eased our billing anxiety. With the recent increase in AI crawler traffic, we used to frequently check bot activity through Observability and monitor which bots were generating traffic. We now spend much less time doing that.

They built more:

Knowing that CDN usage is predictable makes us more willing to adopt caching-oriented approaches. We're now considering broader use of Cache Components and other caching strategies in our Next.js architecture, whereas previously we had to think more carefully about the potential cost impact of additional cache traffic.

This is exactly what we built Flat Rate CDN to do. No surprise bills, predictable pricing, and peace of mind to ship the next project.

Get started

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default. Existing Pro teams can opt in to the new plan:

  1. Select Billing in the navigation.

  2. Browse to Flat Rate CDN and toggle the setting to on.

  3. Choose a capacity tier that corresponds to your typical usage.

  4. Review your selection, which will show subscription costs if you chose a paid Flat Rate CDN tier.

  5. Select Enable to apply.

Learn more about Flat Rate CDN pricing in the documentation.

FAQ

title: Vercel Sandbox routing is now 18x faster globally
description:
Requests to Vercel Sandbox public domains are now routed 18x faster.

Domains created with the sandbox.domain() SDK call are now resolved from the nearest regional replica, instead of a single centralized store. Incoming requests reach the process running in the sandbox with less latency.

Median domain lookup latency dropped from 62ms to 3.4ms (18x faster). The improvement is largest in regions farthest from the previous store: lookups are now up to 112x faster in Sydney (syd1) and up to 146x faster in Cape Town (cpt1), at p99.

This applies automatically to every request to a sandbox domain. There are no pricing changes.

Learn more about Vercel Sandbox in our documentation.

Before each turn, eve retrieves relevant memory and adds it to the model's context. Depending on the provider, memory can be updated automatically after a turn, through tools the agent uses, or through both methods.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

Read the Python documentation to get started.

title: Vercel Connect adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) in public beta. Your apps and agents can access supported services on behalf of signed-in users without separate consent prompts for each service.

  • Admin-managed access: Administrators can grant or revoke access to supported services through the identity provider.

  • Corporate sign-in: Users sign into your app with their corporate account through a compatible identity provider such as Okta.

  • Scoped tokens: Your app requests the scopes it needs, and Connect handles token exchange, caching, and renewal. Access is limited to approved scopes and the user’s existing service permissions.

Enterprise teams can now run Vercel Functions in their own AWS account with Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC). With BYOC, your function code and execution stay inside your security and compliance boundary. Vercel continues to handle deployments, environments, routing, and static assets.

During deployment, you provision functions in your AWS account and Vercel serves everything else. You keep control over function execution with your own IAM permissions, network access, and resource lifecycle policies.

With BYOC, you can:

  • Run Node.js and Python Vercel Functions in your AWS account

  • Meet strict compliance, security, and isolation requirements

  • Connect privately to backends and services in your VPC

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

title: Muse Spark Open now available on AI Gateway
description:
Muse Spark Open from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. The open-weight reasoning model is designed for coding and agentic workflows, including multi-file refactoring, debugging, and understanding large codebases.

Muse Spark Open supports text and image input with a 1M-token context window, allowing agents to work with code and screenshots in the same request. It is available with ZDR and no training, without creating separate provider accounts.

Use meta/muse-spark-open as the model name across all API formats and coding agents. The model is available across the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, the Anthropic-compatible Messages API, and coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select meta/muse-spark-open in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Muse Spark Open in the model playground.

title: Liquid AI's d1-ultra now available on AI Gateway
description:
d1-ultra from Liquid AI is now available on AI Gateway. It is a multimodal decision model for classification, routing, and scoring across text and images, including visual defect inspection and checking damage claims against customer photos.

Rather than generating text, d1-ultra returns structured answers with probabilities. Ask a Boolean question to get the probability of a yes/no answer, use Choice to select among named categories, or use Score to rate an ordered scale. You can ask multiple questions about the same input in one request and use the probabilities to decide when to automate an action or request human review.

d1-ultra is designed for harder real-world decisions, with an emphasis on calibrated probabilities. It supports a 32,768-token context window and is billed on input tokens only, including image input, with no output-token charges.

Use liquid/d1-ultra as the model name. The examples below ask the same question through the AI SDK, OpenAI-compatible Decisions API, and TypeSafe-compatible API:

See the decision models documentation for question types and additional usage details.

title: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta
description:
Vercel Daemons is now in public beta, allowing you to run long-running processes that pull and execute work from Vercel Queues, databases, or third-party systems without requiring an HTTP server:

  • Consumers using Vercel Queues poll mode, Celery, BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Kafka.

  • Temporal or Cadence workers that long-poll their task queues.

  • Self-hosted CI runners for GitHub Actions, GitLab, or CircleCI that poll for jobs without requiring inbound connections.

Daemons run containers on Fluid compute and deploy alongside your app in the same project. Vercel builds your image and maintains the instance count you configure in each region, restarting instances that exit or crash.

Get started by packaging your application and dependencies in a Dockerfile or Containerfile, then adding a daemons entry to one configuration file at your project root. This example uses worker/Dockerfile to run one Celery worker in iad1 (Washington, D.C.):

Set any connection details your worker needs in your project's production environment variables, then deploy to production. Vercel starts the configured instances, and their output appears in your project's Logs. CPU and memory metrics are available with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the Vercel Daemons documentation.

title: Introducing Token Pass
description:
Vercel Token Pass is now in early access for Pro teams. For $30 per month, your team gets $80 in monthly credit for GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3, with more models to come.

Use Token Pass with coding agents such as fx, Command Code, and Pi, or build your own personal agent with the AI SDK. Token Pass runs through AI Gateway, so you can choose your tools and switch between included models using your team’s shared credit.

Token Pass has Zero Data Retention (ZDR) enabled by default. Requests run through selected providers with inference in the US and EU. AI Gateway and the provider delete your prompts and responses after each request, and your prompts aren’t used to train models.

To get started:

  1. Open the Token Pass page in your team’s AI Gateway dashboard.

  2. Activate your subscription, create a Token Pass API key, and follow the setup instructions to connect your agent.

  3. Select GLM 5.3 or Kimi K3, and start building.

The subscription renews monthly unless canceled. Unused credit doesn’t roll over. When your credit runs out, Token Pass requests stop until the next billing period, with no automatic overage charges.

Learn more in the Token Pass documentation.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

  • Deploy an eve agent in Python in one click

title: Backends on Vercel: Python, containers, and Daemons
description:
Last year, we expanded zero-config support for Python and TypeScript backend frameworks. By this summer, developers could deploy their frontend and backend together with Vercel Services and coordinate background work with queues and durable workflows.

Today at Vercel Ship in San Francisco, we are expanding the backend workloads you can run on Vercel. Python on Vercel is now generally available, container support in Vercel Functions enables custom runtimes and system libraries, and we are introducing Vercel Daemons in Public Beta for background workers that pull work and stay running between jobs.

Python is now generally available

You can build your backend in Python with the Vercel infrastructure and development experience you know from your frontend, including local development, previews, and production deployments. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling.

Already, 150,000 teams run Python backends on Vercel, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

SDKs for Python let you use Vercel products from your application, whether you’re storing files in Vercel Blob, sending background jobs to Vercel Queues, coordinating durable steps with Vercel Workflows, running untrusted code in Vercel Sandbox, or streaming model responses and handling tool calls with the AI SDK for Python.

Delphi, which builds AI digital minds from books and talks, moved its Python backend from AWS ECS to Vercel. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs.

Visit the Python knowledge base for framework details and examples.

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. Vercel Services lets you develop and deploy your backend alongside your frontend, while Vercel CDN serves traffic on your domains, Vercel WAF protects it, logs help you investigate issues, and rollbacks restore earlier deployments.

For example, take a video app that uses a container for background processing, preparing a playback copy and thumbnail for each uploaded clip. This Dockerfile packages the Python processor, its dependencies, and ffmpeg to run with Daemons:

When you deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI, Vercel builds the image and stores it in your Vercel Container Registry. Read our containerized Functions deployment guide to get started.

Background workers with Vercel Daemons

Vercel Daemons lets you deploy containers as continuously running background workers on Fluid compute. You choose the number of instances in each region, and Vercel maintains that capacity by restarting processes when they exit or crash.

Daemons launches with support for pull-based workloads, where your code requests work from another system and processes it as it becomes available. That could mean consuming queue messages or fetching pending jobs from a database.

In our example, Daemons runs the video processor continuously as it pulls jobs from Vercel Queues. In vercel.toml, define the Next.js frontend, route requests to it, and add the processor using Dockerfile:

Follow the Daemons deployment guide to add a background worker to your Vercel project.

Run your backends on Vercel

We’re continuing to invest in backend support so more of your existing application can run on Vercel, using the languages, dependencies, and execution patterns it needs.

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

title: Vercel for Enterprise
description:
AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users.

In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x.

Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences.

Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not, and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet.

Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control.

Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar.

Today, we are expanding the platform:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP.

A single control plane for governing enterprise AI

Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP.

Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains.

Control domain

Vercel controls

Deployment governance

Enterprise Managed Users and RBAC

Access governance

Vercel Passport, Deployment Protection, and Vercel Firewall

Integration and data governance

Vercel Connect and Enterprise-Managed Authorization

Model and token governance

AI Gateway, including US-only inference and budget controls

Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics, audit logs, and the Security Dashboard.

Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls.

Deployment governance

Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx.

No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments.

How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform

Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps.

Access governance

Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production.

On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps.

Integration and data governance

Agents are only useful when they can access your systems and data, but that often means using long-standing environment varibles with wide-ranging permissions to your CRM, databases, Slack, and other systems.

Vercel Connect implements connectors with scoped access, and mints tokens for each agent task, meaning agents only access the specific context they need for the job. And now, with Enterprise-Managed Authorization, when employees sign into Vercel through your IdP, agents can use connected services automatically, without a separate authorization prompt.

Connect also integrates with Passport, so individual employee permissions also apply at the integration and data layer. If someone can't see data in a source system, they can't access it through an app or agent either.

Model and token governance

The average enterprise company using Vercel AI Gateway routes across 17 different models. Without a model router, that would require integrating with multiple separate providers, spreading API keys and budget management across platforms.

AI Gateway gives you access to hundreds of models through a single API, with no markup on cost, and Zero Data Retention keeps your data from being stored or trained on. You can also elect to route through US-only providers to maintain compliance.

How Mercor manages model governance at scale

Mercor connects AI labs with subject-matter experts who help train and evaluate models. Their engineers need access to hundreds of models to enable that work, but before migrating to Vercel, access was spread across direct integrations and third-party routers, making stolen credentials a huge risk, and token spend impossible to manage.

They moved their model routing to AI Gateway, and now engineers can access hundreds of models with a single, expiring secret, and they can set budgets per person or project.

In their first 10 days on AI Gateway, they processed 63 billion tokens without hitting any rate limits.

Centralized visibility and security

Vercel Observability gives you a single view for app and agent telemetry across every project, so you can easily manage performance and troubleshoot problems for both internal tools and customer-facing products.

The Security Dashboard flags risks across your team and apps, including missing MFA, unprotected preview deployments, long-lived credentials, and framework vulnerabilities. Each finding links to the settings needed to fix it.

Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS

BYOC on AWS is generally available. With BYOC, application functions execute in your AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

Meta Superintelligence Labs runs on Vercel via BYOC, giving its AI teams the ability to test and deploy ideas quickly, inside their own AWS environment. Leaders at Meta said that in their first week on Vercel, they shipped a month worth of work.

From idea to global scale on one platform

Vercel let's everyone in your company build safely, and makes it easy for engineers to ship the best ideas at global scale, all on a single platform.

That is how we built Vertex, our customer support agent. We were previously using a vendor, but it couldn't answer all of our customers questions. When our support team built agents and skills to cover the gaps and increase our responses times, and we realized they had laid the foundation for the experience we wanted to deliver directly to our customers.

Our GTM engineering team took that foundation and made it production ready with evals and model failover.

Today, Vertex handles 91% of our customer support cases autonomously, processing thousands of tickets a week, and it runs on the same platform where the idea started.

Ship your best ideas, securely

Contact sales to learn more about enterprise governance on Vercel and get a custom demo of the platform.
