title: Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first
description:
This is part 1 of the series "Protect Your Own Service Yourself — Self-Defense Security in the Age of AI." Do the checks you can yourself; when it's hard, EarthLink Network can run the assessment for you, and fix the gaps you can't fix on your own.

Series contents

  1. Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first (this article)
  2. What attackers now hold: when AI runs the attack itself (coming soon)
  3. Before you start: test only what is yours, without breaking production (coming soon)
  4. Testing from the outside (1): setup and the first run (coming soon)
  5. Testing from the outside (2): attack tools and legitimate scanners find different things (coming soon)
  6. Checking the code you wrote: static analysis (coming soon)
  7. Checking the parts you depend on: libraries and packages (coming soon)
  8. Checking your infrastructure settings for gaps (coming soon)
  9. Collect every result in one place and decide what to fix first (coming soon)
  10. How to fix what you found: three ways (coming soon)
  11. When you cannot fix it yourself: a maintenance contract (coming soon)
  12. Keep checking automatically every day — from building to protecting (coming soon)

In the summer of 2025, a free attack tool called Villager went up on a public site where developers share code. You tell it "look into this site," and an AI decides on its own where to look, what to try, and what to do next. In about two months, before the press picked it up, it was downloaded roughly 10,000 times.

That is the starting point for this series. Attack tools like this are now free and available to anyone. The people who attack already have them and are already using them. So instead of finding out after a break-in, check your own service yourself first, find the weak spots, and fix them. That is the most reliable defense you have.

Security is no longer only a problem for companies big enough to be targeted. Even if nobody has heard of you, machines now try every site on the internet, one after another. This part explains why that matters now, and what the series will do.

All 12 parts of this series

Here is the plan, up front.

  1. Part 1 (this one): why do this now. The thinking behind it, and how the series runs.
  2. Part 2: what tools attackers hold today, and what it means for an AI to run an attack by itself. Not how to get them, but what such an opponent can do.
  3. Part 3: what to decide before you start testing. Test on a separate copy of your setup so you do not break the live service your customers use, and never look into anything that is not yours.
  4. Part 4: testing from the outside. Setup and the first run.
  5. Part 5: the results of testing from the outside. We compare what attack tools find with what legitimate security scanners find.
  6. Part 6: checking the code you wrote by reading it without running it (static analysis).
  7. Part 7: checking the parts you depend on (libraries and packages) for known weaknesses. This is where findings tend to pile up.
  8. Part 8: checking your server and cloud settings for gaps.
  9. Part 9: collecting the scattered results in one place and deciding what to fix first, including the risk from partners and parts you are connected to.
  10. Part 10: how to fix what you found. There are three ways.
  11. Part 11: when you cannot fix it yourself, the option of a maintenance contract.
  12. Part 12: keep the checks running automatically every day. From building things to protecting them.

The service we test is promptflow, a service our own company builds and runs.

October 2026: breach announcements kept coming

In October 2026, data breach announcements did not stop. In the US, the count of people affected by the 2025 breach at Oracle's health division (formerly Cerner) rose to about 20 million. Heart monitor maker iRhythm disclosed that data on about 8.2 million people had been stolen. In the UK, online retailer ASOS disclosed a leak of customer data, and Frontline Education, which makes software for schools, disclosed a leak of school staff data. In Japan, the parcel carrier Yamato Transport announced a leak of 5.31 million records of personal data, and one count found more than 40 breach announcements there in about a month.

Ransomware is an attack that locks or steals a company's data and demands payment to give it back. Worldwide, according to the security company Bitdefender, the criminals behind it named 790 organizations as victims in September alone, the month before, 30% more than in September a year earlier.

Numbers like these can feel like someone else's problem. What caught my attention was who the victims were: a parcel carrier, an online store, health care companies, school administration. Ordinary companies, with no special reason to be targeted.

The victims were not special companies

Reading the reports, I noticed something else. The way in was not special either. A partner's server. Setting mistakes in an API (the set entry point that other systems and apps use to request data from a service) or in an admin screen. An old bug in a piece of software. A password that someone reused and that leaked elsewhere. Put them side by side, and these are ordinary paths that many companies have right now.

Take the reused password. Some other service, nothing to do with you, leaks a list of email addresses and passwords. The attacker enters those pairs, one after another, into hundreds of unrelated sites. Wherever someone reused the password, the login goes through. Nobody broke into your site. A password that leaked from some other service, and that your user had reused, simply worked on it. A machine does this nonstop, not a person. So even if your own password handling is solid, someone can get in because of what happened on the user's side.

Attacks also work in a different order now. A human attacker chose a target first, with a motive, and spent time on one company. Automated attacks go through the whole internet mechanically, site after site, and pick up whatever happens to have a hole. Whether your service is famous or large does not matter. If it is public and has a hole, that is enough. So "nobody would bother with a small business like us" does not hold. You are not being targeted; everything is being checked at once.

Attacks no longer need special skills

This is the biggest change. Until recently, attacking took real skill: a person had to work out for themselves where to look and what to try next.

Think of a door lock. The common pin tumbler lock, where you insert a key and turn it, could be picked by a skilled person with thin metal picks, setting the pins one at a time by feel. Few people could do that, and that was part of the protection. Then came devices you simply hold against the lock: press a button, and the lock turns. No skill needed. That is why people moved to locks that are harder to copy and pick, such as dimple keys, with rows of small dents on the surface.

The same thing is happening in security right now.

AI now plans the steps of an attack

Since around the summer of 2025, tools that hand the planning of an attack to an AI have been given away for free.

Villager, from a Chinese company, is the example I opened with. Part 2 covers what it does in detail.

Villager is not the only one. Several tools like it, where AI runs the attack by itself, sit on public code-sharing sites and have been copied many times. How far have they spread? One has about 7,700 copies (forks, where someone copies the project to keep their own version), another about 4,700, another about 2,900. When one gets attention, hundreds of similar copies spread right away. That is how free software works. It is not something anyone can stop.

Some of these are legitimate tools built for defenders, presented as a way to "find and fix the weaknesses in your app." In this series we use both kinds on our own service, because you only learn where someone can really get in by checking the way attackers do it. Then we show how their findings differ.

My point here is not about good or bad. It is a fact: the skill barrier has dropped to almost zero. One short instruction, and anyone, in theory even a child, can move an attack forward. The time when skill itself was the protection is almost over.

Small companies are the least likely to have checked

Small companies are the most exposed to these automated attacks. Large companies have security staff who test their systems regularly, and budget for outside firms. Sole proprietors and companies of a few people have neither. So the businesses that have checked the least are probed by these automated scans just as often as everyone else. They have not checked, so they do not know they have weak spots, and they learn about it only after the leak.

This is why I care about tools that run with one click. If a tool does the planning, a small company without security staff can still run a check at least once. As long as checking takes expert knowledge, people stop at "I know it matters, but we can't." The same thing that lowered the barrier to attack has lowered the barrier to checking. Not all of this is bad news.

Hiding information only hurts the defenders

Whenever I write like this, I get the same pushback: "Don't name those tools. You're giving attackers a lead." I think that idea is backwards.

Attackers do not learn about tools from honest articles like this one. They got them elsewhere, long ago, and that is why they are attacking right now. The pile of breaches in October 2026 is the proof. Keeping quiet did not prevent any of them.

So who is hurt when information is hidden? Only the people with no other way to find it: the defenders. Attackers already know which tools are out there and what they can do; only the defenders do not. They do not even know where they are exposed. That is the most dangerous state to be in.

Defenders benefit from this being public. Once it is known which weakness a tool goes after, software makers can fix it quickly and users can review their settings. If it were hidden, nobody could fix anything, and attackers would quietly keep using it.

It was the same with locks. Keeping a lock's design secret does not help if the lock is weak. A strong lock is strong because it holds even when everyone knows how it works. Software security is the same: do not protect it by hiding, build it to hold up when it is known. That is why, in this series, I name the tools, say what they do, and show the results of checking our own service, without hiding any of it.

First, check your own service yourself

What to do is simple. Take the same tools attackers use, run them against your own service first, find the weak spots, and fix them. If a key that works on almost any lock is on sale, first see whether it works on your own door. If it does, switch to a stronger lock. That is all.

We limit the target to our own service, promptflow, for two reasons. Because it is ours, we decide how far to test, and we can make sure the test copy does not reach real users or outside services. And we are the ones best placed to fix its weak spots. Doing the whole loop of testing, finding, and fixing on something we own seemed the most honest and useful way to show it.

promptflow is a service we build and run for working with AI. Users log in, it holds data, and it connects to other systems through APIs. It has the same kinds of entry points used in the October 2026 breaches, which makes it a good subject. If we find a weak spot in ours, the same spot may be weak in yours. We show the steps exactly as we run them, so you can check the same things on your service.

"Is it safe?" is a call a person makes after testing

I believe that from now on, people's job is to make decisions: AI does the drafting, and people make the final call. "Is my service safe?" is exactly this kind of decision. And a decision needs facts from real testing. Saying "it's probably fine" without testing is not a decision. It is a hope.

Until recently, attackers had the advantage: their attacks were automated, while defenders checked by hand, one thing at a time. Now defenders can use the same automation. If attackers can try with one click, so can we. There is no reason not to use it.

What we will actually do in this series

From Part 4, we test promptflow for real. Here is the approach, without the specific steps yet.

We check from two directions.

  1. From the outside, the way an attacker would: we try the service from outside, just as attackers do. The login screen, the API entrances, the admin screen, files we never meant to make public. We list those entry points, check that each lets in only who it should, and confirm whether a weakness we found can really be reached from outside. Something that is risky in theory and something that can actually be touched from outside are different things.
  2. From the inside, by reading: with your own service, you can see the inside too. The code you wrote, the parts you use (libraries and packages), and your server and cloud settings. We read these three without running them and check for known weaknesses and setting gaps.

Protecting only your own service is not enough. If a partner you connect to, or a system you share with other companies, is broken into, attackers can come in from there; in the October 2026 breaches, one way in was a partner's server. So we also map what your service connects to and which parts and outside services it relies on, and count those risks in the results. That does not mean testing anyone else's site. It means collecting the connections and the known weaknesses in them.

Checking only from outside, or only from inside, leaves gaps. Collect both sets of results in one place, decide what to fix first, and fix it. What you cannot fix yourself, hand to someone who can. That is one full round.

AI tools can chain these checks together without a person giving every instruction. You do not need an expensive AI model or an expert; a cheap model run many times gets you a long way, which is exactly how attackers work too. So even a first-timer can realistically run the whole thing once. From Part 4, I go through it step by step with the promptflow screens.

Checking is also not something you do once. A service keeps changing, and new weaknesses keep being found. If attackers retry automatically, defenders should re-check automatically too. New weaknesses in the parts you use are found almost every day, so the most reliable way is to run the code and library checks automatically every day. Testing from the outside is not a daily job, and it runs against a separate copy, not your live service. The last part of the series shows that setup.

Will testing break my own service?

The natural worry is: "If I use an attack tool on my own service, will it break?" Honestly, depending on how you do it, it can put a load on the service. So Part 3 explains how to test on a separate copy of your setup, or on a copy of the source code, instead of the live service your customers use, and where to draw the line so you do not push too hard. Choose where you test and how hard you push, and there is no need to be afraid. Running your live service without ever checking it is far more dangerous.

Never use these on anyone else's site

One last warning. The tools and ideas in this series are for checking services you own. Never use them on someone else's site, or on any system you do not have the rights to. It breaks the law, and it is the exact opposite of what this series is for. Only check what is yours.

Where the information in this article comes from

What I wrote here about attack tools is based on news reports and public information. The results of testing our own service start in Part 4, with real, unedited screenshots: where we found weaknesses, where we found none, and what was reported as a weakness when it was not.

Next time

Next time, we look inside the tools attackers hold. What does it actually look like, step by step, when an AI runs an attack by itself? As a defender, what should you assume? Again, I will not explain how to get them. The goal is to know what this opponent can do, so you can calmly check your own service.

In this series, in an age when attack tools are free and one click away for anyone, I show step by step how to check your own service yourself and close the gaps before someone else finds them. The target is always our own service; the series does not cover attacking anyone else's site.
If running the checks yourself is hard, EarthLink Network can do the assessment for you. Found a gap you can't fix? We'll handle the fix. Feel free to reach out.
If this was useful, please like and follow.

title: Virtual DOM
description:
In the previous post, we discussed what React really is, the meaning of declarative UI, and its tree-like structure. Now, let’s continue that discussion further.

If you have worked with React, you have probably heard about state, how and why it is used. Don’t worry if you don’t know about it yet.

What is State in React?

State is information that can change over time and affects what a component renders.

Now, assume React renders the component and the user clicks a button. The information about whether the button is clicked or not is stored in this state.

Whenever the user clicks the button, the information in the state changes from its default value to clicked.

The state changes, so React schedules an update. The component is evaluated again. React compares the previous UI and the new UI to determine what needs to change in the actual DOM.

Previous UI vs. New UI

Here, you can see the two UIs: the previous UI and the new UI. So, what is the difference between them?

Understanding the Virtual DOM

To understand the difference, we need to discuss the Virtual DOM.

Assume you already have a UI. Now, you perform some action, and the UI changes.

To track the changes in the UI, React uses an in-memory representation of the updated UI.

To perform reconciliation, React compares both UIs: the previous UI that needs to be updated and the new UI created by React. This is commonly described as the Virtual DOM.

Note: I know this is an oversimplification, but to understand the idea of the Virtual DOM, this mental model is useful.

Using the Virtual DOM, React can determine the required changes instead of rebuilding the entire browser DOM every time the state updates.

The new UI we talked about is the Virtual DOM. Using reconciliation and the Virtual DOM, React updates the specific changes.

What is Reconciliation?

Now, I have used the word reconciliation many times. So, what is reconciliation?

Reconciliation is the process React uses to determine how the current rendered tree, which is the host tree, should change when new data or state produces a new tree, which is commonly referred to as the Virtual DOM.

In a web application, the host environment is generally the browser DOM. React is responsible for the UI programming model and reconciliation.

title: Composing Any Role from 41 Discrete Permissions: A Gulf Security Review
description:
A mid-size logistics firm in Dubai runs its warehouse software with a team of six. One person writes code, reviews her own pull requests, and also signs off on production releases, because there is no one else to do it. A bank in Riyadh runs the opposite problem: forty engineers, three of whom are senior enough to be trusted with a production approval, and all three are already booked on other projects when an incident lands at 2am. Neither org fits neatly into 'Developer, QA, Manager, Admin.' Most software doesn't ask them to. It assumes the org chart it was built for.

This is not a theoretical gap. The GCC's tech-talent shortage is acute enough that a large majority of regional organisations report real skills gaps, and the pattern repeats globally — more than half of European firms report they cannot find qualified developers either. When senior engineering time is the scarcest resource in the building, a permission model that forces you to hire around its assumptions is itself a cost.

Why four fixed roles don't survive contact with a real org

A role-based system with four hardcoded roles makes an implicit claim: that 'who can approve a production release' and 'who can view another team's diagnostics' and 'who can see Face Off scores for their department' are all the same question, answerable by the same label. They are not. A QA lead in Abu Dhabi might need to approve staging promotions for two product lines but should never see payroll-adjacent diagnostic output from a third. A founder running a 12-person shop wears the Developer hat on Monday and the Manager hat when a client calls. Fixed roles either over-grant (give the founder QA powers she doesn't need, because the label bundles them) or under-grant (force her to log in under three accounts to get the access her actual job requires).

Corporate AI 365 doesn't ship four roles. It ships 41 discrete permissions and lets an org compose any role it needs from them — including the four consoles (Employee, Developer, QA, Manager) as starting templates, not fixed destinations.

The mechanism: permissions as atoms, roles as compositions

Each permission is a single, auditable capability: submit a plain-language problem report, view a diagnosis and its confidence score, approve a promotion from Developer to QA, approve QA to production, revert a release, connect or disconnect a git provider, view Face Off scores for a given org level, manage another user's permission set. None of these bundle automatically. A role in the system — 'Senior Backend, Payments Team' — is just a named set of permissions attached to a position in the real org hierarchy, which can itself scope what that role sees. Multi-hat is native: one person can hold two roles with two different permission sets, and the system tracks which hat approved which gate.

This matters at the approval gate specifically, because that's where the governance actually lives. Developer → QA → approval → production exists as real git branches and pull requests, and every transition between them is a permission check plus an audit record — who approved, with what confidence score attached to the diagnosis, at what timestamp. A security reviewer's first question is usually 'show me who could have pushed this to production.' With 41 atomic permissions and an org hierarchy behind them, that answer is a query, not a guess.

It's worth being honest about the cost of this design. Forty-one permissions is not a trivial surface. A system this granular can be misconfigured — an admin who grants broadly 'to be safe' recreates the over-grant problem fixed roles were supposed to avoid, just with more knobs. The templates exist precisely to counter that: start from Employee, Developer, QA, or Manager, and subtract or add individual permissions rather than building from zero. The composability is the point; it isn't an invitation to hand every new hire a custom 41-way grant on day one.

What this buys a lean Gulf team specifically

The payoff shows up at the moment that actually costs money. Large-enterprise production downtime runs to a median of roughly US$9,000 a minute by independent industry estimates — a number that makes 'wait for the one senior engineer who understands this module' an expensive default. With permissions composed this precisely, a non-senior developer can be scoped to run diagnosis and raise a fix to QA, while a senior engineer's scarce time is reserved only for the approval gate that genuinely needs judgment. The AI does the root-cause work — file, class, line, a confidence score, a proposed fix, reproducible because it's cached against a hash of the issue and the code snapshot — and a smaller set of trusted people spend their time on the decision, not the detective work.

It also means the person who notices the problem doesn't have to be an engineer at all. Someone in operations or customer service in Doha can file a plain-language report through the Employee console; the permission model decides who sees what happens next, not whether the report gets filed at all. And the trust boundary stays fixed regardless of how permissions are composed: no role, however broadly granted, can reach a live database. The system reasons over source code and a scripted schema export; if a fix genuinely needs live data, it writes a read-only query for your own developer to run, and the result never leaves your environment.

title: One Trip.com URL, Five Pulls, Twelve Hours: 21 Different Hotels, Six Every Time
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads Trip.com: a city, two dates and a guest count in, one row per hotel out, with the live nightly rate for exactly those dates.

Trip.com is the booking channel for most of Asia and it has no public web API, so a scraper is the only way in. The field I expected to cause trouble was the price. It didn't. What caused trouble was something I hadn't thought to check: which hotels the page shows you at all.

The same URL, five times, one day

My QA runs hit a hardcoded list URL so I can diff the output day over day. On 21 October 2026 five of them fired against a byte-identical URL:

https://www.trip.com/hotels/list?city=723&checkin=2026%2F11%2F20
  &checkout=2026%2F11%2F23&adult=2&children=0&curr=USD&locale=en-XX

Bali, three nights, two adults, USD. Pulls at 00:30, 07:48, 07:55, 08:20 and 12:10 — an 11-hour-40-minute span. Twelve hotel rows each, which is one page, 60 rows total.

Those 60 rows contained 21 distinct hotels. Six appeared in all five pulls. Nine appeared exactly once.

Appeared in Hotels Median nightly
5 of 5 pulls 6 $22
4 of 5 3 $30
3 of 5 3 $89
1 of 5 9 $52

Pairwise, the overlap decays with the gap between requests, and it decays cleanly:

Pair Gap Common rows
07:55 vs 08:20 25 min 12 / 12
07:48 vs 07:55 7 min 11 / 12
00:30 vs 07:48 7 h 8 / 12
08:20 vs 12:10 4 h 8 / 12
07:48 vs 12:10 4 h 7 / 12
00:30 vs 12:10 11 h 40 6 / 12

So this is not per-request randomness. Requests minutes apart come back identical or off by one row. Requests hours apart come back half different. That is the signature of a result set that is assembled and cached, then reassembled later — not a ranking you can treat as stable.

It replicates. Three pulls on 20 October against the 19–22 November window: the two fired a minute apart agreed 12 of 12, the one twenty hours earlier agreed 7 of 12 with both. Two pulls this morning, four hours apart, agreed 7 of 12 — a $260 Kempinski vanished, a $283 resort appeared.

What that does to a number you'd actually report

The prices held almost perfectly still. Across the six hotels present in all five pulls, the nightly rate moved in three of them, by exactly one dollar: $34→$35, $10→$11, $28→$27. Kenran Resort sat at $72 in all five, Moonloka at $16. If you track one named property, Trip.com is boringly consistent and this article is irrelevant to you.

Aggregate those same five pulls and the stillness disappears:

Pull Median nightly Mean nightly
00:30 $31.00 $51.60
07:48 $35.00 $62.80
07:55 $31.50 $61.40
08:20 $31.50 $61.30
12:10 $23.50 $39.00

The mean nightly rate for Bali swung from $39.00 to $62.80 — a 61% spread — on one day, from one URL, with essentially no price changing. Every dollar of that swing is sampling. The 12:10 pull happened to miss the expensive tail: no Anvaya at $110, no Kayon Jungle at $281, no ARNA at $90. The 07:48 pull caught all three.

Which direction it biases is not random either. The six properties that never moved are all in the cheap half — $9 to $72, median $22. The nine one-time visitors have a median of $52 and include $86, $98, $106 and $166. Page one has a sticky cheap core and a rotating expensive tail, and a "city average" built on page one inherits whichever part of that tail it happened to catch.

Asking for more rows is a different question, not a bigger answer

The obvious fix is to pull deeper. It works, but not in the way "more data, same answer" suggests. Three runs on Bangkok this morning, 21–24 November, same two adults, minutes apart:

  • 12 rows: median $38.50, mean $45.10
  • a second 12-row run three minutes later: 11 of 12 the same hotels, zero price differences, order reshuffled
  • 48 rows, thirty seconds after that: 48 distinct properties, median $53.50, mean $75.30

Median $38.50 against $53.50 on the same city, the same dates, the same minute. Page one is not a random sample — it is cheap-skewed, and each extra page walks you up the price distribution. The 48-row run also did not contain 2 of the 12 hotels the first run had just returned.

The practical rule I now use: if you want a city-level statistic, fix the row count and never compare two samples of different depth. If you want coverage, run it more than once and union on hotelId — the churn is working for you then, because five pulls of 12 gave me 21 properties, not 12.

import requests, statistics
from collections import defaultdict

TOKEN = "<APIFY_TOKEN>"
seen = defaultdict(dict)

for _ in range(5):  # five pulls, spaced hours apart by a scheduler
    rows = requests.post(
        "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~tripcom-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items",
        params={"token": TOKEN},
        json={"cityId": 723, "cityName": "Bali",
              "checkIn": "2026-11-21", "checkOut": "2026-11-24",
              "adults": 2, "maxHotels": 48, "currency": "USD"},
    ).json()
    for r in rows:
        if r.get("type") == "hotel" and r.get("price"):
            seen[r["hotelId"]] = r          # last write wins, one row per property

print(len(seen), "distinct hotels")
print("median", statistics.median(r["price"] for r in seen.values()))

Note the type == "hotel" filter. The last row of every run is a free notice row with the run's own accounting — rowsDelivered, chargedTotalUsd, timings. The 48-row Bangkok run reports {"rowsDelivered": 48, "chargedTotalUsd": 0.144} and finished in 28 seconds. Leave it in your dataframe and it becomes a hotel with no price.

Two price fields you should not multiply

While I had 451 priced rows from 22 runs sitting on disk, I checked the arithmetic between price (nightly) and totalPrice (the stay).

totalPrice was larger than price × nights in 451 of 451 rows. Median ratio 1.200, range 1.056 to 1.339. Two things are stacked in there: totalPrice is the number Trip.com prints as incl. taxes & fees, and price is rounded to a whole currency unit, which on a $9 room is an 11% rounding step on its own. I am not going to tell you the tax rate, because Trip.com ships a formatted total and a rounded nightly figure and splitting them is guessing. What I will say is that price * nights is never the number the guest pays, and the error is a fifth, not a rounding wobble.

The discount badges have a smaller version of the same gap. 373 rows carried an originalPrice, and it was above price in all 373 — median implied discount 29.4%. On the 364 rows that also carried an "N% off" tag in dealTags, the discount you compute from the two numbers beat the badge in 341 of them, median by 2.7 points: Lloyd's Inn says 61% off with $80 → $28 next to it, which is 65%. Use the badge as a label and compute your own number, and don't expect them to agree to the point.

The Actor is Trip.com Scraper — hotel cards with the live rate for your dates, property details, and the guest reviews off the hotel page, by city ID or by URL.

When this is the wrong tool

  • You need a booking. This reads public pages. There is no availability hold, no rate code and no reservation here.
  • You need every hotel in a city, exactly once. You will get there by unioning repeated runs, not by one run. If you need a guaranteed complete inventory as of a timestamp, Trip.com's page one will not give you one.
  • You need per-room rate plans. Each row carries the one room Trip.com chose to price for your dates — roomName, roomId — not the hotel's full rate table.
  • You need a tax breakdown. You get the pre-tax nightly figure and the all-in total. The split between them is not published as fields, and I'd rather ship two honest numbers than three invented ones.

If you keep one thing from this: before you trust a scraped ranking, pull it twice an hour apart and count the overlap. A field that disagrees with itself is obvious. A row set that quietly swaps half its members is not, and it moves your averages far harder than any price ever will.

title: I let Stripe grade my tests: building a billing simulator where no expected value comes from my own code
description:
Built for the TestSprite Hackathon, Season 4. Live: tera-orpin-three.vercel.app · Code: github.com/PugarHuda/tera

Founders are afraid to touch pricing, and they are right to be. Move a customer from $29 to $79 on day 17 of a 31-day month and Stripe writes two proration lines you have probably never computed by hand: an "Unused time" credit of −$14.03 and a "Remaining time" charge of $38.23, on top of the $79 renewal. Add a coupon that was applied once, a tax rate that is inclusive, a trial, or a subscription in Stripe's new flexible billing mode, and the invoice your customer sees is no longer something you can predict from the pricing page.

Tera simulates it first. You give it a customer timeline (subscribe, change seats, upgrade, apply a coupon, pause, cancel) and it returns every invoice to the cent, plus the webhook events Stripe will send for it. This post is not really about the simulator, though. It is about the question every test suite eventually has to answer: who decides what the right answer is?

The rule: the engine never writes its own expectations

The easiest way to get a green test suite for a billing engine is to run the engine, save its output, and assert that it does not change. That suite is worthless the day the engine is wrong, because it was wrong when the snapshot was taken too.

So Tera has one rule. Every expected value is derived by hand from the billing rules, written next to its arithmetic, and then replayed in a real Stripe test-mode account with test clocks. Scenario S05 in golden/scenarios.json looks like this:

"math": "remaining 15/31: -round(2900*15/31)=-1403, +round(7900*15/31)=3823",
"expect": [{ "date": "2027-02-01", "lines": [-1403, 3823, 7900], "total": 10320 }]

A script creates the same customer in Stripe, advances a test clock through the timeline, reads back Stripe's invoices and diffs them line by line against both the hand-derived values and Tera's engine. Only when all three agree is the scenario marked verified, and the evidence (invoice ids, test clock id) is committed to the repo. Today there are 130 golden scenarios and all 127 timelines among them match Stripe to the cent. The other three are migration scenarios with no invoices to replay.

When Stripe disagreed with my hand derivation, Stripe won, and I kept the receipts. A coupon applied in the same second as subscribing discounts the next invoice, because Stripe finalizes the first one at creation. A repeating coupon for 3 months lasts three calendar months, not three invoices. A percent discount on a proration comes off the rounded gross. None of those were in my head when I started.

Letting Stripe find the cases I did not think of

Hand-written scenarios only cover what you already suspect. So Tera also runs differential fuzzing: a seeded generator produces random customer timelines, with month-end anchors, Feb 29, random times of day, trials, seat and plan changes, coupons and both tax behaviours. Each one runs through Tera and through Stripe, and any difference is a finding.

Every finding goes through the same pipeline: a targeted Stripe probe to isolate the rule, a new hand-derived golden scenario that pins it, then the engine fix. The fuzzer runs nightly in CI with fresh seeds, in both of Stripe's billing modes. The rules it surfaced are some of the most interesting in the repo. Stripe prorates the unit price to 12 decimals before multiplying by seats, so a credit of exactly 11257.5 lands a cent under the tie. In flexible mode every credit refunds its original debit with the gross and the discount rounded separately.

This week the same approach caught a real gap in usage-based billing. A code audit found the engine silently dropping metered usage on an immediate cancellation. Seven live probes gave the rules: tier lines run only up to the tier the usage reaches, a metered item has no unused-time line, and cancelling with invoice_now bills the usage so far. A follow-up fuzz batch for metered prices then found that Stripe still sends a $0 final invoice after an unused last period. It also found a stale usage window in my own replay script.

Where TestSprite fits

Stripe is the oracle for the engine. TestSprite is the gate for everything a user actually touches.

  • 28 UI tests on every pull request, run by the TestSprite GitHub App against that PR's own Vercel preview. Branch protection requires the TestSprite V3 check. Each test asserts hand-derived amounts in the browser: "Invoice 2 totals $103.20", not "an invoice is shown".
  • The tests live in the repo. Every plan is a JSON file in testsprite/plans/ and every test has hand-written Playwright code in testsprite/code/. A CI check compares both with the cloud project and fails on drift. That matters because an auto-healing run can quietly rewrite stored code, for example pinning a preview URL or loosening an assertion to two words.
  • API tests against the preview, too. TestSprite gives backend tests no target URL, so a small script stores each API test with its base URL pointing at the PR's preview, runs it with auto-heal off, and puts production back.
  • Triage that uses the oracle. When TestSprite V3 fails, a workflow downloads the failure bundle, replays the golden scenarios behind that test on the same preview, and compares them with Stripe's recorded invoices. One PR comment then says either "engine still matches Stripe, so this is a UI regression" or which invoice the engine now gets wrong.
  • A nightly money-math canary on production, plus Playwright user journeys, Schemathesis fuzzing of the OpenAPI spec, Arazzo workflows, Lighthouse budgets and Stryker mutation testing on every PR.

TestSprite caught a real bug before merge on PR #18. A price added in the builder billed $0.00 instead of ¥4,500, because the builder put a metered price first. The fix went in, and the check went green.

What went wrong, honestly

The workspace ran out of TestSprite credits twice during the hackathon. When that happens the check reports "Not enough credits" without running a single test. Nine pull requests hit that wall; the ones that shipped were merged by the repository admin after every other check had passed. They are not hidden: docs/LOOP.md is generated from the GitHub API and lists every PR and every commit's TestSprite verdict. Five went red on real test results, all fixed in the same PR, and nine were blocked by credits. A credit shortfall is not a test verdict, and treating it as one in either direction would make the ledger lie.

A second lesson: every new test layer I added found something about the previous layers. Schemathesis found the OpenAPI spec looser than the validator. Redocly Respect's strict schema checks found my conditional schemas rejecting properties their parent declared. Then my fix for that made Schemathesis unable to generate requests at all. Each layer is cheap. Not running the next one is what gets expensive.

If you build something similar

  1. Pick an oracle that is not your code. For billing it is Stripe's test clocks. For tax it could be a published calculator. For physics, a reference implementation.
  2. Derive expectations by hand and write the arithmetic next to them. Future you will need it when the oracle disagrees.
  3. Let the oracle generate the questions too (differential fuzzing), and turn every disagreement into a pinned example.
  4. Keep your end-to-end tests in the repo and check the cloud copy against it.

Try it: open the simulator on S05, change the upgrade date, and press Verify in Stripe. Your own timeline gets replayed in a fresh test clock and diffed to the cent.

AI disclosure: this post was drafted by an AI agent (Claude Code) from the project's own repository, evidence files and CI history, and published at the author's request. The project itself was built with the same agent.

title: How to Track SEC EDGAR Filings as JSON (Without Maintaining a Scraper)
description:
How to Track SEC EDGAR Filings as JSON (Without Maintaining a Scraper)

If you are building filing alerts, compliance checks or equity-research workflows, SEC EDGAR is the
source: every filing from every US issuer, published minutes after acceptance. The official EDGAR
APIs are free and return JSON — but wiring them up yourself still means declaring a User-Agent the
SEC accepts, staying under its published limit of 10 requests per second, paginating full-text
search results, and handling fields that one endpoint returns while another does not.

Here is how to get the data in two ways, with a real sample of the output.

The official API, in a nutshell

  • Endpoints: the EDGAR application programming interfaces (submissions by CIK, filing metadata, full-text search).
  • No API key: EDGAR's endpoints are anonymous.
  • Politeness rules: send a declared User-Agent with your contact information and stay under the published limit of 10 requests per second; requests that ignore this are rejected.
  • Scope: filing metadata and issuer organisations only. There is no officer or contact data here — personal data stays out of scope, by design.

Option A — call the official API directly 

curl -sS -A "your-app your@email.com" \
  "https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000320193.json" | jq '.filings.recent | .accessionNumber[0:3]'

That works fine for one issuer. The moment you watch a shortlist of companies or run a full-text
search, you are maintaining pagination, date filtering and field reconciliation for every endpoint
you touch.

Option B — run a ready-made Actor

steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor wraps those endpoints on the Apify platform: it handles the declared
User-Agent, the 10 req/s budget, pagination, retries and an output schema check on every run. No SEC
key needed (an optional proxy of your own token keeps your run budget isolated).

Input — by issuer, or by full-text query:

{ "cik": "0000320193", "formTypes": ["10-K", "10-Q", "8-K"], "startDate": "2026-01-01", "maxResults": 10 }

{ "query": "supply agreement", "startDate": "2026-10-01", "endDate": "2026-10-17", "maxResults": 25 }

At least one of cik or query is required.

Run it with one API call:

curl -sS -X POST \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/steadfetch~sec-edgar-monitor/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"cik":"0000320193","formTypes":["10-Q"],"startDate":"2026-07-01","maxResults":5}'

Real output sample (a genuine filing record, as published in the Actor's docs):

{
    "accession_no": "0000320193-26-000020",
    "cik": "0000320193",
    "company_name": "Apple Inc.",
    "form_type": "10-Q",
    "filing_date": "2026-07-31",
    "report_date": "2026-06-27",
    "acceptance_datetime": "2026-07-31T14:01:02.000Z",
    "primary_document_url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000020/aapl-20260627.htm",
    "is_amendment": false,
    "url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000020/aapl-20260627.htm",
    "scrapedAt": "2026-10-19T12:00:00.000Z"
}

One dataset item per filing, validated against the published dataset schema on every run — if a field
type changes upstream, the run fails loudly instead of writing bad rows.

JavaScript and Python

Node.js, with apify-client:

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN });

const { defaultDatasetId } = await client.actor('steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor').call({
  cik: '0000320193',
  formTypes: ['10-K', '10-Q', '8-K'],
  startDate: '2026-01-01',
  maxResults: 10,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(defaultDatasetId).listItems();
console.log(JSON.stringify(items, null, 2));

Python, with apify-client:

import json, os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor").call(run_input={
    "cik": "0000320193", "formTypes": ["10-K", "10-Q", "8-K"],
    "startDate": "2026-01-01", "maxResults": 10,
})
items = client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items
print(json.dumps(items, indent=2))

Runnable versions of all three (curl, Node, Python) plus the sample output live in
steadfetch/examples/sec-edgar-monitor.

What it costs

Pay-per-result pricing on Apify: 5.00 USD per 1,000 filings (0.005 USD per filing) plus a
0.00005 USD run-start fee. Failed requests, retries and empty searches are not charged per result,
and no proxy is billed — EDGAR answers with structured JSON, so no browser is involved.

Fields you get

Field Meaning
accession_no Official accession number of the filing
cik / company_name Issuer identity
form_type 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and the rest of the EDGAR form taxonomy
filing_date / report_date When it was filed and the period it covers
acceptance_datetime EDGAR acceptance timestamp — null when the full-text endpoint omits it; never invented
primary_document_url / url Direct link to the filing document
is_amendment Whether the filing amends an earlier one
scrapedAt Extraction timestamp, on every record

Getting started

Open the Actor page in the Apify Store, run it
from the console or with the API snippets above, and pull the dataset into whatever you already use.

Steadfetch builds public-data Actors that don't break: schema-validated output, official sources
only. More at apify.com/steadfetch.

title: Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration
description:
Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration

Introduction

In this rapidly evolving era of Artificial Intelligence, I wanted to go beyond simply learning about AI and start understanding how it works in real-world applications. My goal is to dive deeper into the world of AI, explore its workflows, understand how Large Language Models (LLMs) operate, and learn how AI agents can reason, use tools, and solve practical problems.

As technology continues to advance, I believe the best way to grow as a developer is to challenge myself by building real-world applications, experimenting with new technologies, and learning from the problems I encounter along the way. I wanted to push my boundaries, strengthen my AI engineering skills, and contribute to the growing AI ecosystem through practical implementation.

That motivation led me to build AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration.

The idea was to create more than a traditional chatbot. I wanted to explore how an AI assistant could interact with external tools, retrieve relevant information, and respond to different user requests through a single conversational interface.

In this article, I'll share my journey of building this project, the technologies I explored, how tool integration works, the challenges involved, and the lessons I learned while developing my practical AI skills.

Project Links

Explore the project and its source code:

  • Live Demo: AI Chat Assistant
  • Frontend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Frontend
  • Backend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Backend

Feel free to explore the code, try the live application, and share your feedback. I'd love to hear your thoughts and suggestions!

1. The Problem: An AI Model Alone Is Not Enough

LLMs are powerful at understanding natural language, generating responses, summarizing content, and explaining technical concepts. However, a standalone model has limitations.

For example:

  • It may not know the latest news or current weather conditions.
  • Its training data may not include recent technical information.
  • It cannot automatically access external services without an integration.
  • It needs additional application logic to interact with APIs and handle errors.

I wanted to solve these limitations by building an assistant that could select the appropriate tools when answering different types of questions.

For example, when a user asks, "What is the weather in Chennai?", the assistant should use a weather service rather than simply generate an answer from its language model.

Similarly, when a user asks a programming question, it can use a relevant technical information source when appropriate.

This led me to explore agentic AI and tool calling.

2. What Is Agentic AI?

Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can work toward a goal by choosing actions, using tools, and incorporating the results into their responses.

A traditional chatbot typically follows a straightforward pattern:

User input → LLM → Response

An agentic assistant can follow a more flexible workflow:

User input → Understand the request → Select a tool → Execute the tool → Process the result → Generate a response

For example, consider this request:

"Find recent technology news and summarize the important points."

The assistant can identify that the user needs current information, invoke a news or search tool, process the returned results, and generate a concise summary.

The LLM handles language understanding and decision-making, while external tools provide capabilities that the model does not have on its own.

An important distinction is that the LLM does not magically gain access to external services. The application must explicitly provide the tools, their descriptions, and the code needed to execute them.

3. Project Architecture

I designed the application around a frontend, a backend API, an LLM integration, and a collection of specialized tools.

The main components are:

Frontend

The frontend provides the conversational interface where users submit questions and view assistant responses.

Backend API

The backend receives requests, manages the conversation flow, coordinates model interactions, executes tool calls, and returns the final response.

LLM integration

The language model interprets user requests, determines when a tool may be useful, and generates natural-language responses from the available context.

Tool integrations

Individual tools connect the assistant to external information sources and services, such as weather, news, web search, Wikipedia, movie information, Stack Overflow, and Notion.

Supporting services

The application also uses supporting infrastructure such as a database and Redis, depending on the feature and workflow, for data persistence and caching.

The overall flow looks like this:

              User
               |
               v
        Frontend Chat UI
               |
               v
          Backend API
               |
               v
          LLM / Agent
               |
        Selects a tool
               |
               v
       Tool Execution Layer
               |
       +-------+--------+
       |       |        |
     Weather  Search   News
       |       |        |
       +-------+--------+
               |
               v
        Tool Result
               |
               v
        LLM Generates
        Final Response
               |
               v
          Frontend UI

This architecture separates the user interface, orchestration logic, and external integrations, making the application easier to extend and maintain.

4. Integrating Multiple Tools

One of the most interesting parts of the project was connecting different capabilities through a single assistant.

Each tool has a specific responsibility.

Weather

The weather tool retrieves weather information for a requested location. This allows the assistant to answer questions that require current or forecast data.

Web Search

The web search tool helps retrieve information from online sources when a question requires information beyond the model's built-in knowledge.

News

The news integration provides access to recent news information, helping the assistant respond to requests about current events.

Wikipedia

Wikipedia provides reference information about people, places, organizations, and general topics.

Movie Information

The movie tool supports queries about films and related information, demonstrating how a specialized API can extend an assistant's capabilities.

Stack Overflow

This integration helps retrieve programming-related discussions and technical information that may be relevant to developer questions.

Notion

The Notion integration connects the assistant to a productivity and knowledge-management platform, where supported operations can help users work with information in their workspace.

The key idea is that these tools are not interchangeable. Each one has its own inputs, outputs, API requirements, and possible failure conditions.

The assistant needs enough information about each tool to select it appropriately.

5. How Tool Calling Works

A tool-enabled LLM workflow generally consists of several steps.

Step 1: Receive the request

The backend receives the user's message and prepares the relevant conversation context.

Step 2: Ask the model to determine the next action

The model evaluates the request and can return either a normal response or a structured tool call, depending on the framework and tool definitions.

Step 3: Execute the selected tool

The backend validates the requested arguments and calls the corresponding function or external API.

Step 4: Return the result to the model

The tool output is passed back into the conversation so the model can interpret it.

Step 5: Generate the final answer

The model converts the available information into a response that is understandable to the user.

Conceptually, a tool definition might look like this:

def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """
    Retrieve weather information for a city.
    """
    # Call the configured weather API here.
    # Validate the response and handle API errors.
    return {
        "city": city,
        "temperature": 28,
        "condition": "Partly cloudy"
    }

This is a simplified example showing the shape of a tool function, not the complete implementation of a production weather integration.

In a real application, the function would retrieve actual weather data, validate the location, handle timeouts, and report errors appropriately.

The LLM should not invent tool results. It should base its answer on the returned information and communicate when reliable data is unavailable.

6. Technology Stack

The project combines frontend development, backend engineering, AI integration, and external services.

The main technologies include:

  • Next.js and React: Building the frontend experience.
  • FastAPI: Exposing backend endpoints and coordinating application logic.
  • Python: Implementing backend functionality and tool integrations.
  • LLM providers: Powering natural-language understanding, reasoning, and response generation.
  • LangChain and related agent tooling: Supporting model and tool integration where configured.
  • PostgreSQL: Providing relational data persistence.
  • Redis: Supporting caching and other appropriate fast-access operations.
  • External APIs: Providing specialized information and capabilities.

Each technology addresses a different part of the system. The frontend handles interaction, the backend coordinates execution, the model processes language, and external APIs provide information or actions.

The exact model, API provider, and available operations depend on the configured integrations.

7. Challenges I Had to Consider

Building an AI assistant involves more than connecting a model to an API. Several engineering concerns become important as the number of tools increases.

Choosing the right tool

Similar user requests can require different tools, and vague questions can be difficult to interpret.

Clear tool descriptions, well-defined parameters, and appropriate model instructions help improve tool selection.

Handling API failures

External services can return errors, enforce rate limits, or respond slowly.

The backend should handle timeouts, validate responses, and return useful error messages rather than allowing one failed integration to break the entire conversation.

Managing API keys

Third-party API credentials should remain on the server and be loaded through environment variables or a suitable secrets-management system.

They should never be exposed in frontend code or committed to a public repository.

Keeping responses grounded

When a question requires current information, the assistant should use the relevant external source instead of presenting unsupported information as fact.

It is also important to distinguish retrieved information from the model's own explanation.

Maintaining a modular architecture

Adding more tools can make backend logic difficult to maintain if every integration is implemented inside a single large function.

Separating tool implementations from orchestration makes it easier to add capabilities, test individual integrations, and handle failures independently.

These considerations helped me understand why reliable AI applications need thoughtful backend engineering in addition to a capable language model.

8. Security and Reliability Considerations

An AI assistant that can access external services needs appropriate safeguards.

Some important practices include:

  • Validate tool arguments before executing them.
  • Apply authentication and authorization to protected endpoints.
  • Use request timeouts and controlled retry policies.
  • Limit tool permissions to the operations the application actually needs.
  • Avoid passing secrets or unnecessary sensitive data into model prompts.
  • Sanitize external content and treat retrieved text as untrusted input.
  • Apply rate limits and usage controls where appropriate.
  • Log useful operational information without exposing credentials or private conversation content.

For integrations that can modify external data, such as creating or updating records, additional permission checks and confirmation steps may be necessary.

These controls help make tool-enabled AI systems safer and more predictable.

9. What I Learned

This project helped me understand how LLMs can become part of a complete software system rather than functioning as isolated text-generation components.

Some of my main takeaways were:

LLMs need reliable tools. A language model becomes more useful for current or specialized questions when it can access appropriate external information.

Backend design matters. Tool orchestration, validation, error handling, authentication, and API integration are essential parts of an AI application.

Modularity improves extensibility. Keeping integrations separate makes it easier to introduce new capabilities without rewriting the entire application.

AI responses need grounding. A polished response is not necessarily a correct one. Reliable results depend on tool quality, context, validation, and clear handling of uncertainty.

Full-stack development and AI engineering complement each other. Building a useful assistant requires frontend interaction, backend APIs, model integration, and operational reliability to work together.

10. What's Next?

There are several ways to improve a multi-tool assistant as it evolves:

  • Add streaming responses for a more interactive experience.
  • Improve conversation memory and context management.
  • Introduce retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for private or domain-specific knowledge.
  • Add structured evaluation to measure tool-selection accuracy.
  • Improve observability with tracing, latency metrics, and error monitoring.
  • Introduce more granular permissions for tools that can modify external data.
  • Explore standardized tool interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where appropriate.

These improvements can help move an experimental AI assistant toward a more reliable and maintainable application.

Conclusion

Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration was an opportunity to explore the intersection of full-stack development and modern AI engineering.

The project demonstrates how a conversational interface, an LLM, a backend orchestration layer, and external tools can work together to answer different types of questions.

More importantly, it reinforced an important lesson: building a useful AI application is not just about choosing a powerful model. It is about designing the systems around that model so it can access reliable information, use tools appropriately, and communicate results clearly.

I'm continuing to explore LLM engineering, agentic workflows, and practical AI integrations, and I'm looking forward to applying these lessons to more complex projects.

If you're building an AI assistant yourself, I'd be interested to hear what tools you're integrating and what challenges you've encountered.

Thanks for reading!

title: Private Receipt Exports: Signed Download URLs and Per-Tenant Object Storage Layout
description:
Use a private bucket per tenant and hand out short-lived signed download URLs. For a SaaS that generates private export files — scanned receipts, CSV extracts, PDF summaries — and lets a user fetch them later, that is the entire answer. No CDN, no file-serving service, no permanent links. Any S3-compatible object storage does this, so the vendor question matters far less than the layout question.

The layout question is where the tenant boundary lives.

Where the storage boundary sits in a receipt pipeline

The system I have in mind is a logistics back office. Drivers photograph fuel and toll receipts, a Python worker pushes each file into storage untouched, an extraction model reads amounts and vendor names out of it, and the finance team later opens a matched expense line and clicks through to the original scan. Auditors care about that last step more than anything else in the pipeline: the extracted JSON is a derived artifact, and the image is the evidence.

So the data flow is: bytes in, one row in Postgres holding tenant_id, bucket, key, checksum and extraction status, and — much later, maybe eighteen months later — a signed URL minted on demand when someone with the right tenant claim asks for the file.

That is the whole boundary. Storage's job begins when the bytes land and ends when the signed link expires.

It does not know what a tenant is. It cannot answer "every receipt from carrier X in March," because object listing filters by key prefix, not by metadata. Both of those facts push you toward the same design: encode tenancy in the bucket and prefix, and keep authorization, search and audit history in your own database where you can join them against everything else. I keep the checksum in that row too, since my eval harness re-scores extraction accuracy against the stored originals and I want a hard guarantee the bytes never drifted.

If you are already assembling a backend out of a dozen vendor dashboards, Infrai is worth trying for exactly this slice: one key and one bill cover object storage next to the other backend services the same worker calls, which removes a credential rotation chore rather than adding one.

One upload, one signed link: the Python code that does it

Here is the part that actually runs. Upload the original, then mint a download link when the finance UI asks for it.

import os
import time
import requests

AUTH = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}


def with_retry(send):
    """One retry policy for every call: back off on 429, honour Retry-After."""
    resp = send()
    for attempt in range(4):
        if resp.status_code != 429:
            return resp
        time.sleep(float(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt)))
        resp = send()
    return resp


def archive_receipt(tenant_id: str, receipt_id: str, pdf_bytes: bytes) -> tuple[str, str]:
    bucket = f"receipts-{tenant_id}"                 # the isolation boundary, one per tenant
    key = f"2026/{receipt_id}/original.pdf"
    resp = with_retry(lambda: requests.put(
        f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}",
        headers={**AUTH,
                 "Content-Type": "application/pdf",
                 "Idempotency-Key": f"receipt-{tenant_id}-{receipt_id}"},
        data=pdf_bytes,
        timeout=30,
    ))
    if resp.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(f"upload rejected: {resp.status_code} {resp.text}")
    return bucket, key


def download_link(bucket: str, key: str, seconds: int = 900) -> tuple[str, str]:
    resp = with_retry(lambda: requests.post(
        f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
        headers=AUTH,
        json={"op": "get", "expires_seconds": seconds},
        timeout=30,
    ))
    if resp.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign rejected: {resp.status_code} {resp.text}")
    signed = resp.json()
    # Hand signed["url"] straight to the browser. Never attach your platform key to it.
    return signed["url"], signed["expires_at"]

Three details in there are load-bearing. The idempotency key means a retried worker never writes the same receipt twice, which matters because a duplicated original is an audit finding, not a rounding error. The presign response carries its own expires_at, so your UI can show the user how long the link is good for instead of guessing. And the returned URL is already authenticated by its signature — sending the platform key along with it is the classic mistake, and it leaks a credential into browser history for no benefit.

There is no SDK to install for any of that. Infrai's storage calls are plain HTTP against one REST API, so the same thirty lines run from a notebook cell while I'm tuning an extraction prompt and from the container that does the work for real.

Should temporary signed links replace a permanent file download service for private exports?

For private files, yes, and the reasoning is mostly about blast radius. A permanent URL is a bearer token that never expires: forward it once in a support thread and it stays live forever. A 15-minute link forwarded to the wrong person is usually already dead. Since a receipt archive is exactly the kind of data you do not want indexed or shared sideways, the expiry is doing real security work.

The catch is that expiring links break bookmarks and emails. Send a customer a signed URL in a monthly statement email and it will be stale by the time they read it. The fix is a redirect endpoint in your own app: the emailed link points at /receipts/<id>/download, that route checks the session's tenant claim, mints a fresh signed URL, and 302s to it. Your app keeps the authorization decision, storage keeps the bytes, and neither one grows a copy of the other's job.

Prefix-only listing shapes this too. If your app database is the only place that knows which tenant owns which key, then every download path must go through code that reads that database — which is exactly the property an auditor wants to see anyway.

What the S3-compatible options actually differ on

The presigned-URL mechanics are close to identical across all of these. What differs is the operational surface around them.

Option How you call it Per-tenant isolation Main limitation
AWS S3 AWS SDK or REST, IAM policies Bucket or prefix, IAM condition keys IAM policy sprawl gets heavy fast
Cloudflare R2 S3 API, no egress fees Bucket per tenant, scoped tokens Fewer regions than S3
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API Bucket per tenant, application keys Thinner ecosystem tooling
MinIO (self-hosted) S3 API you operate Full control, you run the policy engine You own the uptime and the disks
Infrai storage One REST call per action, same key as the rest of the backend Bucket per tenant, private objects only Vendor coverage is S3, R2, OSS and COS

Two limits deserve to be stated plainly rather than discovered later. Infrai's storage does not support public-read objects or permanent public links, which suits an audit archive fine and rules it out for image hosting or a static site. It also lacks object versioning and object lock, so if your compliance team requires write-once-read-many retention with a legal hold, stick with S3 and its Object Lock feature — that is a specialist requirement and a specialist product answers it better.

Lifecycle rules can expire old exports automatically, though the shortest window is one day rather than hours. For temporary CSV exports that is usually fine. Your mileage may vary if your retention policy is measured in minutes.

Retention windows, access logs and the failure modes worth planning for

Keep expiry short and boring: minutes for interactive downloads, and a redirect route for anything that travels through email. Set Content-Disposition on the object so the browser saves receipt-4471.pdf instead of a UUID. Log every mint — user, tenant, key, expiry — because "who looked at this receipt" is a question you will be asked, and storage will not answer it for you. Write the extraction results to a separate key rather than overwriting the original, since there is no conditional write to protect you from a racing worker; a queue with one consumer per tenant is the cheaper fix. Verify the checksum on read before you feed a file back into an eval run.

If that boundary matches your pipeline, the Infrai storage guide on signed download URLs is a reasonable place to start reading. If your requirement is WORM retention or public hosting, the specialist products above remain the better call.

Further reading

  • AWS: sharing objects with presigned URLs
  • AWS: S3 Object Lock
  • Cloudflare R2: presigned URLs
  • MinIO documentation
  • MDN: Content-Disposition
  • Backblaze B2 pricing

title: Make targets big enough to hit (Web HIG tip #12)
description:
Open your site on a phone and try to tap the "×" that closes a banner, the edit icon in a table row, or the second of three pagination numbers. If you hit the wrong one, or have to zoom in first, the target is too small. People with tremors, limited dexterity, or a phone in one hand on a moving bus miss it much more often.

Web HIG tip #12 (Quick #75 / HIG-A11Y-007): Interactive targets MUST be at least 24×24 CSS px. Primary touch actions SHOULD use 44×44 CSS px.

Why it matters

A target is the area that responds to a click or tap, not the icon you can see:

  • A 16px icon with no padding gives the finger a 16px target, even if the design looks roomy around it
  • Small targets packed side by side turn a miss into a wrong action: delete instead of edit, next page instead of previous
  • Icon-only toolbars, close buttons, table row actions, and pagination links are the usual offenders
  • Pointer users with tremors or limited dexterity are affected too, not only touch users

The full HIG covers this in §5.4, Target Sizes, and it separates two levels on purpose. 24×24 CSS px is the MUST (HIG-A11Y-007, severity error), aligned with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA. The WCAG-defined exceptions apply, and the HIG does not redefine them. 44×44 CSS px is a SHOULD, an ergonomic recommendation for primary touch actions. It is not a WCAG AA floor and is not part of HIG-A11Y-007 enforcement, so a 32px secondary button is not a defect. Quick #20 is the companion rule: targets must not overlap in ways that cause mis-taps.

The rule of thumb

Ask: if I tap the middle of the gap between two controls, do I know which one I'll get?

Grow the hit area, not the icon. Padding is usually all it takes.

<button class="icon-button" type="button" aria-label="Close">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16">…</svg>
</button>

/* 16px icon, 24px minimum target, 44px on coarse pointers */
.icon-button {
  display: inline-grid;
  place-items: center;
  min-inline-size: 24px;
  min-block-size: 24px;
}

@media (pointer: coarse) {
  .icon-button {
    min-inline-size: 44px;
    min-block-size: 44px;
  }
}

The visible icon stays the same size. The button around it grows, and that is the part that receives the tap.

Do this instead

  • Measure the clickable box, not the glyph. In DevTools, inspect the <button> or <a>, not the <svg> inside it
  • Use padding or min-inline-size / min-block-size to reach 24×24, and aim for 44×44 on primary touch actions such as submit, add to cart, and the main navigation toggle
  • If a control has to stay visually small, keep enough space around it. WCAG's spacing exception covers an undersized target only when a 24px circle centred on it doesn't intersect another target or another such circle
  • Links inside a sentence are covered by WCAG's inline exception. Footer link lists, tag chips, and breadcrumb rows are not sentences, so give them room
  • Put the size on the component (your IconButton, Chip, Pagination) so every use inherits it, and use your spacing tokens rather than one-off pixel values (Quick #63)

Quick check for your app

Open a page on example.com in your browser's device mode, or on a real phone. Inspect each icon button, close control, chip, and pagination link, and read the box size of the element that has the click handler. Anything under 24×24 needs more size or more space around it. Then try the primary actions with your thumb, one-handed: those are the ones that should reach 44×44. A tool can measure boxes, but only trying it tells you whether the controls are easy to hit.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/27
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/make-targets-big-enough-to-hit-web-hig-tip-12
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/make-targets-big-enough-to-hit-web-hig-tip-12-2n50
  • Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/sastha.bsky.social/post/3mygutvbn5227

title: Fixed vs random effects in Python, and what a Hausman test result actually tells you
description:
Most panel data tutorials stop at "run the Hausman test, and if p < 0.05 use fixed effects." That rule is fine as a starting point, but it hides a few things that matter once you look at real output. So here is a small worked example you can run yourself, with the numbers I got.

The setup

I used the wage_panel dataset that ships with linearmodels: 545 individuals observed over 8 years, with log wages as the outcome. The regressors are experience squared, marital status and union membership.

bash
pip install linearmodels
python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from linearmodels.panel import PanelOLS, RandomEffects
from linearmodels.datasets import wage_panel

df = wage_panel.load().set_index(["nr", "year"])
y = df["lwage"]
X = df[["expersq", "married", "union"]]

the RE model needs an intercept, the FE (within) model does not

X_re = X.copy()
X_re.insert(0, "const", 1.0)

fe = PanelOLS(y, X, entity_effects=True).fit()
re = RandomEffects(y, X_re).fit()
The two sets of estimates
variable fixed effects random effects
expersq 0.0037 0.0032
married 0.1073 0.1316
union 0.0828 0.1035

The random effects numbers for married and union are noticeably larger. That gap is what the Hausman test formalises. If the unobserved person-level effects (ability, motivation, whatever drives wages and also correlates with marrying or joining a union) are correlated with the regressors, the RE estimator picks that correlation up as if it were an effect of the regressor, and the coefficients drift upward.

Computing the Hausman statistic by hand

linearmodels doesn't ship a one-line Hausman test, but the statistic is short:

python
cols = fe.params.index
b = fe.params - re.params[cols]
V = fe.cov - re.cov.loc[cols, cols]

stat = float(b @ np.linalg.inv(V) @ b)
p = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(stat, len(cols))
print(f"Hausman chi2 = {stat:.3f}, df = {len(cols)}, p = {p:.4f}")

Output on this data:

Hausman chi2 = 112.118, df = 3, p = 0.0000

A clear rejection. The RE assumption (effects uncorrelated with the regressors) doesn't hold here, so the fixed effects estimates are the ones to report.

Three things the textbook rule skips

A rejection is evidence against RE, not a proof that FE is right. FE only removes confounding that is constant over the sample window. Anything that changes over time and correlates with both wages and marriage is still in your error term.

You pay for FE with the time-invariant variables. The within estimator can't estimate the effect of anything that doesn't change for a person (education at entry, say, or a fixed demographic). I left those out above for exactly that reason. If they are the point of your study, FE alone won't answer your question, and a Mundlak or correlated random effects specification is worth a look.

The classic Hausman test assumes homoskedastic errors. With clustered standard errors, which is the usual choice in applied work, the difference of covariance matrices isn't the right object anymore. A regression-based version (the Mundlak approach: add the group means of each regressor to the RE model and test them jointly) works with robust errors.

If you'd rather not write code

For a quick check, or to hand something to a colleague who doesn't use Python, there is a panel data regression online tool that fits fixed and random effects models in the browser. Full disclosure: I'm connected to that site. For anything you plan to publish, I'd still keep the script above so the analysis is reproducible.

Curious whether people go Mundlak, or just default to FE and move on.RE model and test them jointly) works with robust errors.
