title: Recurring User Alerts API Explained — 4 Cron Rules for Monthly Weekly Timezone Webhooks
description:
A rate-limited worker pool makes recurring user reminders an API and queueing problem before it becomes a cron problem. Keep the user's calendar intent, turn each due occurrence into a small job, and let workers drain that queue at a known rate. That adds some latency during a burst, but it protects delivery from a burst that exhausts the pool. The same rule applies to monthly and weekly reminders: cron starts the dispatch, while the worker budget decides how quickly the notifications leave the system.

Short answer: store an IANA timezone with the weekly or monthly rule, send a signed public webhook that only records and enqueues an occurrence, and make the worker idempotent. Treat latency and cost as explicit operating choices rather than promises hidden in a cron expression.

Begin with the worker constraint

A cron tick says “start,” not “how much work can run now.” In a B2B SaaS product, a tenant may schedule a digest for the same local minute as many other tenants. Imagine a Monday morning where hundreds of tenants become due together while the same worker pool is processing imports and exports. If every callback renders a template and waits for a provider, the burst consumes connection slots before the scheduler can report success. The scheduler should call an authenticated endpoint, the endpoint should persist an occurrence key, and a queue should hand work to rate-limited consumers. The callback returns after durable enqueue; template rendering and provider calls stay out of the request path. That split makes the latency-versus-cost decision visible: reserve capacity for fast dispatch, or accept queue age and batch the work.

I use (schedule_id, scheduled_for) as the business idempotency key. Queue delivery is commonly at least once, so a retry must map to the same job instead of sending a second reminder. A message identifier alone is too weak: the identifier can change while the user's intended occurrence has not.

Keep the rule visible in operations. Queue age, callback latency, duplicate suppression, and worker utilization tell you whether the pool is draining. CPU by itself does not.

One sentence matters here: bursts are normal.

What should a weekly or monthly reminder API promise about timezone webhooks?

The API should promise calendar intent, not a frozen UTC timestamp. “Tuesday at 09:00 in Europe/Berlin” should remain a local-time rule when daylight-saving rules change. Store the IANA identifier, local wall-clock time, frequency, and a policy version; compute the next UTC instant as derived state and recompute it after each accepted occurrence. A fixed offset such as +01:00 cannot describe future timezone transitions.

Monthly schedules need a declared policy for a date that does not exist. Reject it, clamp to the last day, or choose the next valid day. Any of those can be defensible; silently selecting one makes support and compliance reviews painful. Your mileage may vary when a tenant's sending window or provider quota is stricter than the worker pool.

The public webhook is a narrow bridge, not the reminder engine. Sign the exact raw body with a timestamped HMAC, reject stale timestamps, compare digests in constant time, persist the occurrence, and then return a success response. RFC 2104 defines the keyed-hash construction; the freshness window is an application policy that should match clock-skew and replay-retention decisions.

import hashlib
import hmac


def valid_signature(raw_body: bytes, header: str, secret: bytes, now: int) -> bool:
    try:
        sent_at_text, supplied = header.split(".", 1)
        sent_at = int(sent_at_text)
    except ValueError:
        return False

    # Five minutes is an example policy; choose a window for your clocks.
    if abs(now - sent_at) > 300:
        return False

    signed = f"{sent_at}.".encode() + raw_body
    expected = hmac.new(secret, signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, supplied)

The handler still has to enforce tenant authorization and an idempotency constraint. Authentication answers “who called?”; the occurrence key answers “have I accepted this calendar event already?”

Where do webhook and queue designs fail under load?

The first failure mode is useful work inside the callback. Rendering, calling an email or SMS provider, and waiting for a response couples an internet-facing timeout to every downstream dependency. Return after the ledger write and enqueue; let workers own retries, backoff, suppression checks, and provider-specific rate limits.

The second is an unexamined pause policy. Some schedulers skip occurrences while a schedule is paused, while a business may expect one compensating reminder after resume. Record the pause interval and choose explicitly between “send once after resume” and “skip missed occurrences.” Do not let a retry accidentally decide that policy.

The third is a calendar edge case hidden in a parser. Test a weekly rule across a daylight-saving transition, a monthly rule near the end of a short month, and a leap-day rule. Use a fixed test clock and compare the stored local intent with the derived UTC instant after each transition.

I have spent enough time on OTP and email delivery to distrust a green HTTP response by itself. A 2xx only proves that the bridge accepted a request; it does not prove that a message was delivered. Track scheduled, enqueued, acknowledged, delivered, and suppressed states, and keep reminder content out of logs because destinations and timezone choices are personal data.

How should latency, cost, and endpoint boundaries shape the choice?

Decision Latency-leaning option Cost-leaning option
Dispatch Poll frequently and reserve worker capacity Batch due occurrences on a slower cadence
Retry Short backoff with a dead-letter review path Fewer attempts with explicit operator review
Calculation Derive each next occurrence immediately Derive it when a worker claims the schedule
Security Signature, replay cache, and tenant limits Signature with a smaller replay store

The trade-off is concrete. A public HTTPS webhook is a good boundary when the ingress can be authenticated and monitored. It is not suitable for a private-only service unless a public gateway forwards into the private worker plane. A queue with at-least-once delivery is a poor fit for a side effect that cannot be made idempotent; use a workflow system or an application-level ledger when the process needs joins, long-running compensation, or an audit trail across steps.

Do not make a unit price the main decision. Measure queue wait, callback time, duplicate rate, and worker utilization with the same tenant mix you expect in production. I'm not sure any single scheduler's “timezone support” label tells you how it handles invalid monthly dates, pause recovery, or replay, so require those behaviors in an acceptance test.

A small rollout that keeps the calendar honest

Start with one tenant and a staging endpoint. Generate weekly and monthly occurrences around a daylight-saving change, a short month, and a leap day. Replay each signed callback and verify that the ledger creates one job for one occurrence.

Then cap concurrency below the provider's documented limit, watch queue age, and exercise the pause and resume policy. Roll out by tenant cohort. Keep the calendar policy version beside each schedule so a later policy change does not silently rewrite existing intent.

The durable design is deliberately plain: calendar data, an occurrence ledger, a narrow webhook, and a worker loop. Cron is only the trigger.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview
  • https://www.iana.org/time-zones

title: SlothPulse: I wrote the code. Gemma can draft the standup.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.

💡 What I Built

After a day of writing code, “what did you do today?” shouldn’t require another Git archaeology session.

I built SlothPulse to turn recent commits and a terminal error into a standup draft using Gemma running locally through Ollama. One command produces three Markdown sections: completed work, blockers, and suggested next steps.

Every item has a receipt pointing back to its source, so you can check anything suspicious before sharing the draft. The note stays in a local file.

🎥 Demo

Open the recorded demo → — click a source badge to inspect its commit or error, or watch the 48-second video.


python3 slothpulse.py --since today --error-file error.txt

An excerpt from the actual saved draft:

### 🛠️ What I Did Today
- Fixed issue where export job IDs were lost during retries. [^C1]

### 🐛 Blockers & Bugs
- User-reported: KeyError: 'result' while downloading job results. [^E1]

### 🚀 Next Steps
- Suggested: Investigate the origin of the KeyError and potential data access issues in worker.py. [^E1]

The full captured run summarizes five commits and one traceback in 10.33 seconds inside the CLI. The fixture uses fictional authors and a deliberately fake key; the tiny worker really raises the captured error. The video replays timestamped output, including the measured wait.

💻 Code

TengByte / slothpulse

A 100% local, privacy-first CLI that turns Git commits and error traces into developer digests with Ollama and Gemma.

Setup and source · Exact input and output · Build log

🛠️ How I Built It

The first version produced a tidy recap—and attributed a pasted error to SlothPulse itself, although its source was unspecified. That unsupported connection mattered more than the formatting.

I moved the model’s response to JSON with required source keys. Every commit gets a C key. Each reported error gets an E object containing both its summary and investigation step. Python assigns their references and renders the Markdown.

That pairing came from another real failure: an error investigation cited an unrelated commit. Both IDs existed, so checking whether a source was known had missed the problem. Keeping the error and its follow-up together removes that particular mismatch.

The CLI validates coverage and reference types, retries an invalid plan once, and saves no digest if the second attempt fails. A valid reference still cannot prove that a sentence is correct; human review stays in the workflow.

The application uses Python’s standard library: subprocess for Git, urllib.request for Ollama, and json for the response contract. No external Python packages. The code is MIT licensed.

🔒 Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Commit subjects and traces can contain private project details. Downloaded Gemma weights let the recap run on the same machine as that context, without a hosted inference account or API key. The model download needs internet access; generation stays local.

SlothPulse checks model metadata before sending context, rejects cloud-backed models, and bypasses HTTP proxies. The tested Ollama server runs with OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1. These checks trust the local server and its metadata.

Before generating, --preview shows the sanitized input without a model call or file write. Common credential patterns are masked, but masking is best effort: preview it, and treat saved notes as potentially confidential.

🦥 The Lazy Payoff

The chore becomes reviewing a draft instead of assembling one from scattered context. To check this beyond the demo fixture, I ran SlothPulse on this project’s six real commits, using local Gemma on an Apple M5 / 16 GB:

Invocation Whole process time
Model initially unloaded 13.619 s
Immediate repeat 8.720 s

Review caught one important correction among the six completed-work items: Gemma turned “submission handoff” into “submitted,” while this entry was still a draft. The receipt made that mismatch easy to locate. The raw output and the corrected version are both preserved in the repository trial.

This was an AI-assisted source check, not a human standup study. Manual preparation time and human editing effort remain unmeasured. The earlier nine-run synthetic benchmark and 23 unit tests check workflow behavior and failure boundaries; factual accuracy still needs review.

🏆 Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma — local Gemma drafts the summaries and investigation steps.

Codex assisted with implementation, testing, demo preparation, and this article. More engineering notes: tengli.dev.

title: I built SiteScope, a free technical SEO audit tool that ranks what to fix first
description:
For my college course I built SiteScope (vikramyadav.me), a free technical SEO audit tool. You enter a site, it crawls every page it can reach, and it tells you what to fix first. No sign-up needed to run an audit. If you want, you can create an account to have your sites re-audited daily or weekly.

The problem

Two things bugged me about free SEO checkers.

First, most test a single URL and hand back an unordered list. SiteScope follows internal links and the XML sitemap and checks every page it finds (up to 300 per audit). Then it ranks issues with one rule:

priority = severity × share of pages affected

A missing alt text on every page outranks a broken link on one page; a 5xx on half the site outranks both.

Second, a lot of sites load their content with JavaScript. SiteScope reads raw HTML, the way most AI crawlers do, so you can check whether your content needs JavaScript to show up. The tool itself uses no JavaScript framework. Every page, including the report, is server-rendered, because a tool that talks about JavaScript SEO should be readable by a crawler that runs none.

It also checks broken links, duplicate and near-duplicate pages (SimHash), the internal link graph (click depth, PageRank, orphan pages), titles, meta descriptions, H1s, canonicals, noindex and more. Reports download as PDF or JSON, and re-running an audit shows what was fixed and what is new since last time.

Tech stack

  • FastAPI (Python 3.12) with Jinja2 templates; audits run as FastAPI background tasks
  • PostgreSQL 16, where each finished result is one JSONB column
  • Docker Compose with an Nginx reverse proxy and Certbot
  • Azure VM: one small VM (2 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM) running two containers
  • Cloudflare for DNS and proxying
  • httpx + asyncio for crawling, BeautifulSoup for parsing, NetworkX for the link graph

What I learned

  • A URL fetcher is an SSRF hole. If a stranger can type any URL, they will try the cloud metadata service or localhost. The guard refuses private, loopback and reserved addresses, checks every redirect hop, and connects to the exact IP it checked, so DNS rebinding can't swap the address in between.
  • Don't trust a header anyone can send. My per-IP limit read Cloudflare's CF-Connecting-IP, but anyone hitting the server's IP directly could send that header with a new value each time. Now it only believes that header when the connection really comes from Cloudflare's IP ranges, and the limit lives in Postgres so a restart doesn't reset it.
  • Keep dependencies small on a small VM. NetworkX's PageRank pulled in numpy and scipy, so I wrote my own PageRank and tested it against the reference. The scheduled re-audits run as a background task inside the app, with no cron, Celery or Redis.
  • Severity alone gets the order wrong. Multiplying by the share of pages affected fixed it.
  • An SEO tool shouldn't create thin pages. Report pages send noindex and are disallowed in robots.txt.
  • DNS moves need care. Switching nameservers to Cloudflare replaces the whole zone, so I recreated the existing records first and issued SSL before turning on the proxy.

What's next

Some things are still open: score-drop emails are waiting on an SMTP provider, and external link checks stop at 200 links per audit.

Try it at vikramyadav.me and see the code on GitHub. Feedback welcome!

title: How to Build a Finance AI Agent With Audit Trails, Controls, and Human Oversight
description:
Here’s a truth about building AI agents for finance that nobody puts in the tutorial: the agent intelligence is maybe 30 percent of the work. The audit trail, the access controls, the human oversight checkpoints, the compliance documentation, that’s the other 70 percent. And that 70 percent is what determines whether your agent runs in production or gets killed in the compliance review before it processes a single transaction.

We learned this the expensive way on our first finance AI agent deployment. Built a beautiful underwriting agent. Elegant reasoning. Clean tool use. Impressive accuracy on test data. The compliance team looked at it for two hours and rejected it because they couldn’t answer one question: “If a regulator asks why the agent recommended denying this loan application, can you show them the exact data and reasoning that produced that recommendation?”

We couldn’t. The agent worked. It just didn’t prove it worked. And in finance, working without proving it is the same as not working.

This article is the guide we wish existed when we started. It covers the audit trail architecture, the access control design, the human oversight implementation, and the code patterns that make a finance AI agent not just functional but auditable, controllable, and compliant.

If you’re building agents that touch money, customer data, or regulatory workflows, this is the engineering that separates a demo from a deployment.

The audit trail isn’t logging. It’s the primary deliverable

Most developers think of audit trails as application logging. Write some events to a log file. Query them when something goes wrong. That’s not what finance compliance requires.

A finance audit trail must capture what data the agent received, what reasoning it applied, what tools it called, what each tool returned, what decision it reached, how confident it was, and what action it took, for every single transaction. And it must store this immutably for seven to ten years in a format that a non-technical regulator can review.

Here’s the data model:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional
import hashlib
import json


class EvaluationType(Enum):
    DETERMINISTIC = "deterministic"
    AI_ASSISTED = "ai_assisted"
    HUMAN_REVIEWED = "human_reviewed"


class ActionType(Enum):
    AUTO_APPROVED = "auto_approved"
    AUTO_DENIED = "auto_denied"
    ESCALATED = "escalated"
    PENDING_REVIEW = "pending_review"


@dataclass
class AuditRecord:
    """Immutable record of every agent decision."""
    record_id: str
    timestamp: datetime
    agent_id: str
    agent_version: str

    # What was evaluated
    transaction_id: str
    transaction_type: str
    input_data_hash: str          # SHA-256 of exact input
    input_data_snapshot: dict      # Frozen copy of input state

    # How it was evaluated
    evaluation_type: EvaluationType
    rules_applied: list[str]       # Rule IDs for deterministic checks
    model_version: Optional[str]   # For AI-assisted evaluations
    prompt_hash: Optional[str]     # For reproducibility

    # What was concluded
    decision: ActionType
    confidence: Optional[float]
    reasoning_chain: list[dict]    # Step-by-step reasoning

    # What happened next
    escalated_to: Optional[str]
    human_reviewer: Optional[str]
    human_decision: Optional[str]
    human_override_reason: Optional[str]
    human_decision_timestamp: Optional[datetime]

    # Integrity
    previous_record_hash: Optional[str]  # Chain integrity
    record_hash: str = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self):
        """Compute hash for tamper detection."""
        content = json.dumps({
            'record_id': self.record_id,
            'transaction_id': self.transaction_id,
            'input_data_hash': self.input_data_hash,
            'decision': self.decision.value,
            'timestamp': self.timestamp.isoformat(),
            'previous_hash': self.previous_record_hash
        }, sort_keys=True)
        self.record_hash = hashlib.sha256(content.encode()).hexdigest()

Two fields in this model deserve specific attention.

input_data_hash and input_data_snapshot serve different purposes. The hash proves that the data hasn’t been modified since the decision was made. The snapshot preserves the exact data state at decision time, because the source data in the ERP may change after the agent evaluated it, and the regulator needs to see what the agent saw, not what the database currently contains.

previous_record_hash creates a chain where tampering with any historical record breaks the hash chain on every subsequent record. This isn’t blockchain, it’s a simple integrity mechanism that makes after-the-fact modification detectable.

The storage architecture matters:

class AuditStore:
    """Append-only audit storage with hot and cold tiers."""

    def __init__(self, hot_store, cold_store, retention_years=7):
        self.hot = hot_store      # PostgreSQL - last 90 days, fast queries
        self.cold = cold_store    # S3 + Parquet - long-term, cost-efficient
        self.retention = retention_years

    async def append(self, record: AuditRecord) -> str:
        """Write to hot store. Never update. Never delete."""
        # Verify chain integrity
        last_record = await self.hot.get_latest(record.agent_id)
        if last_record and record.previous_record_hash != last_record.record_hash:
            raise IntegrityError("Chain broken - previous hash mismatch")

        await self.hot.insert(record)
        return record.record_hash

    async def archive(self, older_than_days=90):
        """Move aged records to cold storage. Hot store stays fast."""
        records = await self.hot.get_older_than(older_than_days)
        await self.cold.write_parquet(records)
        # Mark as archived in hot store - never delete
        await self.hot.mark_archived(records)

The append-only constraint is non-negotiable. No updates. No deletes. No “soft deletes.” If a record needs correction, you append a correction record that references the original. The original stays forever.

The access control layer: least privilege isn’t optional

The agent’s service account should have exactly the permissions it needs and nothing more. This sounds obvious. In practice, it’s the control that most teams get wrong because scoping permissions precisely requires understanding every data access and system interaction the agent performs.

class AgentPermissions:
    """Define and enforce what the agent can access and do."""

    def __init__(self, agent_role: str):
        self.role = agent_role
        self.permissions = self._load_permissions(agent_role)

    def _load_permissions(self, role: str) -> dict:
        """Each agent role has explicit read/write scopes."""
        roles = {
            "ap_processor": {
                "read": [
                    "invoices",
                    "purchase_orders", 
                    "goods_receipts",
                    "vendor_master",        # Read vendor info
                    "approval_matrix",      # Read routing rules
                ],
                "write": [
                    "invoices.status",       # Update processing status
                    "invoices.match_result", # Record match outcome
                    "approval_queue",        # Route for approval
                ],
                "blocked": [
                    "payments.execute",     # Cannot trigger payments
                    "vendor_master.modify", # Cannot change vendor data
                    "general_ledger",       # No GL access
                    "payroll",              # No payroll access
                    "treasury",             # No treasury access
                ],
                "amount_ceiling": 100_000,  # Escalate above this
            },
            "underwriting_analyst": {
                "read": [
                    "loan_applications",
                    "credit_bureau_data",
                    "financial_documents",
                    "compliance_rules",
                ],
                "write": [
                    "applications.risk_assessment",
                    "applications.recommendation",
                    "escalation_queue",
                ],
                "blocked": [
                    "applications.approve",  # Cannot approve loans
                    "applications.deny",     # Cannot deny loans
                    "disbursement",          # No access to funds
                ],
                "amount_ceiling": None,  # All amounts escalate
            }
        }
        return roles.get(role, {"read": [], "write": [], "blocked": []})

    def check_access(self, operation: str, resource: str) -> bool:
        """Enforce permission before every system interaction."""
        if resource in self.permissions.get("blocked", []):
            raise PermissionDenied(
                f"Agent role '{self.role}' is blocked from '{resource}'"
            )

        allowed_resources = self.permissions.get(operation, [])
        if resource not in allowed_resources:
            raise PermissionDenied(
                f"Agent role '{self.role}' lacks '{operation}' on '{resource}'"
            )
        return True

The blocked list is as important as the read and write lists. Explicitly defining what the agent cannot access, even when those resources exist in the same system, creates a documented boundary that compliance teams can review. An AP processing agent that has no path to the payroll system, the treasury system, or the general ledger is an agent whose blast radius is bounded by design.

The amount_ceiling field is the operational authority limit. Transactions above this threshold escalate to a human regardless of how confident the agent is. The ceiling is a business decision, not a technical one, set by the finance leadership based on the organisation’s risk tolerance.

Human oversight: the checkpoint architecture

Human-in-the-loop for finance agents isn’t “a human can review if they want.” It’s a set of defined checkpoints where the agent must stop, present its work, and receive human authorisation before proceeding.

class OversightCheckpoint:
    """Defines when and how the agent pauses for human review."""

    def __init__(self, rules: list[dict]):
        self.rules = rules

    async def evaluate(
        self, 
        transaction: dict,
        agent_assessment: dict,
        audit_trail: list[AuditRecord]
    ) -> CheckpointDecision:
        """Determine if human review is required."""

        for rule in self.rules:
            if self._matches(rule, transaction, agent_assessment):
                return CheckpointDecision(
                    requires_human=True,
                    reason=rule["reason"],
                    reviewer_role=rule["reviewer_role"],
                    context=self._assemble_context(
                        transaction, agent_assessment, audit_trail
                    ),
                    sla_hours=rule.get("sla_hours", 24)
                )

        return CheckpointDecision(requires_human=False)

    def _matches(self, rule, transaction, assessment) -> bool:
        """Check if this transaction triggers a checkpoint."""
        checks = {
            "amount_exceeds": lambda: (
                transaction.get("amount", 0) > rule.get("threshold", 0)
            ),
            "confidence_below": lambda: (
                assessment.get("confidence", 1.0) < rule.get("threshold", 0.85)
            ),
            "new_counterparty": lambda: (
                transaction.get("counterparty_history_days", 999) < 
                rule.get("minimum_days", 90)
            ),
            "exception_type": lambda: (
                assessment.get("exception_type") in 
                rule.get("escalation_types", [])
            ),
            "regulatory_flag": lambda: (
                assessment.get("regulatory_flags", []) != []
            ),
        }

        check_fn = checks.get(rule["condition"])
        return check_fn() if check_fn else False

    def _assemble_context(self, transaction, assessment, trail) -> dict:
        """Give the human everything they need to make a decision."""
        return {
            "transaction_summary": transaction,
            "agent_recommendation": assessment.get("recommendation"),
            "agent_confidence": assessment.get("confidence"),
            "agent_reasoning": assessment.get("reasoning_chain"),
            "relevant_history": self._get_relevant_history(transaction),
            "applicable_rules": assessment.get("rules_checked"),
            "escalation_reason": assessment.get("escalation_reason"),
            "suggested_action": assessment.get("suggested_action"),
            "audit_trail": [r.record_id for r in trail[-5:]],  # Last 5 steps
        }


# Checkpoint rules configuration
CHECKPOINT_RULES = [
    {
        "condition": "amount_exceeds",
        "threshold": 100_000,
        "reason": "Transaction exceeds autonomous authority limit",
        "reviewer_role": "senior_finance",
        "sla_hours": 4
    },
    {
        "condition": "confidence_below",
        "threshold": 0.85,
        "reason": "Agent confidence below threshold",
        "reviewer_role": "domain_specialist",
        "sla_hours": 8
    },
    {
        "condition": "new_counterparty",
        "minimum_days": 90,
        "reason": "Counterparty has less than 90 days of history",
        "reviewer_role": "risk_analyst",
        "sla_hours": 24
    },
    {
        "condition": "regulatory_flag",
        "reason": "Transaction flagged for regulatory review",
        "reviewer_role": "compliance_officer",
        "sla_hours": 4
    },
]

The _assemble_context method is where the oversight becomes genuinely useful rather than merely procedural. A human reviewer who receives “please review this transaction” makes a worse decision than one who receives the transaction data, the agent’s recommendation, the reasoning chain, the applicable rules, and the suggested action. The context assembly is what makes human oversight efficient, the human starts with understanding, not investigation.

The sla_hours field is the detail that operational teams care about. A checkpoint without a response deadline creates a queue that grows without bound. The SLA ensures that escalated transactions are reviewed within a defined window, and transactions that aren’t reviewed within the SLA trigger secondary escalation.

Putting it together: the compliant agent loop

Here’s how the components compose into a complete agent execution loop:

class FinanceAgent:
    """A finance agent that's auditable, controlled, and supervised."""

    def __init__(self, tools, permissions, checkpoints, audit_store, llm):
        self.tools = tools
        self.permissions = permissions
        self.checkpoints = checkpoints
        self.audit = audit_store
        self.llm = llm

    async def process(self, transaction: dict) -> ProcessingResult:
        trail = []

        # Step 1: Deterministic compliance checks first
        compliance_result = await self._run_compliance_checks(transaction)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "compliance_check", 
            EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC, compliance_result
        ))

        if not compliance_result.passed:
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="compliance_failed",
                details=compliance_result.failures,
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 2: AI-assisted assessment where judgment is needed
        assessment = await self._run_ai_assessment(transaction)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "ai_assessment",
            EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED, assessment
        ))

        # Step 3: Check if human oversight is required
        checkpoint = await self.checkpoints.evaluate(
            transaction, assessment, trail
        )

        if checkpoint.requires_human:
            trail.append(await self._audit(
                transaction, "escalated",
                EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED, 
                {"reason": checkpoint.reason}
            ))
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="pending_human_review",
                context=checkpoint.context,
                reviewer=checkpoint.reviewer_role,
                sla=checkpoint.sla_hours,
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 4: Execute within authority
        self.permissions.check_access("write", f"{transaction['type']}.status")

        if transaction.get("amount", 0) > self.permissions.permissions.get(
            "amount_ceiling", float("inf")
        ):
            trail.append(await self._audit(
                transaction, "amount_escalation",
                EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC,
                {"ceiling": self.permissions.permissions["amount_ceiling"]}
            ))
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="escalated_amount_ceiling",
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 5: Execute and document
        action_result = await self._execute_action(transaction, assessment)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "action_executed",
            EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC, action_result
        ))

        return ProcessingResult(
            status="completed",
            action=action_result,
            audit_trail=trail
        )

    async def _audit(self, transaction, step, eval_type, data) -> AuditRecord:
        """Every step gets an immutable audit record."""
        record = AuditRecord(
            record_id=generate_uuid(),
            timestamp=datetime.utcnow(),
            agent_id=self.agent_id,
            agent_version=self.version,
            transaction_id=transaction["id"],
            transaction_type=transaction["type"],
            input_data_hash=hash_data(transaction),
            input_data_snapshot=freeze(transaction),
            evaluation_type=eval_type,
            rules_applied=data.get("rules", []),
            model_version=self.llm.model_version if eval_type == 
                EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED else None,
            prompt_hash=data.get("prompt_hash"),
            decision=data.get("decision", ActionType.PENDING_REVIEW),
            confidence=data.get("confidence"),
            reasoning_chain=data.get("reasoning", []),
            escalated_to=data.get("escalated_to"),
            human_reviewer=None,
            human_decision=None,
            human_override_reason=None,
            human_decision_timestamp=None,
            previous_record_hash=await self.audit.get_latest_hash(
                transaction["id"]
            )
        )
        await self.audit.append(record)
        return record

The execution order matters. Compliance checks run first, deterministic, binary, fast. If the transaction fails a regulatory requirement, there’s no point running the AI assessment. The AI assessment runs second, only for transactions that need interpretive evaluation. The checkpoint evaluation runs third, comparing the transaction characteristics and agent confidence against the oversight rules. The action execution runs last, only for transactions that passed compliance, received a confident assessment, and didn’t trigger a checkpoint.

Every step produces an audit record. The complete chain for a single transaction typically contains four to six records, each linked to the previous by hash. A regulator reviewing a decision can trace the complete chain: what data came in, what compliance checks passed, what the AI assessed and why, whether a human reviewed it, and what action was taken.

The testing that makes compliance teams comfortable

The code above gets you an architecture. The testing below gets you the approval to deploy it.

# Golden test set: known-outcome transactions for regression testing
class ComplianceRegressionSuite:
    """Run against every agent update, every prompt change, every model version."""

    def __init__(self, golden_set_path: str, drift_threshold: float = 0.02):
        self.golden_set = load_golden_set(golden_set_path)
        self.threshold = drift_threshold  # Max 2% decision drift

    async def run(self, agent: FinanceAgent) -> RegressionResult:
        results = []
        for case in self.golden_set:
            actual = await agent.process(case.transaction)
            results.append({
                "case_id": case.id,
                "expected_decision": case.expected_decision,
                "actual_decision": actual.status,
                "match": actual.status == case.expected_decision,
                "confidence": actual.audit_trail[-1].confidence
            })

        match_rate = sum(r["match"] for r in results) / len(results)
        drift = 1.0 - match_rate

        return RegressionResult(
            passed=drift <= self.threshold,
            match_rate=match_rate,
            drift=drift,
            failures=[r for r in results if not r["match"]],
            recommendation="BLOCK" if drift > self.threshold else "APPROVE"
        )

The golden test set contains 300 to 500 transactions with known correct outcomes, labelled by experienced finance professionals, not by the development team. Every agent update, every prompt change, and every model version upgrade runs against this set. If the decision outcomes drift by more than 2 percent from the baseline, the update is blocked.

This regression suite is what we point to when compliance asks “how do you know the agent still works correctly after a change?” The answer is: we run it against 500 transactions where we know the right answer, and we block any change that moves the outcomes by more than 2 percent.

For a deeper dive into the full development lifecycle, from workflow assessment through architecture selection, integration patterns, and deployment, our guide on how to build finance AI agents covers the engineering decisions we make before writing any agent code.

What most teams get wrong

Three patterns consistently cause compliance rejections or production failures.

Building the audit trail as an afterthought. If the audit architecture isn’t designed before the agent logic, the audit records won’t capture the right data at the right granularity. Retrofitting audit trails onto a working agent means re-engineering the decision flow to emit records at each step, which is more expensive than building it in from the start.

Testing with synthetic data only. Compliance teams want to see the agent’s performance on real transactions, transactions that humans have already processed with known correct outcomes. Synthetic test data proves the code works. Real test data proves the agent works on your actual business workflows.

Treating the human oversight as a failure mode rather than a design feature. The checkpoint architecture isn’t the system failing and asking for help. It’s the system correctly identifying which transactions need human judgment and routing them efficiently. The 20 to 30 percent of transactions that escalate aren’t a limitation, they’re the system working as designed.

The bottom line for finance developers

A finance AI agent that works but can’t prove it works is a demo, not a deployment. The audit trail, the access controls, and the human oversight checkpoints are what transform working code into a production system that compliance teams approve, regulators can examine, and operations teams trust.

Build the audit architecture first. Design the permissions before the agent logic. Define the oversight checkpoints with the compliance team, not for them. Test against real transactions with known outcomes. And treat every deployment as the beginning of a continuous proving process, not the end of a build project.

For teams ready to build finance agents that survive audit, the bespoke AI agent development practice at Dextra Labs designs and deploys agents with the compliance architecture described in this article as a foundational requirement, not an add-on. The audit trail, the access controls, and the oversight checkpoints are built into the agent from day one, because in finance, working without proving it is the same as not working.

title: Media User Reminders: Node.js Cron Webhook Queue Handoffs Past 900 Seconds
description:
Short answer: for a media subscription renewal reminder, let cron call a public HTTPS endpoint that only enqueues work; let a queue worker do the potentially slow send. A 900-second cron ceiling makes “send every reminder in the scheduled request” a fragile design, especially when a billing-date spike arrives.

The mental model is small: cron is the alarm, the queue is the waiting room, and the worker is the person doing the calls. The trigger should acknowledge quickly. The worker can retry a delivery, record an idempotency key, and keep processing after the trigger has returned.

For this boundary, Infrai is worth testing when you want one plain REST API for both the cron admission and queue publish calls. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and includes runnable examples, so a Node.js team can inspect a capability and send HTTP without installing another SDK.

Why a 900-second deadline changes reminder design

Cron is a clock, not a batch runtime. Its single execution limit is 900 seconds. If a publisher tries to look up thousands of accounts, render messages, and call an email provider in one run, the last pages can still be running when the clock closes. A timeout then looks like a scheduling failure even though some messages were already sent.

There is a second boundary that is easy to miss: the cron target must be a public HTTP URL. Push delivery also requires a public HTTPS endpoint. A private service name, localhost address, or VPN-only route isn't reachable from the scheduler. Check the run history for failures, but don't treat its output as your application log; only the first 4 KB is retained, so the trigger and worker should emit their own structured events.

That is the whole fix.

The trigger admits work, and the worker owns delivery. For a renewal due at 09:00, put a stable reminder ID in the message, not a mutable row snapshot. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the send handler must make the provider call idempotent (or record a sent marker under that same ID) before acknowledging the message. FIFO deduplication only covers a five-minute window; it isn't a substitute for consumer idempotency.

Consider a deadline-day spike: 18,000 subscribers become eligible in one hour, but the public handler has only enough time to validate the batch and publish chunks. The worker drains those chunks at the provider's safe rate, records renewal_2026_09_12_1842 before acknowledging, and retries a 429 with backoff. If the process dies after provider acceptance and before acknowledgement, the same ID is seen again and the sent marker suppresses a second message. This is a longer path than a one-shot cron script, but each step has an observable state and a bounded retry; that is what keeps a 900-second limit from deciding which subscribers get contacted.

How should Node.js reminders use cron, a public HTTPS endpoint, and a queue worker?

Start with a public HTTPS route such as /hooks/reminder-admission. Its job is deliberately boring: authenticate the scheduler, accept the reminder batch identifier, publish one message per bounded unit of work, and return a 2xx response. It must not wait for email or SMS delivery. If the endpoint cannot be reached publicly, fix the network boundary or place a small public relay in front of the private worker; do not point cron at an internal hostname and hope retries will repair reachability.

The queue message can carry { reminderId, dueAt, attempt }. reminderId is the idempotency key used by the worker. dueAt lets the worker reject stale work or choose a fresh template, while attempt makes retry policy visible in logs. Keep payloads well below the 256 KB message limit and delay no more than seven days. Retention tops out at 30 days, and acknowledging a message removes it, so copy the fields you need into your own audit store.

Here is the smallest publisher I would keep near the public trigger. It uses an explicit method, an environment key, a client idempotency key, and a bounded retry for HTTP 429. The route and field names come from the scheduling API's discovery surface; there is no SDK to install.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const message = {
  queue: "media-renewal-reminders",
  payload: { reminderId: "renewal_2026_09_12_1842", dueAt: "2026-09-12T09:00:00Z", attempt: 0 },
  idempotency_key: "renewal_2026_09_12_1842"
};

for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/queue/publish`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json"
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(message)
  });

  if (response.ok) break;
  if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
    throw new Error(`queue publish failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
  const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250;
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
}

The worker then claims a message, checks its own sent-record table with reminderId, sends once, and acknowledges only after the provider confirms acceptance. A network timeout after the provider accepted the message is the classic duplicate-send case; the idempotency record is what makes a retry safe. Your mileage may vary with provider semantics, so verify whether the downstream API offers an idempotency key or use a transactional outbox plus a sent marker.

Which scheduling option fits the boundary?

The right comparison is operational shape, not a leaderboard. GitHub Actions schedules are convenient for repository-owned maintenance, but a media reminder service still needs a reachable handler and a separate worker when volume spikes. RabbitMQ gives mature acknowledgements and consumer controls; it is a strong choice when your team already operates a broker and needs its routing model. Temporal or Airflow are better when the job is a long, branching workflow with durable state and joins. Inngest and Trigger.dev sit between a hosted trigger and a full workflow engine: they suit teams that want managed retries and developer-facing functions, while a plain queue remains easier to inspect with existing worker tooling.

Option Good fit Friction or limit for renewal reminders
A cron trigger plus queue worker A short public admission request and bursty sends You own idempotent consumers and application logging
GitHub Actions schedule Repo-local housekeeping and small, predictable batches Public webhook and worker lifecycle still need design
RabbitMQ Teams needing broker-level acknowledgements and routing More infrastructure and credentials to operate
Temporal or Airflow Multi-step workflows, joins, and durable orchestration Heavier control plane than a single enqueue-and-send path
Inngest or Trigger.dev Managed function retries with a developer-centric workflow surface Another hosted execution model and its event semantics to learn

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the main pain is integration friction: its discovery endpoint describes capabilities and runnable examples, and the same REST convention covers cron and queue calls. Infrai also uses a one key, one bill model across that boundary, which removes a small but recurring credential and invoice reconciliation task. One key can cover those backend capabilities, so a Node.js service can stay with plain HTTP instead of adding another SDK and credential set. I would recommend it for the public admission and queue boundary, not as a replacement for a workflow engine. The concrete advantage is fewer integration surfaces to review: discovery, auth, and request envelopes follow one convention while you swap the downstream sender behind your worker.

The catch is important. Infrai does not provide DAG orchestration, a fan-out/join primitive, native debounce, or topic-style one-to-many delivery. Choose Temporal or Airflow for a renewal process that must wait on several independent approvals, and choose RabbitMQ when you need its richer broker topology. Stick with a direct provider integration when the extra platform boundary would add more review work than it removes.

What should you observe after the handoff?

Track three timestamps: scheduled time, enqueue time, and provider-accepted time. Add the reminder ID, queue message ID, attempt count, and response status to each application log line. The cron run history is useful for spotting a failed trigger, but its truncated output cannot explain a whole batch. A small dashboard that separates “not admitted,” “waiting,” “retrying,” and “accepted” will tell you which side of the boundary needs attention.

Test the awkward paths on purpose: an unreachable public URL, a 429 from the queue API, a worker restart after provider acceptance, and a duplicate delivery inside and outside the five-minute FIFO window. Those tests expose the real contract. A green cron run alone does not prove that a subscriber received a reminder.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the cron and queue reminder guide and verify the request schema before wiring production traffic.

References

  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/inngest-functions
  • https://trigger.dev/docs/documentation/introduction
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: 5 Nodejs Checks for Batched Metric Updates to Dashboard Channels in 2026
description:
TL;DR: Collect changed presence series over a short window, publish them as one batch, and have each media workspace apply that diff; periodically send a full snapshot so a reconnecting dashboard converges even after it missed updates. The deciding constraint is the delivery guarantee at fan-out, not how lively the chart looks.

For a newsroom workspace showing which editors, producers, and reporters are online, an Express process should not turn every presence change into its own outbound request. A brief batching window absorbs a burst into one request while remaining short enough for the roster to feel live. Keep the publishing contract behind an application-owned adapter, too: the route and payload boundary stay put if the service behind that capability changes.

That is the operational recommendation. The rest is the runbook I would want beside the alert, because a green dashboard cannot prove that a disconnected browser received anything.

1. What page should fire when fan-out falls behind?

Page on a user-visible freshness or convergence failure, not on raw publish volume. A burst of 300 contributor changes can legitimately become one batch; request count falling during that burst is therefore evidence of batching, not evidence of loss. The useful signal is whether the online roster stops converging after publishes continue.

Ask the uncomfortable question first: what page fired? If the answer is merely "the realtime dashboard looks unusual," the monitor has confused a picture with a guarantee. Instrument the path as three separate facts: a change entered the short collection window, a batch was handed to the publisher, and a later snapshot gave clients a recovery point. Those facts describe the failure domain without inventing an exactly-once promise.

This is the postmortem frame: the missed update is not the root cause; the absence of a bounded recovery path is.

2. How should Nodejs push batched metric updates to a dashboard channel?

The Express-side collector should hold only changed series during a small, explicit window, coalesce repeated changes to the same series, and submit the resulting set through POST /v1/realtime/publish/batch. Batch publishing turns a burst into a single request. Do not infer a universal window duration from somebody else's traffic: the correct value is the largest delay your workspace can tolerate before "online" feels false.

Short wins here.

There is a real trade-off. A wider window reduces request pressure but makes presence stale; a narrower one feels immediate but gives up much of the batching benefit. Record the selected window as an operating parameter, then test it under a synchronized reconnect burst rather than tuning it by eye. This also keeps the Node.js handler boring: accept the change, place it in the collector, and let one publisher own flushing.

Infrai is one candidate for that publisher when an application wants one key and one REST contract across a verified surface of 295 routes in 20 modules. Its discovery surface is self-describing, and the same adapter boundary lets the service behind the capability move without changing calling code. That is useful here because the presence algorithm remains an application decision rather than becoming vendor-shaped. It doesn't remove the need to define recovery semantics.

The following Go publisher accepts a batch body that has already been validated against the discovery schema. Keeping the body in a file makes the transport example runnable without guessing undocumented fields. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and a unique BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY, then pass the JSON filename as the only argument.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 {
        panic("usage: publisher batch.json")
    }
    body, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    idempotencyKey := os.Getenv("BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/realtime/publish/batch", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    panic("publish remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

3. Treat every diff as disposable and every snapshot as recovery

A reconnecting browser may have missed one or several diffs. Do not ask the next diff to repair an unknown gap; send a full snapshot periodically, and make applying it replace the client's current workspace roster. Between snapshots, clients apply only the changed series from each batch.

This split is deliberately asymmetric. Diffs optimize the normal path. Snapshots repair uncertainty.

A practical verification drill has four steps:

  1. Connect two dashboard clients to the same shared workspace.
  2. Disconnect one client while several online states change and the connected client receives batched diffs.
  3. Reconnect the isolated client before a full snapshot, then verify that no test assumes an unproven replay guarantee.
  4. Wait for the scheduled snapshot and verify that both rosters converge to the same full state.

The evidence to retain is the batch boundary, snapshot boundary, workspace identifier, and client-observed convergence result. A screenshot is weak evidence. It cannot tell an incident responder whether the browser recovered through replay, a snapshot, or luck.

4. Compare products by recovery contract, not feature count

Ably, Pusher Channels, and PubNub are real alternatives, but their documentation exposes different concepts and those concepts should shape the test plan. Ably documents connection state recovery and message continuity; Pusher Channels documents presence channels and their membership events; PubNub documents Presence separately from message persistence. These are objective interface differences, not a ranking. Read the linked product documentation before assigning any of them a guarantee that its name merely suggests.

Option Contract to inspect for this workload Boundary to test
Ably Connection state recovery and channel continuity Whether the intended disconnect duration and client state qualify for recovery
Pusher Channels Presence-channel membership events How reconnect and resubscribe rebuild the member view
PubNub Presence plus the separately documented persistence behavior Which state comes from presence and which recovery requires stored messages or an application snapshot
Infrai Batch publish behind a consistent REST capability contract Application-owned periodic snapshots and diff application

The fair decision rule is narrow: choose the option whose documented recovery contract matches the failure you are willing to tolerate, then prove that behavior with a disconnect test. Use an application snapshot when the contract does not establish that every missed diff will return. WebRTC is not a substitute for that analysis; its standard covers peer connections, while this job is server-mediated workspace presence and dashboard fan-out.

No vendor row earns a pass from a successful happy-path demo.

5. Verify rollback before enabling the publisher

Rollout should begin with observation: build batches and record their size and age while the existing delivery path remains authoritative. Next, enable the batch publisher for a bounded workspace cohort and run the disconnect drill. Promotion requires both acceptable freshness on the connected client and convergence after the full snapshot on the reconnected client.

Rollback is a routing decision, not a data repair strategy. Stop sending batched diffs through the new publisher, restore the prior authoritative path, and immediately issue a full snapshot through that path so clients do not preserve an ambiguous partial roster. Keep snapshot generation independent from diff batching; coupling them creates the exact common-mode failure the snapshot is meant to repair.

At 3 a.m., the runbook should answer three things without dashboard archaeology: which workspace stopped converging, whether batch publication continued, and when the last full snapshot completed. If those answers are available, an operator can distinguish publisher trouble from a reconnect recovery gap and can roll back without claiming that a missing diff was delivered.

References

  • Ably connection state recovery: https://ably.com/docs/connect/states
  • Pusher Channels presence channels: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/presence-channels/
  • PubNub Presence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/presence/overview
  • PubNub Message Persistence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/storage
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
