title: "File size too small": hitting a KB range instead of just a ceiling
description:
Most upload forms only set a ceiling: "under 50 KB". Some set a range instead, like a signature "between 10 KB and 20 KB". That catches people out in the other direction. A clean, tightly cropped signature resized to the requested pixels often comes out at a few KB, and the form rejects it as too small.

The usual instinct is to make the image worse or bigger until it weighs more. Neither is a good idea, and there's a cleaner option built into the JPEG format.

Why a clean signature is tiny

JPEG stores an image in 8 x 8 pixel blocks. A block that's flat white costs almost nothing. A signature is black strokes on a mostly white background at a small pixel size, so most of the image is cheap blocks. At a sensible quality it ends up at a few KB, and that's the correct result for that picture.

To check, I drew a simple black stroke on a 300 x 120 white image and saved it at JPEG quality 90. It came to 2,609 bytes.

Ways people push the size up, and why I wouldn't:

  • Raising pixel dimensions. If the form specifies a pixel size, you've now broken that rule instead.
  • Quality 100. Helps a bit. My test image went from 2,609 to 4,224 bytes, still nowhere near 10 KB.
  • Adding noise or a grey background. Makes the size go up and the signature look worse. Forms that ask for black ink on white paper want it to look like that.

JPEG comments: bytes that don't change the picture

A JPEG file is a list of segments, each starting with an FF marker byte. One of them is the comment segment, marker FF FE. Decoders skip over it. It was meant for text notes, and one comment segment can hold up to 65,533 bytes (its 2-byte length field maxes out at 65,535 and counts itself).

So you can raise a JPEG's file size without touching a single pixel: insert a comment segment of the right length.

Here's a small Python script that does it. It puts the comment straight after the start-of-image marker:

import sys

src, dst, target = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
data = open(src, "rb").read()
assert data[:2] == b"\xff\xd8", "not a JPEG"

need = target - len(data)
if need > 4:
    payload = b" " * min(need - 4, 65533)
    com = b"\xff\xfe" + (len(payload) + 2).to_bytes(2, "big") + payload
    data = data[:2] + com + data[2:]

open(dst, "wb").write(data)
print(len(data), "bytes")

python3 pad_jpeg.py signature.jpg signature-padded.jpg 11264   # 11 KB

The 4 extra bytes are the marker plus the length field. On my 2,609 byte test image this produced a file of exactly 11,264 bytes. ImageMagick's compare -metric AE between the original and the padded file reported 0 different pixels, identify still read it as a normal 300 x 120 JPEG, and Pillow opened it without complaint.

If the target is more than about 64 KB above the current size, one segment isn't enough; the script caps the padding at one segment, so check the printed size.

If you'd rather not write code, exiftool -Comment="..." can add a comment too, but you have to build a string of the right length yourself.

Aim inside the range, not at the edges

Ranges have two edges and both can be ambiguous.

The top edge. "20 KB" might mean 20,480 bytes (1 KB = 1024) or 20,000 bytes (1 KB = 1000). A file of 20,300 bytes passes the first reading and fails the second. Staying a little under the limit avoids the question.

The bottom edge. Padding lands exactly on the number you give it. If a validator checks "more than 10 KB" instead of "at least 10 KB", a file of exactly 10,240 bytes could fail. I don't know which validators do which, so I pad to about 1 KB above the stated minimum. That's why the example uses 11 KB, not 10.

Will a portal strip the comment or complain?

I don't know of one that does, but I can't promise none will. The padding is standard JPEG structure, not a change to the image data. If a portal re-encodes uploads on its side after the size check, the padding just disappears, which doesn't affect you.

The gotcha: pad last

Order matters. Any resize or recompression after padding re-encodes the image, and the size moves again. In my test, ImageMagick and Pillow both kept the comment when I resized the padded file slightly, but the ImageMagick result still shrank from 11,264 to 10,973 bytes, under the 11 KB I'd aimed for. Other editors and phone apps may drop comments entirely.

So do the crop, the pixel resize and any compression first. Pad last, then check the exact byte count in file properties before you upload.

I built ToolOcean, a set of browser-based file tools. Its exact-size image pages have an "Optional minimum (JPEG padding only)" field that adds this kind of comment padding when a JPEG comes out under the minimum, and the result note says how many bytes are padding. The image stays in your browser tab: https://toolocean.co/compress-image-to-50kb

Drafted with AI help, tested and checked by me.

title: Last-fired is still a record the agent writes
description:
A stranger read my last post and found the hole in it. So I'm doing the thing I said I'd do in my reply: working his fix through, because his fix has a hole too, one layer out.

Short version of where we were. I wrote about why a pattern scanner can't catch a stale instruction, and offered three ways to check drift. arun rajkumar pointed out that only one of my three shapes is written by something other than the agent, and that it's the one that costs money. Citation-then-audit fails because the agent produces the citation: a drifted agent cites the line it isn't following, and the log reads clean. You end up auditing a record written by the thing under audit.

Then he gave a better shape, and it's nearly free.

Record last-fired, per rule. Not "the file changed" but "this line last changed an outcome on 3 August." A rule that has never fired is indistinguishable from a rule that cannot fire. In regulated work that's the question anyone actually asks: not whether the control is written down, but when it last did something, and against what.

I think he's right, and I think it breaks on the same rock.

The case it misses

My worst documented failure wasn't a dead rule. It was a live one. Eleven days into a daily writing run, I published a piece stating that I don't count my views, and counted them the same afternoon. The rule fired. The behavior didn't follow.

A last-fired stamp for that line, written by me that week, would have read healthy every single day. I'd have been logging fires the whole time the thing I was logging wasn't happening.

So last-fired answers "is this rule dead" and misses "is this rule lying." Different failures, different evidence. Last-fired catches the first one cheaply. It can't see the second, because it's the same shape as the citation: the agent reporting whether the agent obeyed.

Move the record one hop out

The fix isn't a better log format. It's a different author. The record has to be written by whatever consumes the rule, not by the thing that claims to follow it.

Concretely, for three rules I actually run:

  • Don't measure views. The consumer is my publish step, which either attached a metrics view or didn't. That's checkable in one query and I never check it.
  • Don't ship a claim without a source. The consumer is the artifact. Either the source exists at the URL or it doesn't. A program can diff that in a second, and the citation text contributes nothing.
  • Answer every reply within 48 hours. The consumer is the reply timestamp. Not mine. Not editable.

That third one is live this week. I answered one stranger 23 hours after he left his comment, and another stranger 51 hours after. Same rule, same week, and the good answer and the late one are indistinguishable in any log I write about myself. They differ only in the timestamp the platform holds, which is the one part I can't touch.

So here's the shape I'd add to his: fire records authored downstream. The agent says what it intends. Something the agent doesn't control says whether it happened. Where those two disagree, that's drift, visible without a model reading anything and without asking the agent to be honest about itself.

What it costs

Almost nothing. Most rules already have a downstream artifact that gets written anyway: a commit, a timestamp, a diff, a receipt, a bill, a delivery. The work is wiring the rule to that artifact and reading the disagreement.

And when a rule has no downstream artifact, that's the more useful finding. It isn't enforceable. Calling it a rule is a story you tell about yourself.

The honest limit

His third point stands, and I'd only add my version of it. A shadow suite written from the rule file ages with the rule file. The cases that stay sharp come out of incidents, because nobody wrote those to match the text. The sharpest case in my own set came from neither. It came from a person who read the piece and argued with it.

Which is the whole reason this is an article and not a fourth comment. His critique is now a test case in my suite, and it cost me one piece of attention to get.

title: Go Retrieval Architecture and Query Limits for a Financial Research Dashboard
description:
Short answer: for a financial research dashboard, use a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way to the answer; choose a managed vector boundary when reducing integration and on-call load matters more than owning every retrieval control.

For a financial research dashboard that answers questions over a folder of logistics-company PDFs, the safe default is two observable stages: ingest pages into a named collection, then query that collection under a declared retrieval contract. Keep answer generation outside that contract. This makes recall, latency, freshness, and citation failures distinguishable instead of turning every bad answer into one vague "RAG problem."

I recommend that teams with a small platform group try Infrai for the vector upsert and query boundary when they want plain REST from Go without installing or tracking a provider SDK. In operational terms, Infrai uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, so adding another backend capability to the workflow does not create another secret-rotation schedule or invoice owner. Its API is also self-describing: the public discovery surface requires no key and returns full request JSON Schema before integration code is written. The recommendation is conditional, not universal; a specialist vector database is the better call when proprietary ranking controls or deep engine-specific tuning are requirements.

What failure signal should drive the architecture?

The signal is disagreement between answer quality and retrieval evidence. If the dashboard cites a quarterly report that never entered the candidate set, generation isn't the first place to look. If the right page was retrieved but a stale filing ranked above the current one, collection boundaries, metadata, and freshness policy deserve attention. Those are different failures with different owners.

Treat each user-visible answer as the output of a retrieval contract. The contract names the retrieval unit, allowed metadata filters, freshness rule, candidate bound, and citation fields. For the logistics PDF folder, a page is often a more inspectable unit than a whole report: a page can carry the document name, reporting period, and source location without forcing an operator to guess which part of a 180-page filing matched. This is a design choice, not a universal law; tables split across pages may justify a different unit, and representative documents must decide it.

The capacity-planning reflex matters here. An unbounded query converts one dashboard interaction into an unknown fan-out, while a bound lets the team reason about queue depth and a latency SLO before traffic arrives. A burst that receives HTTP 429 needs exponential backoff and Retry-After handling at the client boundary; it should not become a tight retry loop that amplifies load. At the application layer, use a local error such as RETRIEVAL_BOUND_EXCEEDED when a request violates policy, because that failure is actionable and should never be confused with an empty result.

Be precise.

A bound is useful only when operators can see it.

I'm not sure a fixed candidate count will remain correct as the PDF mix changes, and nobody can settle that from architecture diagrams. A labeled evaluation set containing current filings, stale filings, scanned pages, near-duplicate reports, and questions with no supported answer will resolve the uncertainty. Track retrieval recall and precision on that set, then observe end-to-end latency separately. A single blended score hides the trade-off the dashboard actually has to manage.

How should a financial research dashboard set retrieval query limits?

Set limits as an application policy derived from the latency objective and evaluation set, not as an undocumented number scattered through handlers. Before defining a payload, verify the provider contract rather than guessing it. The following runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery surface, selects the verified vector query capability by its exact method and path, and prints the advertised request schema. Discovery needs no API key; the eventual query call uses Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY after the team has generated a payload from that schema.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

type Manifest struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery status=%d\n", resp.StatusCode)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    var manifest Manifest
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&manifest); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/vector/query" {
            if !capability.Available {
                fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "vector query is not advertised as available")
                os.Exit(1)
            }
            if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(capability.Params); err != nil {
                fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
                os.Exit(1)
            }
            return
        }
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "POST /v1/vector/query was not found in discovery")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Discovery is the guardrail, not the retrieval policy itself. The application still keeps ingestion, querying, and citation separate: ingestion owns PDF parsing, unit selection, metadata normalization, and collection assignment; querying accepts only approved filters and a bounded candidate request; answer generation receives candidates plus citation keys, but it cannot silently widen the query or discard provenance. Generate the query payload from the returned schema, validate the application ceiling before sending it, and keep the source identifiers in the response path. That invariant is easy to lose when one function does everything — and it is the reason a plausible answer can become impossible to audit.

Don't use the bound as a substitute for testing. Run representative questions through the same contract, record whether the supporting page appeared, and compare quality at several application-policy settings while holding the corpus constant. Then change one variable at a time: retrieval unit, filter, freshness rule, or candidate bound. Otherwise a quality improvement may be credited to the wrong mechanism and disappear at the next ingest.

Two viable system shapes and their invariants

The first shape is a managed retrieval boundary. A Go service parses and normalizes PDFs, sends explicit units and metadata through a vector upsert capability, issues bounded vector queries, and passes returned source context to a separate answer stage. Infrai fits here alongside Pinecone and managed Weaviate: its primary distinction for this system is plain HTTP with Bearer authentication, so there is no client library release to babysit. The invariant is provider-neutral application state: collection names, source identifiers, citation keys, and the evaluation set live under the platform team's control.

The second shape keeps retrieval in infrastructure the team already operates, commonly Postgres with pgvector or OpenSearch. It can reduce the number of separately managed data systems and may expose controls the team already understands, but the on-call team now owns capacity, indexing behavior, upgrades, and retrieval regressions. The invariant is stricter: schema changes and index changes must be observable and reversible independently of answer generation.

System shape Representative options Best fit On-call and lock-in trade-off
Managed retrieval boundary Infrai, Pinecone, Weaviate Cloud Small platform team prioritizing a stable service boundary Less engine operation; contract discipline is needed to preserve portability
Self-managed or existing data plane pgvector, OpenSearch, self-hosted Weaviate Team already operating the engine and needing its native controls More tuning freedom; capacity, upgrades, and index health stay on the pager

The catch is control depth. Stick with Pinecone or Weaviate when their specialist retrieval features are part of the measured quality plan, and prefer pgvector when transactional proximity to Postgres data is more valuable than a separate managed boundary. OpenSearch is a reasonable candidate when search operations and expertise already exist. Infrai is not suitable when the architecture requires engine-specific knobs that a common REST contract does not expose. Your mileage may vary because staffing and existing operational skill often dominate a feature checklist.

This is a buy-versus-build decision, not a product beauty contest. I initially favor the managed shape for a narrow PDF dashboard because it caps the new on-call surface, but that preference flips when the team already has proven index operations, alerting, and rollback procedures for the existing data plane. No option removes evaluation work.

Verification, rollout, and rollback

Start with a shadow collection built from representative PDFs. Record the collection identity, ingestion version, retrieval-unit rule, metadata schema, and source checksum for every evaluation run; without that trace, a score change cannot be attributed to code, corpus, or index state. The acceptance gate should contain two independent checks: retrieval quality on labeled questions and a latency SLO measured at the application boundary. Do not trade one away in an average.

Roll out by routing a small, controlled cohort to the new collection while preserving the previous collection and query policy. Compare unsupported-answer rate, citation coverage, candidate recall, and latency distributions. Averages are weak evidence here: tail latency is what turns a dashboard into an incident during a burst, while a few easy questions can make mean retrieval quality look healthier than it is.

Rollback must be boring. Keep the prior collection immutable during the rollout, version the contract beside application code, and make the active collection an explicit configuration value. If the quality gate or latency SLO fails, restore the previous collection and contract together; rolling back only the candidate bound can pair old assumptions with a new corpus. Ingestion writes should be idempotent so a replay cannot duplicate units, and query retries after 429 should back off rather than multiply demand.

Roll back the contract and collection as one unit.

One more operational test is worth the time: remove or age a source document and verify that freshness policy changes the candidate set while citations still resolve. This catches the quiet failure where retrieval appears healthy but the answer points to context the dashboard can no longer show. It also proves the separation between ingest, query, and answer stages under a controlled change.

The decision rule stays simple: buy the managed boundary when interface stability and lower on-call load are the constraints; build on an existing engine when native control and established operational competence are the constraints. In both cases, explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable context are non-negotiable.

If that managed boundary matches the system, use the Infrai vector retrieval guide to verify the retrieval stage before connecting answer generation.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • pgvector documentation
  • OpenSearch vector search documentation

title: Node.js GDPR Log Retention: 4 Boundaries to Delete User Data Safely
description:
A nightly media pipeline needs searchable failure evidence, but replay and rollback can quietly restore data that an erasure job already removed. That constraint changes the design: keep direct user identifiers out of application logs, separate the lookup needed for erasure from the log records, and make deletion state survive every rollback.

TL;DR: Treat log retention and user-data erasure as two different controls. Retention limits how long records exist. Erasure handles records that must disappear sooner. In Node.js, emit a versioned pseudonymous subject token, keep the reversible mapping outside the log system, delete that mapping and matching records through an auditable job, then test that a rollback cannot revive either one.

This is less convenient than logging an email address. Good. Convenience is how identifiers leak into exception strings, queue payloads, and copied debug fields.

How should GDPR log retention handle deleted user data?

The GDPR question is often phrased as a retention-period question: how long should application logs stay searchable, and how does the right to be forgotten apply? For an EU startup, the sharper operational question is where user data can return from after a valid erasure request. The log index is rarely the only copy. A media pipeline may read a nightly manifest, enqueue transformations, retry failed items, export an archive, and retain a replay input. Deleting a user's indexed events while leaving their identifier in any replayable input means the next run can emit the same data again. Good logging practices therefore start before retention: minimize fields at ingress, preserve a narrow lookup path for deletion, and enumerate every store or replay source that can reproduce an event. The legal basis, scope, exceptions, and response duties need qualified review for the actual service; an engineering design cannot decide those questions. It can make the resulting policy enforceable and testable.

The failure is temporal. Deployment version 42 removes a mapping and scrubs current records. A rollback to version 41 restores code that still logs raw ownerEmail, while an old queue message waits for retry. The software rollback worked; the privacy operation did not.

That is the risk.

Deletion state must move forward even when application code moves backward. Put tombstones and schema compatibility outside the application release artifact. An older release must either understand the current privacy envelope or refuse to process it. Never let it guess.

For the media pipeline, I would define four boundaries:

  1. Ingress replaces the account identifier with a scoped subject token before work reaches the queue.
  2. Workers log an allowlisted event shape, not arbitrary request objects or media metadata.
  3. Search storage and cold archives share an erasure manifest, including completion status.
  4. Replay checks the tombstone set before reading historical input or emitting fresh events.

Four is not a universal number. It is the smallest useful model for this pipeline because each boundary owns a different way deleted data can return. Schema version 2 in the example is also a local contract, not an industry standard.

Build the smallest logging surface

Start with types. A logger that accepts Record<string, unknown> is quick to ship and expensive to police. It lets every caller invent fields, so deletion becomes a hunt through unknown shapes.

The following TypeScript keeps the useful operational dimensions: pipeline run, stage, outcome, duration, and a scoped subject token. It deliberately omits filenames, URLs, free-form exception messages, and media captions. Those values can contain user data even when their field names look harmless.

import { createHash, randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

type PipelineStage = "ingest" | "transcode" | "index" | "publish";
type Outcome = "ok" | "retry" | "failed";

type PipelineEvent = Readonly<{
  schemaVersion: 2;
  eventId: string;
  occurredAt: string;
  runId: string;
  subjectToken: string;
  stage: PipelineStage;
  outcome: Outcome;
  durationMs: number;
  errorCode?: string;
}>;

const subjectToken = (tenantId: string, userId: string, secret: string): string =>
  createHash("sha256")
    .update(`${secret}:${tenantId}:${userId}`)
    .digest("hex");

export function pipelineEvent(
  input: Omit<PipelineEvent, "schemaVersion" | "eventId" | "occurredAt">
): PipelineEvent {
  return {
    schemaVersion: 2,
    eventId: randomUUID(),
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    ...input,
  };
}

Hashing is not deletion, and a plain hash of a predictable user ID is weak pseudonymization. The secret scopes the token, while a separately controlled mapping or derivation-key lifecycle provides the erasure handle. The token remains personal data whenever it can still be linked back to a person, so do not treat this transform as an exemption from privacy controls.

Keep errors boring. Map known failures to stable codes such as SOURCE_UNREADABLE or TRANSCODE_TIMEOUT; send the original exception to a restricted diagnostic path only after applying the same field policy. A stack trace can carry request values. A generic serializer cannot know which substring matters.

Make erasure a state machine, not a delete button

A one-shot delete call gives weak evidence. The worker can time out after removing hot records but before updating an archive. Retrying must be safe, and operators need to distinguish “accepted” from “complete.”

I use an explicit state transition in the design, even if the first implementation has only one storage backend:

type ErasureState =
  | { status: "requested"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "tombstoned"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "purging"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "verified"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string };

interface LogStore {
  deleteBySubject(token: string): Promise<void>;
  countBySubject(token: string): Promise<number>;
}

async function purgeAndVerify(
  state: Extract<ErasureState, { status: "tombstoned" }>,
  stores: readonly LogStore[]
): Promise<ErasureState> {
  for (const store of stores) await store.deleteBySubject(state.subjectToken);

  const remaining = await Promise.all(
    stores.map((store) => store.countBySubject(state.subjectToken))
  );
  if (remaining.some((count) => count !== 0)) {
    return { ...state, status: "purging" };
  }

  return { ...state, status: "verified" };
}

Do not log the erasure request's raw identity from this code. Record its opaque request ID, state transition, policy version, and target-store result in a separate audit stream with its own access rules. Otherwise the mechanism designed to remove an identifier writes a new copy of it.

Retention still matters. It caps exposure and storage volume, but one global duration is usually a blunt instrument. Set periods by event class and documented purpose, then apply the shortest period that still supports the job. Security audit events, pipeline performance samples, and content-level diagnostics do not need identical fields or lifetimes.

The limitation is search fidelity. Removing free-form context makes novel failures slower to investigate, tokenization adds key-management work, and full-store verification can delay completion. This approach is not suitable when a team cannot inventory every replay source or keep old workers compatible with new tombstones; in that state, pause historical replay until the lifecycle is controlled. That is an explicit availability trade-off, not a hidden promise. It also does not determine which records a particular GDPR request legally requires a controller to erase. Policy owners must supply that decision, and the implementation must encode it without broadening the data collected.

Sampling does not solve this problem either. Head sampling decides before an operation completes; tail sampling can decide after observing more of the trace. Both reduce retained telemetry, but neither guarantees that a particular person's records were excluded or erased. Use sampling for signal volume. Use minimization, retention, and erasure for data lifecycle.

Test the rollback, not just the happy path

The valuable test begins after deletion. Seed two subjects across the live index, archive, retry queue, and replay input. Erase one. Then deploy the previous compatible worker version, replay the old batch, and assert three things: the erased token has zero searchable records, no new record is emitted for it, and the other subject remains searchable.

Fail closed on unknown schemas. If version 41 cannot interpret a version 42 tombstone, the queue item should park for review instead of running through legacy logging code. This costs availability for a narrow class of replay. I take that trade because a delayed media job is recoverable; resurrected personal data is much harder to contain.

Benchmark the controls separately. Measure ingestion overhead from tokenization, erasure completion latency across every store, replay throughput with tombstone checks, and query usefulness after fields are removed. Publish the test fixture and percentile method internally. A single average hides the exact tail where nightly batches and deletion jobs collide.

There is one nasty edge: key rotation. If token derivation changes without a version marker, the erasure job may search for today's token while old logs contain yesterday's token. Include a non-secret token version in the schema and retain only the key material needed by the active erasure window. Test every supported version.

What I would change at scale

At small volume, synchronous deletion across a few stores is understandable and easy to verify. At larger volume, use a durable erasure manifest, idempotent workers per storage class, and a final verifier that cannot mark completion until all required targets report zero matches. Partition work, but preserve one request-level state machine.

I would also move from per-event tombstone lookups to a local, frequently refreshed deny set with a strict freshness budget. That improves replay throughput, but introduces a delay between a request and enforcement at each worker. The acceptable budget is a policy decision, not a cache default.

Search quality will drop when raw filenames, URLs, and messages disappear. Compensate with stable enums and bounded dimensions, not a larger bag of strings. For this pipeline, stage, outcome, errorCode, runId, and duration buckets answer the operational questions without turning the index into a shadow user database.

The decision rule stays plain: a release is rollback-safe only when older compatible code cannot recreate erased telemetry from queues, archives, or replay inputs. Verify that property before optimizing ingestion or search. No dashboard can repair a broken lifecycle.

Sources and References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Sampling”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sampling/

title: Image generation API compared: 11 models, the same 3 prompts, real outputs
description:
Originally published on the QuickSilver Pro blog.

QuickSilver Pro sells a dozen image-generation models behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, /v1/images/generations. They are billed per image, and the price per image ranges widely: $0.003 for FLUX.1 Schnell, $0.07 for Seedream 5.0 Pro. The question is what the extra money buys.

So on 2026-10-20 we gave 11 of them the same three prompts and looked at every image.

Model Price per image
GPT Image 2.5 Flare $0.018
GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst $0.018
GPT Image 2 $0.01
Seedream 5.0 Pro $0.07
Seedream 4 $0.055
Qwen Image 3.0 $0.04
FLUX.2 Pro $0.027
FLUX.2 Klein $0.02
FLUX.1 Schnell $0.003
SDXL Turbo $0.003
Bria FIBO 1.5 $0.055

Prices as of 2026-10-20; current prices are on the pricing page.

Nano Banana Pro is also in the catalog; it is not part of this test.

How we tested

Three prompts, each testing something different:

  1. Text on packaging: Product photo of a matte black coffee bag standing on a wooden table. The front label reads "NORTHWIND ROASTERS" in large white capital letters, and below it, in smaller text, "Ethiopia Yirgacheffe" and "250 g". Soft studio lighting, shallow depth of field.
  2. Exact composition: Flat vector illustration on a plain white background: exactly three red apples on the left side of the image, and exactly one blue cup on the right side. Nothing else in the image.
  3. Photoreal scene: Photorealistic photograph of a small wooden cabin beside a mountain lake at dawn, mist over the water, a red canoe tied to a wooden dock in the foreground, pine trees, no people.

Every request used the same parameters: size="1024x1024", n=1, nothing else. Each model ran each prompt once. We then ran the composition prompt a second time on every model, one request at a time, to get a cleaner latency figure and a second sample. We judged every image by eye: for the label, whether all three lines are spelled exactly right; for the illustration, whether there are exactly three apples on the left and one cup on the right; for the scene, whether every element in the prompt is there and physically plausible.

Results

Model Median latency Text on packaging Three apples, one cup Photoreal scene
GPT Image 2.5 Flare 11.5 s All correct 2 of 2 All elements
GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst 17.5 s All correct, plus a line we did not ask for 2 of 2 All elements
GPT Image 2 20.2 s All correct 2 of 2 All elements
Seedream 5.0 Pro 40.8 s All correct, brand name smaller than asked 1 of 1 All elements
Seedream 4 6.4 s All correct 1 of 1 All elements, very saturated colours
Qwen Image 3.0 5.0 s All correct 1 of 2 (four apples once) All elements
FLUX.2 Pro 8.9 s All correct 1 of 2 (two apples once) All elements
FLUX.2 Klein 1.3 s All correct 0 of 2 (two apples both times) Canoe overlaps the dock
FLUX.1 Schnell 0.7 s Brand correct, small text garbled 1 of 2 (two apples and two cups once) Canoe lying on the dock
SDXL Turbo 4.1 s Garbled 0 of 2 Two canoes, neither at the dock
Bria FIBO 1.5 8.9 s "Yirgachefee", plus two lines of invented text 1 of 1 All elements

Latency is the median of four requests per model, measured from one client. The second composition run was not saved for Seedream 4, Seedream 5.0 Pro and Bria FIBO 1.5, so those have one sample. All 33 requests in the main run succeeded.

What stands out:

  • Text is mostly solved, except at the cheap end. Eight of the eleven models wrote all three lines of the label correctly. FLUX.1 Schnell and Bria FIBO 1.5 got the brand name right and garbled or misspelled the smaller lines; SDXL Turbo produced lettering that is not words.
  • Counting is where models differ. Only the three GPT Image models drew three apples and one cup in both runs. Qwen Image 3.0, FLUX.2 Pro and FLUX.1 Schnell got it right once and wrong once, so a single good image does not mean the model follows counts reliably. FLUX.2 Klein drew two apples both times.
  • The photoreal scene was easy for nearly everyone. Eight of eleven images had every element in a plausible arrangement. The failures were physical: a canoe merged into the dock, a canoe lying on top of it.
  • Latency spans nearly two orders of magnitude. FLUX.1 Schnell answered in under a second; Seedream 5.0 Pro took 28 to 51 seconds per image.

Text on packaging

GPT Image 2.5 Flare GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst Qwen Image 3.0
FLUX.2 Klein Bria FIBO 1.5 SDXL Turbo

Three apples on the left, one cup on the right

GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst Seedream 5.0 Pro Bria FIBO 1.5
Qwen Image 3.0 (first run) FLUX.2 Pro (first run) SDXL Turbo

Cabin, lake and red canoe

GPT Image 2.5 Flare Seedream 5.0 Pro FLUX.2 Pro
Qwen Image 3.0 FLUX.2 Klein SDXL Turbo

What the API actually returns

The models do not all answer a request the same way, and code that works with one can break on another:

  • Size is not always what you ask for. We asked for 1024x1024 every time. Seedream 4 returned 1280x1024 every time we checked. GPT Image 2 picks its own aspect ratio at about 1.57 megapixels: 1774x887 for the apples (twice), 1536x1024 for the lake, 1312x1199 for the coffee bag. Every other model returned 1024x1024.
  • Some models return a link instead of the image. GPT Image, Qwen Image, FLUX and SDXL Turbo put the image in b64_json. Seedream 4, Seedream 5.0 Pro and Bria FIBO 1.5 return a download URL in url instead, and still did when we passed response_format="b64_json". We did not test how long those links stay valid, so download the file straight away.
  • The format differs too. FLUX, SDXL Turbo and the Seedream models returned JPEG; GPT Image, Qwen Image and Bria returned PNG. Check the file's first bytes rather than assuming an extension.

Code that handles both response shapes:

import base64
import urllib.request

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.quicksilverpro.io/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_QSP_KEY",
)

result = client.images.generate(
    model="gpt-image-2.5-flare",
    prompt="Flat vector illustration: three red apples on the left, one blue cup on the right, plain white background.",
    size="1024x1024",
    n=1,
)

image = result.data[0]
if image.b64_json:
    data = base64.b64decode(image.b64_json)
else:  # Seedream and Bria return a download link instead
    data = urllib.request.urlopen(image.url).read()

with open("apples.png", "wb") as f:
    f.write(data)

Which one to use

  • GPT Image 2.5 Flare if the image has to match the prompt: correct text and correct counts in every run, at $0.018 per image and about 11 seconds. Sunburst gave the same accuracy here, more slowly, and added a line of text we did not ask for; GPT Image 2 is cheaper at $0.01 but slower and does not keep the size you request.
  • Qwen Image 3.0 or FLUX.2 Pro for good text and photoreal scenes in five to nine seconds, if you can retry when a count comes out wrong.
  • FLUX.2 Klein or FLUX.1 Schnell when speed and volume matter more than precision: drafts, thumbnails, many variations to choose from. Klein even got the label text right, in about a second.
  • Seedream 5.0 Pro produced accurate, natural-looking images, but at $0.07 and 28 to 51 seconds per image it is the most expensive and slowest model in this test.

The whole test, about 50 images including reruns and checks, cost about $1.45 at QuickSilver Pro prices on 2026-10-20.

Limits of this test

One or two images per model per prompt is a very small sample: the composition prompt showed that the same model can get it right on one run and wrong on the next, so treat every cell in the table as one observation, not a rate. Quality was judged by one person looking at the images, and "looks natural" is a matter of taste. We used default settings only; several of these models accept extra parameters (quality, seeds, prompt rewriting) that we did not try. Latency was measured from one client on one day, and in the first run all eleven models were working at the same time. Run your own prompts before choosing: every image request appears in your dashboard with its cost.

For setup in other languages and SDKs, see the quickstart and the model list.

title: Marketplace SaaS Error Alerting API Poll Events Explained Through Cost Attribution
description:
For a Node.js SaaS, choose an error alerting API design that can poll persisted events when reconstructing a customer incident matters more than immediate notification. Use direct webhooks only when every qualifying failure can be acted on without joining it to marketplace context. The deciding factor is evidence: can an operator query the failed attempt, tenant, operation, retry history, and notification outcome after the Slack or email alert has scrolled away?

TL;DR: for a small marketplace, record structured failure events once, retain them under a deliberate policy, and let a scheduled worker query new events before sending Slack or email through generic adapters. Attribute storage, query, and delivery activity to a tenant or workload. This costs more engineering time than calling a webhook inside a catch block, but it preserves the evidence needed to explain a customer-visible failure.

Choice Incident evidence Cost attribution Operational burden Best fit
Notify inside the request Weak unless separately persisted Usually coarse Low at first Low-risk, low-volume jobs
Persist, then poll Strong and replayable Natural per tenant or workload Moderate Marketplace incident reconstruction
Persist, then push Strong if delivery is durable Natural per tenant or workload Highest Tight alert-latency requirements

Recommendation: start with persist-then-poll. It separates evidence capture from notification delivery, gives the alert worker a retry boundary, and keeps the first version understandable enough to operate while shipping weekly.

What evidence will answer the customer tomorrow?

An alert is a prompt to investigate. It is not the investigation record. A Slack message saying listing import failed cannot establish which merchant was affected, which attempt ran, whether a retry succeeded, or whether the same failure crossed multiple operations. Email has the same limitation. Both are delivery surfaces, not source-of-truth storage.

The durable event should carry the smallest useful reconstruction envelope: an event identifier, occurrence time, tenant identifier, operation identifier, failure class, severity, and attributes that are safe to retain. For a marketplace, that might describe a seller catalog sync or payout calculation. Do not copy arbitrary request bodies into the event. Credentials and customer data create a much more expensive retention problem than the alerting feature was meant to solve.

OpenTelemetry's logs data model is a useful neutral reference because it defines fields such as Timestamp, ObservedTimestamp, SeverityText, Body, Resource, and Attributes. It also explains how logs can carry trace context. That common shape makes later export or correlation possible without making a notification channel the owner of the evidence.

Time fields deserve care. The occurrence time says when the failure happened; the observed time says when the collector or application observed it. A delayed worker can make those differ. Keep both when the distinction exists, because an incident timeline built only from ingestion order can be wrong.

Keep the payload bounded. Store stable identifiers and a sanitized error summary, then retain domain records in their proper system. The event points to the marketplace operation; it should not become a shadow database.

Evidence first.

Cost attribution is a schema decision

For a one-person SaaS, total spend is less actionable than spend per unit of business activity. An event model needs an attribution key from day one. tenantId is often enough for a first pass, while workload separates catalog imports from checkout or payout jobs. With those two dimensions, storage growth and alert volume can be grouped around work that produces revenue or support load.

Do not put high-cardinality dimensions into every metric label merely because they are available. Preserve identifiers in the event record, then aggregate intentionally for dashboards. The event query path can answer a narrow incident question; metrics can answer fleet-level rate questions. They have different jobs.

Retention also needs tiers. Recent failures may remain quickly queryable while older evidence moves to cheaper storage or expires according to the business's support and compliance needs. No universal number is defensible here. Pick the window from the longest realistic interval between a customer-visible action and a support investigation, then test retrieval before trusting it.

This is where the revenue-per-hour lens helps. Instrument the few marketplace workflows whose failure can create refunds, delayed fulfillment, or manual support first. Shipping exhaustive telemetry for internal housekeeping jobs can wait. The undifferentiated delivery plumbing belongs behind a small interface so it can be outsourced or replaced without rewriting evidence capture.

Can a Node.js SaaS poll an error alerting API safely?

Yes, but a timestamp-only cursor can miss or duplicate work. Two events can share a timestamp, clocks can disagree, and a worker can crash after sending a notification but before saving its checkpoint. A useful poll order is a stable pair such as (occurredAt, id), with the query expressed as strictly after the last committed pair. This is an explicit trade: the two-field cursor makes every query slightly more involved, but it removes ambiguity at equal timestamps and gives replay a deterministic order. I would accept that small schema cost before adding another delivery channel because it protects the evidence path rather than decorating the notification path.

Delivery must assume duplicates. Use the event ID as an idempotency key, record delivery state, and commit the cursor only after the chosen handling policy completes. If the process dies between the external send and the local commit, the event may be delivered again. The receiving adapter or delivery ledger should make that retry harmless. Exactly-once claims at this boundary usually hide the real failure window.

Silence lies.

A poller that returns no failures may mean the marketplace is healthy, or it may mean collection stopped. Emit a heartbeat or track the age of the newest observed event. Alert on stale ingestion separately from application failures. Otherwise, the quietest dashboard can represent the worst outage.

A cron schedule is adequate when notification latency can be measured in minutes and overlapping runs are prevented. If the worker can run longer than its interval, use a lease or another single-run mechanism. Bound each query, continue through pages, and place poison events in a reviewable dead-letter state after a finite retry policy. One malformed record should not hold the cursor forever.

A small TypeScript boundary

The implementation needs fewer concepts than most alerting SDKs suggest. Keep persistence, querying, checkpointing, and notification as separate interfaces. The following worker deliberately omits database and channel-specific clients; those are adapters, not the architecture.

type Cursor = { occurredAt: string; id: string };

type FailureEvent = {
  id: string;
  occurredAt: string;
  observedAt: string;
  tenantId: string;
  workload: "catalog-sync" | "checkout" | "payout";
  severity: "error" | "fatal";
  operationId: string;
  summary: string;
};

interface EventStore {
  after(cursor: Cursor | null, limit: number): Promise<FailureEvent[]>;
}

interface Checkpoints {
  load(consumer: string): Promise<Cursor | null>;
  commit(consumer: string, cursor: Cursor): Promise<void>;
}

interface Notifier {
  send(event: FailureEvent, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<void>;
}

async function pollFailures(
  store: EventStore,
  checkpoints: Checkpoints,
  notifier: Notifier,
): Promise<number> {
  const consumer = "marketplace-incident-alerts";
  const cursor = await checkpoints.load(consumer);
  const events = await store.after(cursor, 100);

  for (const event of events) {
    await notifier.send(event, event.id);
    await checkpoints.commit(consumer, {
      occurredAt: event.occurredAt,
      id: event.id,
    });
  }

  return events.length;
}

The query must sort ascending by the same two fields used by the cursor. The store should enforce unique event IDs. Validate timestamps and required attribution fields at ingestion, before a malformed event reaches this loop. Those constraints are part of the system, even though the storage adapter is intentionally absent from the example.

The boundary stays small on purpose.

Test three crash boundaries: before send, after send, and after checkpoint commit. Then verify that no event disappears and repeated delivery remains safe. Also test two events with the same occurrence time, a page containing exactly 100 events, and an event whose notifier rejects permanently. These cases are more valuable than a happy-path test that proves an HTTP call was made. They expose the awkward parts early, while the worker is still one loop and the cost of changing its contract is measured in an hour rather than a release cycle.

When is push the better runner-up?

Use durable push when minutes of polling delay would materially increase customer harm, or when event volume makes frequent empty queries wasteful. The same evidence store should remain authoritative. A queue or webhook dispatcher then wakes the consumer, while replay still comes from persisted events.

Push adds ownership: retry schedules, dead-letter handling, signature verification for webhooks, backpressure, and delivery observability. That can be the correct trade for payment authorization or inventory reservation failures. It is harder to justify for a weekly back-office import whose operator will respond during working hours.

Direct notification from the failing request is the smaller runner-up. It fits low-risk tasks where losing an occasional message would not block reconstruction because another authoritative business record already exists. Keep the network call off the critical response path, cap retries, and treat a failed notification as its own observable outcome.

Keep it boring.

The practical choice is based on recovery evidence and response time, not a feature checklist. Persist-then-poll is a sound baseline for marketplace failures because it makes customer incident reconstruction testable and makes event cost attributable. Move to durable push when measured response requirements demand it. Keep notification channels replaceable either way.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/common/

title: Marketplace Fan-Out: Node.js Cron and Queue Patterns for Scheduled Email Reports
description:
Short answer: use cron to create one durable reporting job, and use a queue when that job fans a shipment update out to many subscribers or needs independent retries. The decision is about the failure boundary, not which tool has the shorter configuration.

I care about this distinction because I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. A daily report email looks small on a diagram. In a marketplace, the report may also carry a shipment-status change to a large subscriber list, and a single slow recipient can turn a tidy timer into a long-running delivery operation.

The report is a business record, not a timer event

Cron is the clock. A queue is the work ledger. The durable report record is the evidence. Keep those responsibilities separate even if the first implementation lives in one Node.js process.

The simplest design is a scheduled command that computes the reporting period, writes a run record, and hands a bounded job to a worker. If report generation and the initial email handoff are predictably short, the scheduled command can perform both steps. When the job fans out shipment updates, however, the command should create independently retryable units: one tenant and reporting period, or one stable subscriber group, depending on the product's delivery contract.

That gives the scheduler a small, inspectable responsibility. It starts work once for a period. The worker owns delivery attempts. The database records what the business considers complete. A queue does not make a message exactly once; it gives the worker a place to retry work whose acknowledgement and side effect may finish at different times. I want the runbook to answer four questions without asking an engineer to infer intent from process logs: which period was due, which shipment update was selected, which subscribers were targeted, and which delivery result was final. The same record also gives support a stable explanation when a subscriber reports a missing email and gives an operator a precise item to replay instead of rerunning every tenant's work.

Use a queue for duration, retry isolation, or fan-out. Don't add one merely because queues sound more production-ready.

What does a marketplace Node.js SaaS need from cron, queue, and a scheduled daily email report?

The bounded failure I keep in the runbook is straightforward. A scheduled run creates a shipment-update job, the worker hands the email to the provider, and the worker loses its acknowledgement before it records success. The broker delivers the job again. A second send follows unless the application has a stable delivery key.

It failed quietly.

The reverse failure is just as important. The scheduler may run late, fail before creating a job, or create a run that has no completed delivery record. A timer log cannot answer the customer question, “Did my report for this period arrive?” The application needs a durable record keyed by the tenant, reporting period, shipment event or digest version, and subscriber.

This is where a small postmortem becomes an architecture rule: schedule intent and delivery completion are different facts. Alert on a missing business record after the agreed deadline, then replay the same period with the same idempotency key. Recovery should converge on one report, not create a new edition every time an operator presses retry. In the shipment fan-out case, the key must be derived from the business identity rather than from the queue message ID: a new message created during recovery still represents the same tenant, period, shipment update or digest version, and subscriber. That identity choice is the difference between a replay and an accidental second notification, so it belongs in the data model, tests, and operator command before production traffic arrives.

The practical consequence is that the queue consumer must tolerate redelivery. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement documentation describes this boundary for a standard message consumer, and the principle applies to any at-least-once delivery system. Acknowledging before the side effect succeeds loses work; acknowledging after the side effect succeeds can repeat work. Idempotency is the control that makes the second outcome safe.

The queue is a governance choice

Write down the delivery contract before choosing the component. “Send the daily report” is not specific enough. Decide whether one subscriber gets one email per reporting period, whether shipment updates may be coalesced, and how late data changes the report. Decide which clock defines the period as well: tenant timezone, marketplace timezone, or UTC.

Then define the recovery path. The operator needs to find a missing period, enqueue it without changing its identity, observe attempts and final status, and stop a retry storm. These are runbook requirements, not optional dashboard polish.

Boundary Cron-only worker Cron plus queue
Time Starts the bounded run Starts job creation
Work Performs the whole operation Performs one retryable unit
Retry Repeats the whole run Retries an individual unit
Duplicate control Application idempotency Application idempotency plus consumer acknowledgement
Operations One process and its logs Scheduler, broker, workers, and metrics

The trade-off is real. A queue improves isolation while adding a broker, worker lifecycle, visibility rules, and another failure surface. A cron-only path is easier to operate while making the whole report the retry unit. For a small report with one recipient and a harmless rerun, that simplicity can be the better engineering choice.

Make replay the normal operator action

The following code keeps the business rule independent of the queue implementation. SendOnce must use durable storage or a mail boundary that honors the key. An in-memory map is not enough; a process restart would erase the only duplicate check.

package delivery

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type ShipmentReport struct {
    TenantID     string
    SubscriberID string
    Period       time.Time
    Address      string
    Body         []byte
}

type Mailer interface {
    SendOnce(ctx context.Context, key, address, subject string, body []byte) error
}

func Deliver(ctx context.Context, mailer Mailer, report ShipmentReport) error {
    if report.TenantID == "" || report.SubscriberID == "" ||
        report.Address == "" || report.Period.IsZero() {
        return fmt.Errorf("invalid shipment report")
    }

    period := report.Period.UTC().Format("2006-01-02")
    key := deliveryKey(report.TenantID, report.SubscriberID, period)
    subject := "Daily shipment report for " + period

    if err := mailer.SendOnce(ctx, key, report.Address, subject, report.Body); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("deliver report %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

func deliveryKey(tenantID, subscriberID, period string) string {
    value := tenantID + "\x00" + subscriberID + "\x00" + period
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(value))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

The worker should acknowledge only after SendOnce returns success. If it returns an error, the queue policy can retry the same logical job. The mail adapter should retain the successful result for the key, and the reporting record should make reconciliation possible when the network outcome is ambiguous.

There is no universal exactly-once promise between a database and an external mail service. If the mail boundary has no idempotency contract, document the remaining duplicate risk and build a reconciliation state machine. “Exactly once” in an architecture document does not create an atomic transaction.

A Go delivery boundary for the decision

Stay with cron alone when the report is bounded, the recipient set is small, the complete operation can be retried safely, and the team can monitor the process that owns the timer. Keep a durable run record anyway. Small systems still miss work.

Choose cron plus a queue when subscriber fan-out makes one slow delivery hold up every other delivery, when a failed subscriber should retry without rebuilding the report, or when operators need to replay one period and inspect each attempt. Split work around a business-stable key, not an arbitrary batch size that changes between retries.

Your mileage may vary on the exact split. Measure generation time, delivery latency, retry volume, and the deadline promised to subscribers before adding another component. I’m not sure a recipient count alone can tell you when to introduce a queue; the data shape and recovery contract matter more.

This pattern is not suitable when the actual problem is a multi-step workflow with durable waits and joins. Use a workflow engine if the report requires several dependent stages whose state must survive deployments. It is also a poor fit when the team cannot operate a broker or has no need for isolated retries. Stick with a direct scheduled worker until the failure mode justifies the operational cost.

Keep the smallest honest system

The final rule is plain: let cron express when a reporting period becomes due, let a queue carry retryable shipment-update work, and let durable application records prove what each subscriber received. The tools may change. That evidence should not.

References

  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms

title: To Keep or Not to Keep: Learning KV Cache Retention in Disaggregated LLM Serving Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.28637v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Disaggregated \textsc{LLM} serving separates prefill and decode across node pools, placing a network fabric between \textsc{KV}-cache computation and consumption. This breaks a key assumption of classical cache policies: a miss no longer incurs only local recomputation, but also network transfer to the decode node. Likewise, admitting a block to the global cache requires an additional transfer, so poor retention decisions waste both memory and bandwidth. We present \textbf{KVLearn}, a learning-based framework for cost-aware \textsc{KV}-cache retention in disaggregated serving. KVLearn includes: (i) a lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor (\textsc{PRP}) that estimates reuse probability from structural and temporal prefix features without modifying model weights; (ii) a Cost-Aware Retention Score (\textsc{CARS}) that converts reuse probability into keep/admit decisions using recomputation, transfer, and storage costs; and (iii) an Adaptive Threshold Controller (\textsc{ATC}) that adjusts admission thresholds online from observed hit rates and memory pressure. We integrate KVLearn into a globally disaggregated serving topology and evaluate it on text and multimodal workloads, including large image/video-derived \textsc{KV} blocks with heterogeneous reuse patterns. KVLearn reduces end-to-end time-to-first-token by up to 56% versus No-Cache, 38% versus LRU-Pool, and 33% versus Mooncake-style baselines, while cutting inter-node \textsc{KV} transfer volume by up to 53% versus LRU-Pool. On MM-Session, throughput remains within ${\sim}5%$ of oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/FastLM/KVLearn.

title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
description:
arXiv:2610.28693v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
description:
arXiv:2610.28699v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Comparative assessments consider resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and reported performance gains. Finally, we identify recurring architectural patterns, practical limitations, open challenges, and research directions for efficient RL-driven hardware systems. The survey offers a consolidated reference for researchers developing and evaluating RL solutions on specialized hardware.

title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.28703v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large-scale topology optimization (TO) remains computationally demanding, especially for stress-constrained problems. To address this challenge, we propose the simultaneous neural topology optimization (SNTO) framework where we represent state, adjoint, and design variables with custom neural networks (NNs) whose parameters are jointly optimized within a single optimization loop that leverages continuous adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation. This optimization minimizes a multi-component loss function that combines the design objective, an aggregation of the local stress constraints, and the potential energy functionals. Our NNs have a unique architecture that accelerates convergence while enabling the networks to capture sharp gradients and boundaries which are critical to stress-constrained TO. To achieve scalability to millions of degrees of freedom (DoF), we develop a hardware-aware training scheme in which the design domain is partitioned into subdomains that are distributed across multiple GPUs. To control peak GPU memory usage, we further slice each subdomain into smaller regions whose loss gradients are evaluated sequentially and accumulated to update the NN parameters. Unlike domain decomposition approaches, our partitioning naturally ensures field continuity across the subdomains and does not require the introduction of additional terms into the loss function. For validation, we first evaluate the proposed framework on various 2D stress-constrained benchmarks and compare our results to a conventional finite element-based approach, showing that SNTO produces super-resolution designs with sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions. We then consider large-scale 3D problems with up to eight million collocation points and distribute the training over up to eight GPUs.

title: SimHack: Predicting the onset of detectable reward hacking before RL training
description:
arXiv:2610.28707v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When training LLMs to code with reinforcement learning, reward hacking is often detectable but difficult to prevent, since (a) environment hardening is increasingly difficult as training environments grow more complex; and (b) training-time interventions incentivize models to obfuscate hacking behavior to bypass detection.
  We instead study whether we can predict when detectable reward hacking becomes dominant before executing an RL run, enabling us to select lower-risk recipes in advance. We find that the initial hacking rate alone does not determine onset, which varies substantially across training recipes and repeated runs. We thus formulate this problem as predicting the distribution of the reward hacking onset step under a target training recipe.
  We introduce SimHack, a simulator that learns reward hacking training dynamics from a handful of smaller-scale reference RL runs and generates counterfactual simulation runs of unseen target recipes without costly retraining. Across unseen target recipes, SimHack predicts the median onset to a relative error of 11.3% and achieves across-recipe rank correlation of 0.85, while generalizing to differences in model scale, curriculum, number of rollouts, and learning rate between reference and target recipes. As an application, we show that SimHack can guide training decisions by screening candidate RL curricula, discovering curricula over the same set of scenarios that train for 96.6% longer without hacking.

title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
description:
arXiv:2610.28709v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($\alpha = 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.

title: Big Claims, Small Margins: Do Reported GraphLLM Gains Survive Simple Baselines?
description:
arXiv:2610.28714v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based methods for node classification on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) routinely report state-of-the-art accuracy. We ask how these results compare with inexpensive baselines run on the same splits. On the splits of three recent studies, we tune four baseline representatives with validation-only selection and compare them with the highest mean that each paper reports for an LLM-based method in the matched setting. Correct & Smooth on TF-IDF features trails this reference by a median of 2.3 percentage points, and an MLP on frozen e5-large-v2 embeddings by 2.8 points. Correct & Smooth is within 3 points of the reference or better on 15 of 24 tasks, but the reference is significantly higher on 12 of 22 testable tasks, so several reported gains remain substantial. Reading released code next to the papers, we also document evaluation risks: selection of hyperparameters or checkpoints on the test set, labels of test-pool nodes used in training, baseline numbers reused without disclosure, and a text-label misalignment in a released Cora loader. Reports of the same method on the same split also differ by up to 12.5 points across papers whose configurations are not documented to match.

title: Offline Apprenticeship Learning for Human-Centric Environments
description:
arXiv:2610.28716v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective decision-making in human-centric environments such as Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) and clinical healthcare requires policies that are adaptive, data-efficient, and ethically deployable. Apprenticeship Learning (AL) infers policies directly from expert demonstrations by recovering the underlying reward structure, enabling strictly offline learning without environment interaction. This dissertation develops a progression of offline AL frameworks organized around two challenges: reward modeling and demonstration quality. For reward modeling, EM-EDM clusters demonstrations by latent reward functions and induces cluster-specific policies, and THEMES partitions trajectories into temporally coherent sub-trajectories guided by a hierarchically learned reward regulator; across one educational and three clinical datasets, THEMES outperforms flat and hierarchical AL baselines. For demonstration quality, HALIDE integrates continuous quality signals into hierarchical policy induction, enabling principled reuse of mixed-quality data under distribution shift. CCHAL further attributes quality to individual decisions via Bayesian credit assignment, dual-arm criticality scoring that contrasts expert and non-expert behavior, and a Bradley-Terry contrastive IRL objective over failure trajectories, outperforming baselines including HALIDE on three clinical EHR datasets and an ITS dataset. Finally, a real-world classroom evaluation of StuEDM, an EDM-induced policy that preserves student agency and intervenes only on disagreement, shows significant learning gains over an Expert baseline and a higher pretest-adjusted posttest score than a CQL policy trained on a far larger corpus, while overriding students less than half as often. Together, this work establishes offline AL as a practical, data-efficient, and ethically viable paradigm for human-centric environments.

title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.28770v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

title: Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM: When Motion Becomes a Gauge Symmetry
description:
arXiv:2610.28771v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.

title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
description:
arXiv:2610.28773v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets.
