title: How to launch an 8-GPU RTX PRO 6000 instance on EcoHash
description:
An eight-GPU instance in EcoHash's Atlanta region gives you a whole node: eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with 96 GB of VRAM each, 200 vCPUs, 1,352 GB of RAM, and up to 5,260 GiB of temporary local scratch space. You can start with an EcoHash container image or bring the stack you already use.

This walkthrough covers the choices that matter before you launch, how to connect afterward, and where to put files you need to keep. Open GPU Instances in the console to follow along. You will need an account with enough credit for the configuration you select.

Choose Atlanta and all eight GPUs

Click Launch Instance, give the instance a name, and select atl for Atlanta. Under GPUs per Instance, choose 8x.

The configuration summary now shows the whole node dedicated to this instance. The eight GPUs provide 768 GB of total VRAM, with 96 GB on each GPU. That is memory distributed across eight devices; your serving or training software must support using multiple GPUs to take advantage of it.

Selecting eight GPUs allocates the whole node. Check the resource summary for your chosen region.

Pick a container for the work you want to run

The EcoHash Images tab offers several starting points. Their names include the installed software versions, so check the dropdown rather than relying on a tag from an old tutorial.

Use the inference image for vLLM, Jupyter for notebooks, or a base image for your own stack.

  • GPU Inference: vLLM configured for the RTX PRO 6000. This is the starting point for serving an LLM. It is a large image, so the first launch on a node may spend several minutes downloading it.
  • GPU Base: a CUDA and PyTorch environment for installing your own software. Choose the CUDA version your workload needs.
  • CUDA Bare: a CUDA 13.0 image without a framework, for building your environment from a smaller starting point.
  • GPU Jupyter: JupyterLab and an ML environment for browser-based notebook work.

The optional Startup Command runs when the instance starts. Use it to launch your application or model server. If you leave it blank, the image's default command applies. Make sure that command keeps the container running.

Bringing your own image

Open Images under Registry and click Add Image. Enter a display name and the full image reference, including its tag. For example, registry.example.com/team/eval:v1.0 is the format; replace it with your real registry and image.

A public image needs only its reference. Private images also need credentials with pull access.

For a private registry, provide its username and a read/pull access token. The form displays guidance for the registry you enter. AWS ECR login tokens expire after 12 hours and cannot be saved for this workflow; use a public ECR repository or arrange for EcoHash's account to have pull access.

Before saving the image, check these requirements:

  • Architecture: build for linux/amd64. On an Apple Silicon Mac, include --platform linux/amd64 in your docker buildx build command.
  • CUDA: use CUDA 13.0 or earlier for the configuration described here.
  • GPU support: your framework and CUDA extensions must support Blackwell sm_120. Check the specific build you are using, especially if you compile extensions yourself.
  • SSH: EcoHash configures SSH automatically for Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine-based images. Include OpenSSH yourself for other base distributions.

Save the image, return to the launch form, and select it under Custom / Registry.

Set up SSH and an HTTP endpoint

Enable SSH access and add your public SSH key in the launch form. Keys are applied when the instance starts, so do this before launching. Keep the matching private key on your own computer.

If you want to call a model server or another HTTP application, enable Expose a public service URL and enter the port your application listens on inside the container, such as 8000.

The endpoint forwards to the HTTP port inside your container.

Your application must listen on 0.0.0.0, not only on 127.0.0.1. A process bound to localhost can run normally inside the container while remaining unreachable through the public URL.

Choose the runtime and attach storage

Select No end time if you want the instance to run until you terminate it. The form explains the credit hold and hourly deductions. This setting does not keep an instance running after the account runs out of credit.

Alternatively, choose a fixed estimated duration if you want an automatic end time. Read the billing summary before launching; it changes with the number of GPUs and the duration you select.

Attach persistent storage before starting work you need to keep.

A cloud drive attaches to one instance at a time. A shared filesystem can be attached to several instances. Both are retained after the compute instance ends. Choose a cloud drive for files used by this instance, or a shared filesystem when several instances need the same datasets, weights, or results.

Treat /workspace as temporary. Its local scratch data is erased when the instance ends, including when it stops because your account balance runs out. Write results you need to keep to an attached cloud drive or shared filesystem.

Review the GPU count, image, SSH keys, service port, duration, and storage attachments. Then click Launch. Allow extra time for the first download of a large container image.

Connect and check your application

Once the instance is running, its detail page shows the SSH command, the public URL if you enabled one, and a web terminal you can open in the browser. Copy the SSH command from that page rather than constructing the hostname or port yourself.

In the terminal, run:

nvidia-smi

For this configuration, the output should list eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Check that your application can see all eight before starting a long job.

The public URL requires your console login or an EcoHash API key. To call it from a script, send the key in an Authorization: Bearer header. Paths after /service pass through to your application: /service/v1/models reaches the container as /v1/models.

For a vLLM server exposing that route, copy the instance's public URL and test it with:

export ECOHASH_SERVICE_URL="https://api.ecohash.com/gpu-instances/INSTANCE_ID/service"
# Set ECOHASH_API_KEY in your environment before running this request.
curl --fail-with-body "${ECOHASH_SERVICE_URL%/}/v1/models" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ECOHASH_API_KEY}"

Replace INSTANCE_ID with your instance ID, or use the full URL copied from the console. A ready vLLM server should return a model list. For another application, use one of its own HTTP routes instead.

If the request fails, check that the application has finished starting, listens on 0.0.0.0, and uses the same port you entered in the console. Also confirm that your request includes a valid API key.

Before ending the session, confirm that your outputs are on persistent storage. Terminate the instance when you are finished to stop compute charges.

Open GPU Instances to configure a node, or read more about launching an instance and container images.

title: A Single SQL Constraint Can Save Your Database From Bad Data — Do You Know Which One?
description:
Imagine you are building an order management system.

Your "customers" table contains 10,000 customers. Your "orders" table contains 500,000 orders.

Everything works perfectly.

Then one day, an application inserts an order for "customer_id = 99999".

The problem? Customer 99999 does not exist.

Your database now contains an order that cannot be linked to a valid customer.

Your reports may become unreliable. Your joins may not return the expected information. Your team may spend hours investigating a data-quality problem that could have been prevented.

The solution is not another SQL query. It is a database constraint.

Let's explore how SQL developers prevent these problems and learn some common SQL interview traps along the way.

  1. CREATE TABLE: Start With the Right Structure

First, create a customer table.

CREATE TABLE customers (
customer_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
customer_name VARCHAR2(100) NOT NULL
);

Notice two important constraints:

  • "PRIMARY KEY" ensures that every customer has a unique, non-NULL identifier.
  • "NOT NULL" prevents a customer record from being inserted without a name.

Now create an orders table.

CREATE TABLE orders (
order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
customer_id NUMBER,
order_amount NUMBER(10,2)
);

At first glance, everything looks fine.

But there is a hidden problem.

Nothing in this table definition prevents an order from referencing a customer who does not exist.

How do we fix it?

  1. FOREIGN KEY: Protect Table Relationships

Add a foreign key.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
REFERENCES customers(customer_id);

Now the database enforces the relationship.

If someone tries to insert an order with a non-NULL customer ID that does not exist in "customers", the database rejects the operation.

Why is this important?

Because your database should not depend entirely on every application developer remembering to validate every relationship correctly.

Interview takeaway: A foreign key enforces referential integrity at the database level.

One important detail: a nullable foreign key can contain "NULL" unless the column is also defined as "NOT NULL".

  1. ALTER TABLE: Change Structure Without Recreating the Table

Business requirements rarely remain the same forever.

Suppose you now need to store customer email addresses.

Do you need to drop the table and create it again?

No.

ALTER TABLE customers
ADD email VARCHAR2(150);

The new column is added to the existing table, and existing rows are retained.

You can also use "ALTER TABLE" to add or remove constraints and modify columns, subject to database-specific rules and existing data.

In production, always review dependencies before changing a schema. A column modification or removal can affect reports, stored procedures, applications, and downstream data pipelines.

  1. DROP vs TRUNCATE vs DELETE: The SQL Interview Trap

An interviewer asks:

"You have a table containing 10 lakh records. You want to remove all records but retain the table structure. Which command would you use?"

Many candidates immediately answer "DELETE".

But let's understand the differences.

DROP — Remove the Table

DROP TABLE orders;

This removes the table itself, including its data and associated table objects such as indexes and constraints.

Use it only when the table is no longer needed.

TRUNCATE — Remove All Rows

TRUNCATE TABLE orders;

This removes all rows while retaining the table structure.

There is no "WHERE" clause, so you cannot use it to remove only selected records.

DELETE — Remove Selected Rows

DELETE FROM orders
WHERE order_amount < 1000;

This removes only rows matching the specified condition.

You can also delete all rows by omitting the "WHERE" clause.

Important Oracle interview tip: DDL statements such as "DROP" and "TRUNCATE" have implicit-commit implications. Do not assume you can roll them back like an ordinary uncommitted "DELETE".

Always verify the target table and understand the transaction behavior before running destructive commands.

  1. COMPOSITE PRIMARY KEY: When One Column Is Not Enough

Consider an order-items table.

A single order can contain several products, and the same product can appear in different orders.

CREATE TABLE order_items (
order_id NUMBER,
product_id NUMBER,
quantity NUMBER,
unit_price NUMBER(10,2),

PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)

);

Why use two columns in the primary key?

Because the combination of "order_id" and "product_id" identifies each row.

For example:

  • "(101, 10)" identifies product 10 in order 101.
  • "(101, 20)" identifies product 20 in order 101.
  • "(102, 10)" identifies product 10 in order 102.

These combinations are different.

But inserting "(101, 10)" a second time would violate the composite primary key.

This concept is useful when designing junction tables, order details, and many-to-many relationships.

  1. CHECK CONSTRAINT: Prevent Invalid Values

Suppose an order amount must never be negative.

You can enforce that rule at the database level.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT chk_order_amount
CHECK (order_amount >= 0);

Now an insert or update that violates the constraint is rejected.

One subtle detail: a "CHECK" constraint alone does not reject "NULL" values. If the amount must also be present, define the column as "NOT NULL" or add an appropriate constraint.

This is the kind of detail that separates memorizing SQL syntax from understanding how database rules actually work.

Your SQL Interview Challenge

Before you leave, try this question without looking up the answer.

You have two tables:

  • "customers", containing customer information.
  • "orders", containing customer orders.

You must prevent an order from referencing a customer who does not exist.

Which solution is best?

A. Create an index on "orders.customer_id".

B. Add a foreign key referencing "customers.customer_id".

C. Use "ORDER BY customer_id".

D. Add a "CHECK" constraint requiring "customer_id > 0".

Pause and decide before reading further.

Correct answer: B — Add a foreign key.

An index can improve access performance, but it does not enforce the relationship. Sorting rows does not enforce data integrity, and checking that an ID is positive does not establish that the customer exists.

A foreign key directly enforces the required relationship.

The key principle is simple:

Good database design makes invalid data harder to create.

Want to Master SQL DDL for Interviews?

We've covered the fundamentals, but there is much more to learn.

What happens when you need a many-to-many relationship? When should you use "ON DELETE CASCADE"? How do you modify existing constraints safely? What mistakes do interviewers expect SQL developers to avoid?

I've brought these topics together in a detailed guide on Sankalan Data Tech.

The complete tutorial covers:

  • "CREATE", "ALTER", "DROP", and "TRUNCATE" with practical examples
  • Primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, and check constraints
  • One-to-many and many-to-many relationships
  • Composite primary keys and junction tables
  • Constraints versus triggers
  • Common interview mistakes and follow-up questions
  • 21 SQL interview questions with answers

👉 Continue learning with the complete SQL DDL guide:

https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/ddl-manage-tables-relationships-sql-faq.html

If you are preparing for a SQL developer, Oracle PL/SQL, or data engineering interview, work through the examples and understand the reasoning behind each constraint instead of simply memorizing syntax.

Save this post for revision, and test yourself on the interview questions in the full guide.
