title: Screen Sizes & Viewport Cheat Sheet for 2026
description:
Screen Sizes & Viewport Cheat Sheet for 2026

Every responsive bug report starts the same way: "it looks broken on my phone." Then you spend ten minutes hunting for that phone's viewport width — one site lists the panel resolution, another lists a viewport from two generations ago, and a third just says "various."

This is the cheat sheet I keep coming back to: the device viewports worth testing in 2026, the framework breakpoints next to them, and the three numbers — resolution, viewport, DPR — that developers constantly mix up. All values below are portrait CSS-pixel references. Treat heights as references, not guarantees: mobile browser bars, keyboards and zoom change the visible height, while width stays comparatively stable.

Phone viewports worth testing

Eleven models cover nearly every width your layout will meet in production, from the narrow 360px Android baseline to the 440px Pro Max class. The full model-by-model reference lives in the iPhone viewport sizes table and the device screen sizes index.

Device CSS viewport Panel resolution DPR
Galaxy S25 360 × 780 1080 × 2340 3
iPhone SE (3rd gen) 375 × 667 750 × 1334 2
Galaxy S25 Ultra 384 × 832 1440 × 3120 3.75
iPhone 14 390 × 844 1170 × 2532 3
iPhone 16 393 × 852 1179 × 2556 3
iPhone 17 402 × 874 1206 × 2622 3
Pixel 10 412 × 923 1080 × 2424 2.625
iPhone Air 420 × 912 1260 × 2736 3
Pixel 10 Pro 427 × 952 1280 × 2856 3
iPhone 16 Plus 430 × 932 1290 × 2796 3
iPhone 17 Pro Max 440 × 956 1320 × 2868 3

Patterns worth internalizing:

  • Modern iPhones cluster tightly. Everything from the iPhone 14 to the 17 sits between 390 and 440 CSS pixels wide, all at DPR 3. If your layout survives 390, 402 and 430, it survives the current iPhone line.
  • Android is wider at the edges. The base Galaxy line still reports 360px — the narrowest mainstream target, and the one that exposes cramped toolbars and rigid dialogs first.
  • DPR is not always a whole number. The Pixel 10 ships at 2.625 and the S25 Ultra at 3.75. Hard-coding "retina = 2x or 3x" assumptions into image pipelines is how blurry hero images happen; serve srcset steps and let the browser pick.
  • Shared widths hide differences. Several models share a viewport width while differing in height, DPR and safe areas. A matching reference is a starting point for testing, not proof two devices render identically.

Tablets and laptops, briefly

Tablet viewports overlap small-laptop widths, which is why "tablet layout" and "small desktop layout" so often collide around 1024px.

Device / class CSS viewport / workspace Panel resolution
iPad mini (A17 Pro) 744 × 1133 1488 × 2266
Classic iPad reference 768 × 1024 —
iPad (10th gen) / iPad Air 11" 820 × 1180 1640 × 2360
iPad Pro 11" (M4) 834 × 1210 1668 × 2420
iPad Pro 13" (M4) 1032 × 1376 2064 × 2752
Budget laptop (WXGA) 1366 × 768 1366 × 768
MacBook Air 13" (M3) 1470 × 956 2560 × 1664
MacBook Pro 14" (M4) 1512 × 982 3024 × 1964
1080p panel at 125% scaling 1536 × 864 1920 × 1080

Two things to notice. First, laptop "workspace" values are scaled: a 2560 × 1664 MacBook Air panel gives CSS a 1470 × 956 layout space, and OS scaling — not the panel — decides what your media queries see. Second, the classic 768 × 1024 iPad reference refuses to die; it is still a useful portrait test width even though current iPads report larger viewports.

Tailwind vs. Bootstrap breakpoints

Both frameworks are mobile-first min-width systems, but their thresholds only agree at 768px. The side-by-side reference, with a live checker that tracks your current width against both systems, is the responsive breakpoint checker.

Tier Tailwind Bootstrap
Base 0–639px (base) 0–575px (xs)
Small sm 640px sm 576px
Medium md 768px md 768px
Large lg 1024px lg 992px
Extra large xl 1280px xl 1200px
Largest 2xl 1536px xxl 1400px

Practical consequences:

  • A layout that switches to two columns at Bootstrap lg (992px) does so 32px earlier than the same layout at Tailwind lg (1024px). Porting components between the two without adjusting expectations shifts every boundary.
  • Tailwind expresses its thresholds in rem (640px = 40rem at the default root size), Bootstrap in px. If a user changes their browser's root font size, rem-based breakpoints move and px-based ones don't — a classic source of "works on my machine."
  • Test the pixel below each threshold, not just the threshold itself: 639, 767, 1023, 1279 and 1535 are where the old layout makes its last stand.

If you only keep one testing set, make it 360, 393, 430, 768, 1024, 1366, 1536 and 1920 — narrow Android, common iPhone, large phone, tablet portrait, tablet landscape, small laptop, large laptop and desktop. The reasoning behind that set is laid out in the common screen resolutions reference.

Check your own device, live

Tables tell you what a device should report. Your actual browser may disagree — because of zoom, OS display scaling, an installed web app shell, or a keyboard eating half the screen. When a bug is on your desk, measure the real thing:

  1. Open the viewport size checker on the device in question.
  2. Read three values: viewport (window.innerWidth × innerHeight), DPR (window.devicePixelRatio), and the active Tailwind/Bootstrap range.
  3. Resize or rotate and watch the values update; then paste the report straight into the bug ticket, so QA reproduces at your width instead of guessing.

For screenshot and image bugs, multiply the CSS slot by the live DPR: a 360px-wide slot on a DPR 3 phone needs a 1080px asset to stay sharp, and exporting at the panel resolution "to be safe" just ships megabytes nobody asked for.

The three numbers everyone confuses

Most screen-size confusion is one paragraph away from disappearing:

Physical resolution is the panel's pixel grid — 1179 × 2556 on an iPhone 16. It describes hardware. Your CSS never sees it directly. CSS viewport is the area the page renders into, in CSS pixels — 393 × 852 on that same phone. Media queries, breakpoints and layout respond to this number and only this number. DPR is the ratio between them: how many physical pixels paint one CSS pixel. It drives image sharpness (and screenshot dimensions), but it does not change which breakpoint is active.

So when a spec sheet brags about a huge resolution, divide by DPR before you panic: what lands in your stylesheet is the viewport. And when a user reports a "tiny" screen, ask for their viewport and DPR — not their panel resolution — before you touch a single media query.

TL;DR

Test widths, not devices: 360–440px covers current phones, 768–1032px covers tablets, and scaled laptop workspaces matter more than panel resolutions. Keep resolution, viewport and DPR in separate mental buckets, verify your own browser live instead of trusting spec sheets, and always check the pixel just below the breakpoint.

title: Small SaaS Custom Metrics Dashboard — 4 Push API and Pull Model Boundaries
description:
For a small SaaS evaluating a Prometheus alternative, send each completed game-data batch through an idempotent push API, then expose reconciled custom metrics to the dashboard; do not treat either a successful push or a successful pull scrape as proof that the nightly pipeline produced correct data. The deciding constraint is signal quality: the service needs to distinguish late, duplicated, partial, and invalid batches without turning every log line into a metric, regardless of whether Grafana or another dashboard renders the result.

TL;DR: For a nightly pipeline, push one bounded completion record per batch into a durable receiver, derive low-cardinality metrics there, and retain structured logs as the audit trail. A pull endpoint remains useful for live process health. The two transport models solve different failure windows, so combining them is often clearer than declaring either one the universal winner.

This architecture decision record uses four boundaries: batch identity, acceptance, reconciliation, and publication. They matter more than the choice of dashboard.

Should a small SaaS push or pull custom metrics?

The concrete workload is a gaming pipeline that transforms a night's events into searchable structured logs and a small custom-metrics dashboard. Operators need to answer questions such as: Did every scheduled shard finish? Which game mode produced rejected records? Is the apparent drop in processed events real, or did telemetry arrive late?

Four invariants keep those answers defensible. First, every batch has a stable identifier derived from the scheduled run and shard, not from an individual retry. Second, accepting an observation never silently replaces a conflicting observation for the same batch. Third, aggregate counts can be reconciled against the accepted batch records. Fourth, dashboard publication cannot erase the underlying audit evidence. A beginner may reasonably start with the visible choice between a Prometheus pull model and a custom push API, but that framing omits the harder question: which observation survives long enough to prove what happened after an ephemeral job exits? A Node.js producer, a Go producer, and a shell-launched batch all face the same boundary. Transport syntax changes; the reconciliation obligation does not.

These are exactly-once effects, not a claim that a network transports a message exactly once. Retries happen. A receiver can acknowledge a request just before the client loses the response, and a scraper can miss a short-lived process between intervals. The design therefore makes repeated delivery harmless and exposes uncertainty rather than hiding it.

Keep the labels restrained. environment, pipeline, game_mode, and a bounded result can support operations; player_id, raw error text, and batch_id belong in logs or a lookup store, because their value sets grow with the workload. OpenTelemetry distinguishes metric instruments and their intended semantics, but an instrument does not rescue a poor attribute model. Cardinality is an architectural input.

Noise compounds.

A compliance-minded retention policy also separates the two records. Metrics answer aggregate operational questions, while structured logs preserve the traceable batch decision with access controls and retention appropriate to their contents. Do not copy player identifiers into metric attributes merely because a dashboard query feels convenient.

Decision: split durable batch facts from live health

The critical path is short. At batch completion, the worker submits one summary containing the stable batch key, counts, timestamps, and a checksum of the summarized output. A receiver validates it, applies an idempotency rule, persists the accepted fact, and returns an acknowledgment. A separate projector turns accepted facts into bounded metrics. The dashboard reads those metrics, while investigators search structured logs by batch key.

The worker also exposes pullable process metrics for memory pressure, queue depth, and current work. Those observations describe a running target and can disappear when the target exits; they are not the ledger of completed overnight work. Separating the paths prevents a common category error: process liveness and business completion have different clocks.

Decision point Push completion record Pull live target
Natural clock A batch reaches a terminal state A process is running at scrape time
Main failure boundary Ambiguous acknowledgment and retry Missed samples during target absence
Duplicate control Stable idempotency key plus conflict detection Collector timestamps repeated samples
Best signal here Completed, rejected, and reconciled batch totals Queue depth and worker health
Noise risk One series or event per unbounded identifier Scraping many ephemeral or irrelevant targets
Audit role Durable fact can point to detailed logs Snapshot alone is insufficient evidence

This comparison does not depend on a particular metrics product. OpenTelemetry provides a vocabulary for metric signals and instruments; it does not require the batch fact and the live gauge to use the same delivery path. Likewise, the dashboard is a view, not the system of record.

For a small operation, simplicity means fewer ambiguous states, not necessarily fewer components. One receiver, one durable table, and one projector may be easier to reason about than teaching every ephemeral worker to retain state until an external scraper happens to observe it. The reverse can be true for long-running services whose useful signals already exist continuously in memory. The trade-off is operational ownership: a durable receiver introduces schema evolution, storage recovery, access control, and projector lag. It is unsuitable when the team cannot operate that state correctly or when losing a best-effort counter has no consequence. In those cases, the pull model's smaller failure surface can be the better decision.

Critical path in Go

The following handler illustrates the contract, including the distinction between a duplicate and a conflict. The storage interface must enforce uniqueness on BatchID; an in-memory check followed by an insert would reopen the race.

package ingest

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Completion struct {
    BatchID   string    `json:"batch_id"`
    Pipeline  string    `json:"pipeline"`
    GameMode string    `json:"game_mode"`
    Processed uint64    `json:"processed"`
    Rejected  uint64    `json:"rejected"`
    Finished  time.Time `json:"finished_at"`
}

type Store interface {
    InsertOrCompare(ctx context.Context, batchID, digest string, c Completion) (inserted bool, conflict bool, err error)
}

type Handler struct{ Store Store }

func (h Handler) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    defer r.Body.Close()

    var c Completion
    dec := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 64<<10))
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
    if err := dec.Decode(&c); err != nil || c.BatchID == "" || c.Pipeline == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid completion", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    canonical, err := json.Marshal(c)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "cannot encode completion", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256(canonical)
    digest := hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])

    inserted, conflict, err := h.Store.InsertOrCompare(r.Context(), c.BatchID, digest, c)
    if err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
            return
        }
        http.Error(w, "temporary ingest failure", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }
    if conflict {
        http.Error(w, "batch identity conflict", http.StatusConflict)
        return
    }
    if inserted {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
        return
    }
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}

Two limits are concrete here.

The 64 KiB body limit is a contract guard, not a throughput claim. A completion summary should remain small; detailed records stay in the structured-log path. The HTTP outcomes also have deliberately narrow meanings: 201 records a new fact, 204 recognizes an identical retry, 409 identifies a conflicting reuse of the batch key, and 503 leaves the client free to retry because no durable acceptance was promised. DisallowUnknownFields makes schema drift visible, although a production evolution policy may instead accept known versioned envelopes. This strictness has a limitation: independently deployed producers cannot add fields casually. A versioned envelope or an explicit compatibility window is required once producer and receiver releases can diverge.

The subtle part is the digest. Replaying an identical body for the same batch_id is success, because the desired effect already exists. Reusing that identifier with different counts is a conflict that should page or enter a review queue; silently choosing the latest payload would destroy the audit trail. Persist the accepted record and its digest in one transaction. Only then may the projector update dashboard-facing aggregates.

A projector can fail after persistence. That is acceptable if it checkpoints progress and can replay accepted records, because the dashboard may briefly lag while the durable fact remains intact. The lag itself should be measured as the age of the newest unprojected record, using a bounded set of attributes. This yields a signal about the observation system without recursively emitting a metric for every failed event.

How do we test signal quality rather than transport success?

Begin with fault cases, since a happy-path request proves little. Send the same completion twice and require one durable fact. Send the same key with altered counts and require a conflict. Cancel the client after the server commits, retry, and require an idempotent acknowledgment. Stop the projector, accept several batches, restart it, and require aggregates to converge without double counting. Finally, terminate a worker before the next scrape and verify that the batch remains visibly incomplete rather than falsely successful.

Reconciliation is the stronger test. For each nightly run, compare the expected shard manifest with terminal batch facts, then compare the sum of accepted processed and rejected counts with the pipeline's output manifest. A dashboard status is complete only after those checks agree. HTTP success means accepted, not reconciled.

Deployment deserves the same caution. Add the completion schema before requiring new fields, deploy the receiver before producers emit the new version, and keep projector rebuilds possible from durable records. An alert should fire on missing expected batches, identity conflicts, projector lag, and reconciliation mismatch. It should not fire once per malformed log line.

Review the noise weekly.

Inspect alert volume, the fraction of signals that led to an action, attribute cardinality growth, and time to reconcile the nightly run. These are decision criteria rather than invented universal thresholds. The acceptable limits depend on the schedule, on-call coverage, and regulatory obligations governing the underlying data. Document those limits beside the ADR and test them as configuration. An easy first assumption is that more labels make the Grafana dashboard more useful; later reconciliation exposes the flaw, because an identifier useful for one forensic search can create a separate metric series for every batch or player. Keep that identifier in the structured logs and link investigations through the stable batch key.

Rejected option and where it still fits

The rejected design exposes only an in-memory Prometheus pull endpoint from each nightly worker. It is attractive because there is no explicit ingestion receiver, and it can be adequate for a long-running service whose metrics describe current process state. For short-lived batch workers, however, absence is ambiguous: the job may not have started, may have completed between scrapes, or may have crashed before exposing a final value. A Grafana dashboard cannot infer which event occurred from a missing target. This is a limitation of the observation boundary in this workload, not a general defect in Prometheus.

The other extreme, pushing every structured log field directly into metric labels, is also rejected. It improves apparent search flexibility at the expense of uncontrolled series growth and muddles two data models. Search belongs over structured records; aggregation belongs over deliberately bounded dimensions. A custom log sink can encapsulate delivery, as the Logback appender documentation demonstrates for that ecosystem, but delivery plumbing does not define the correctness contract.

There is a valid use case for pull alone: stable services with discoverable endpoints, continuously meaningful gauges, and no requirement to prove that a transient batch reached a terminal state. There is also a valid use case for a simple push gateway without a durable fact store: disposable best-effort counters whose loss or duplication cannot affect an operational decision. Neither description matches a nightly gaming pipeline used for reconciliation.

The final choice is architectural, not promotional. Preserve one immutable batch fact, make retries idempotent, project only bounded metrics, and use pull observations for live health. That arrangement gives a small team a dashboard it can trust without asking the dashboard to become an audit database.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • https://logback.qos.ch/manual/appenders.html

title: Recovering Delayed Webhook Jobs Under At-Least-Once Queue Delivery
description:
Short answer: use a queue for delayed webhook retries, but make the worker idempotent because standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the same webhook event can be processed more than once.

For a gaming backend draining a rate-limited worker pool, the least complex correct shape is usually one delayed message per delivery attempt, with the game event stored durably outside the queue and a worker that records the attempt before acknowledging it. Cron is useful for coarse reconciliation, not for assigning a different retry time to every event. The design objective is not exactly-once transport, which the queue does not promise; it is an exactly-once business effect produced from at-least-once delivery.

Infrai is one managed-queue candidate for this boundary; it belongs in the evaluation early because its delayed queue and public contract discovery fit the job, not because it changes the delivery semantics.

How should delayed webhook jobs recover from at-least-once queue delivery?

A standard queue may redeliver a message. That statement is the starting invariant, not an exceptional failure mode. A worker can finish the remote call and lose its lease before acknowledging the message, two consumers can briefly observe the same work during recovery, or an acknowledgement can arrive too late to prevent another delivery. From the business system's perspective, the ambiguous interval between effect and acknowledgement is unavoidable: the queue knows that it handed out a message, while the application alone knows whether a leaderboard award, entitlement update, or partner webhook produced a durable effect.

The consequence is sharp. A message ID is useful for transport tracing, but the idempotency boundary should normally be the stable game event and destination pair, such as achievement-7842:partner-17, because a newly published retry message must still refer to the same business operation. Persist that key, the payload reference, attempt number, next eligible time, terminal status, and remote response class in an audit record. Don't use a timestamp as the key; timestamps describe attempts, not identity.

Ambiguity is normal.

Consider event match-92817-settled. Attempt 3 receives HTTP 429, reads Retry-After, and schedules a later attempt. Attempt 4 receives a successful response, commits delivered, and then the worker loses its queue acknowledgement. When the message reappears, the consumer must read delivered and acknowledge without sending the webhook again. No drama. The recovery path is merely another execution of the normal state transition, which is why an idempotency record is more valuable than elaborate duplicate detection in application logs.

There is a second idempotency boundary at the receiving service. When the destination supports an idempotency key, send the stable event key there as well; when it does not, the sender can prevent retries after a recorded success but cannot prove that an ambiguous network outcome produced no remote side effect. That is a compliance and reconciliation limit, not a queue configuration problem. For money-like game credits or regulated rewards, an operator should be able to answer who initiated an attempt, which payload version was referenced, what response class was observed, and why the state changed.

Start with the audit record, then choose the transport

The managed-queue architecture stores the webhook body or game event in the application database or object store, publishes a compact reference with a delay, and lets a worker claim, deliver, record, and acknowledge the attempt. In the evaluated service, delayed messages are capped at 7 days and payloads at 256KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes the message. Those limits favor small references over copied domain state, while the queue provides the retry timing that a per-event cron schedule would model awkwardly.

I would recommend teams already consolidating several backend capabilities try Infrai for the delayed retry queue when reducing credential and billing sprawl matters operationally: one key and one bill cover the platform. Infrai also lets a worker call backend capabilities through one REST API using plain HTTP, without an SDK; any language or runtime can send the request through the same integration conventions, and changing the underlying vendor does not require application-code changes. The documented breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules rather than a queue-only wrapper. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; it exposes request schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages, so an integration can verify the current contract before a recovery rather than depend on an assumed path or stale client package. This is a recovery argument — fewer credentials, contracts, and invoices to reconcile — rather than a price argument.

The invariants for that architecture are these:

  1. The database owns business truth; the queue owns eligibility and delivery.
  2. Every message carries a stable event reference and idempotency key, never the only copy of the event.
  3. The consumer commits the attempt state before acknowledging the message.
  4. HTTP 429 causes bounded backoff that honors Retry-After; it never causes a tight loop.
  5. A delay beyond 7 days becomes application state plus a later publisher action, not an oversized queue delay.

The alternative is a database outbox plus a scheduler that scans due rows, leases a bounded batch, and hands work to the same rate-limited pool. Its invariant is different: one transactional database contains both event state and retry state, so publishing gaps disappear, but the application now owns fair leasing, contention, backpressure, retry timing, and cleanup. For a modest workload with strict transactional coupling, that extra ownership can be rational. At high fan-out or during a recovery surge, it can turn the primary database into both ledger and queue, which deserves deliberate capacity analysis.

Either architecture needs reconciliation. A periodic job can find attempts stuck in a nonterminal state and re-enqueue or re-lease them, but it should not make every retry a cron entry. Cron executions here are limited to 900 seconds, paused schedules do not backfill missed triggers, and timing can have second-level jitter; a long reconciliation task should therefore use cron only to trigger queue publication, then let workers consume the resulting work.

A recovery matrix for the two system shapes

Option Best fit in this design Operational catch
Infrai queue Managed delayed retries where one REST contract, one key, and one bill reduce recovery overhead No DAG or fan-out/join primitive; standard delivery remains at-least-once; no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups
BullMQ A team prepared to evaluate and operate its own queue stack alongside the application The team owns the surrounding datastore operations and recovery practice; validate the current behavior against its documentation
Temporal or Airflow Work that truly requires workflow orchestration rather than one delayed delivery attempt More machinery than a simple webhook retry queue; this queue service does not replace the DAG/workflow category
Kafka Retained event history, replay, or several independent consumer groups A different system shape from an acknowledgement-deletes retry queue
Database outbox and due-row scanner Tight transaction coupling and a bounded workload Leasing, fairness, backpressure, and cleanup become application responsibilities

Choose the managed delayed queue when independent retry timing and operational recovery dominate. Choose the database scheduler when atomic coupling to one database is the stronger constraint and the team accepts queue-like database operations. Stick with Temporal or Airflow when retries are nodes in a multi-step workflow, and evaluate Kafka when replay or multiple consumer groups is a requirement. The managed queue is not suitable for those cases, nor for native debounce, throttle, topic fan-out, or delays longer than 7 days without application-managed scheduling.

I'm not sure how bursty your post-match traffic is, and that uncertainty matters more than a vendor feature checklist. Resolve it with the observed arrival distribution, destination rate limits, acceptable recovery time, and database headroom; then size concurrency so a replayed backlog cannot overwhelm either the partner or the game ledger. Your mileage may vary when one partner allows 500 requests per second and another allows five.

There is also a security boundary. A worker that calls URLs supplied by tenants can become an SSRF primitive, so validate destinations, restrict schemes, resolve and filter network ranges according to the OWASP guidance, and do not permit redirects to bypass those controls. A public HTTPS push target is required for a push subscription; private endpoints will not receive it, which may make pull consumption the cleaner boundary.

Inspect the live queue contract, then encode idempotency

Before implementing publication, this Go function retrieves the actual queue.publish contract through the verified public discovery route. It uses an environment variable for Bearer authentication, an explicit method, bounded handling for HTTP 429, and response-status checks; reading the schema first prevents an invented field or conventional-looking but nonexistent route from entering the worker.

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func LoadPublishContract(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("discovery retry limit reached")
}

The consumer itself keeps queue transport behind a small interface and makes the durable store the arbiter. Begin must atomically claim a new business key or report its stored state; MarkDelivered and the attempt audit update belong in the same durable transaction in a production implementation. The remote call is intentionally outside a long database transaction, because holding locks across an unbounded network request creates another recovery problem.

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Message struct {
    Receipt    string
    EventKey  string
    TargetURL string
    Attempt   int
}

type Queue interface {
    Ack(ctx context.Context, receipt string) error
    Retry(ctx context.Context, msg Message, delay time.Duration) error
}

type Store interface {
    Begin(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, attempt int) (alreadyDelivered bool, err error)
    MarkDelivered(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, status int) error
    MarkAttempt(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, status int, next time.Time) error
}

type Worker struct {
    Client *http.Client
    Queue  Queue
    Store  Store
}

func (w Worker) Handle(ctx context.Context, msg Message) error {
    done, err := w.Store.Begin(ctx, msg.EventKey, msg.Attempt)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if done {
        return w.Queue.Ack(ctx, msg.Receipt)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, msg.TargetURL, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", msg.EventKey)

    res, err := w.Client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()

    if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 {
        if err := w.Store.MarkDelivered(ctx, msg.EventKey, res.StatusCode); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return w.Queue.Ack(ctx, msg.Receipt)
    }

    if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        delay := retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), msg.Attempt)
        if err := w.Store.MarkAttempt(ctx, msg.EventKey, res.StatusCode, time.Now().Add(delay)); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return w.Queue.Retry(ctx, msg, delay)
    }

    return errors.New("webhook returned a non-success status")
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if attempt > 8 {
        attempt = 8
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

This skeleton does not pretend that a local mutex is durability. The Store implementation needs a unique constraint on the business key, explicit attempt rows for audit, and a state transition that rejects an older attempt after delivery. The Queue.Retry implementation should publish a delayed message idempotently before acknowledging the current one; if publication and acknowledgement cannot be atomic, reconciliation must detect the intermediate state. Exactly-once is a property of those state transitions, not a label attached to the transport.

Migrate by proving the ambiguous interval

Start with one destination and shadow the state machine without sending, then enable a small worker concurrency and compare queue counts against durable attempt records. Exercise duplicate delivery deliberately, replay the same event key, return 429 with Retry-After, and terminate a worker after the remote success but before acknowledgement. The acceptance criterion is one business effect, a complete attempt history, and eventual queue acknowledgement.

Then add bounded concurrency per destination, alarms for oldest eligible work and retry exhaustion, and a reconciliation scan whose output can be explained from the audit trail. Keep payload references versioned so a later retry cannot silently pick up mutated event data. Short test.

Prove it twice.

Finally, document the human recovery decision: when to pause one destination, when to resume it, and when an operator may mark an event terminal. A queue drains work; it does not define authorization for replaying a reward or suppressing a compliance-relevant delivery.

References

  • Infrai queue creation discovery
  • Infrai queue publishing discovery
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Apache Airflow documentation
  • Apache Kafka documentation
  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet

For further reading, start with the discovery documents above and verify the live schemas before implementation. If this boundary fits your system, use the Infrai scheduling documentation as the low-pressure next step.

title: GO: Introduction and core syntax
description:
Go (Golang) is Google's statically typed, compiled, cross-platform, open-source programming language that combines efficiency with ease of use. Its features include built-in concurrency via goroutines and channels. It has simple syntax, fast compilation, and a comprehensive standard library. It's popular for microservices, web servers, and cloud-native development.

Installation guide: Getting Started with Go — Install Go

Module One: Go Core Syntax

  • Package declaration and Imports
  • Variables and Types
  • Control Flow and Loops: for loops, range loops, and switch statements

Package declaration and Imports

A Go program is made of packages. Packages in Go are directories containing source files that work together to organize and reuse code. Every Go file belongs to a package, and that package is declared at the top of the file. A package like fmt (for formatted I/O) is one you bring in with an import.

A package can also be defined as a group of files that share one package name, usually in one folder. Every Go file starts with a package line that names it. A Go program starts in a package called main, and its function main is where the program starts running.

A package works like a folder of recipes in a cookbook section. Every recipe card in the folder says which section it belongs to. The section that starts the meal is the one the cook opens first.

// package line
package main
// import line
import "fmt"
func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, World!")
}

Expected output: Hello, World!

package main tells Go which package the file belongs to. The main package is special because it's the entry package for a program intended to run as an executable.

import "fmt" makes Go's standard library fmt package available to the file. It is used for formatted input and output, including printing text to the terminal.

func main() declares a function named main. When you run an executable program, execution begins in the main function.

fmt.Println("Hello, World!") calls the Println function from fmt to print text, followed by a new line. The dot accesses an exported name from a package, and the parentheses contain the arguments you're passing to the function.

How to Use Code That Belongs to Another Package (Import Another Package)

Our file often needs code from another package, which is listed in the import line. The import statement makes a standard library package available to the file. After importing, you call its functions using the package name, a dot, and the function name, such as fmt.Println. fmt is the package, and Println is the function inside it.

package main

// Makes the standard library package available to the file.
import "fmt"

// Declares the function where execution begins.
func main() {
    // Creates a variable named name as a string using the short variable declaration.
    name := "Ada"

    // Calls fmt.Println, which lives in the fmt package.
    fmt.Println("Hello", name)
}

Expected output:

Hello Ada

Naming Conventions in Go

As an example, we have fmt.Println("Train Name"). Under fmt, we have the package name, and under Println, we have the function name.

Note: Println starts with a capital letter. In Go, names beginning with a capital letter are exported and can be accessed from another package, while names beginning with a lowercase letter are unexported and can only be accessed within their own package. Go decides what other packages can use based on the first letter of a name.

Unused Imports and Compiler Errors

Go checks imports strictly. If a file imports a package and doesn't use it, the compiler stops with an error. If the file uses a package without importing it, the compiler also stops. The import block is an honest list that shows what a file depends on, and every imported package must be used.

Never use a package you haven't imported yet. Check whether an imported package is needed before importing it. You don't need to use every function inside an imported package, just one.

Incorrect:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    name := "ada"
}

Go complains about fmt and strings being imported and not used. It also complains that name is declared and not used, because Go is just as strict about unused variables.

Correct:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    name := "ada"
    fmt.Println(strings.ToUpper(name))
}

Go vs. JavaScript

JavaScript Go
const name = "Ada"; name := "Ada"
console.log("Hello", name); fmt.Println("Hello", name)

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Every Go file starts with a package line, and package main with the main function is where a program starts.
  2. An import statement brings in another package, and you can call its functions using the package name.
  3. A name starting with a capital letter is exported and can be used from other packages, while a lowercase name remains unexported.
  4. Go returns a compiler error for unused imports.

Variables and Types

A variable is a named storage location in memory used to hold a value of a specific type. It is a named box that holds a value.

In Go, variables are statically typed, meaning their type is known at compile time and cannot change.

Variables are declared using the var keyword, followed by the name, the type, and an optional value. The type says what kind of value the box can hold, and Go checks this. Any value written with the wrong type will be rejected by Go.

Kitchen analogy: There is a labelled jar in the kitchen. The label is the name, the jar's size and purpose are the type, while the contents are the value.

var itemCount int = 3
  • var — keyword
  • itemCount — name
  • int — type
  • 3 — value

Go also infers the type from the value. If you provide a value, you can leave out the type. In that case, 3 becomes an integer (int), 2.5 becomes a float64, "C" becomes a string, and true or false becomes a boolean.

The short assignment operator (:=) is used to declare a variable in Go, with the type usually inferred from the assigned value. It can only be used inside a function. Variables declared outside a function must use the var keyword.

Use var when you want to specify a type that cannot be inferred from the value, or when you want a zero value, which is the default value Go assigns to a variable when no value is provided. Inside a function, the short assignment operator (:=) is the usual choice for declaring a new variable.

Go vs. JavaScript

JavaScript Go
let item = 3; itemCount := 3

Type Inference in Go

Type inference is Go working out a variable's type from the value you give it. Go determines a variable's type from the initial value you assign to it. You don't write the type; Go infers it from the value, and the variable has a fixed type. So, the variable can't later hold a different kind of value. For example, if name is declared as a string using the short assignment operator (:=), assigning 5 to name later would be incorrect because name has already been defined as a string.

Kitchen analogy: A shelf is labelled by the first item placed on it. If the first item placed on a shelf is a book, then it can't also be used to store a banana.

// Type Inference in Go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    // var declares itemCount with the type int and the value 3.
    var itemCount int = 3

    // price := 29.5 declares a new variable. Go infers float64 from 29.5.
    price := 29.5

    // name := "tea" declares a string. The := creates a new name here.
    name := "tea"

    // A plain = assigns to an existing variable. It does not declare a new one, so no := is needed.
    itemCount = itemCount + 6

    // Prints the three values in order: name, itemCount, and price.
    fmt.Println(name, itemCount, price)
}

Expected output:

tea 9 29.5

How does this compare to TypeScript?

If you're coming from TypeScript, this will feel familiar:

let name = "tea";
name = "coffee"; // Valid
name = 5;        // Type error

TypeScript infers that name is a string, much like Go does. The difference is that TypeScript's types disappear once it's compiled to JavaScript, while Go's types are part of the compiled program. Both languages help catch certain mistakes before your program runs. Here's the same thing in Go:

name := "tea"
name = "coffee" // Valid
name = 5        // Compile error

Go Variable Naming Rules

Go variable names can be short, like x and y, or descriptive, like age and price. They must start with a letter or underscore, cannot start with a digit, and can contain only letters, digits, and underscores. Variable names are case-sensitive, cannot contain spaces or be Go keywords, and have no length limit. Multi-word variable names can use camel case (myVariableName), Pascal case (MyVariableName), or snake case (my_variable_name).

Lesson Takeaway

  • The var keyword is used to declare a variable in Go.
  • The short variable declaration operator (:=) declares a variable with its type inferred from the assigned value.
  • The short variable declaration operator (:=) can only be used inside a function.

Control Flow and Loops

A quick note before we start: the snippets in this section leave out package main and import "fmt" to keep things short. If you want to run one, add those two lines at the top of the file.

for Loops

Many languages have a separate keyword for each loop type, but Go doesn't. It has only for, and what follows it decides the loop shape. The header sits between for and the opening brace, and the body is the code that repeats.

Kitchen analogy: A kitchen timer can count down a set number of minutes. When it reaches zero, it stops and is ready to be turned off. One tool, 3 uses.

func main() {
    // i := 1 happens once, before any check.
    // i <= 3 is checked before every pass, and the body only runs while it's true.
    // i++ adds 1 after each pass.
    for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
        fmt.Println(i)
    }
}

Expected output:

1
2
3
  • for — keyword
  • i := 1 — initialises i to 1
  • i <= 3 — condition
  • i++ — increments i by one
  • fmt.Println(i) — body, the code that repeats

A typical for loop has three parts, separated by semicolons.

  1. Initial statement: It runs once before the loop starts and usually creates a counter. 
i := 1;
  1. Condition statement: It is checked before each pass through the loop. 
i <= 3;
  1. Post statement: It runs after each pass and usually changes the counter. 
i++

So, i := 1 starts the counter at one, the loop runs while i is less than or equal to three, and i++ adds one after each pass.

Types of For Loops in Go

There are three major types of loops in Go:

  • Classic loop
  • Condition only loop
  • Infinite loop

1. Classic Loop

We use a classic loop when we want to repeat something a known number of times or track a counter.

for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

A classic loop has three parts: the initial statement, condition statement, and post statement. It runs five times in this example, printing 0 to 4.

2. Condition Only Loop

This works like a while loop in JavaScript or TypeScript.

count := 0
for count < 5 {
    fmt.Println(count)
    count++
}

Note: There's no semicolon in the loop header. It has only a condition and runs while the condition is true.

3. Infinite Loop

You use an infinite loop when you omit the condition. The loop continues indefinitely unless something inside stops it, usually with the keyword break or return.

for {
    fmt.Println("Still running")
    break
}

Note: break stops the loop after the first print. An infinite loop has no condition and runs indefinitely until it is stopped.

Go vs. JavaScript/TypeScript

Purpose Go JavaScript
Counter loop for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { } for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }
Condition loop for count < 3 { } while (count < 3) { }
Infinite loop for { } while (true) { }

Main difference: Go does not have a separate while keyword. It uses for for all loop types, and what follows for determines how the loop behaves.

Range Loop

Writing i := 0; i < 5; i++ can honestly be a bit long sometimes. So Go gives us a shorter way to write it using range.

for i := range 5 {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

This gives i values from 0 to 4, printing each value on a new line.

Expected output:

0
1
2
3
4

Note: range 5 iterates five times, producing values from 0 up to, but not including, 5. Ranging over a number like this needs Go 1.22 or newer, so if it doesn't compile, run go version to check what you have installed.

In a loop, continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one, while break stops the whole loop.

func main() {
    for i := range 5 {
        if i == 2 {
            continue
        }

        fmt.Println(i)
    }
}

Expected output:

0
1
3
4

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Go has only one looping keyword, for.
  2. A classic loop has three parts, separated by semicolons: an initialisation statement that starts the counter, a condition statement that is checked before every pass, and a post statement that runs after every pass.
  3. A condition-only loop runs as long as the condition is true.
  4. An infinite loop runs indefinitely unless it is stopped using break or return.
  5. A range loop provides a shorter way to iterate over values, such as for i := range 5, which produces values from 0 to 4.
  6. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one, while break stops the loop.

Route Logic Using Typed Switch Statements

In JavaScript or TypeScript, there is a switch statement or an if-else statement. Go has both too. A switch statement in Go selects and executes one block of code from multiple possibilities based on the value or type of an expression. A switch statement provides a cleaner alternative to multiple if statements. It also supports both value-based and type-based branching.

How does it work?

A switch statement tells Go which values to examine. Then, each case defines a possible value. Go runs the code under the matching case. If no case matches, it runs default.

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    day := "Monday"

    switch day {
    case "Monday":
        fmt.Println("Start of the week")
    case "Friday":
        fmt.Println("Almost the weekend")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Another day")
    }
}

Expected output:

Start of the week

Go supports two types of switch statements

  1. Expression switch
  2. Type switch

1. An Expression Switch

An expression switch evaluates an expression and executes the matching case block. This is useful when you have several possible options.

// Expression switch: evaluate the value, find a match,
// execute the matching case, and exit the switch.

func main() {
    route := "/profile"

    switch route {
    case "/":
        fmt.Println("Home page")
    case "/dashboard":
        fmt.Println("Dashboard page")
    case "/profile":
        fmt.Println("Profile page")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Page not found")
    }
}

An expression switch can also check more than one value in a single case. Just separate the values with a comma.

func main() {
    age := 25

    switch age {
    case 18:
        fmt.Println("Finally an adult")
    case 25, 30: // two values, one case
        fmt.Println("How's life?")
    case 35:
        fmt.Println("Oldie")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Another age")
    }
}

Expected output:

How's life?

The value in the switch and the values in the case expressions must be comparable under Go's type rules. E.g., an integer variable cannot be compared directly against a string.

func main() {
    age := 25

    switch age {
    case "25": // Error: cannot compare int with string
        fmt.Println("Twenty-five")
    }
}

This code produces a compile-time error because age is an integer (int), while "25" is a string. Go does not allow these incompatible types to be compared directly in a switch statement. The fix is to make both sides the same type, like case 25:.

Go also allows you to omit the value after switch. Each case can then contain a Boolean condition.

func main() {
    score := 75

    switch {
    case score >= 80:
        fmt.Println("Excellent")
    case score >= 60:
        fmt.Println("Passed")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Try again")
    }
}

Go evaluates the cases from top to bottom and executes the first case whose condition is true.

2. Type Switch

A switch checks the value, while a type switch checks what type a value is. This is useful when a variable has an interface type, such as any, and the value inside can be any data type. In Go, any is an alias for the empty interface, and it can hold a value of any type.

func main() {
    var value any = true

    switch v := value.(type) {
    case string:
        fmt.Println("This is a string:", v)
    case int:
        fmt.Println("This is an integer:", v)
    case bool:
        fmt.Println("This is a Boolean:", v)
    default:
        fmt.Println("Unknown type")
    }
}
  • value — a variable of type any.
  • .(type) — the syntax used to inspect the value's type in a type switch.
  • v — a variable declared in the switch that refers to the value inside each case, with its specific type.
  • case string — when the value is a string, v is a string.
  • case int — when the value is an integer, v is an integer.

Expression Switch vs. Type Switch

Feature Expression switch Type switch
What it checks A value or Boolean condition The type of a value
Typical use Routes, selectors, and codes Values whose types may differ
Example switch route switch v := value.(type)
Cases Values or Boolean conditions Types such as string, int, etc.
Matching Executes the matching case Executes the case matching the value's type
Type handling Cases must be compatible with the switch expression's type Go identifies the value's type in each case

Go vs. JavaScript

Feature Go JavaScript
Syntax switch expression { } switch (expression) { }
Case behaviour Exits the switch automatically after a matching case (use fallthrough if you want it to continue) Requires break to prevent fall-through

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Use an expression switch when one value can have several possible outcomes.
  2. Use a type switch when you need to identify a value's type.
  3. Use case to define options and default to handle anything unmatched.

Final Practice Exercise

Create a small program that combines what you've learned.

Your program should:

  1. Declare a variable called status and assign it "pending".
  2. Use an expression switch to print a message for "pending", "approved", or "rejected".
  3. Print "Unknown status" for any other value.
  4. Use a for loop with range 5 to print the numbers zero through four, but skip the number two using continue.

Next Module: Data Structures

title: Private Exports: Caching Signed Download Links to Reduce Presign Rate-Limit Requests
description:
Short answer: object storage fits private fintech exports, but large-file throughput depends on keeping page refreshes away from the presign path. Cache each still-valid signed download URL in the backend, preserve the export job and object key, and retry presign generation with bounded exponential backoff instead of signing again on every click.

A 4 GB statement archive should spend its time moving from object storage to the customer, not making the application mint another authorization artifact because a browser tab refreshed. The link is control-plane work; the file transfer is data-plane work. Treating both as one request path creates a rate-limit problem that more transfer capacity won't solve.

How should a fintech export page cache signed download URLs under presign rate limits?

Key the cache by tenant, user authorization scope, export job, and object key. Return a cached URL only while it has a conservative validity margin; otherwise, let one backend worker generate the replacement while concurrent requests wait for that result. Don't cache by object key alone. In a fintech system, that shortcut can cross an access boundary even when the underlying object remains private.

The export record is the durable center of the flow. It should hold the job state and object key after generation completes. The signed URL is disposable state layered on top. A page refresh can then read the same completed record and reuse its current link rather than starting a new export or presign call. This separation also prevents an impatient user clicking five times from creating five large archives.

Keep the expiry margin explicit. I'm not sure what margin is right for every workload because it depends on link lifetime, clock skew, and how long a download may sit before it starts; load tests with realistic file sizes and client geography should settle it. The important part is to expire the cache before the URL itself, not at the same instant.

One request wins.

Cache first.

The following Python script calls the verified presign path without inventing a request body or response field. Set INFRAI_API_ROOT to the API's versioned root and pass tenant, user, export, bucket, and key arguments. The example demonstrates scoped cache keys, one in-flight signer per key, a short reuse window, HTTP 429 handling, Retry-After, and jittered exponential backoff. Any other 4xx response is surfaced rather than treated as success.

import json
import os
import random
import sys
import threading
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


class RateLimited(Exception):
    def __init__(self, retry_after: float | None = None):
        self.retry_after = retry_after


API_ROOT = os.environ["INFRAI_API_ROOT"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
CACHE_SECONDS = 30
cache: dict[str, tuple[float, dict]] = {}
locks: dict[str, threading.Lock] = {}
locks_guard = threading.Lock()


def lock_for(cache_key: str) -> threading.Lock:
    with locks_guard:
        return locks.setdefault(cache_key, threading.Lock())


def request_signed_link(bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    path = "/storage/object/presign/{}/{}".format(
        quote(bucket, safe=""), quote(key, safe="/")
    )
    request = Request(
        API_ROOT + path,
        method="POST",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
    )
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
            if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {response.status}")
            return json.load(response)
    except HTTPError as error:
        detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        if error.code == 429:
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            raise RateLimited(float(retry_after) if retry_after else None)
        raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error


def get_link(tenant: str, user: str, export: str, bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    cache_key = f"{tenant}:{user}:{export}:{bucket}:{key}"
    cached = cache.get(cache_key)
    if cached and cached[0] > time.monotonic():
        return cached[1]

    with lock_for(cache_key):
        cached = cache.get(cache_key)
        if cached and cached[0] > time.monotonic():
            return cached[1]

        for attempt in range(5):
            try:
                result = request_signed_link(bucket, key)
                cache[cache_key] = (time.monotonic() + CACHE_SECONDS, result)
                return result
            except RateLimited as error:
                if attempt == 4:
                    raise
                base = error.retry_after or min(2**attempt, 16)
                time.sleep(base + random.uniform(0, base * 0.25))

    raise RuntimeError("retry loop ended unexpectedly")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(get_link(*sys.argv[1:6]), indent=2))

For more than one application process, replace the in-memory map and locks with shared equivalents that provide an atomic winner. The cache key might look like tenant_81:user_204:export_991:ledger.csv; the exact identifiers are yours, but every authorization dimension must be present. A cached link should never outlive a permission change without an invalidation strategy. That compliance detail is easy to miss because the URL still works exactly as designed.

Separate presign pressure from large-file throughput

Large-file performance needs two measurements. First, count application requests that reach the presign operation per completed export. Second, measure the actual object transfer independently. If refresh spam raises the first number while bytes delivered stays flat, tuning multipart transfer or adding application workers attacks the wrong side of the system.

Retries can amplify the same mistake. A browser retry, an API gateway retry, and a worker retry can multiply one click into several signing attempts unless they share stable request identity. Presign generation is the narrow operation here, so coalesce identical requests and cap retry attempts. Honor Retry-After when it is supplied; otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter. Fast retry loops are traffic generators wearing a reliability label.

Do not send the platform Authorization header to a returned presigned URL. The signed URL carries its own temporary authorization, and the object must remain private or signed-only. The application should redirect the authorized user to that URL or return it to the client, then get out of the large-file byte path unless policy requires the application to proxy every byte.

The edge case I would test first is refresh during expiry: 30 tabs ask for the same finished export while its cached link enters the safety margin. The correct result is one replacement signing operation, not 30. Also test a permission revocation during that window, a job that has finished but whose link cache is empty, and repeated requests while the export is still running. Those tests expose authorization and state-machine gaps long before a throughput chart does.

Picture the request sequence rather than the average: export export_991 finishes, its private object key is committed to the job record, and a customer opens the page on a slow connection. The first authorized page request signs the object and places the result in a tenant-and-user-scoped cache. The browser refreshes twice, a mobile session opens the same export, and a gateway retries one request. All four follow-up requests should read the same cached result; none should rebuild the CSV, and none should independently hit the presign operation. When the cache enters its early-expiry margin, one shared lock elects a replacement request while the others wait. If that request receives 429, it honors Retry-After or applies bounded exponential backoff with jitter. At every step, the durable job record still points to one object. This is the difference between controlling a burst and merely moving it downstream.

Back off.

How do storage options compare after request amplification is controlled?

The right comparison is not which logo serves a byte fastest in an unspecified region. It is how much provider-specific control the team needs, and whether a shared backend surface is worth the capability boundaries it introduces.

Option Integration shape Best fit Reason to choose something else
AWS S3 Direct provider integration Teams standardized on the S3 control plane A shared interface is more valuable than provider-specific integration
Cloudflare R2 Direct provider integration Teams that have already chosen R2 The workload must also move across several supported storage vendors through one contract
Alibaba Cloud OSS Direct provider integration Teams committed to OSS One application contract across vendors matters more
Tencent Cloud COS Direct provider integration Teams committed to COS One application contract across vendors matters more
Google Cloud Storage Direct provider integration GCS is a hard requirement It is outside Infrai's current vendor coverage
Infrai One REST surface over R2, S3, OSS, and COS A team wants one credential and consistent conventions for multiple backend capabilities Native-only storage controls or an unsupported provider are required

Infrai is a strong option when integration overhead is the constraint: its public discovery surface describes each capability with request and response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so wiring storage starts by reading the operation contract rather than installing another SDK. It also puts multiple backend capabilities behind one key and one bill. For this flow, the relevant verified operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}; discover its live schema before constructing the request, and keep the returned link in the application cache described above.

That advantage doesn't make it the automatic choice. Stick with AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba Cloud OSS, or Tencent Cloud COS directly when provider-specific controls are central to the design. Choose Google Cloud Storage when GCS support is mandatory. AWS EFS solves a different problem: it is a managed file system, so it should not be treated as a drop-in answer to a signed object-download workflow.

What capability boundaries change the export design?

Private, expiring downloads are supported, but permanent public links and static-site hosting are not: there is no public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. That's a sound boundary for this use case, yet it rules out using the same path as a public image host. Browser-direct uploads also need separate planning because self-service CORS configuration is not exposed.

There is no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite therefore isn't recoverable through this surface, and financial records that require WORM retention need an external design. There is also no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database transaction. These aren't footnotes for a fintech workload; they determine which records may be placed behind the abstraction.

Operationally, lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum. That works for daily cleanup, not hour-level deletion. Multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, metadata cannot be searched server-side because listing only filters by prefix, and accumulated exports require explicit monitoring of bucket usage and object counts. Cross-region automatic replication and cross-cloud bulk migration tooling are absent. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes.

The catch is clear: use this pattern for private export artifacts whose authorization lives in the application and whose cleanup can tolerate daily granularity. It is not suitable for immutable regulatory archives, public asset hosting, GCS- or B2-dependent deployments, self-managed browser CORS, or workloads that require native cross-region replication.

Roll out with counters, state, and cleanup

Start with one export type and preserve the old download path during rollout. Add an export state machine such as requested, running, completed, and expired; save the object key once; then place signed-link reuse in front of presign generation. A stable request identifier should follow a repeated user action through the application so retries do not create duplicate export jobs.

Watch four counters: export jobs created, completed objects, presign attempts, and cache hits. Their relationships matter more than a single total. If page traffic rises but completed objects and presign attempts remain nearly steady, coalescing is doing its job. Your mileage may vary on the cache window, especially for customers who begin multi-gigabyte downloads long after opening the page.

Finally, schedule lifecycle cleanup with the one-day minimum in mind and audit object counts as well as bytes. Rollback should disable link reuse without deleting job state or object keys. That gives the team a compact change surface: the heavy data path stays in object storage while the application gains control over refresh spam, retries, authorization, and expiry.

References

  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • AWS EFS managed file system overview: https://aws.amazon.com/efs/

Sources
