title: Delayed Webhook Queue Publish Explained 7 Nightly Cron Trigger Batch Worker (Latency/Cost)
description:
For a fintech shipment update fanout, the least complex reliable choice is a nightly cron trigger that batches pending webhooks into a durable queue, then lets workers publish with idempotency and backoff. Keep the trigger boring. Put the cleverness in observability and recovery.

Short answer: use a queue when delayed webhook delivery can tolerate seconds or minutes of waiting; use a direct publish path only when the subscriber contract demands sub-second latency and you can absorb its cost.

The dispatch decision in one table

Pattern Pick this when Main cost Failure to watch
Direct publish from the transaction One or two subscribers, strict latency, short request budgets Coupled availability and request time A slow endpoint delays the database request
Transactional outbox plus queue Events must not disappear when a commit succeeds A relay and queue to operate Duplicate delivery after a retry
Nightly cron batch into a queue Pending work is acceptable overnight and spend is the primary constraint Delivery is intentionally delayed A growing backlog hides until morning
Workflow scheduler Delays, branches, and human review are part of the process More state and operational surface State-machine complexity exceeds the job

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. A hosted task service, BullMQ backed by Redis, and Temporal-style workflows all solve different slices of the same problem. Their APIs and durability guarantees differ, so compare the contract you need rather than the logo on the dashboard.

How should a cron trigger queue pending webhooks for a nightly batch?

Start with a durable record. When the shipment status changes, write an outbox row in the same database transaction as the status update. A separate publisher claims rows that are ready, creates a queue message, and marks the row as enqueued. This is the transactional outbox pattern: the business write and the intent to publish commit together, while delivery happens later.

The cron trigger is only a nudge. It should select a bounded batch, such as 500 rows, and enqueue work with a stable message key. It must be safe to run twice. A lock or lease prevents two schedulers from claiming the same rows, but the worker still needs idempotency because queues commonly provide at-least-once delivery.

Here is a small Node.js example. It uses generic interfaces so the same shape can sit over a cloud task queue, Redis-backed queue, or an internal broker.

type PendingWebhook = {
  id: string;
  shipmentId: string;
  endpoint: string;
  payload: unknown;
  attempts: number;
};

interface PendingStore {
  claimReady(limit: number, leaseSeconds: number): Promise<PendingWebhook[]>;
  markEnqueued(id: string, messageId: string): Promise<void>;
  markDelivered(id: string): Promise<void>;
  reschedule(id: string, nextAttempt: Date): Promise<void>;
}

interface Queue {
  enqueue(messageId: string, body: PendingWebhook): Promise<void>;
}

export async function nightlyEnqueue(store: PendingStore, queue: Queue) {
  const batch = await store.claimReady(500, 300);
  for (const item of batch) {
    const messageId = `shipment-webhook:${item.id}`;
    await queue.enqueue(messageId, item);
    await store.markEnqueued(item.id, messageId);
  }
}

One small detail matters: the message ID comes from the outbox ID, not from the current time. That gives you a deduplication key you can inspect in logs. If enqueue succeeds and the process dies before markEnqueued, the next cron run may publish the same item again. That is expected. Make the receiver—or your delivery ledger—treat item.id as an idempotency key.

What does the worker publish, retry, and measure?

The worker owns the network call. It sets a bounded timeout, sends an idempotency key, and records the response class. A 2xx response marks delivery. A timeout or 5xx response gets exponential backoff with jitter. A 4xx response usually needs quarantine and an operator decision; retrying a permanently invalid signature forever just burns queue capacity.

export async function deliver(
  item: PendingWebhook,
  store: PendingStore,
  fetcher: typeof fetch,
) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 8_000);
  try {
    const response = await fetcher(item.endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "content-type": "application/json",
        "idempotency-key": item.id,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(item.payload),
      signal: controller.signal,
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      await store.markDelivered(item.id);
      return;
    }

    if (response.status >= 400 && response.status < 500) {
      await store.reschedule(item.id, new Date("2099-01-01T00:00:00Z"));
      return;
    }

    const delaySeconds = Math.min(3_600, 2 ** item.attempts * 30);
    await store.reschedule(item.id, new Date(Date.now() + delaySeconds * 1000));
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

The 2099 date is a readable quarantine sentinel for this example; production code should use an explicit dead-letter state. Do not hide that distinction in a generic retry helper.

Measure the path as a timeline: outbox_created, queue_enqueued, worker_started, request_finished, and delivered. The useful metrics are age of the oldest pending row, batch size, enqueue lag, delivery latency, retry count, and dead-letter count. Alert on age and error rate, not on a single slow request. Logs should carry shipment ID, webhook ID, message ID, attempt, and a trace ID. That lets an on-call engineer answer “where did this update stop?” without replaying the entire night.

Which queue shape fits latency versus cost?

If customers watch a shipment screen in real time, a nightly batch is the wrong shape. Use the outbox relay continuously and let workers drain small messages; the extra queue operations buy lower latency. If the webhook is a reconciliation hint consumed by a back-office job, a 15-minute or nightly batch can be rational. Your mileage may vary when subscribers are spread across time zones or have contractual delivery windows.

A queue service usually charges for requests and retained work; Redis-backed queues shift cost toward always-on capacity and operations; workflow engines charge for state transitions and add visibility for multi-step processes. I’m not sure which line item dominates for your traffic until you chart messages per shipment, retry probability, and retention hours. Cost belongs beside latency in the design review, never in place of a delivery guarantee.

The catch is operational ownership. A cron plus queue is not suitable when each webhook needs human approval, calendar-aware waits, or a long saga; stick with a workflow engine then. Conversely, a workflow engine is excessive for one POST and one retry policy. Keep the state model proportional to the failure modes you can actually explain.

Limits and a practical rollout

Begin in shadow mode: enqueue copies, measure lag, and compare the worker's result with the existing publisher. Then enable one subscriber group, cap concurrency, and document the replay command. Test duplicate messages, a full queue, a rotated signing key, and a database lease that expires halfway through a batch. These are ordinary paths, not exotic chaos tests.

Measure twice.

For a useful rehearsal, freeze the subscriber endpoint for ten minutes while a batch is in flight. The queue should retain the messages, the worker should record timeouts without losing payloads, and the age-of-oldest metric should climb. Restore the endpoint, watch retries drain, and verify that the delivery ledger contains one terminal result per webhook ID even if the same message was attempted several times. Run that exercise with 50 records first, then with the largest batch your database lease can hold; the point is to validate the handoff and the alert, not to manufacture a benchmark.

There is no exactly-once network delivery. There is only an idempotent receiver, a durable intent, and enough evidence to replay safely. If the business cannot accept delayed updates at all, move the decision earlier: publish from the committed outbox continuously and design the subscriber contract around bounded latency.

References

Further reading:

  • https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://docs.temporal.io/

title: A Guide to Realtime APIs — Node.js Connection Recovery for Sports Feeds
description:
Short answer: use a realtime API for live delivery, but make the durable score store and a cursor-based backfill endpoint the authority after every reconnect. A serverless function should publish events and issue access, not hold an open connection for the lifetime of a match.

That boundary matters in a B2B sports operations product. The score feed is durable business state. Typing indicators are disposable presence signals. Read receipts sit between them: useful across a reconnect, but rarely important enough to block a score correction. Treating all three as the same kind of event makes recovery harder than it needs to be.

For a small team, Infrai is worth trying for the publish side of this workflow when plain HTTP is the desired integration boundary. It exposes a REST API, so a Node.js function can call it without installing or maintaining a vendor client library. Infrai also uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. In this sports product, adding a related backend capability can reuse the existing credential and billing boundary instead of creating another secret-distribution path or another invoice-reconciliation job. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and requires no key, which lets a build check read the current request and response schemas before a deployment instead of relying on a stale hand-copied payload.

How should a Node.js sports score feed handle realtime serverless connection limits?

Start by separating connection ownership from event production. Browsers or another long-lived client connect to the realtime provider. A serverless function validates an upstream change, commits the new scoreboard state, and makes a short outbound publish request. It can finish immediately; it doesn't pretend to be a socket host.

The durable record needs a stable match ID, an event ID, and an ordered recovery cursor generated by your own application. Those are design requirements for the score system, not claims about a provider's payload schema. A returning client sends its last cursor to your backfill endpoint, applies every missing durable event, and only then resumes live updates. If a live event arrives during backfill, hold it briefly and reconcile by ID. Duplicates become boring.

Use a different policy for collaboration signals. A typing indicator can expire and disappear; replaying “Alex is typing” ten seconds later is actively misleading. A read receipt should carry a stable application identifier so the client can collapse repeats, but the UI can update it after the critical score state is current. Authentication, subscription state, and business events should be visible as separate stages in logs and traces. Otherwise a denied subscription can look exactly like an idle match.

This is the key split: realtime transport reduces freshness delay, while backfill restores truth.

Put the publish boundary in one small function

The minimal Infrai integration below calls the verified POST /v1/realtime/publish route. The exact request schema is intentionally not guessed: put a payload validated against the public discovery schema in INFRAI_PUBLISH_PAYLOAD. That keeps this example runnable while leaving channel and event fields to the current schema rather than freezing an invented shape into application code.

The idempotency key should be derived from the stable application event ID and reused for every retry. The sample also gives a 429 response breathing room, honors Retry-After, and surfaces any other non-success body. It uses Node's built-in fetch, so there is no realtime SDK version to babysit.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const eventId = process.env.SCORE_EVENT_ID;
const rawPayload = process.env.INFRAI_PUBLISH_PAYLOAD;

if (!apiKey || !eventId || !rawPayload) {
  throw new Error(
    "Set INFRAI_API_KEY, SCORE_EVENT_ID, and INFRAI_PUBLISH_PAYLOAD",
  );
}

const payload: unknown = JSON.parse(rawPayload);
const sleep = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const value = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (!value) return 500 * 2 ** attempt;

  const seconds = Number(value);
  if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);

  const date = Date.parse(value);
  return Number.isNaN(date) ? 500 * 2 ** attempt : Math.max(0, date - Date.now());
}

async function publishScoreEvent(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": eventId,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      await sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt));
      continue;
    }

    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Publish failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }

    return body ? JSON.parse(body) : null;
  }

  throw new Error("Publish retry budget exhausted");
}

publishScoreEvent()
  .then((result) => process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`))
  .catch((error: unknown) => {
    process.stderr.write(`${error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)}\n`);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  });

Keep database commit and publication as two observable steps. If an execution ends after the commit but before publication, an outbox worker can retry the same event ID; the fixed idempotency key prevents a retry from double-applying at the publish boundary. The client still deduplicates because delivery and processing are separate concerns. This sounds fussy until a score correction, a reconnect, and a repeated event occur within the same few seconds. Then it is the whole system.

Don't publish before the authoritative write. A subscriber could display a score that the recovery API cannot return yet, leaving a reconnect to move the UI backward. The safer sequence is validate, commit, enqueue or record the outbox item, publish, and mark that item complete. Exact transaction machinery depends on the database and queue already in the stack; I'm not sure there is one right choice without knowing those constraints.

Compare the boundary, not the demo

Most realtime demos look convincing on one laptop. The useful comparison is less glamorous: who owns the socket, where history lives, how authorization is refreshed, and what a client does with duplicate delivery. Provider choice follows from that boundary.

Option Sensible fit Boundary to verify before committing
Infrai A serverless publisher that benefits from a plain HTTP surface and no required client SDK Validate the current publish request schema through discovery; keep durable history and recovery cursors in the application
Ably A team evaluating a specialist managed realtime product Confirm connection, history, ordering, and token-renewal semantics against the product's current documentation
Pusher Channels A product already designed around the Channels ecosystem Confirm reconnect behavior, authorization flow, and retained-history expectations for the selected plan
Supabase Realtime A team whose data and access model already live in Supabase Confirm how database changes, presence, and application-managed backfill divide responsibility
Cloudflare Durable Objects A team willing to own more coordination logic on Cloudflare Confirm object lifecycle, placement, persistence, and client recovery behavior for match rooms

This table is a shortlist, not a synthetic benchmark. No latency or uptime numbers are implied. Run the same match script against each serious candidate: connect late, drop the network, refresh authorization, deliver one event twice, and reconnect while a correction is being written. Record which component answers each step. A lower median delivery time can't rescue a design that has no defined recovery source.

Stick with Ably or Pusher when a specialist realtime product's documented connection model is the center of the architecture and your team accepts its client integration. Supabase is the more coherent candidate when the source data and authorization model are already there. Durable Objects deserve evaluation when per-match coordination logic is valuable enough to operate explicitly. Infrai is not suitable as a substitute for the application's durable event history; its fit here is the HTTP publication handoff.

Make reconnect and partial failure ordinary

A clean reconnect flow has a small state machine: disconnected, authenticating, subscribed, backfilling, and live. Expose those states rather than compressing them into a green or red connection dot. The UI can then say “catching up” while it applies missing scores, suppress stale typing signals, and queue read-receipt updates behind the score recovery. A subscription expiry is an authentication event. It should not erase the last confirmed scoreboard.

Test at realistic latency, including a delayed backfill response racing a fresh live event. Also test a duplicate with the same stable ID, a gap in cursor order, an expired credential, and an authorization denial for the wrong customer or match. 401, 403, and 429 are different facts and should land in different counters. Don't turn them into one “realtime failed” alert.

Partial failure is normal. A publish request can be rate-limited while the score commit remains valid; the outbox retains the handoff and retries it. A browser can lose its connection while other subscribers remain live; only that browser backfills. A read receipt can lag while the score is correct; the product stays useful. These distinctions keep a transient transport condition from becoming a fabricated business incident.

The read path deserves the longer test because it carries recovery. Seed a match with a known ordered event set, connect a client after event 20, interrupt it after event 27, and write events 28 through 35 while that client is offline. Reconnect with 27 as the last applied cursor, but deliberately delay the backfill response while event 35 also arrives over the restored live connection. Deliver event 31 twice. Expire the old credential during the same run, issue a valid replacement through the normal application flow, and verify that the subscription resumes without resetting confirmed state. Now make an operator type a correction note before the disconnect and stop before reconnecting; the old typing indicator must not reappear. Send the note's read receipt twice and confirm that its stable application ID collapses the duplicate without delaying the scoreboard. At the end, compare the client's materialized score with the authoritative snapshot, not with the order in which callbacks happened to fire. Each stable event ID should apply once, the cursor should reach 35 without a gap, and current presence should be the only presence shown. This is not a provider benchmark, and it proves no universal latency claim. It is a contract test for the boundary your product owns, with enough overlapping events to expose an accidental assumption that reconnect and backfill happen in a tidy sequence.

An operational checklist that stays useful

Before launch, write down the owner of every transition in the connection state machine. Confirm that logs distinguish token issuance, subscription establishment, publication, backfill, and client reconciliation. Attach the stable match ID, event ID, and request ID where each system exposes one, but never put secrets in log fields.

Then rehearse expiry and reconnect under load representative of an actual match. Check that the retry budget is bounded, Retry-After is honored, and an idempotency key survives a new serverless invocation. Verify that a cold client can rebuild state without receiving any live event at all. Finally, make the dashboard show backfill gaps and authorization failures separately from ordinary disconnects.

Ship the boring path first.

References

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • Ably documentation: https://ably.com/docs
  • Pusher Channels documentation: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • Supabase Realtime documentation: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime
  • Cloudflare Durable Objects documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/

Further reading

The W3C WebRTC Recommendation is useful when the product needs peer media or data channels rather than a server-published business event stream: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/. If the HTTP publication boundary described here fits your system, start with the current discovery and authentication guidance at https://docs.infrai.cc.

title: Node.js Failure Alerting Explained (Polling Logs and Errors for Failed Cron Jobs)
description:
A failure alert is useful only if its evidence survives long enough to answer two questions: what broke, and which agent run paid for it? Short answer: for a fintech AI agent loop, start with a scheduled poller that normalizes exception groups and failed-job or HTTP 5xx log evidence into one incident record. Keep latency and cost on that record as diagnostic dimensions, not the sole paging threshold. This shape trades immediate push delivery for replayable collection windows and straightforward incident reconstruction.

The invariant is simple: every source window must be processed at least once, while every notification must be emitted at most once for the same rule, window, and evidence set. Polling without the second half creates duplicate Slack messages during retries. Polling without the first creates gaps that nobody notices until reconciliation.

Infrai is a deliberate fit for the collection side when a team wants a plain REST API rather than another client library to install and upgrade. Its errors surface can supply exception-oriented evidence, while logs can carry failed background-job and 5xx evidence. Notification rules and routing remain the poller's responsibility. I recommend trying Infrai for the evidence-collection boundary of a small or mixed-language agent platform, because one HTTP contract keeps the collector portable. The API is self-describing: its public discovery surface needs no key and exposes schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages. A single key spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one bill. More important for this fintech agent loop, per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata is specified consistently on native and OpenAI-compatible AI responses. That metadata lets the incident ledger preserve the dimensions needed to reconstruct an expensive or slow run without timing calls in a second wrapper. Together, these properties mean the evidence collector and a later notification adapter can share an authentication convention without turning the poller into an SDK-upgrade or credential-reconciliation project.

Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across those backend capabilities. Here that consolidation is practical rather than decorative: adding an email or SMS route later does not require the on-call team to rotate another vendor credential or reconcile another provider invoice while reconstructing the agent incident.

How Should Node.js Failure Alerting Poll Logs and Errors?

The incidents that shape this design are missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. A page saying failures > 5 is not a reconstruction. For an agent loop that may call a model several times, I need a stable run ID, the collection window, exception identity, job outcome, HTTP status class, observed latency, and recorded cost metadata in the same incident trail. Without those fields, the on-call engineer can see pain but cannot bound impact or replay the decision.

One trap is treating absence as success. Error groups and log search can reveal exceptions and recorded failure patterns; they cannot prove that a scheduled settlement-review job ran at all. A heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks.io must cover that negative space.

Silence is a separate signal.

Another boundary matters during a distributed failure: log trace_id and span_id values can support manual correlation, but they do not produce a distributed trace query or span tree. If the investigation depends on causal traversal across services, use a tracing system. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, and session replay also belong elsewhere.

Two viable system shapes

The first shape is scheduled evidence polling. A cron-triggered worker reads overlapping time windows, normalizes evidence, evaluates thresholds, persists its cursor and deduplication key, then calls Slack, email, or another webhook. Its invariants are a durable cursor, overlap between windows, deterministic incident keys, idempotent notification delivery, and a separate heartbeat. The overlap prevents a record arriving near a boundary from falling through; the incident key prevents that overlap from paging twice.

The second shape is streaming ingestion into a specialist alert engine. Applications and collectors send telemetry continuously; the alert engine owns evaluation, grouping, muting, and notification routing. Its invariants are durable ingestion, bounded evaluation delay, rule-version history, and deduplication across retries. This is the better default when seconds matter, routing policy is complex, or a staffed team already operates the alert platform.

Both work. For a modest agent fleet where incident reconstruction is the primary decision axis, I choose polling first: a five-minute evidence window is easy to replay, audit, and compare against the agent run ledger. I would choose streaming for fraud controls or payment authorization paths where waiting for the next schedule is itself unacceptable.

The polling worker should use error groups or events for exception alerts and log search for failed jobs and 5xx patterns. Exact log-search filters are not declared in the discovery parameters, so the adapter must validate its query shape against the live discovery contract and representative staging data before production use. Do not bury guessed filter fields in the evaluator. Keep that uncertainty at the adapter boundary.

Fair comparison by operating boundary

Option Natural operating shape Strong fit here Boundary to keep visible
Infrai REST evidence source plus a team-owned scheduled evaluator Portable collection across mixed services, with public discovery for contract inspection No native alert rules, push channels, heartbeat monitoring, or span-tree queries
Sentry Specialist error monitoring Exception grouping and workflows when application errors dominate A separate heartbeat is still needed for work that never starts
Datadog Managed observability and alerting platform Central rules and routing when logs, metrics, and traces already live there Broader platform ownership and instrumentation are part of the decision
Grafana Cloud Hosted observability around telemetry backends Alert evaluation close to existing metrics and logs Rule and data-source operations replace the small poller's simplicity
Healthchecks.io Dead-man's-switch monitoring for scheduled work Detecting job never ran or job never finished It complements exception and log evidence rather than replacing them

This is not a feature-score exercise. Sentry is a stronger choice when exception triage is the center of gravity. Datadog or Grafana Cloud is more appropriate when native alert evaluation, routing, and distributed telemetry are already organizational standards. Healthchecks.io fills the blind spot every error-query design has: nothing was emitted because nothing ran. Infrai fits when the desired system shape is a thin, language-neutral evidence boundary and the team is comfortable owning the rule engine.

A small evaluator that will not double-page

The preventative path below intentionally starts after vendor-specific retrieval. Adapters translate their responses into Observation; the evaluator owns the policy. That split keeps undeclared search filters out of business logic and makes recorded incident fixtures replayable in tests.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    ID, AgentRun, Kind string
    LatencyMS          int64
    CostUSD            float64
}

type Incident struct {
    Key       string
    WindowEnd time.Time
    Count     int
    RunIDs    []string
    CostUSD   float64
    MaxMS     int64
}

func fetchEvidence(client *http.Client, key, url string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: status %d: %s", url, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: rate limit persisted after retries", url)
}

func evaluate(end time.Time, threshold int, observations []Observation) (Incident, bool) {
    unique := make(map[string]Observation)
    for _, o := range observations {
        if o.ID != "" && (o.Kind == "exception" || o.Kind == "failed_job" || o.Kind == "http_5xx") {
            unique[o.ID] = o
        }
    }
    if len(unique) < threshold {
        return Incident{}, false
    }

    ids := make([]string, 0, len(unique))
    runs := make(map[string]struct{})
    incident := Incident{WindowEnd: end.UTC(), Count: len(unique)}
    for id, o := range unique {
        ids = append(ids, id)
        runs[o.AgentRun] = struct{}{}
        incident.CostUSD += o.CostUSD
        if o.LatencyMS > incident.MaxMS {
            incident.MaxMS = o.LatencyMS
        }
    }
    sort.Strings(ids)
    for run := range runs {
        incident.RunIDs = append(incident.RunIDs, run)
    }
    sort.Strings(incident.RunIDs)
    material := end.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339) + "|" + strings.Join(ids, ",")
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(material))
    incident.Key = hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
    return incident, true
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    groups, err := fetchEvidence(client, key, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/groups")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    search, err := fetchEvidence(client, key, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("retrieved error_groups_bytes=%d log_search_bytes=%d\n", len(groups), len(search))

    end := time.Date(2026, 10, 8, 10, 5, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    observations := []Observation{
        {ID: "evt-17", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "http_5xx", LatencyMS: 1840, CostUSD: 0.031},
        {ID: "evt-18", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "exception", LatencyMS: 1920, CostUSD: 0.014},
        {ID: "evt-18", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "exception", LatencyMS: 1920, CostUSD: 0.014},
    }
    incident, fire := evaluate(end, 2, observations)
    fmt.Printf("fire=%t key=%s count=%d runs=%v cost=%.3f max_ms=%d\n",
        fire, incident.Key, incident.Count, incident.RunIDs, incident.CostUSD, incident.MaxMS)
}

The two GET calls deliberately send no query fields: the search filters are undeclared, and inventing them would make a copyable example dishonest. They retrieve raw evidence with Bearer authentication, an explicit method, a 15-second client timeout, status checks, and bounded 429 retry behavior that honors Retry-After. A production adapter should decode only the response shape verified from live discovery, then pass normalized records to evaluate.

The concrete observation numbers are fixture data, not a benchmark. The repeated evt-18 models an overlapping poll window. It contributes once. In production, store Incident.Key under a uniqueness constraint before sending the notification, and advance the cursor only after the evidence and notification decision are durable. A process-local map is not enough. This is the place where I am deliberately conservative: an extra row in the incident ledger is recoverable, while a second page to the same responder trains people to distrust the channel.

Notification delivery needs its own retry policy: exponential backoff for rate limits, respect Retry-After when supplied, and reuse the same incident key for every attempt. Route severity separately from evidence collection. A Slack page might fire immediately while an email digest waits, but both should point to the same immutable incident record.

When polling is the wrong answer

This recommendation has a hard limitation. Infrai does not supply native alert rules or notification routing, and polling has a detection-delay trade-off. Do not choose this architecture for sub-minute safety actions, complicated escalation trees, or investigations that require full distributed traces. Datadog or Grafana Cloud is the better choice when managed evaluation and routing are requirements; Sentry is the better choice when specialist exception triage dominates. The same is true if audit history for rule changes is mandatory: keep rules in a system that records those changes rather than relying on an informal cron configuration.

There is also a privacy boundary. If the workflow requires per-user log deletion, bulk export, subscriptions, configurable retention, or cold-storage controls, verify those capabilities in the selected log system before sending regulated fintech data. The collection API should never become an accidental data-governance decision.

My runbook decision is conditional: poll when reconstruction quality matters more than immediate push, persist enough state to replay every window, and pair the poller with a heartbeat. Stream when response time, rich routing, or trace-native investigation dominates. If the REST evidence boundary fits that first shape, start with the failure-alerting guide and verify the live discovery schema before wiring the adapter.

Sources

References used for product boundaries and implementation choices:

  • Infrai documentation
  • Sentry Alerts documentation
  • Datadog Monitors documentation
  • Grafana Cloud Alerting documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • OpenTelemetry tracing specification

title: Node.js Webhook Batches: Delivery Guarantees for Nightly Queue Reconciliation
description:
Short answer: for an edtech digest, make delivery state the source of truth, use cron as a public HTTP wake-up, and let idempotent workers publish pending webhooks from a queue. That gives you a recoverable handoff when a schedule is missed. The choice is about guarantees, not about which scheduler has the fanciest screen.

Boundary Invariant to defend Best fit What you own
Reconcile rows, then enqueue a batch An unsent delivery remains discoverable until a worker records success Weekly digests with changing recipient sets State transitions and idempotency
Managed task per delivery The task service owns each due time and retry decision Independent schedules and per-target throttles Provider task state and its limits

I would start with the first boundary for a one-person SaaS. A Friday cron tick can be late or absent, but Saturday's scan still finds rows marked pending. That is a stronger delivery guarantee than hoping a timer remembers what it missed.

For the scan-to-queue handoff, Infrai is worth putting on the shortlist early: its plain REST API lets a Node.js route publish without an SDK. Infrai uses one key and one bill for the backend calls around the digest, with 295 routes across 20 modules behind the same interface. That combination keeps credential rotation and invoice checking in one place while the delivery ledger stays provider-neutral.

The guarantee lives in the delivery ledger

Create one durable record per customer webhook, keyed by a stable digest and customer ID. Store pending, enqueued, delivered, and failed as business states, not as guesses derived from queue metrics. The scheduled endpoint selects a bounded page where scheduled_for <= now, claims it, and publishes messages. A worker sends the callback, writes the result, and only then acknowledges the queue message.

Picture the failure on a real Friday: the scheduler reaches the endpoint, the process publishes half a page, and the network drops before the response is written. On Saturday, the reconciliation query cannot trust the old HTTP response, so it looks at durable delivery state, republishes stable IDs with an idempotency key, and lets the worker decide whether the callback already succeeded. The queue may contain two copies; the customer still receives one digest because the worker's business write is the gate. That is more code than a timer, but it is code you can inspect when a school asks where its digest went.

This ordering matters. Standard queues are at-least-once, so a worker can see the same message twice. The send operation must be idempotent on the delivery ID; FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes, far shorter than a weekly recovery window. A retry after a timeout must not create a second digest at a school.

There is a second invariant: the business transaction that creates a digest and its delivery row must commit together. A transactional outbox is a useful pattern for that boundary. It keeps a healthy queue from masking an application write that never happened.

Tiny state machines beat clever cron expressions.

That is the contract.

How should a Node.js cron trigger queue publish for delayed webhook batches?

Cron does not host application code. It calls a public http_url, so deploy a small Node.js route that performs the scan and exits. A single run is capped at 900 seconds; it should never loop over customer HTTP calls. Keep each message below 256 KB, keep delays at or below seven days, and remember that acknowledged messages are deleted rather than retained for Kafka-style replay.

The route below shows the handoff. The array stands in for a database query so the example is runnable; production code should claim rows transactionally and leave them recoverable until the worker records delivery.

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

type Delivery = { id: string; customerId: string; digestWeek: string };
const pending: Delivery[] = [
  { id: "digest-1042", customerId: "school-18", digestWeek: "2026-W34" },
  { id: "digest-1043", customerId: "school-27", digestWeek: "2026-W34" },
];

const pause = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function publishBatch(tasks: Delivery[]): Promise<unknown> {
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
  const idempotencyKey = `digest-${tasks[0].digestWeek}`;
  const messages = tasks.map((task) => ({ id: task.id, body: JSON.stringify(task) }));

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ queue: "weekly-digest-webhooks", messages }),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    const detail = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429) throw new Error(`publish failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    await pause(Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt);
  }
  throw new Error("publish remained rate-limited after five attempts");
}

createServer(async (request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "POST" || request.url !== "/jobs/reconcile-digests") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }
  try {
    if (pending.length) await publishBatch(pending);
    response.writeHead(202, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ enqueued: pending.length }));
  } catch (error) {
    const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error";
    response.writeHead(502, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ error: message }));
  }
}).listen(port);

The scheduler should call the public HTTPS deployment of POST /jobs/reconcile-digests. The handler batches the handoff and returns; workers own slow destinations. A 429 honors Retry-After, while other status codes expose their response body. If cron was paused, the next scan reconciles every still-pending row instead of replaying a calendar event that never existed.

Two architectures, one uncomfortable question

The reconciliation queue is a ledger-driven architecture. Its recovery rule is simple: any row not durably marked delivered is eligible for a future scan. This is a good match for a weekly digest where recipients change and missed work must be found.

It also makes the support story legible.

The managed-task architecture creates one scheduled task per webhook. Google Cloud Tasks is a credible choice when each destination needs its own retry and schedule controls. BullMQ is practical when Redis is already part of the Node.js stack and keeping queue code in-process is more valuable than a hosted boundary. Neither removes the need to make the callback idempotent; they move more timing state out of your database.

Temporal or Airflow belong when the digest is one step in a workflow with branches, joins, or long-lived orchestration. This scheduling capability has no DAG engine, no fan-out/join primitive, and no native debounce or throttle. Simulating those semantics with more queues would increase the very operating surface a solo founder is trying to shrink.

The uncomfortable question is: who can prove a missed run was recovered? With the ledger shape, the answer is a query over pending rows. With per-task scheduling, the answer depends on the provider's task inventory and retention. Pick the answer you can inspect during a support ticket.

Where a plain REST boundary earns its keep

Infrai is a deliberate option for the scan-to-queue leg when a Node.js service should make a plain HTTP request without installing an SDK. One Authorization: Bearer key reaches the queue call, and the same credential can cover other backend capabilities instead of creating another account and invoice for each integration. That reduces credential rotation and billing reconciliation work, which is a real operating cost for a one-person team.

The platform also exposes 295 routes across 20 modules behind that consistent interface, with public discovery and runnable examples in ten languages. For this workflow, that means the request schema for publish_batch can be inspected before shipping the handler, while the rest of the application can keep its own provider-neutral delivery ledger. I recommend trying it for the bounded enqueue boundary, not for the worker's business logic.

The catch is capability fit. Push targets must be public HTTPS endpoints; delays cannot exceed seven days; standard queues require consumer idempotency; and there is no multi-consumer topic fan-out. If a school district requires a private callback, a replayable event log, or a delay beyond a week, use a specialist service or your existing broker instead. The right recommendation has a stop sign.

A weekly shipping test

Run one failure drill before calling this reliable: pause the cron schedule, leave several deliveries pending, resume it the next day, and verify that one scan enqueues each stable ID exactly once at the business boundary. Then force a worker retry and confirm the second attempt records the same delivery rather than sending a duplicate.

I'm not sure there is a universal page size for every tenant mix. Lock duration, webhook rate limits, and the database decide that number. Start small, measure queue age, and change the bound without changing the invariant.

Ship weekly. Outsource the undifferentiated handoff only after the ledger tells you what “done” means.

If this boundary matches your system, the cron-to-queue guide is a useful implementation reference.

References

  • Google Cloud Tasks overview
  • Transactional Outbox pattern
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: How to Auto-Update an updated_at Column: MySQL ON UPDATE vs a Database Trigger vs the ORM
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: A DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP fills updated_at only once, at insert. On MySQL, add ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP to the column; on PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite, write a trigger; or let the ORM set it, which works on every database but misses every write that does not go through the ORM. Pick the database side when scripts, admins or other services write to the table, and the ORM side when only one application does.

Whether updated_at should be set by the database or by the ORM comes down to one question: does anything besides your application write to the table? The database side means MySQL's ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP column clause or a trigger everywhere else; the application side means Rails timestamps, Django's auto_now, Eloquent or Prisma's @updatedAt. A column default alone never moves after the row is created.

The short version: if anything other than your application writes rows (a migration backfill, a support engineer in psql, a second service, a bulk update_all), keep it in the database. If one application owns every write, the ORM is simpler and portable. The rest of this post is what each option does on the edge cases that decide it, and the schema changes that break each one later without an error. Every database behaviour below was run on MySQL 8.4.11, PostgreSQL 18.3, SQL Server 2022 and SQLite 3.54.0 in throwaway containers; the ORM behaviour is quoted from each framework's documentation or source.

Why DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is not enough

Most schemas start the same way. On MySQL:

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
    updated_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6)
);

Both columns get the insert time. After that, updated_at is an ordinary column, and an UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' leaves it exactly where it was. A default is a value for a missing column at insert, on every database. Keeping a "last changed" time current is a separate job, and each database gives you a different tool for it.

How to auto update updated_at column: the three options

MySQL ON UPDATE PostgreSQL trigger ORM (auto_now, @updatedAt, Rails timestamps)
Available on MySQL TIMESTAMP and DATETIME only Any database with triggers (SQL Server and SQLite below) Any database
An UPDATE that changes nothing Column unchanged Column moves Rails sends no UPDATE; Django's save() moves it
An UPDATE that sets updated_at itself Your value is kept Your value is overwritten Rails and Prisma keep it, Django's auto_now overwrites it
Raw SQL and scripts Covered Covered Not covered
Bulk updates Covered Covered Eloquent sets it; Django QuerySet.update() and Rails update_all do not
Renaming the column The clause follows the column Next UPDATE fails Change the model
Where it shows up In the column definition In a trigger, outside the table In application code

The rows that decide it are the bulk and raw writes, and the rename, so each option gets its own section.

MySQL: ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP

MySQL is the only one of the four with a column clause for this:

updated_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6)

It fires only when a row's values actually change. UPDATE orders SET status = 'new' on a row whose status is already new reports 0 rows changed and leaves updated_at alone, which matches the MySQL manual: an auto-updated column "remains unchanged if all other columns are set to their current values". An UPDATE that sets updated_at explicitly keeps the value it was given, which is how a data fix can backdate a row on purpose. The clause works on DATETIME as well as TIMESTAMP, and with fractional seconds the precision has to match on both sides: CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) for a TIMESTAMP(6) column.

The trap is in later migrations. ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY updated_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) replaces the whole column definition, and since it does not repeat the clause, the clause is gone. MySQL accepts the statement without a warning. Before it, information_schema.columns.EXTRA read DEFAULT_GENERATED on update CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6); after it, DEFAULT_GENERATED. The column keeps its old values and stops moving, and nothing notices until someone asks why a row edited yesterday says it was last changed in March. RENAME COLUMN, by contrast, keeps the clause.

PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite: a trigger

PostgreSQL has no column clause, so the column is kept current by a BEFORE UPDATE trigger:

CREATE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.updated_at := now();
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON orders
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

PostgreSQL also ships the same thing as an extension, moddatetime, in contrib: CREATE EXTENSION moddatetime; then CREATE TRIGGER ... BEFORE UPDATE ON orders FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION moddatetime(updated_at);. It saves writing the function and accepts only timestamp or timestamptz columns.

Three behaviours differ from MySQL, and all three were reproduced on 18.3:

  • It fires on every UPDATE, changed or not. UPDATE orders SET status = status moves updated_at. Adding WHEN (OLD.* IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.*) to the CREATE TRIGGER gives MySQL's no-op behaviour back; an explicit value is still overwritten.
  • It overwrites an explicit value. UPDATE orders SET updated_at = '2020-01-01' stores the current time instead, with the plpgsql function and with moddatetime. A backfill that needs to set historic times has to disable the trigger first.
  • now() is the start of the transaction, not the moment of the update. Every row a long transaction touches gets the same time. Use clock_timestamp() in the function if you need the wall clock.

SQL Server and SQLite use an AFTER UPDATE trigger that runs a second UPDATE on the same row. That second update does not fire the trigger again because recursive triggers are off by default on both (is_recursive_triggers_on = 0, PRAGMA recursive_triggers returns 0). On SQL Server:

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at ON orders AFTER UPDATE AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    IF UPDATE(updated_at) RETURN;
    UPDATE o SET updated_at = SYSUTCDATETIME()
    FROM orders o JOIN inserted i ON i.id = o.id;
END;

And on SQLite:

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at AFTER UPDATE ON orders
WHEN NEW.updated_at IS OLD.updated_at
BEGIN
    UPDATE orders SET updated_at = strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%f', 'now') WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

Both keep an explicit value, and both still move the column on a no-op UPDATE. The SQL Server guard has a catch: UPDATE(updated_at) is true whenever the column is in the SET list, even with its old value, so an ORM that writes every column on save makes this trigger return every time and the column never moves. Drop the guard if your ORM does that.

The weakness of a trigger is that it names the column in a place the column does not know about. Rename updated_at to modified_at and PostgreSQL accepts the rename, then fails the next UPDATE on the table with record "new" has no field "updated_at" from the plpgsql function, or "orders" has no attribute "updated_at" from moddatetime. Dropping the column does the same. The migration succeeds; the first write after the deploy is what fails. SQL Server fails the same way after sp_rename, which at least prints a caution. SQLite is the exception: it rewrites the trigger body on RENAME COLUMN, though a dropped column still breaks the next UPDATE with no such column: NEW.updated_at. A generated column is no way out here, since it cannot call now().

The ORM: auto_now, @updatedAt and Rails timestamps

Rails, Django, Laravel's Eloquent and Prisma all set updated_at themselves, in application code, so the same model works on every database and the behaviour is visible in the codebase. The cost is every write that does not go through that code path, and the frameworks document where that is:

  • Django: auto_now is "only automatically updated when calling Model.save()", not by QuerySet.update().
  • Rails: update_all "does not trigger Active Record callbacks or validations", so it does not touch updated_at either.
  • Prisma: @updatedAt is "implemented at Prisma ORM level", so a raw SQL UPDATE leaves it alone.
  • Eloquent is the exception for bulk writes: its query builder's update() adds updated_at to the values, so Order::where(...)->update([...]) sets it. A DB::table('orders')->update() does not.

Add a manual fix run in a SQL console, a nightly script, or a second service written in another language, and updated_at is right for some writes and stale for others. That is acceptable when the column is for display. It is not when an incremental export, a cache, or a sync job reads WHERE updated_at > :last_run, because a stale row is a row that sync never sends.

Which should you use: MySQL ON UPDATE, a trigger or the ORM?

  • One application owns every write, and updated_at is informational: let the ORM do it. It is portable and it lives next to the model.
  • Anything reads updated_at to decide what changed (sync, export, cache invalidation): put it in the database, because the database sees every write. On MySQL that is the column clause; elsewhere a trigger, with the WHEN clause if no-op updates should not count. Database-side fixes coverage, not ordering: now() is when a transaction started, so a long transaction that commits after a sync run can stamp rows earlier than that run's :last_run. Query with an overlap, such as updated_at > :last_run - interval '5 minutes', and make the sync idempotent.
  • Both at once is harmless when the column is for display: MySQL and the SQLite trigger keep the value the ORM wrote, and a PostgreSQL trigger replaces it with its own now(). For sync, pick one clock, the database's, since the application servers' clocks and time zones are not the database's.

Whichever you choose, the column's behaviour now depends on something the CREATE TABLE may not show, which is what makes it easy to lose in a later migration.

How Schemity keeps updated_at in the schema

To design the next one without losing this, the schema, not the application, has to carry the decision. Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git.

On MySQL, the clause is part of the column in the diagram. Import SQL and the live reader both read ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, and the field dialog has an "On update, set to the current time" tick on TIMESTAMP and DATETIME columns. Because the diagram holds it, every MODIFY in the migration SQL Schemity writes restates it, so changing the column's type or default does not quietly drop it the way a hand-written MODIFY does. Converting a MySQL diagram to another database leaves the clause out and says so in the conversion notes (ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) "is left out: PostgreSQL has no column that sets itself on update"), rather than writing a column that looks the same and stops moving.

With the default removed and the tick left on, the planned migration still carries the clause:

On PostgreSQL, the mechanism lives outside the table, and the diagram is honest about that. Import SQL keeps CREATE EXTENSION moddatetime and writes it back as CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS moddatetime; setup SQL that runs before the tables, but the trigger and its function are not part of a table in the diagram: they are counted among the skipped statements, and updated_at reads as a timestamptz column with its now() default.

When you rename or drop updated_at in a diagram connected to the database, impact analysis reads the table's triggers from the catalogue and names each one, with the warning that it fails the next time it runs if it uses what changed. That is the error above, shown before the migration rather than after the deploy.

When you design the next table, the template every new entity starts from is the place to settle the columns once: created_at and updated_at with their types and defaults, so the question of how updated_at stays current is asked for every table rather than remembered for some.

Related reading

Why a trigger and not a generated column is the right tool for now() is in generated column vs trigger. For the type of the column itself, timestamp or timestamptz, see timestamp vs timestamptz. SQLite drops a table's triggers during a table rebuild, which is how an updated_at trigger disappears in changing a SQLite column type. And the MySQL round-trip benchmark is where Schemity's own loss of ON UPDATE was found and fixed.

title: Toán Tử (Operators) Trong Java
description:
Toán tử là những ký hiệu được sử dụng để thực hiện các phép toán và so sánh trong lập trình. Java cung cấp nhiều loại toán tử khác nhau, bao gồm: 

I. Toán tử số học (Arithmetic Operators)
II. Toán tử bit (Bitwise Operators)
III. Toán tử so sánh (Comparison Operators)
IV. Toán tử logic (Logical Operators)
V. Toán tử điều kiện (Conditional Operators)
VI. Toán tử gán (Assignment Operators)
Ảnh mô tả các loại toán tử trong java.<!--more-->

Ⅰ. Toán tử số học

Sử dụng cho các phép toán cộng, trừ, nhân, chia, modulo (lấy dư).

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

+

Phép cộng

a + b

-

Phép trừ

a - b

*

Phép nhân

a * b

/

Phép chia

a / b

%

Phép chia lấy dư

a % b

++

Tăng thêm 1

a + 1

--

Giảm đi 1

a - 1

Ⅱ. Toán tử bit

Các toán tử bit thực hiện các phép toán trên các bit của số nguyên.

Toán tử

Mô tả

~

Phủ định NOT: Trả về giá trị phủ định của một bít. Chuyển đổi các bit 1 thành 0 và ngược lại.

&

Toán tử AND: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 chỉ khi cả hai bit đều là 1, 0 trong các trường hợp khác.

|

Toán tử OR: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 nếu một trong hai bit là 1, 0 trong trường hợp cả hai bit đều là 0.

^

Toán tử Exclusive OR: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 chỉ khi hai bit khác nhau, 0 trong trường hợp hai bit giống nhau.

>>

Dịch phải: Dịch các bit của số nguyên sang phải một số vị trí nhất định. Các bit trống được lấp bằng bit dấu (0 cho số dương và 1 cho số âm).

<<

Dịch trái: Dịch các bit của số nguyên sang trái một số vị trí nhất định. Các bit trống được lấp bằng bit 0.

Ⅲ. Toán tử so sánh

Các toán tử so sánh dùng để so sánh các giá trị và trả về kết quả dạng boolean.

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

==

Bằng nhau

a == b

!=

Khác nhau

a != b

>

Lớn hơn

a > b

<

Nhỏ hơn

a < b

>=

Lớn hơn hoặc bằng

a >= b

<=

Nhỏ hơn hoặc bằng

a <= b

Ⅳ. Toán tử logic

Các toán tử logic làm việc với các toán hạng Boolean. Các toán tử quan hệ được sử dụng trong các cấu trúc điều khiển.

Toán tử

Mô tả

&&

Toán tử (AND) đọc là “Và”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu cả hai toán hạng đều là True.

False: nếu ít nhất một toán hạng là False.

||

Toán tử (OR) đọc là “Hoặc”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu ít nhất một toán hạng là True.

False: chỉ khi cả hai toán hạng đều là False.

^

Toán tử XOR đọc là “Hoặc ngoại trừ”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu chỉ một trong hai toán hạng là True.

False: nếu cả hai toán hạng đều là True hoặc cả hai đều là False.

!

Toán tử (NOT) đọc là “Không”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu toán hạng là False.

False: nếu toán hạng là True.

Ⅴ. Toán tử điều kiện

Toán tử điều kiện, còn được gọi là toán tử ba ngôi, là một loại toán tử đặc biệt trong Java được sử dụng để xác định điều kiện và trả về giá trị tương ứng dựa trên điều kiện đó. Nó là một cú pháp ngắn gọn để thay thế cho các câu lệnh if-else truyền thống. Bạn sử dụng cú pháp sau:

Cú Pháp 
<điều_kiện> ? <giátrị_khiđúng> : <giá_trị_khi_sai>

Giải thích các thành phần:

↳ <điều_kiện>: Biểu thức logic trả về giá trị true hoặc false.

↳ <giátrị_khiđúng>: Giá trị được trả về nếu <điều_kiện> là true.

↳ <giá_trị_khi_sai>: Giá trị được trả về nếu <điều_kiện> là false.

↳ Nếu điều kiện đúng: Trả về giá trị sau dấu ?.

↳ Nếu điều kiện sai: Trả về giá trị sau dấu :.

Main.java 
public class Main {

   public static void main(String[] args) {

      int age = 20;

      String message = (age >= 18) ? "Bạn đã đủ tuổi" : "Bạn chưa đủ tuổi";

            System.out.println(message); // In ra "Bạn đã đủ tuổi"

    }

}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Bạn đã đủ tuổi

Ⅵ. Toán tử gán

Toán tử gán mở rộng trong Java là những toán tử kết hợp phép toán và phép gán trong cùng một biểu thức. Giúp cho việc viết code ngắn gọn và dễ đọc hơn.

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

=

Gán giá trị của toán hạng phải cho toán hạng trái.

c = 10

+=

Cộng và gán Thực hiện phép toán cộng giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c += a tương đương với c = c + a

-=

Trừ và gán Thực hiện phép toán trừ giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c -= a tương đương với c = c - a

*=

Nhân và gán Thực hiện phép toán nhân giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c *= a tương đương với c = c * a

/=

Chia và gán Thực hiện phép toán chia giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c /= a tương đương với c = c / a

%=

Lấy số dư và gán Thực hiện phép toán chia lấy phần dư giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c %= a tương đương với c = c % a

&=

AND và gán Thực hiện phép toán bitwise AND giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c &= a tương đương với c = c & a

^=

XOR và gán Thực hiện phép toán bitwise XOR giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c ^= a tương đương với c = c ^ a

<<=

Dịch trái và gán Dịch trái c với số bit bằng giá trị của a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c <<= a tương đương với c = c << a

>>=

Dịch phải và gán Dịch phải c với số bit bằng giá trị của a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c >>= a tương đương với c = c >> a

title: Railway Says Some Customer Secrets May Have Been Decrypted. What Should Teams Do?
description:
A platform can encrypt a secret at rest and still face a serious incident if an attacker reaches a path that exposes its decrypted value. Railway's October 21 security notice says an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted customer environment variables and obtained the decrypted contents of some of them.[1]

Railway has not said that every customer was affected. Its initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset, while its precautionary recommendation applies to all users.[1] This is an evolving incident, so check Railway's notice and status page before acting on older summaries.[2]

What Railway has disclosed

Railway says the affected systems store customer environment variables. Those values can include API keys, database access, or credentials for private registries.[1] The company also says it believes the incident is part of a broader series of attacks against platform companies intended to reach AI inference providers. That is Railway's assessment, not a publicly described attack chain.[1]

Railway paused builds and deployments while investigating.[1] Its status updates on October 22 added response guides, including credential rotation and checks for unusual usage at connected services.[2] At 02:19 UTC on October 22, Railway said builds were still offline and some remediation steps requiring a redeploy would have to wait.[2]

The public notice does not explain how the third party gained access, how many accounts were affected, or which specific variables were exposed.[1] Railway says it will contact customers it confirms were affected.[1] Avoid treating either the possible subset or the platform-wide precaution as a confirmed count. The first is Railway's initial assessment; the second is its response advice.[1]

Rotate credentials at the service that issued them

Changing a value in a hosting dashboard does not necessarily invalidate the old credential. A leaked API token can remain usable until its issuing provider revokes it. A database password remains valid until the database accepts a new one and the old one is disabled.

For each secret stored in Railway, identify the system that issued it, then replace it there. Update the corresponding Railway variable when the platform allows it, and revoke the old value. Railway recommends rolling all environment variables, including API keys and private registry credentials.[1]

For database credentials, coordinate the change with the database itself. AWS defines rotation as updating the credential in both the secret store and the database or service that accepts it.[4] Changing only one side can leave the application or database using an outdated value.[4]

Prioritize credentials that can create bills, expose customer data, or grant broad access. Include AI provider keys, cloud access, database passwords, source-control tokens, and private package credentials if they were stored in the affected platform. Railway's notice explicitly includes environment variables and private registry credentials in its recommendation.[1]

Keep a short record of each credential: owner, issuing service, affected application, replacement status, and old-key revocation status. AWS recommends limiting access to secrets, monitoring their use, and rotating credentials as part of secret management.[3]

Check for use you do not recognize

Review the logs at the service that issued each credential, as Railway recommends reviewing service logs for unusual activity.[1] Look for requests, deployments, access locations, or usage patterns the team cannot explain. Railway's status page has published service-specific guides, including checks for unusual activity at AI providers, cloud accounts, databases, and other connected services.[2]

A lack of suspicious entries does not prove that a credential was not accessed. Logs may have limited retention or may not capture every relevant action. Treat log review as one part of the response, alongside replacement and revocation.

Plan for a paused deployment pipeline

A rotation is not complete if the running application still depends on the old value. But during Railway's response, teams could not deploy new versions while builds were paused. Railway's status page said some remediation steps required a redeploy and had to wait for builds to return.[2]

That creates an operational tradeoff: revoke an old credential immediately and risk breaking the live service, or keep it active while waiting to deploy the replacement. There is no universal answer. For a credential with clear signs of misuse, containment may outweigh availability. For a production database password with no safe way to update the running app, coordinate the change with the database and platform status, and use Railway's service-specific guidance.[2] Avoid making a rushed change that locks out the application without actually revoking the old credential.

The lesson is about the full secret lifecycle

Encryption at rest is important, but it is not the whole security boundary. Applications and platforms must eventually retrieve usable credentials to connect to databases, cloud accounts, registries, and APIs. The important questions are also who can access those values, how access is monitored, and how quickly a credential can be replaced and revoked.

AWS recommends limiting access to secrets, monitoring their use, and rotating credentials as part of secret management.[3] These controls cannot prevent every breach. They can reduce the number of systems a stolen credential can reach and shorten how long it remains useful.[3]

For developers, keep a secret inventory. Record which service issued each key, what it can access, how to revoke it, and which deployment depends on the replacement. AWS's guidance on limiting access and monitoring secret use supports planned secret management.[3]

Railway's disclosure is still developing. Treat its published guidance as the source for the platform response, and check the incident page for new updates before redeploying.[2]

Sources

[1] Railway, Security Disclosure: Wednesday October 21st
[2] Railway, Platform incident updates
[3] AWS, Secrets Manager best practices
[4] AWS, Rotate AWS Secrets Manager secrets

title: AWS RDS Explained: Launch, Secure, and Scale a Managed Database
description:
By Vishal Patil | #vishalcloudjourney

Running a database on your own EC2 instance means you are also the DBA. You patch the OS, schedule backups, set up replication, and wake up when the disk fills. Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) takes that operational work off your plate so you can focus on your application. In this hands-on guide, you'll launch a MySQL database on RDS, lock it down, connect from EC2, test automatic failover, and learn how to scale reads.

What Is Amazon RDS?

Amazon RDS is a managed service for relational databases. You choose the engine and size, and AWS handles the heavy lifting.

Supported engines: Amazon Aurora (MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible), MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, and Db2.

What AWS manages for you

  • Hardware provisioning and OS patching
  • Automated backups and point-in-time recovery
  • Database software patching during a maintenance window
  • Multi-AZ failover
  • Monitoring through CloudWatch

What you still manage

  • Schema design, queries, and indexes
  • Security groups, network placement, and user access
  • Choosing instance size and storage
  • Cost control

Note: With standard RDS you don't get SSH or OS-level access to the underlying host. That's the trade-off for a managed service.

What You Will Build

  • A security group setup where only your EC2 app server can reach the database
  • A private MySQL RDS instance with encryption and automated backups
  • A connection from EC2 to the database
  • A Multi-AZ standby and a failover test
  • (Optional) A read replica

Architecture:

EC2 app server (ec2-app-sg) → RDS MySQL primary (rds-sg, AZ-a)
                                  ↓ synchronous replication
                              RDS standby (AZ-b), takes over on failure

Key Concepts in 60 Seconds

  • DB instance: The managed database server you pay for.
  • DB subnet group: The subnets (in at least two AZs) where RDS is allowed to place your database.
  • Multi-AZ: A standby copy in another AZ, kept in sync, that takes over automatically if the primary fails. It's for availability, not for read scaling.
  • Read replica: An asynchronously updated copy used to scale read traffic.
  • Automated backups: Daily backups plus transaction logs, kept for 1 to 35 days, enabling point-in-time restore.
  • Snapshot: A manual backup that stays until you delete it.
  • Endpoint: The DNS name your application uses to connect. Always use the endpoint, never an IP.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions for RDS, EC2, and VPC
  • A VPC with subnets in at least two AZs (the default VPC works)
  • A running EC2 instance (Amazon Linux 2023) to act as your app server, or you can launch one in Step 4

Cost note: RDS bills while the instance is running, and Multi-AZ roughly doubles the instance cost. Check the current Free Tier terms for your account and follow the cleanup section at the end.

Step 1: Create the Security Groups

Use two security groups so the database is reachable only from your app server.

App security group (ec2-app-sg) attached to your EC2 instance

  • Inbound: SSH (22) from your IP, or use EC2 Instance Connect or Session Manager

Database security group (rds-sg)

  • Inbound: MySQL/Aurora (3306) from ec2-app-sg (select the security group as the source, not 0.0.0.0/0)

This is the single most important RDS security habit: never open your database port to the internet.

Step 2: Check the DB Subnet Group

  1. Go to RDS → Subnet groups.
  2. The default VPC already has a default subnet group covering its subnets.
  3. For your own VPC, create a subnet group and add subnets from at least two AZs.

Step 3: Create the Database

  1. Go to RDS → Databases → Create database.
  2. Choose Standard create and engine MySQL.
  3. Template: Free tier or Dev/Test, depending on what your account shows.
  4. Settings:
    • DB instance identifier: mydb-rds
    • Master username: admin
    • Credentials: choose Managed in AWS Secrets Manager (recommended), or set a strong password yourself
  5. Instance configuration: a small burstable class such as db.t4g.micro or db.t3.micro.
  6. Storage:
    • Type: General Purpose SSD (gp3), 20 GiB
    • Enable storage autoscaling with a sensible maximum
  7. Connectivity:
    • VPC and subnet group: your chosen ones
    • Public access: No
    • VPC security group: rds-sg
  8. Additional configuration:
    • Initial database name: appdb
    • Automated backups: enabled, retention 7 days
    • Encryption: enabled (this must be chosen at creation)
    • Deletion protection: on for anything important
  9. Click Create database. It takes a few minutes to reach Available.
  10. Open the database and copy its Endpoint.

Step 4: Connect from EC2

  1. Connect to your EC2 instance (launch one with ec2-app-sg in the same VPC if you don't have one).
  2. Install a MySQL client: 
   sudo dnf install -y mariadb105
  1. Connect using the RDS endpoint: 
   mysql -h <your-rds-endpoint> -u admin -p

If you used Secrets Manager, open the secret in the console and choose Retrieve secret value to get the password.

  1. Create a table and add data: 
   USE appdb;
   CREATE TABLE visitors (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50));
   INSERT INTO visitors (name) VALUES ('Vishal'), ('AWS Builder');
   SELECT * FROM visitors;

You now have a working managed database that only your app server can reach.

Step 5: Turn On Multi-AZ

  1. Select your database and click Modify.
  2. Under Availability, choose Create a standby instance (Multi-AZ).
  3. Choose Apply immediately and confirm.

RDS creates a standby in another AZ and keeps it synchronized. Your endpoint stays the same.

Step 6: Test Failover

  1. Select the database, then Actions → Reboot.
  2. Check Reboot with failover? and confirm.
  3. Watch the Events tab and the database's AZ. The standby is promoted, and the AZ changes.
  4. Re-run your SQL query. Your data is still there, and the same endpoint works.

Expect a short interruption (typically a minute or two) while DNS flips to the new primary. Your application should retry failed connections.

Step 7 (Optional): Add a Read Replica

  1. Select the database and choose Actions → Create read replica.
  2. Give it an identifier such as mydb-rds-replica.
  3. Once available, point read-heavy queries at the replica's endpoint and keep writes on the primary.

Replication is asynchronous, so replicas can lag slightly behind the primary.

Multi-AZ vs Read Replica

Multi-AZ Read Replica
Purpose High availability and failover Read scaling
Replication Synchronous Asynchronous
Takes traffic normally No (standby only) Yes (reads)
Automatic failover Yes No (manual promotion)

Security Best Practices

  • Keep Public access set to No and place the DB in private subnets.
  • Allow access only from application security groups.
  • Use Secrets Manager for credentials and rotate them.
  • Enable encryption at rest (KMS) and enforce SSL/TLS connections.
  • Turn on deletion protection and automated backups.
  • Use IAM to control who can modify or delete DB instances.

Cost Tips

  • Pick the smallest instance that meets your needs and resize later.
  • Use Multi-AZ for production, but not for throwaway labs.
  • Stop or delete dev databases you aren't using. (A stopped RDS instance is automatically started again after 7 days.)
  • Delete old manual snapshots you no longer need.
  • Consider Reserved Instances for steady, long-running databases.

Common Issues and Fixes

Problem Likely cause Fix
Connection times out rds-sg doesn't allow 3306 from your app's SG Add the inbound rule with ec2-app-sg as source
Can't connect from your laptop Database is private (public access: No) Connect through EC2, a bastion, or Session Manager
Access denied for user Wrong username or password Re-check credentials or the Secrets Manager value
Unknown database Initial DB name wasn't set Run CREATE DATABASE appdb;
Storage full warnings Autoscaling off or limit reached Enable storage autoscaling or increase size

Clean Up

To avoid charges:

  1. Delete the read replica first (if you created one)
  2. Turn off deletion protection, then delete the DB instance
  3. Decide whether to keep a final snapshot (it costs storage) and whether to delete automated backups
  4. Delete leftover manual snapshots
  5. Delete the security groups and the EC2 instance if no longer needed
  6. Delete the Secrets Manager secret if you created one just for this lab

Conclusion

Amazon RDS lets you run production-grade relational databases without managing servers, patches, or backups by hand. With private networking, Multi-AZ, and automated backups, you get a secure and resilient foundation in minutes. Next, try adding a read replica, enabling Performance Insights, or moving to Aurora to see how far managed databases can go.

If you found this helpful, let's connect and keep learning together.

Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
