GBase Database Silent Installation: 6 Common Errors and How to Fix Them
description:
Silent installation helps automate GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment, but a failed installation can interrupt an otherwise straightforward process. In most cases, the first places to check are the response file, installation permissions, component dependencies, and available disk space.

Here are six common issues to investigate when ids_install -i silent fails.

1. License Acceptance Is Missing

A silent installation needs the license acceptance parameter. Check that your response file contains the following setting:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Alternatively, pass the parameter directly to the installer:

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

If the license acceptance parameter is missing or incorrectly configured, the installation may stop before completing.

2. The Response File Path Is Incorrect

The installer cannot read parameters from a response file that does not exist or is inaccessible.

Check the file first:

ls -l /opt/bundle.properties

Confirm that the path specified by -f matches the actual file location and that the user running the installation has read permission.

For example:

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

If the command references the wrong directory or filename, correct the path before investigating more complicated causes.

3. The Installation Directory Has Incorrect Permissions

Directory permissions can prevent the installer from creating or updating files.

Inspect the target directory:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase

Check whether the installation process has the necessary permissions to write to the directory. If the directory already exists, also check its ownership and whether existing files could interfere with the installation.

Do not change ownership blindly. Choose permissions based on the installation procedure and the account intended to manage the database software.

4. Selected Components Have Missing Dependencies

A response file may specify multiple components through SELECTED_FEATURES. Some selected components may require additional dependencies or supporting packages.

If the installation fails during component setup:

  • Review the selected features in the response file.
  • Check the installation logs for dependency or package errors.
  • Install any required dependencies.
  • Remove unnecessary components from the selection if they are not needed for the current deployment.

Avoid removing components simply to make the installation pass. First identify the component responsible for the failure, then adjust the configuration accordingly.

5. There Is Not Enough Disk Space

A silent installation can fail if the target filesystem does not have enough free space for the installation files and temporary files.

Check available capacity:

df -h /opt

Also check the filesystem used for temporary files if the installer extracts packages under /tmp or another temporary directory.

If space is insufficient, clean up unnecessary files or select an appropriate filesystem with enough capacity. Remember that the installation package itself is not the only space requirement: extraction and installation can require additional temporary storage.

6. The Instance Initialization Runs as Root

Installing the GBase Database program and initializing a database instance are separate operations with different execution requirements.

Running ids_install as root is permitted. However, the instance initialization script must be run as the gbasedbt user.

If initialization is performed as root, files or directories may receive incorrect ownership, causing problems when the database instance is started or managed by gbasedbt.

Before starting the instance, verify that the relevant installation and instance files have the expected ownership. Follow the product's installation procedure to correct any ownership problems rather than repeatedly rerunning initialization commands.

A Practical Troubleshooting Order

When troubleshooting a failed GBase Database silent installation, check the following in order:

  1. Response file: Confirm that the file exists, is readable, and contains valid parameters.
  2. License acceptance: Verify LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE or pass the command-line parameter.
  3. Permissions: Check the installation directory and the account running each step.
  4. Components: Review SELECTED_FEATURES and any dependency errors.
  5. Disk space: Check both the installation filesystem and temporary storage.
  6. Instance initialization: Make sure initialization is performed as gbasedbt, not root.

This order helps separate configuration problems from operating-system and instance-management issues.

Final Thoughts

Automating GBase Database deployment is not just about running ids_install -i silent. A reliable installation also depends on a valid response file, correct permissions, sufficient disk space, and proper separation between software installation and instance initialization.

When a silent installation fails, start with the response file and the installation logs before changing multiple settings at once. Identifying the first failing step is usually more effective than repeatedly rerunning the installer without knowing what went wrong.

title: Map pointer coordinates into the canvas drawing buffer
description:
Convert the pointer position into drawing-buffer coordinates before drawing a marker on a resized canvas. The event reports viewport coordinates, while the drawing buffer has its own width and height.

For a canvas displayed at half its buffer width, one CSS pixel covers two buffer pixels. Subtracting the canvas position gives a local CSS coordinate. Multiply that value by the buffer-to-display ratio before drawing a marker or choosing a crop boundary.

function canvasPoint(canvas, event) {
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (rect.width === 0 || rect.height === 0) return null;
  return {
    x: (event.clientX - rect.left) * canvas.width / rect.width,
    y: (event.clientY - rect.top) * canvas.height / rect.height
  };
}

This example assumes an axis-aligned canvas with no CSS border or padding and no rotation or skew. Put a decorative border on a wrapper. The bounding rectangle includes border and padding, so those would need separate handling if placed on the canvas itself.

The returned coordinates describe the canvas buffer. If the drawing context has a transform, or if the photo is letterboxed inside that buffer, mapping into the photo requires another step. Reject clicks outside the displayed photo before calculating a crop.

Check the mapping near both corners after resizing the page. If a marker follows the pointer near the upper-left corner but drifts near the lower-right, check the scale conversion. Read the current rectangle for the interaction; a rectangle saved before a layout change can be stale.

Reference: MDN

title: Collections and the Catalog: How a Database Remembers What Exists
description:
Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 3

Once I had page zero written to disk with those magic bytes NOSQLITE_DB___P8, I had a brief moment of satisfaction. I opened a hex editor, saw my custom signature staring back at me, and felt like I was actually getting somewhere.

Then reality set in.

I had an empty file with a header and absolutely no way to store anything useful yet. If you open a database, what is the very first thing you do? You create a collection. In SQL, you write CREATE TABLE. In MongoDB, you just start writing to a collection or create one explicitly. But what actually is a collection when you are sitting in front of a raw binary file?

It is not a folder on your hard drive. It is not some magical in-memory table. At the byte level, a collection is just a string name tied to a starting page number somewhere inside that single file.

My first lazy thought when planning this was tempting: why not just keep a HashMap<String, Vec<Document>> in memory and dump it to disk as a JSON blob when the program exits?

That would have taken an hour to write. But that is what you do if you are building a toy in Python or Node, and it completely misses the point of this experiment. If the power cuts out, your in-memory map is gone. If you copy the database file to another computer, that catalog has to travel with it inside the exact same file. The file has to be completely self-contained. It has to know its own collections, where they live, and how many documents they hold.

That meant building a catalog page.

The Table of Contents for Your Database

Think about a book. Before you read chapter three, you flip to the table of contents. The table of contents does not contain the story. It just tells you: Chapter 3 starts on page 45.

The catalog in nosqlite is literally just that table of contents.

For every collection you create, the engine needs to remember exactly three things:
What is the collection's name?
What page number does its first document live on?
How many documents are currently inside it?

That is all. If you know those three things, you can find the data, display counts in the shell, and know where to start scanning.

Where does this table of contents live? It gets its own dedicated page in the file. Specifically, it lives on page 1, sitting right after the file header. If you remember from the previous article, the file header on page 0 stores a field called catalog_page that holds the value 1. When the database boots up, it reads page 0, checks catalog_page, and immediately loads page 1 into memory.

The Anatomy of the Catalog Page

Let us look at how page 1 is laid out in memory and on disk.

// Catalog page layout:
//
// +-------------------------------+
// | Page Header                   |   16 bytes (generic header on every page)
// +-------------------------------+
// | collection_count (u32)        |    4 bytes (how many collections exist)
// +-------------------------------+
// | entries...                    |   packed one after another
// +-------------------------------+
//
// Each entry looks like this:
//
// +-------------------------------+
// | collection_name (\0)          |   variable length, null-terminated
// +-------------------------------+
// | first_document_page (u64)     |    8 bytes
// +-------------------------------+
// | document_count (u64)          |    8 bytes
// +-------------------------------+

The first 16 bytes belong to the generic page header that every single page in nosqlite has. That header records the page number, the page type (in this case, PageType::CollectionCatalog), and a couple of reserved bytes.

Right after those 16 bytes, we store 4 bytes for collection_count. This is an unsigned 32-bit integer that tracks how many collections currently exist in the database.

Why do we need this count? Because without it, a loop reading through the file would have no idea when to stop. It would keep reading random bytes until it crashed or hit corrupted memory. With collection_count, the reader knows upfront: there are 3 collections here, so read exactly 3 entries and then stop.

The catalog header size is therefore 20 bytes:

pub const CATALOG_HEADER_SIZE: usize = PAGE_HEADER_SIZE + 4; // 16 + 4 = 20

Since a page is 4096 bytes total, that leaves 4076 bytes for collection entries. In an embedded database where you usually have five, ten, or maybe thirty collections, 4076 bytes is plenty of room.

Null Terminators and C Strings

Here is the struct that represents a collection entry in Rust:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct CatalogEntry {
    pub name: String,
    pub first_document_page: u64,
    pub document_count: u64,
}

In Rust, this looks clean and friendly. But when this struct gets serialized into raw bytes on disk, we have to make an important choice: how do we store the string name?

In modern high-level languages, a string always carries its length with it. But at the raw binary level, there are two classic approaches. You can either use a Pascal string, where you write a length byte first and then the characters, or you can use a null-terminated C string, where you write the characters and end with a literal zero byte (\0).

I chose the null-terminated C string approach.

When you create a collection named "users", the engine writes the ASCII bytes for u, s, e, r, s, followed by 0x00. In hex, that is 75 73 65 72 73 00. That zero byte acts as a red light for the reader. The reader walks forward byte by byte, and the instant it sees a zero, it knows the name is finished.

Right after that zero byte, we write 8 bytes for first_document_page and 8 bytes for document_count, both encoded as little-endian unsigned 64-bit integers.

This brings up a fascinating detail about variable-length binary layouts. Because collection names can have different lengths, the entries do not have a fixed size. A collection named "users" takes 6 bytes for the name plus 16 bytes for the two u64 numbers, totaling 22 bytes. A collection named "audit_logs_v2" takes 14 bytes for the name plus 16 bytes for the numbers, totaling 30 bytes.

Because of this, you cannot simply calculate an offset with math like index * entry_size. You cannot jump directly to the fifth collection. You have to start at byte 20 and walk forward with a cursor, reading each entry to know where the next one begins.

Why the Catalog Struct Is Completely Empty

When you look at the source code in crates/nosqlite-core/src/catalog/catalog.rs, you find something that might look bizarre at first:

pub struct Catalog;

The struct has no fields. It holds no data in memory. It is a zero-sized type.

Every single method on Catalog takes a reference to a Page or Pager and acts directly on the byte buffer:

impl Catalog {
    pub fn initialize(page: &mut Page) {
        page.set_page_type(PageType::CollectionCatalog);

        // collection_count = 0
        page.data[PAGE_HEADER_SIZE..PAGE_HEADER_SIZE + 4]
            .copy_from_slice(&0u32.to_le_bytes());
    }
}

Let us look closely at what 0u32.to_le_bytes() is doing here, because this is fundamental to how systems programming works.

The number 0 as an unsigned 32-bit integer occupies 4 bytes. The method to_le_bytes() converts that number into a 4-byte array in little-endian order, where the least significant byte comes first. For zero, that array is just [0, 0, 0, 0]. If the count were 1, it would be [1, 0, 0, 0].

The call to copy_from_slice takes those 4 bytes and copies them directly into page.data starting at offset 16. That is how the collection count is set to zero when the database is first formatted.

Why did I make Catalog stateless instead of storing a Vec<CatalogEntry> inside it?

Because holding an in-memory copy of the catalog creates two sources of truth. What happens if your in-memory list says there are three collections, but a disk write failed and the file only has two? Now your program is in an inconsistent state, and debugging that will make you question your career choices.

By making Catalog stateless, the page itself is always the single source of truth. Every time we need to create, delete, or list collections, we read the page, do the work, and flush the page. There is zero risk of in-memory cache drift.

Creating a Collection: The Journey of a Write

When you type create users in the shell, here is the exact journey that command takes through the engine.

First, the engine calls the pager to load the catalog page into memory. The pager gives back a 4096-byte mutable slice of memory representing page 1.

The engine reads the first 4 bytes after the page header to find out how many collections already exist. Let us say collection_count is 2.

Next, it has to make sure we are not creating a duplicate. It sets a cursor variable to offset 20 (the start of the entries). It loops twice, reading each existing collection name using a helper function called read_cstring. If any name matches "users", it stops immediately and returns an error. We do not allow duplicate collections.

If no duplicate is found, the cursor is now pointing to the exact byte where the previous entry ended. That is our insertion point.

The engine checks whether there is enough space left on page 1 for the new entry. The new entry needs 6 bytes for "users\0", 8 bytes for the page pointer, and 8 bytes for the document count, which is 22 bytes. If the page has enough room, it writes the string bytes, writes 8 bytes of zero for first_document_page (since a new collection has no documents yet), and writes 8 bytes of zero for document_count.

Then it goes back to offset 16, increments the collection_count from 2 to 3, and writes the new count back to the page buffer.

Finally, the pager marks the page as dirty and flushes it to disk.

Notice how simple and mechanical that is. There is no query planner, no schema validator, no background worker. It is just reading a small buffer, checking for duplicates, appending 22 bytes, incrementing a counter, and writing the page back.

Listing Collections with a Cursor

Reading the list of collections reverses that entire process:

pub fn list(pager: &mut Pager) -> Result<Vec<CatalogEntry>> {
    let page = pager.read_page(pager.header.catalog_page)?;
    let count = Self::collection_count(&page)?;
    let mut cursor = CATALOG_HEADER_SIZE;
    let mut entries = Vec::new();

    for _ in 0..count {
        let name = read_cstring(&page.data, &mut cursor)?;
        let first_document_page = read_u64(&page.data, &mut cursor);
        let document_count = read_u64(&page.data, &mut cursor);

        entries.push(CatalogEntry {
            name,
            first_document_page,
            document_count,
        });
    }

    Ok(entries)
}

The cursor pattern is one of the most useful patterns in binary parsing. A cursor is simply a usize variable that keeps track of where we are currently reading in the byte slice.

When read_cstring(&page.data, &mut cursor) runs, it starts at cursor, reads characters until it hits 0x00, constructs a Rust String, and advances cursor past the zero byte.

Then read_u64 reads the next 8 bytes as a little-endian number and advances cursor by 8. Then it does it again for document_count.

After looping count times, the function returns a clean Vec<CatalogEntry> ready for the shell to print.

Now, someone who took a computer science algorithms class might look at this and say: wait, that is an O(n) linear scan. Why didn't you build a B-tree or a hash map for the catalog?

Because context matters. The entire catalog page is 4096 bytes. That is 4 kilobytes. A modern CPU can scan 4KB of contiguous memory in its L1 cache in a fraction of a microsecond. If you have 20 collections, an O(n) linear scan takes virtually zero time. Building a complex B-tree just to store 20 collection names would be textbook over-engineering. Never pay for complexity you do not actually need.

Deleting a Collection: The Shift-Left Trick

Deleting a collection is where the byte manipulation gets interesting.

When someone deletes a collection, you cannot simply write zeros over its entry and leave a hole in the middle of the page. If the reader encounters a gap of zeros, it will either think the collection name is an empty string or get confused about where the next entry begins. The entries must always remain packed tightly together.

To solve this, I used a shift-left strategy.

Imagine a row of physical books sitting on a shelf. If you remove the book in the middle, you get an empty gap. What do you do? You slide all the books to the right of that gap one position to the left. The gap disappears, and all the books are neatly packed again.

In Rust, the standard library provides a method called copy_within on slices that does exactly this:

page.data.copy_within(entry_end..used_end, entry_start);

copy_within takes a source range of bytes and copies them to a new destination offset inside the exact same slice. It safely handles overlapping memory regions, which is crucial because when you slide bytes to the left, the source and destination overlap.

After sliding the bytes left, we decrement collection_count by 1.

What happens to the leftover bytes at the far right of the entries region? Nothing! We do not even need to zero them out. Because collection_count is decremented, the reader will stop reading earlier and will never look at those leftover bytes. They will simply be overwritten the next time a new collection is created.

When a collection is deleted, we also free any document pages that belonged to it so they can be reused later. We will see how page reuse works when we talk about the free-page list.

Preventing Catastrophe with a Lock File

Above the Catalog and the Pager sits the Database struct. This is the main entry point that the shell and external applications interact with:

pub struct Database {
    pager: Pager,
    lock_path: PathBuf,
    _lock_file: File,
}

Notice that field named _lock_file with the leading underscore.

In Rust, if you declare a variable or a field and never call any methods on it, the compiler will yell at you about an unused variable. The underscore tells the compiler: I know this looks unused, but please leave it alone.

And leaving it alone is the whole point!

When Database::open is called, it creates a small file next to the database with a .lock extension. It opens that file and stores the open file handle inside _lock_file.

As long as the Database instance exists in your program, that file handle remains open. When your program finishes or the Database goes out of scope, Rust drops the struct. Rust's ownership system automatically closes the file handle, and the operating system releases the lock.

This is the classic RAII pattern, which stands for Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. You acquire the resource on creation, and cleanup happens automatically on destruction. You do not have to remember to call a close() method.

But what happens if the power cord is pulled out of the wall while the database is running?

If the system crashes violently, the .lock file remains sitting on the hard drive even though the process is dead. If another program tries to open the database later, it sees the .lock file and thinks the database is still in use.

To solve this, nosqlite checks for stale locks on startup:

pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<Self> {
    let lock_path = path.with_extension("lock");

    if lock_path.exists() {
        let stale = match read_lock_file(&lock_path) {
            Ok(lock) => !process_exists(lock.pid),
            Err(_) => true,
        };

        if stale {
            eprintln!("Removing stale lock file");
            let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&lock_path);
        } else {
            return Err(Error::DatabaseLocked);
        }
    }
    // ... proceed with opening
}

When nosqlite creates a lock file, it writes the current process ID into it. On startup, if a lock file exists, the engine reads that PID and asks the operating system: is a process with this ID currently running?

If the answer is no, the previous process died without cleaning up. The lock is stale. nosqlite deletes the file and continues opening normally. If the process is still running, the database is genuinely in use by another instance, and the engine refuses to open to prevent data corruption.

It is a simple, pragmatic mechanism that prevents two processes from destroying the same database file while handling unexpected crashes gracefully.

Where We Stand

At this point in the project, nosqlite had a solid foundation.

It could format a file, stamp its magic bytes, maintain a catalog of collections, slide bytes around safely during deletions, and protect the file from concurrent access with process locking.

You could open the shell, run create users, run create orders, and run list. The database would print:

users: 0 documents
orders: 0 documents

Everything worked. But every single collection had first_document_page set to 0.

It was like having a filing cabinet with neatly labeled folders, but every single folder was completely empty. We had built the entire organizational structure of a database without storing a single byte of actual user data.

That changes in the next article.

In Part 4, we finally put real data into those folders. We take a JSON string typed into the terminal, break down why storing raw JSON is a terrible idea, convert it into binary BSON format, allocate document pages, link them together in a chain, and write our very first document to disk.

title: CVE-2026-89111: SSRF in a Multi-Tenant SDK and the OAuth Credentials Behind It
description:
CVE-2026-89111: SSRF in a Multi-Tenant SDK and the OAuth Credentials Behind It

A server-side request forgery in a cloud SDK sounds like a lower-tier finding until you consider what the SDK is holding. For CVE-2026-89111 in the SAP Cloud SDK for Python, the answer is OAuth2 client credentials in multi-tenant SAP Business Technology Platform environments.

The disclosure

CVE-2026-89111 is rated 10.0 and affects SAP Cloud SDK for Python versions below 0.45.2. The flaw is server-side request forgery. Public reporting reviewed here notes that no in-the-wild exploitation had been observed at the time of writing, which distinguishes it from the KEV-listed issues covered elsewhere in this series.

Severity without exploitation is still severity. A 10.0 SSRF in a library that handles tenant-scoped credentials deserves attention before someone builds an exploit.

Why SSRF in an SDK is different

SSRF in a web application lets an attacker make the server issue requests on their behalf, typically to internal endpoints the attacker cannot reach directly.

SSRF in a shared SDK is a different shape. The SDK runs inside the customer's application, and that application holds credentials issued for its tenant. If request construction can be influenced so that the credential-bearing call goes to an attacker-chosen destination, the outcome is credential exfiltration rather than internal port scanning.

The distinction matters for impact assessment. A traditional SSRF is an access bypass. This one is closer to a credential leak: the tenant's OAuth2 client secret, presented to the wrong host, is a durable compromise.

The multi-tenant dimension

The affected environment is described as multi-tenant BTP. Two aspects deserve emphasis.

First, credentials in this environment authorize access to services across a subscription. A leaked client credential is not a read-only token for one endpoint; its scope is defined by the service instance it was created for.

Second, SDKs are consumed by application developers rather than operated by platform teams. The library version in use is often decided by a dependency lock file and updated when someone runs an upgrade. That makes remediation a code change in every consuming application, distributed across teams.

This is why library vulnerabilities with credential impact age badly. There is no single appliance to patch, and the dependency may sit several levels deep.

Practical remediation

  1. Identify consuming applications. Search dependency manifests and lock files for the SDK. Container images reveal what actually shipped, which is often more accurate than repository manifests.
  2. Upgrade to 0.45.2 or later in each application, then rebuild and redeploy so the runtime image contains the fixed version.
  3. Verify at runtime. Log or assert the SDK version during startup. A repository that declares the fixed version and an image that contains the old one is a common mismatch.
  4. Rotate client credentials for tenant service instances where the vulnerable version was deployed in an environment that processes untrusted input.
  5. Review outbound traffic. If the SDK's request destinations are logged or observable, examine historical records for calls to unexpected hosts.

Step five is where an SSRF can be confirmed or ruled out in retrospect. Most organizations have proxy or egress logs that would show a credential-bearing request leaving for an unexpected destination, and few have looked at them for this reason.

The dependency problem this exposes

Credential-handling libraries occupy a privileged position in an application's dependency graph and are usually treated like any other package. They get updated on a release cadence, not a security one.

The practical improvement is to classify dependencies that hold credentials separately from those that do not, and apply a faster update policy to the first group. That is a policy change, not a tooling purchase, and it directly reduces the window in which a flaw like this one remains deployed.

References

  • SAP, Security notes portal (SAP Security Note for CVE-2026-89111; version 0.45.2 is the fixed release per public reporting).
  • NVD, CVE-2026-89111.
  • Week 42 2026 security summary citing the CVSS 10.0 rating and BTP credential scope: security report.

title: Managing Google Play Testers Programmatically: Email Lists, Google Groups, and the API
description:
Managing Google Play Testers Programmatically: Email Lists, Google Groups, and the API

Tester management is the unglamorous part of Android releases. Somewhere between "the build is ready" and "users have the beta," there's a list of emails to create, sync, prune, and babysit — done by hand in the Console, it eats an hour every release. Worse, for new personal developer accounts, sloppy tester management is the top reason the mandatory 14-day closed testing period fails: testers who never opted in don't count, and you find out only when Google rejects your production application.

This guide covers the three ways to manage testers on Google Play, when each one scales, and how to drive the whole thing through the API so your tester list stays correct without manual Console clicking.

The Three Tester-Management Methods

1. Email lists (Console-managed)

Under a closed track's Testers tab, create named email lists and paste addresses directly. Simplest option: no external tooling, Google handles opt-in emails.

Limits: 2,000 testers per list, 50 lists per track — more than you'll ever recruit. The constraint is operational: bulk add/remove is manual in the Console UI. If your testers rotate frequently, this gets old fast.

2. Google Groups

Instead of pasting emails, point the track at a Google Group — membership is the tester list. This is the method that scales: anyone who can manage the group (a community manager, a script, a signup form) can add or remove testers without touching the Play Console.

The trade-off: testers must be group members and opt in via the Play testing link — membership alone grants nothing. Document that two-step flow wherever you recruit, or you'll get tickets from people who joined the group but can't see the beta.

3. The open testing link (not closed, but relevant)

Open testing uses a public opt-in link rather than a managed list — anyone with the link can join. It doesn't satisfy the closed-testing requirement for new accounts. Keep it straight: closed tracks need explicit tester lists; open tracks need a link and a feedback funnel.

Which Method Scales When

  • Solo dev / small team, stable tester pool: email lists. Ten minutes of setup, zero maintenance tooling.
  • Community beta (50–500 testers), rotating membership: Google Groups. Let moderators manage membership; the Console just reads the group.
  • CI-driven QA: the API. Your pipeline adds contractor emails when a sprint starts and removes them when it ends.
  • Enterprise with compliance requirements: Google Groups plus audit logging on membership changes — you get a paper trail the Console lists don't provide.

Driving Tester Lists Through the API

The Play Developer API exposes tester management through the transactional Edits API — the same one used for automated uploads. The flow:

  1. Create an edit (edits.insert) for your package.
  2. Call edits.testers.update with the track name (internal, alpha, beta, or your custom closed track) and a Testers resource body specifying your email lists, Google Groups, or both.
  3. Commit the edit (edits.commit).

The Testers resource lets you mix methods on one track — an email list for core QA plus a Google Group for the community beta. Typical automation patterns:

  • Nightly sync: diff your canonical roster (CRM, spreadsheet, signup database) against current track testers via edits.testers.get, and push additions/removals. Kills the classic drift where someone who left months ago still gets beta builds.
  • Onboarding: when a tester signs up, add them to the list and send the opt-in link automatically. The biggest drop-off isn't recruitment — it's the gap between "I signed up" and "I opted in." Closing it programmatically is the highest-leverage automation here.
  • Offboarding on release: when a build graduates from closed to production, archive the tester list for that track so the next testing cycle starts clean.

One caution: the Edits API is transactional, so concurrent edits to the same track can conflict. Serialize tester-management jobs — don't run a sync and a release upload against the same track simultaneously.

Keeping 20+ Testers Engaged for the 14-Day Requirement

For new personal developer accounts, Google requires at least 20 opted-in testers continuously engaged over the 14 days before you can apply for production access. "Opted in" is operative — a tester who never clicked the link, or who opted in then uninstalled, doesn't count.

What actually works:

  • Recruit 30–40, not 20. Attrition is real. People lose interest, switch devices, or never complete opt-in. A 50% buffer is the minimum.
  • Give testers something to do. "Install the app" retains nobody. Ship a one-page test script: three tasks to complete, one form to fill. Testers with assignments stay active; testers without them churn by day three.
  • Communicate on a schedule. A short message at day 1 (welcome + opt-in link), day 5 (what to test this week), and day 12 (final feedback call) keeps the cohort warm. Automate these alongside your tester-list sync.
  • Monitor opt-in status weekly. The Console shows per-tester opt-in state. Anyone not opted in by day 3 gets a nudge; anyone still not in by day 7 gets replaced.

Removing Inactive Testers (and Why It Matters)

Dead weight distorts your signal: crash reports from testers who installed once and vanished pollute pre-launch data, and for the 14-day requirement, inactive testers create false security — your list says 25, but only 14 are genuinely engaged.

Hygiene rule: zero sessions in 7 days gets one re-engagement message, then removal at day 14. Keep an alumni list for easy re-recruiting.

Common Pitfalls

  • Testers not opted in. The single most common failure. Being on the list ≠ opted in. Verify in the Console, not in your spreadsheet.
  • Wrong track. Internal-track testers don't count toward closed-track requirements. Double-check which track your automation targets.
  • Stale builds. Testers on an old build reporting fixed bugs wastes everyone's time. Tie tester notifications to your release pipeline so a new build always triggers an update nudge.
  • Device coverage blindness. Twenty testers all on Pixel phones tells you nothing about Samsung or Xiaomi quirks. Recruit across manufacturers and Android versions deliberately.
  • Ignoring the feedback. A beta program that collects feedback into a void trains testers to stop giving it. Acknowledge reports, even briefly.

Managing testers is an operations problem, and operations problems are what APIs are for. Whether you run a five-person QA rotation or a 500-strong community beta, the google play manage testers API lets you treat your roster like infrastructure — versioned, synced, self-maintaining — instead of a spreadsheet someone updates when they remember.

If the 14-day requirement itself is the blocker — recruiting and retaining 20+ genuine testers for two straight weeks is genuinely hard for a solo dev with no audience — 14-day closed testing coordination services exist to run that process for you, from recruitment through the full 14-day window.

About the author: This guide was written by the team at Play Console Store, an independent marketplace helping Android developers with Google Play publishing — account setup, verification, and closed testing. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Google LLC.

title: A Practical CI/CD Pipeline: Build Once, Tag by Commit, Deploy Anywhere
description:
A good CI/CD pipeline is boring. Every change goes through the same steps, deploys look the same every time, and rolling back takes seconds.

This post builds a minimal pipeline for a containerised app using GitHub Actions. The principles also apply to other CI systems and cloud providers.

Principles first

  1. Build once. Create a single artefact (a container image) and promote that same artefact through staging and production. Don't rebuild per environment, or you're not testing what you ship.
  2. Make artefacts immutable. Tag images with the commit SHA. Avoid deploying latest, because you can't tell what it is or roll back to it reliably.
  3. Keep config out of the image. Environment variables and secrets come from the environment at runtime.
  4. Automate the check after deploy. A deploy isn't done until a health check passes.

Step 1: Test and build on every push 

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint --if-present
      - run: npm test

  build:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

Pull requests run tests only. Merges to main also build and push an image tagged with the exact commit.

Step 2: A small, secure Dockerfile 

FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

Multi-stage builds keep the final image small, and USER node avoids running as root.

Step 3: Deploy the exact image

How you deploy depends on your platform (ECS, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, a VM with Docker, and so on). The pattern is the same: tell the platform to run the image tagged with this commit SHA.

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - name: Deploy image
        run: |
          echo "Deploying ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} to staging"
          # replace with your platform's command, for example:
          # kubectl set image deployment/app app=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Wait for health check
        run: |
          for i in {1..20}; do
            if curl -fsS https://staging.example.com/healthz; then exit 0; fi
            sleep 5
          done
          echo "Health check failed" && exit 1

  deploy-production:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # add required reviewers in repo settings
    steps:
      - name: Deploy the same image
        run: echo "Deploying the same SHA to production"

Using GitHub Environments lets you add required approvals for production and keep secrets separate per environment.

Step 4: Add a real health endpoint 

app.get("/healthz", async (req, res) => {
  try {
    await db.query("SELECT 1");     // check critical dependencies
    res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" });
  } catch {
    res.status(503).json({ status: "unhealthy" });
  }
});

Keep it fast and cheap. Platforms use it to decide whether to send traffic to a new version, and your pipeline uses it to decide whether a deploy succeeded.

Step 5: Rollback is just another deploy

Because every image is tagged with a commit SHA, rolling back means deploying the previous known-good SHA. No rebuild required.

# example: redeploy the previous version
kubectl set image deployment/app app=ghcr.io/org/app:<previous-sha>

Practice this before you need it. A rollback you've never tried isn't a plan.

Beyond the basics

  • Secrets: prefer short-lived credentials via OIDC (for example, GitHub Actions to AWS, Azure or GCP) over long-lived keys stored in secrets.
  • Infrastructure as code: manage cloud resources with Terraform or similar, reviewed through pull requests.
  • Progressive delivery: canary or blue/green releases reduce the impact of a bad deploy.
  • Observability: logs, metrics and alerts tied to each release, so you can see when a deploy changed behaviour.
  • Database migrations: make them backward-compatible so old and new versions can run side by side during a rollout.

Checklist

  • [ ] One build, promoted across environments
  • [ ] Images tagged by commit SHA, never latest
  • [ ] Config and secrets injected at runtime
  • [ ] Health check gates every deploy
  • [ ] Manual approval for production
  • [ ] Rollback tested

What does your deployment pipeline look like, and what's the one thing you'd change?

Further reading: Cloud DevOps Solutions
