title: Node.js AI Image Generation: Decode Errors in Compatible Object Storage
description:
Short answer: S3-compatible object storage is a good home for AI-generated images when a worker uploads the PNG buffer as binary, verifies the stored metadata before its database commit, and serves the result with a presigned link instead of a permanent public URL.

A malformed base64 decode error is usually an ownership mistake at an interface. A PNG already has bytes; turning those bytes into text for a queue, then decoding them again before upload, creates room for a data-URL prefix, missing padding, or a second decode. Decode at the documented generation boundary once, validate the bytes, and keep the rest of the path binary.

Small rule. Large consequence.

What signal says a Node.js generated PNG needs an object-storage runbook?

The signal is simple: the application accepts a generation, yet the delivered object cannot later be read or no longer has the expected size and image/png type. A successful generation request is not the success event. For the storage SLO, success means a durable object whose metadata has been checked, followed by a database record that points to it.

That distinction matters during capacity planning. Base64 expands a payload and encourages a team to carry large strings through components that should only carry job identifiers. Make the object key deterministic, for example userId/jobId.png, put that key and a job ID in the queue, and let the worker retain ownership of the buffer. The resulting sequence is easy to reason about: write bytes, inspect bytes, then publish the database state.

This is also a server-side workflow. The bucket model has CORS rules, but there is no independent route to configure them, so browser-direct upload cannot be treated as self-service. Keep the upload worker on the server when that policy must be predictable.

How should a Node.js service place a generated PNG in S3-compatible object storage?

Use PUT, then the metadata endpoint, then the database transaction. The runnable Go worker below shows the wire behavior required for the same Node.js pipeline: it reads the generated PNG buffer, checks its signature, sends a binary object write with an explicit method, retries only rate limiting with exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After, and checks the response status before any application state changes. INFRAI_BASE_URL is set to the service API base URL by deployment configuration; the three routes in the program are the supported storage routes.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func send(method, endpoint, apiKey, idempotencyKey string, body []byte) (*http.Response, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        if method == http.MethodPut {
            req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil || resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return resp, err
        }
        io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after bounded retries")
}

func require2xx(resp *http.Response, action string) error {
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
        return nil
    }
    body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    return fmt.Errorf("%s rejected: status=%d body=%s", action, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    bucket, userID, jobID := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET"), os.Getenv("USER_ID"), os.Getenv("JOB_ID")
    png, err := os.ReadFile(os.Getenv("PNG_FILE"))
    if err != nil || apiKey == "" || baseURL == "" || bucket == "" || userID == "" || jobID == "" {
        panic("PNG_FILE, INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BASE_URL, STORAGE_BUCKET, USER_ID, and JOB_ID are required")
    }
    if len(png) < 8 || !bytes.Equal(png[:8], []byte{0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a}) {
        panic("PNG_FILE is not a PNG buffer")
    }

    key := url.PathEscape(userID) + "/" + url.PathEscape(jobID) + ".png"
    putURL := baseURL + "/storage/object/put/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + key
    put, err := send(http.MethodPut, putURL, apiKey, "image:"+userID+":"+jobID, png)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := require2xx(put, "upload"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    headURL := baseURL + "/storage/object/head/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + key
    head, err := send(http.MethodGet, headURL, apiKey, "", nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := require2xx(head, "metadata check"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("verified %s; the database commit may proceed\n", key)
}

Compare the returned content length and content type to the original buffer and image/png before the commit. A rejected response body should be surfaced to the job operator rather than silently discarded. I'm not sure which response representation an individual image generator uses, so confirm that provider's documented response shape at the one decode boundary; the binary-storage rule does not change.

The verification step deserves more attention than it usually gets in an image pipeline review. A PUT proves that the write request received a response; it does not make the database row truthful by itself. Read the metadata with the supported head route, compare the observed byte count to len(png), compare the stored type to the type the worker sent, and only then make the image visible to the rest of the application. If that comparison fails, retain the job state for investigation and do not publish a record that points users at an object whose representation has not been confirmed. This keeps the failure boundary narrow: the generator has produced bytes, the storage worker has either verified those bytes or has not, and the database has a state that reflects that fact. It also gives an on-call engineer a useful place to measure the gap between generated jobs, verified objects, and committed records, instead of treating every accepted generation as successful delivery.

Verification and rollback belong in the database

There is no object versioning, object lock, or If-Match conditional write protection. If a user can regenerate userId/jobId.png, coordinate the overwrite in a database row or queue: claim one active writer, write the object, verify it, and advance the record last. An object write by itself cannot offer strict concurrency control.

For a reversible product action, assign every generation a new immutable key and switch the database pointer transactionally after metadata verification. Rollback then means restoring the prior pointer. An overwritten object cannot be recovered as a version, so it is not a rollback plan.

Lifecycle expiration can remove retired objects, but its shortest interval is one day. It won't clean hourly scratch data, multipart fragments need their own cleanup process, and metadata is not server-searchable: listing filters by prefix only. Maintain a database index for retention, reporting, and incident work.

Which storage option fits the on-call model?

This is a buy-versus-build choice, not a naming exercise. The image path needs private binary storage, deterministic keys, and temporary delivery; the remaining questions are who owns the data plane, which access controls are already familiar, and how many control planes the platform team must carry.

Option Fits when Operational trade-off
AWS S3 AWS-native controls already govern the platform Adds AWS account, policy, and billing administration when the rest of the stack is elsewhere
Cloudflare R2 The application already operates around Cloudflare Adds a vendor control plane to access review and incident procedures
MinIO Self-hosted S3 compatibility is required The team owns capacity, upgrades, durability design, and the storage SLO
Infrai Several backend capabilities benefit from one provider relationship Private signed delivery fits; permanent public hosting, versioning, WORM retention, GCS/B2 coverage, and cross-region replication do not

Infrai is worth considering when one key and one bill across backend capabilities reduce credential sprawl and month-end invoice reconciliation. That is an access-management advantage, not a substitute for storage operations.

The catch is fit. Stay with AWS S3 for deep AWS-native controls, Cloudflare R2 for an edge-centered application, and MinIO when data-plane ownership is worth the on-call load. This private-storage workflow is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public image links, finance-grade immutable retention, or browser uploads that require independently managed CORS. An authorized reader can receive a temporary presigned link through the supported presign route; treat it as access, not as a public asset identity.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest

title: I Migrated a Cloudflare Agents Workspace and Measured Everything: What Changes When the Storage Format Changes?
description:
The difference was not the table names.

TL;DR

On October 20, 2026, Cloudflare Agents switched its Workspace implementation from @cloudflare/shell to @cloudflare/computer. The change is not just a new API name. It changes how files are stored. The old implementation stored one row per path, with the file contents base64-encoded in that same row. The new one separates inodes and chunks, storing content-addressed blobs in 512 KiB pieces.

I ran the old and new implementations in the same Durable Object and compared the data before and after migration.

  • The tables are different, so old files are invisible after switching without migration. They are still there, though.
  • Storing a whole file in one row changes the size limit and performance. The old implementation hit a limit at about 6 MiB, and its 1 MB read/write cycle was 13.5 times slower.
  • The schema is versioned, so it migrates forward automatically but cannot go backward.
Aspect Old @cloudflare/shell New @cloudflare/computer
Tables cf_workspace_<namespace> vfs_* / _vfs_*
Representation of one file One row (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY) Inode + 512 KiB chunks
Where content lives Base64 in the same row's content column Blob addressed by SHA-256
Observed file-size limit About 6 MiB without R2 No single-row limit; content is chunked
1 MB write + read 87.25 ms 6.45 ms
Same content at two paths Stored twice Both paths share one blob row
Reopen with old implementation Works Fails with EIO

Test code: GitHub repository

Here is the main point upfront.

The old and new implementations differ in storage format, not API. Once you understand that, the reason files disappear after switching without a migration, why the file-size limit changes, why the new implementation is faster, and why you cannot switch back all follow from the same underlying change. The migration guide says to copy files manually because the tables differ. The deeper difference is their structure, not their names.

This article expands on my talk about migrating a Cloudflare Agents Workspace with measurements I could not fit into the presentation. It is for people using Cloudflare Agents who are preparing to move to @cloudflare/computer.

1. The announcement

On October 20, 2026, Cloudflare posted this changelog:

Think and Agent Skills now use the workspace from @cloudflare/computer as well as the filesystem tools.
@cloudflare/shell is deprecated, and so is Think's createExecuteTool. These will no longer be developed nor supported from today onwards.

On the same day, Cloudflare published @cloudflare/think@0.21.0, @cloudflare/computer@0.6.0, and agents@0.29.0. @cloudflare/shell also received version 0.5.0 that day to announce its deprecation. npm's deprecated flag applies retroactively to earlier versions too, so 0.4.3 shows the same warning.

The migration guide itself had landed earlier, in PR #2564 on October 14. It did not arrive at the same time as the announcement.

The Changelog also says:

This is a breaking change. @cloudflare/computer stores files in different tables from @cloudflare/shell, and there is no automatic data migration between workspace formats.

“Different tables.” That is where I started. Let's see how different they are.

2. The old Workspace stored one file per row

A Workspace is where an agent stores its files. A model interacts with them through read, write, edit, and ls; the files themselves live in Durable Object SQLite.

The old @cloudflare/shell schema is included in the migration guide:

CREATE TABLE cf_workspace_default (
  path             TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_path      TEXT NOT NULL,
  name             TEXT NOT NULL,
  type             TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(type IN ('file','directory','symlink')),
  mime_type        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'text/plain',
  size             INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  storage_backend  TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'inline' CHECK(storage_backend IN ('inline','r2')),
  r2_key           TEXT,
  target           TEXT,
  content_encoding TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'utf8',
  content          TEXT,
  created_at       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  modified_at      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch())
);

It is straightforward: the path is the primary key, and the metadata and content live in the same row. The content column holds file contents, base64-encoded for binary files.

Large files are handled separately. The default threshold is 1,500,000 bytes. Files above that threshold are moved to R2, leaving only an r2_key in the row. If no R2 bucket is provided, the implementation logs a warning and keeps the file inline:

if (size >= this.threshold && !r2)
  console.warn(`[Workspace] File ${path} is ${size} bytes but no R2 bucket was provided. Storing inline.`);

This “put everything in one row” design matters later.

3. The new Workspace separates inodes and chunks

The new @cloudflare/computer uses several tables:

Table Stores
vfs_dirents Parent inode + name → child inode
vfs_nodes Inode metadata (type / mode / mtime / size / link_target)
vfs_chunks Inode + chunk index → blob SHA-256
vfs_blobs SHA-256 → size and last-reference time
vfs_blob_bytes SHA-256 → actual bytes
vfs_meta schema_version and revision counter

Path resolution walks vfs_dirents from the root (inode = 1). File contents are split into 512 KiB chunks, each stored in vfs_blob_bytes as a blob keyed by SHA-256:

const CHUNK_SIZE = 524288;

The tables start with vfs_ or _vfs_, so they do not collide with cf_workspace_*. Both formats can coexist during migration.

From here, I measured what follows from the structural difference.

4. Consequence #1: switching does not make old files visible

I put both implementations on the same Durable Object. Splitting them across two DO namespaces would not test migration on the same storage. I switched between them inside one class.

I wrote 13 items with the old implementation, initialized the new one, and tried reading them:

Read through old Workspace before switch → {found: true, length: 23}
Initialize new Workspace
Read /workspace/notes.md through new     → ENOENT no such file
Read /notes.md through new               → ENOENT no such file
New-side tree                            → [{path: "/workspace", type: "dir"}]

The new implementation could not see the files.

If I stopped here, the article would say “the data is gone.” That would be quick—and wrong.

Add two controls

“Not visible through the new implementation” does not tell us whether the original write failed. In the same run, I verified that the old Workspace could still read the file both before and after switching:

Read through old before switch        → {found: true, length: 23}
Read through old after switch         → {found: true, length: 23}
Rows in cf_workspace_default          → 14 (same as before)

The old implementation could still read the file after the switch. The row count had not changed either.

The data was not gone. The new implementation was looking somewhere else. A table listing showed both formats coexisting:

cf_workspace_default
computer_execution_runtime
sqlite_sequence
vfs_blob_bytes   vfs_blobs    vfs_changes   vfs_chunks
vfs_dirents      vfs_manifests  vfs_meta    vfs_nodes
_vfs_fetch_cursor  _vfs_mounts  _vfs_push_cursor
_vfs_sync_operations  _vfs_sync_skips  _vfs_watermark

I also learned that all vfs_* tables are created as soon as you call new Workspace(). They do not wait for the first filesystem operation. The schema_version was 10.

5. Consequence #2: the size limit changes when everything fits in one row

The old implementation base64-encodes file contents and puts them in one cell. A 4 MB file becomes 5,592,408 base64 characters.

Meanwhile, the Durable Objects Limits page says:

Item Documented limit
Maximum string, BLOB, or table row size 2 MB
KV key size Key and value combined cannot exceed 2 MB

A 4 MB file should not fit in the old Shell. I predicted that while designing the benchmark and prepared files of 1 KB, 100 KB, 1 MB, and 4 MB.

They all worked.

My prediction was wrong.

4 MB → storage_backend=inline, content_encoding=base64,
       content_len=5,592,408 → read-back SHA-256 matches
8 MB → Error: string or blob too big: SQLITE_TOOBIG

I got the same result in local Miniflare and a deployed production Durable Object.

Measurement: where is the actual limit?

Stepping through the library would only reveal its implementation constant, not the underlying limit, so I called ctx.storage.sql and ctx.storage.kv directly to find the boundary. Each probe used a new Durable Object.

Largest accepted  8,388,627 bytes
Smallest rejected 8,388,628 bytes

8 MiB is 8,388,608 bytes. TEXT, BLOB, and a KV value all failed at the same boundary.

That is four times the documented 2 MB. I repeated probes around the boundary on a new Durable Object and got the same result. I reported it in cloudflare-docs#34502. Since I could not rule out 2 MB being the guaranteed limit and 8 MiB merely an implementation allowance, I did not open a PR asserting a new limit; I attached a reference branch instead.

Why does the old implementation stop at 6 MiB?

The old Shell hit its own boundary below the raw SQL limit:

Largest file accepted by shell.writeFileBytes  6,291,408 bytes (8,388,544 base64 chars)
Smallest rejected                             6,291,409 bytes (8,388,548 base64 chars)

Base64 expands the content by about 4/3, so that works out to roughly 6 MiB of file data.

I could not explain why the Shell fails earlier than raw SQL at 8,388,627 bytes. I reproduced its DDL, indexes, INSERT statement, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE clause, and base64 string, then ran them against the same Durable Object. Raw SQL accepted the value. I also suspected that UPSERT might duplicate the value through excluded, but an UPSERT against an existing row accepted the same size.

The stack trace points to the Shell's INSERT:

Error: string or blob too big: SQLITE_TOOBIG
  at Object.run (index.js:367:17)
  at Workspace.writeFileBytes (index.js:652:22)

I stopped there. For practical purposes, remember that “without R2, the old Shell's file-size limit is about 6 MiB.”

The new Computer splits content into 512 KiB chunks, so this particular wall is gone. Files of 8 MB, 16 MB, and 32 MB all worked. Chunking may look like a performance design, but it also changes the size limit.

6. Consequence #3: base64 conversion on every operation is slower

I hit an oddity here: Date.now() does not advance inside a Worker. In production, even a 4 MB write was recorded as 0ms. It advanced in local Miniflare, so at first I thought I was misreading the production logs.

I measured from outside instead. I sent one request that repeated the operation 60 times and a control request that did nothing, then divided the difference by 60. The table shows the median of seven runs:

Size Old Shell New Computer
1 KB 1.58 ms -0.75 ms
100 KB 4.92 ms 0.80 ms
1 MB 87.25 ms 6.45 ms

I cannot draw conclusions from the 1 KB and 100 KB results. As the negative value shows, the differences are buried in HTTP round-trip variance.

At 1 MB, the gap was clear: 13.5×. The old Shell base64-encodes a 1 MB file into one row on every write and decodes it on every read, adding overhead. My measurement includes the write and the read together, so I cannot say which one is slower on its own.

7. Consequence #4: content addressing enables deduplication

The new implementation uses the blob's SHA-256 as its primary key. The same bytes can be shared by files anywhere in the tree.

I wrote the same 512 KiB of content to two paths and counted rows in vfs_blobs:

Initial blob count                 → 0
Write identical content to path 1  → 1
Write identical content to path 2  → 1  (no increase)
Control: write different content  → 2  (increases)

Without the control, I could not distinguish deduplication from an implementation that never added a blob at all. The different byte sequence confirmed that a second row is created when the content differs.

The old implementation stores content per path, so putting the same file in two places uses storage twice.

8. Consequence #5: there is nowhere to put some metadata

The old FileInfo has mimeType, createdAt, and updatedAt. The new WorkspaceStatResult has only these fields:

{ name, inode, mode, mtime, size, isFile, isDirectory, isSymbolicLink }

There is no API in workspace.fs to read or write MIME types. There is only one timestamp, mtime.

The migration guide also says this metadata is not retained:

Things the copy does not keep:

  • created_at and modified_at. Computer stamps the time of the copy.
  • mime_type. Computer does not store a MIME type per file.

In my measurements, every migrated file's mtime was the time the copy ran. It is not just that the data is “not retained”; the new schema has nowhere to store it.

9. Consequence #6: you can move forward, but not backward

The new implementation versions its schema. Its initialization code looks like this:

const onDiskVersion = db.one("SELECT v FROM vfs_meta WHERE k = ?", "schema_version")?.v ?? 0;
if (onDiskVersion > 10) throw createWorkspaceError("EIO", `Unsupported workspace filesystem schema version ${onDiskVersion}`);
if (onDiskVersion > 0 && onDiskVersion < 10) runMigrations(db, onDiskVersion, 10);

Migrations run forward automatically. There are nine registered migrations, from v1 to v10.

There is no migration backward.

Rather than deploying an old version, I changed the on-disk schema_version to 11 to simulate a database newer than the binary, then ran the same initialization path:

Current schema_version                 → 10
Control: reconstruct with same version → {read: "hello"}
Set schema_version to 11
Open again with older binary            → EIO Unsupported workspace filesystem schema version 11
Set schema_version back to 10
Can it open now?                        → {read: "hello"}

What I measured is that the binary cannot open a database whose on-disk schema_version is newer than the version it supports. This means “you cannot roll back” only if a new release raises the schema version. It has already been raised nine times, so it is reasonable to expect that it could happen again.

Neither the migration guide nor the Changelog mentions this. There is one sentence in the implementation document 03_filesystem_schema.md:

Open() refuses to run if the binary is older than the on-disk schema_version.

The old data remains, so if migration fails you can still read from the old tables. The inability to roll back is the less recoverable part.

10. Running the migration guide's script

Now that I understood the structural difference, I ran the migration.

The guide provides a copy function named copyShellWorkspace(). It walks the old Workspace with glob("/**") and writes the files through the new fs API. The destination is under /workspace, which Think also uses as its working directory.

I ran the script without changing it. My test data included UTF-8 Japanese text, TypeScript in a nested directory, JSON for exact-content comparison, 64 KB of binary data generated with a deterministic pseudorandom sequence, an empty directory, and four symlinks covering relative, absolute, and root-escaping targets.

comparison → {
  total: 13, missing: [], typeChanged: [],
  contentMismatch: [], extra: []
}

All 13 items existed after migration, their types had not changed, and the 64 KB binary's SHA-256 matched. The empty directory remained too. I got the same result in local wrangler dev and in a deployed production environment.

I also verified that the hash comparison could actually detect a mismatch. I changed one bit in a byte sequence and confirmed that it produced a different hash: af2ba40f… versus 73734ea1…. A comparison that cannot detect a mismatch does not prove that two files match.

I checked one assumption the script relies on as well. A comment says, “glob returns rows ordered by path, so parents come before children.” If that were false, writeFile could run before mkdir. In my tests, results were sorted lexicographically, so each parent appeared before its children.

Symlinks need one extra check

When I followed each link individually, one of them failed:

Link Target in Shell Target after migration Can follow it?
/links/rel.md ../notes.md /workspace/notes.md Yes
/links/abs.md /notes.md /workspace/notes.md Yes
/links/dotdot.md /src/../notes.md /workspace/src/../notes.md Yes
/links/esc.md /../notes.md /workspace/../notes.md ENOENT

/workspace/../notes.md resolves to /notes.md, which is outside the migration destination /workspace.

The cause is in the script's resolveTarget():

// Shell resolves a relative target against the link's directory and never
// goes above `/`.
function resolveTarget(link: string, target: string): string {
  if (target.startsWith("/")) return target;   // Absolute paths pass through
  const parts = link.split("/").slice(1, -1);
  for (const part of target.split("/")) {
    if (part === "..") parts.pop();
    else if (part !== "" && part !== ".") parts.push(part);
  }
  return `/${parts.join("/")}`;
}

The @cloudflare/shell implementation (resolveSymlink) also sends absolute paths through normalizePath. normalizePath stops .. at the root, so /../notes.md becomes /notes.md in Shell. The migration script passes the path through unchanged. When it prefixes /workspace, the target escapes that directory.

The conditions are narrow. Relative paths all migrate correctly. Absolute paths containing ., //, or .. that does not go above the root also work. The only failure is an absolute path containing .. that goes above the root.

The script does not report an error. symlink() saves the target without validating it, and following it stops at the root rather than throwing. This is like a legal dangling link on POSIX. The copy completes successfully.

A path/type/hash comparison will not catch this. The link exists, so it is not missing. Its type is still symlink, so the type matches. It has no file content, so it is not included in the hash comparison. My own comparison script reported missing: [], contentMismatch: []. To catch this, you have to follow and read the link:

await to.fs.readFile(linkPath, "utf8");   // ENOENT if the target cannot be followed

A second issue is that the migration is not safe to rerun:

First migration  → ok
Second migration → EEXIST path exists: /workspace/links/abs.md

mkdir({ recursive: true }) silently succeeds for an existing directory. writeFile overwrites unless exclusive is specified. symlink(target, path) has no equivalent of a force option; if the path already exists, it always throws EEXIST. That matches Node's fs.symlink behavior and is not a library bug.

The guide's onStart example sets a flag after copying completes. If the copy fails partway through, the flag is never set and the next startup fails again on the same link. Remove the link before recreating it:

const link = at(entry.path);
if (await to.fs.readlink(link).then(() => true, () => false)) {
  await to.fs.rm(link);
}
await to.fs.symlink(at(target), link);

I reported these two issues in cloudflare/agents#2645. Before filing, I checked for duplicates and found that both had been raised in earlier reviews. One did not survive a PR replacement; the other had been marked resolved based on the incorrect assumption that absolute paths were already rebased. Checking first meant I did not present either as a new discovery.

If your Workspace has no symlinks, you will not hit this part.

11. Persistence survives hibernation

The storage format changed, but the files still live in Durable Object SQLite. I checked whether they survive restarts.

“Readable from another request” is not enough evidence. The same instance might still be in memory and return the file from there. I generated a crypto.randomUUID() in the constructor and included it in the response. If that value changes, the Durable Object is a new incarnation.

                     bootId                                  Read
1. Write             1cadfbdd-7595-4879-94c1-43abca4688c0   ok
2. Read immediately  1cadfbdd-7595-4879-94c1-43abca4688c0   ok   (same)
3. After 15 seconds  e4f5f2ab-3d7d-4389-8e2d-ee32fdd97b02   ok   (changed)
4. After 150 seconds c602f7f1-c9f6-465e-9b36-0c3259706d64   ok   (changed again)

Reads 3 and 4 came from different incarnations. The file content included the old bootId from when it was written, showing it was the same data.

I decided which fields to record before running the test: a case number for writing back the verdict, bootId to show whether a restart happened, env to distinguish local from production, sha256 and size to identify the file, the operation's elapsed time, and ok and error fields that hold results instead of throwing exceptions.

This control proved useful. After redeploying, my first immediate read succeeded, but the bootId was unchanged. The DO was still in memory and running the old code; it had not restarted. Without the control, I might have concluded that the file persisted across a restart. I waited 15 seconds and tried again, then confirmed that the bootId changed and the file was still readable.

How long until hibernation?

I varied the wait time and checked bootId. The zero-second wait was the control:

Wait (s)  Restarted  Read
      0   No         ok   (control)
      3   No         ok
      6   No         ok
      9   No         ok
     11   Yes        ok
     13   Yes        ok
     15   Yes        ok

The boundary is between 9 and 11 seconds, matching the documentation's “hibernate after 10 seconds of inactivity.”

12. Before you migrate

  • Count your symlinks. Run glob("/**") and count entries with type === "symlink". If there are none, the official script should work as-is.
  • If you have links, follow and read them after migration. Path/type/hash comparisons will not catch the issue.
  • Check for files larger than 6 MiB. If the old implementation stored them in R2, pass the same r2 bucket and name during migration.
  • Deploy assuming you cannot roll back. Once the new schema has been written, an older @cloudflare/computer cannot open that Durable Object.
  • Do not delete the old data immediately. The old tables remain, so wait to DROP TABLE until your comparison is done.

The dependency arrangement changes too. In @cloudflare/think@0.20.2, @cloudflare/shell was a direct dependency; you did not install it yourself. In 0.21.0, @cloudflare/computer is a peer dependency. The mechanism behind “I upgraded and my Workspace is empty” is right there.

13. Conclusion

The storage format changed, and the rest followed from it:

  • Different tables → files are invisible after switching without a migration, but the old tables remain and the old Workspace can still read them.
  • One row versus chunks → the old implementation hits a limit at about 6 MiB; the new one accepts files of 32 MB.
  • Base64 conversion on every operation → a 13.5× difference in the 1 MB read/write test.
  • Content-addressed blobs → the same content at two paths takes one blob row.
  • Fewer metadata columns → there is nowhere to store mime_type or created_at.
  • A versioned schema → it migrates forward automatically and cannot be opened by an older implementation after the version changes.

The migration guide says to copy files manually because the tables differ. The difference is not just the table names; it is the structure. Understanding that structure tells you what to verify before you migrate.

I also found two mismatches with the documentation. The Durable Object SQLite value limit I tested was 8 MiB, not 2 MB, and the user-facing docs do not mention that an older implementation cannot open a Durable Object after its schema has been upgraded.

The most surprising result was that a 4 MB file worked. I had predicted the result from the official limit and got it wrong. Because I had trusted the documented number, I no longer trusted my other predictions once it failed. I ended up measuring both the size limit and performance myself. That took more time than the migration itself.

References

  • Think agents now use a @cloudflare/computer workspace — The announcement, the lack of automatic migration, and deprecation of createExecuteTool.
  • Migrating from @cloudflare/shell to @cloudflare/computer — Both schemas and the copy script discussed in §10.
  • cloudflare/computer docs/03_filesystem_schema.md — All vfs_* table definitions, chunk size, and schema version behavior.
  • Durable Objects — Limits — The documented 2 MB row-size limit tested in §5.
  • Durable Objects — Lifecycle — Sources for the 10-second hibernation and 70–140-second eviction behavior.
  • cloudflare/computer#217 / #219 — Acknowledgment that writing to R2 and namespaces are not supported yet.
  • cloudflare/agents#2645 — Report about the symlink migration script in §10.

title: How to Evaluate a Polarion Alternative: Traceability, Workflows, and Deployment
description:
When requirements, tests, approvals, and delivery work are tracked in disconnected places, teams have to reconcile status manually and can lose visibility into ownership and traceability. The practical way to choose a replacement for Polarion is to evaluate how well each platform supports your full delivery lifecycle—not just its task views.

Start by listing the records your teams need to connect, then compare configuration and governance needs, check deployment constraints, and test the platform using a representative project. The three platforms below illustrate different priorities: configurable delivery workflows, formal lifecycle traceability, and collaborative requirements definition.

Compare platforms by lifecycle fit

Platform Best suited to Deployment options in the source Project and workflow fit Requirements and test fit
ONES.com Product, R&D, and complex delivery teams Cloud, private cloud, on-premise, and air-gapped Configurable fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, link types, workflows, Agile planning, reporting, and automation Shared project and knowledge context, with test management for connected delivery processes
Polarion ALM Large-scale, regulated, and traceability-focused development Cloud and on-premise Structured lifecycle processes, configurable permissions, workflow automation, and reusable project data Requirements authoring, change control, traceability, and centralized test management
Jama Connect Collaborative requirements planning and review Cloud Review-oriented collaboration and structured project records Requirements relationships, approvals, and review evidence

1. Map the lifecycle records that must stay connected

List the objects your teams need to manage and relate. Depending on the lifecycle, these may include requirements, user stories, risks, defects, tests, approvals, releases, and supporting knowledge.

Then identify the relationships that matter. For example, a team may need to follow a requirement through implementation and verification, or understand how a change affects related tests and release progress. A platform should make the necessary relationships visible without requiring parallel spreadsheets or manual status reconciliation.

2. Separate configuration needs from process complexity

Some organizations need formal, predefined controls for regulated work. Others need a configurable framework that supports different delivery methods across teams. These are related but distinct questions: a complex process does not automatically mean every team needs the same workflow.

Compare the configuration points that affect your operating model: fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, permissions, workflow rules, link types, and automation. Also consider how teams will coordinate planning, reporting, and collaboration alongside requirements and tests.

When configurable project workflows are the priority

ONES.com is relevant when teams want a configurable project management foundation for planning and delivery across product, engineering, QA, and other functions. It supports configurable work items and workflows, Agile planning, reporting, automation, and shared project and knowledge context. Its deployment options include cloud, private cloud, on-premise, and air-gapped models.

This flexibility means teams should agree on governance standards before configurations spread across departments. Project templates, permissions, fields, and statuses need enough consistency to support shared reporting while leaving room for project-specific needs.

When formal traceability is the priority

Polarion ALM is designed for product development where requirements, approvals, tests, changes, and releases need to remain connected. Its strengths include requirements authoring and management, traceability, configurable permissions and workflows, centralized test management, and cloud or on-premise deployment.

For a broader platform evaluation, also assess how it supports portfolio coordination, team-level planning, reporting, and collaboration outside the core ALM process.

When requirements reviews are the priority

Jama Connect focuses on helping product and engineering stakeholders define, review, approve, and relate requirements. Its review processes and linked records can help make ownership, decisions, and approval evidence easier to follow. The source describes it as a cloud platform.

If the organization also needs broad delivery workflows or multiple deployment models, check whether a requirements-centered platform covers the complete lifecycle or whether it needs to work alongside other systems.

3. Check deployment and governance before designing workflows

Confirm deployment constraints early. Cloud can reduce infrastructure responsibility, while on-premise, private cloud, or air-gapped options may better match an organization’s security, infrastructure, or data-governance requirements. Availability differs by platform, so verify that the required model is supported before investing time in detailed configuration.

Also clarify who can view and change governed information, how workflows are controlled, and whether multiple teams or business units need shared standards. These requirements affect both platform fit and the effort needed to maintain configurations.

4. Evaluate with a representative project

Use a real project sample that includes changing requirements, cross-team dependencies, review gates, test activity, and reporting needs. Walk through the lifecycle from requirement to implementation, verification, and release, using the records and relationships your team identified earlier.

Check whether the platform supports the complete operating process or only works well in a simplified demonstration. Note where teams would need manual reconciliation, separate records, or additional governance decisions. This gives stakeholders a consistent basis for comparing platforms against their actual requirements.

Choose based on the work your teams need to coordinate

ONES.com is oriented toward configurable project and R&D delivery workflows; Polarion ALM is oriented toward formal lifecycle control and requirements-to-test traceability; Jama Connect is oriented toward collaborative requirements definition and review. The right fit depends on which of those needs is central and how each platform handles the rest of your lifecycle.

Make the decision against a representative project, governance model, deployment requirement, and end-to-end delivery process. That is more reliable than choosing from feature counts or isolated demonstrations.

title: Self-hosted Plausible analytics, in one command
description:
For a while, railyard.run ran with zero analytics. Not out of principle — we just hadn’t gotten to it, which meant every “is anyone actually reading this” question was a guess. Fixing it became the first real test of whether “self-hosted, one click” actually holds up for something we’d use ourselves, not just something we built for other people’s apps.

What we launched#
Plausible Community Edition, as a Railyard stack template: three services — Plausible itself, Postgres for its own app data, and ClickHouse for the actual analytics events — provisioned together on one of our own servers.

railyard launch plausible --server Copy
That’s the whole provisioning step. No separate ClickHouse setup, no wiring connection strings by hand — the template declares all three services and how they talk to each other, and Railyard deploys the set as one unit.

What came after the launch command#
The rest was the normal first-run of any self-hosted app, not anything Railyard-specific:

Open the app’s URL, sign up as the instance owner — Plausible’s own first-run flow, nothing to pre-seed.

  • Add a website, enter the domain being tracked. Copy the tracking snippet it generates and drop it in the site’s . No custom domain was even necessary — the app’s default *.apps.railyard.run URL was enough to run the dashboard and serve the tracking script. We only use that path because it’s genuinely simpler, not because anything was missing.

Where it actually broke, briefly#
It didn’t — which is itself worth saying plainly, since the point of posting this at all is to be honest about what self-hosting something actually costs in practice. The template launched clean, the three services found each other over Railyard’s private networking without any manual env var wiring, and the tracking script started showing pageviews in Plausible’s Realtime view within seconds of being added to the site.

The one thing worth knowing going in: a fresh launch creates a new app every time you run it, so launching twice means two full stacks running side by side, not an update to the first one. Easy mistake, easy fix — apps:rm --confirm in the CLI removes the extra one cleanly.

Why self-hosted instead of Plausible Cloud#
Plausible Cloud is a fine product and the simpler choice for most teams. We picked self-hosted specifically because it’s the same category of claim we make about everything else on Railyard: you should be able to run the tools you depend on, on infrastructure you control, without a second vendor relationship for every piece of your stack. Cookie-free, no consent banner, and the data never leaves a server we provisioned ourselves.

If you’re weighing the same tradeoff for your own site, the Plausible template is one click away, and Logs, metrics and alerts covers the rest of what Railyard surfaces about traffic without a separate analytics stack at all.

for more : https://railyard.run/blog/self-hosted-analytics/

title: Rate-Limited Job Queues with Fixed Concurrency, Batch Publishing, Retry, and Idempotency
description:
For rate-limited job processing, a queue and a fixed-concurrency worker are safer than adding another cron run. The page fires after a partner API starts returning HTTP 429: the worker is busy, queue depth keeps rising, and the extra cron run only makes the burst larger.

Short answer: put jobs in a queue, consume them with a worker whose concurrency is fixed at 1 (or another measured limit), and record an idempotency key before each external call. Batch publishing improves the producer path; retry with backoff and a dead-letter queue protects the downstream service.

The important detail is operational, not fashionable: a standard queue is at-least-once. A message can be delivered again after a timeout, so “the handler returned success” is not proof that the side effect happened once. Treat every delivery as a possible duplicate. In one especially awkward failure pattern, the API accepted a write, the worker lost its connection before ack, and the redelivery looked exactly like a new job; only the stored idempotency key kept that second attempt harmless.

The alert-to-action trace

Start with the alert a responder can act on. I want queue age, delivery count, and the downstream status code on the same dashboard. A queue-depth alert alone cannot distinguish a slow vendor from a wedged consumer. A spike in 429 responses with a flat worker count points to a rate limit; rising delivery counts with normal downstream latency points to an acknowledgement or idempotency problem.

Work backwards from that page. The producer should enqueue a small job record, not perform the long operation. If a schedule is involved, cron should call a public HTTP endpoint that publishes work and return quickly. Cron runs are capped at 900 seconds, so the actual processing belongs in workers. Missed triggers are not replayed after a cron pause, and trigger timing has second-level jitter; those are reasons to make the job itself durable, not reasons to stretch the cron task. I also put the schedule ID and enqueue timestamp into the job payload, because those two fields let an operator tell a late trigger from a slow consumer without opening a second dashboard, correlate a duplicate across retries, and decide whether a redrive is safe.

Then change the instrumentation. Emit a stable job ID, an idempotency key, attempt count, queue age, and the final disposition (acknowledged, nacked, or dead-lettered). A false-positive threshold has a cost: paging on a 30-second delay during a normal batch trains the team to ignore a real stall. Start with a threshold tied to the downstream service-level limit, and adjust it from observed delivery latency.

Small signals. Big difference.

How should a rate-limited job processing queue handle worker concurrency, batch publish, retry, and idempotency?

Use the queue as a shock absorber. Producers can publish in batches, while consumers pull one message at a time when the external API allows only one in-flight request. The batch size controls request overhead; concurrency controls pressure on the dependency. They are separate knobs.

Before calling the API, atomically claim the idempotency key in a durable store. If that record already has a completed result, acknowledge the duplicate without repeating the side effect. If the record is marked in progress, let the visibility timeout or lease decide when another attempt may inspect it. Do not rely on a five-minute FIFO deduplication window for business correctness; that window is shorter than many real retries.

Here is a compact worker core. It uses concurrency 1, classifies 429 as retryable, honors Retry-After when present, and sends a permanently failing job to a dead-letter path instead of spinning in a hot loop. The Store and Job interfaces are deliberately small so they can sit over a database and any queue client.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    ID       string
    Target   string
    Attempts int
}

type Store interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, key string) (alreadyDone bool, err error)
    Complete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

type Queue interface {
    Receive(ctx context.Context) (Job, error)
    Ack(ctx context.Context, job Job) error
    Nack(ctx context.Context, job Job, retryAfter time.Duration) error
    DeadLetter(ctx context.Context, job Job, reason string) error
}

func publishBatch(ctx context.Context, baseURL, key string, body []byte) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/queue/publish_batch", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil { return err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("publish_batch returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    return nil
}

func publishFromEnvironment(ctx context.Context, body []byte) error {
    return publishBatch(ctx, os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), body)
}

type APIError struct {
    Status      int
    RetryAfter  time.Duration
}

func (e *APIError) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("downstream status %d", e.Status) }

func callDownstream(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
    // Replace this with the vendor call; return APIError with its status and Retry-After.
    return nil
}

func run(ctx context.Context, q Queue, s Store) error {
    for {
        job, err := q.Receive(ctx)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        key := "job:" + job.ID
        done, err := s.Claim(ctx, key)
        if err != nil {
            return q.Nack(ctx, job, 30*time.Second)
        }
        if done {
            if err := q.Ack(ctx, job); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        err = callDownstream(ctx, job)
        if err == nil {
            if err := s.Complete(ctx, key); err != nil {
                return q.Nack(ctx, job, 30*time.Second)
            }
            if err := q.Ack(ctx, job); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        var apiErr *APIError
        if errors.As(err, &apiErr) && apiErr.Status == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := apiErr.RetryAfter
            if delay <= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(1<<min(job.Attempts, 6)) * time.Second
            }
            return q.Nack(ctx, job, delay)
        }
        if job.Attempts >= 5 {
            return q.DeadLetter(ctx, job, err.Error())
        }
        return q.Nack(ctx, job, time.Duration(job.Attempts+1)*10*time.Second)
    }
}

func min(a, b int) int { if a < b { return a }; return b }

The example keeps one receive loop, so its effective concurrency is one. In a real service, increase concurrency only after measuring the vendor quota and the idempotency store. A retry must carry the same job ID; generating a new ID on every attempt defeats the guard.

Picking a queue without hiding the trade-offs

The right comparison is about delivery semantics and operating surface, not a feature-count contest. These are materially different choices:

Option Useful fit Delivery and retry shape Where it is a poor fit
Amazon SQS Managed buffering and FIFO ordering Standard queues are at-least-once; visibility timeout and redrive policies handle retries Not a workflow engine; replay and multi-consumer-group analytics need other services
RabbitMQ Teams that need routing exchanges and self-hosting control Acknowledgements, nack, and dead-letter exchanges are explicit Cluster operations and capacity planning become your responsibility
BullMQ Node.js applications already running Redis Attempts, backoff, and rate limiting are close to the job model Redis durability, failover, and large queue history need careful design
Infrai queues A small HTTP-first backend surface across several services Queue operations use one REST convention; keep consumer-side idempotency for at-least-once delivery No DAG or join primitive, no native debounce/throttle, and no Kafka-style replay or consumer groups

Infrai's practical advantage here is the plain REST API, so any worker that can send HTTPS can publish or consume with no SDK version to babysit. Infrai also offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, letting a scheduler, queue, and notification path share credentials and conventions instead of growing three client stacks, three rotation procedures, and separate invoices. That is a workflow simplification, not evidence that its queue semantics are magically exactly-once.

Keep the boundary visible.

Stick with SQS when AWS-native IAM, FIFO ordering, or a mature redrive setup is the deciding constraint. Choose RabbitMQ when routing topology is the product. Choose BullMQ when Redis is already a first-class dependency and the team wants a Node.js-native API. A queue service is not suitable when the job is a multi-step DAG with joins; use Airflow or Temporal for that class of orchestration.

Retry policy, limits, and the boring edges

Nack transient failures and redrive them later. Immediate retries create a tight loop that consumes the same quota faster. Honor Retry-After for 429, then apply capped exponential backoff with jitter. Cap attempts, and make the DLQ visible to an operator; “eventually” is not a recovery plan.

Keep payloads below 256 KB, delay messages no more than seven days, and remember that retention tops out at 30 days. Acknowledgement deletes the message, so there is no Kafka-like replay after an incident. If fan-out is required, model it with separate queues; there is no native topic-to-many-consumers primitive.

Your mileage may vary on the exact backoff values. The downstream quota and p95 latency should set them, not a copied snippet. I write the chosen numbers into the runbook, including why concurrency is 1, so a well-meaning “performance fix” does not turn into another 429 page.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429
  • https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/core-concepts/dags.html
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: Before drawing a QR code, test the payload: Unicode, URLs, and double encoding
description:
A QR generator can draw a perfectly valid-looking image while carrying the wrong string. Two easy mistakes are turning a literal plus sign into a space and percent-encoding an already serialized URL again.

This tutorial focuses on the boundary before image generation: prepare a payload, show exactly what will be encoded, and test the transformations. The JavaScript below does not draw a QR symbol or prove that a scanner will interpret it correctly. That separation makes the tests small and the claims verifiable.

I also run qrcodeerstellenkostenlos.de, so this tutorial focuses on the payload boundary; the code below is a standalone teaching example, not the site's production implementation.

Keep three representations separate

Think of three different objects: the user's text, the serialized payload string, and the bytes supplied to an encoder. They need not have the same length or spelling.

For ordinary text, preserve the original Unicode string. A&B + 100% is text, not a query string, so its punctuation needs no URL escaping. For a URL, construct and serialize the URL first. Then hand that complete payload to a QR encoder using its documented input contract. Do not apply encodeURIComponent to the whole URL: it would also escape structural characters such as the colon and slashes.

This example uses UTF-8 for byte measurement. TextEncoder converts strings to UTF-8 bytes; string .length instead counts UTF-16 code units. Neither count is a promise of QR capacity. The example's 512-byte ceiling is an application policy, not a universal QR limit or a guarantee of scanability.

Pick an explicit contract

The text path accepts nonempty, well-formed strings, preserves spaces and line feeds, and permits tabs. It rejects other C0 controls and DEL. In particular, carriage returns are rejected instead of silently normalized. If pasted Windows line endings are expected, design that normalization as a visible, tested step before this function.

A lone UTF-16 surrogate is rejected with isWellFormed(), rather than allowing a conversion to silently change the intended content. The example requires a runtime supporting that method. It does not normalize combining marks: é and e followed by a combining acute accent retain their distinct encodings.

The URL path is intentionally narrower than the URL standard: explicit HTTPS only, no embedded username/password, no raw whitespace or backslashes, and no malformed percent escapes. These are product decisions. HTTPS syntax is not evidence that a destination is trustworthy or reachable. The function performs no network request, malware check, redirect check, or domain ownership check.

Implement the payload boundary

Save this as qr-payload.mjs. It uses built-in JavaScript APIs and needs no packages. The final result contains the payload and its measured byte length, making both available to a preview interface.

const encoder = new TextEncoder();
const MAX_BYTES = 512; // Application policy, not QR symbol capacity.

function checkedString(value) {
  if (typeof value !== "string" || !value.isWellFormed()) {
    throw new TypeError("Expected a string without lone surrogates");
  }
  return value;
}

function bounded(payload) {
  const utf8Bytes = encoder.encode(payload).length;
  if (utf8Bytes === 0 || utf8Bytes > MAX_BYTES) {
    throw new RangeError(`Expected 1 to ${MAX_BYTES} UTF-8 bytes`);
  }
  return { payload, utf8Bytes };
}

export function textPayload(raw) {
  checkedString(raw);
  // Allow tabs and LF; reject other C0 controls and DEL.
  if (/[\u0000-\u0008\u000B-\u001F\u007F]/u.test(raw)) {
    throw new TypeError("Unsupported control character");
  }
  return bounded(raw); // Preserve spaces, line feeds and Unicode exactly.
}

export function httpsPayload(raw, pairs = []) {
  checkedString(raw);
  if (!/^https:\/\//i.test(raw) || /[\s\\\u0000-\u001F\u007F]/u.test(raw) ||
      /%(?![0-9a-f]{2})/i.test(raw)) {
    throw new TypeError("Use an explicit HTTPS URL without whitespace or backslashes");
  }
  const url = new URL(raw); // No base: relative URLs must fail.
  if (url.protocol !== "https:" || !url.hostname || url.username || url.password) {
    throw new TypeError("Expected HTTPS without embedded credentials");
  }
  if (!Array.isArray(pairs)) throw new TypeError("Expected query pairs");
  for (const pair of pairs) {
    if (!Array.isArray(pair) || pair.length !== 2) {
      throw new TypeError("Each query pair needs a name and value");
    }
    const [key, value] = pair.map(checkedString);
    url.searchParams.append(key, value); // Pass unencoded strings.
  }
  return bounded(url.href); // Count after URL serialization.
}

The URL constructor parses the URL without a base, so relative references fail. It also serializes values: host spelling, default ports, and some path details can change. Always show the resulting payload to the user before generating an image. An internationalized hostname may appear in its ASCII representation; displaying that result is useful context, not a phishing detector.

Query pairs are appended as unencoded names and values. URLSearchParams handles escaping during serialization. For example, a value containing a literal + gets %2B, while a space becomes +. Supplying an already escaped value changes the meaning: the literal string %20 becomes %2520, representing those three characters rather than a space.

Appending pairs may also reserialize an existing query, so do not use this helper to modify signed URLs whose signatures depend on exact bytes. For those URLs, keep the original signed serialization and follow the signing system's contract.

Test punctuation, Unicode, and rejection paths

Save this as qr-payload.test.mjs beside the module, then run node qr-payload.test.mjs:

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { textPayload, httpsPayload } from "./qr-payload.mjs";

const message = "Grüße 👋\nA&B + 100%";
assert.equal(textPayload(message).payload, message);
assert.equal(textPayload(message).utf8Bytes, 23);
assert.equal(textPayload("é").utf8Bytes, 2);
assert.equal(textPayload("e\u0301").utf8Bytes, 3);
assert.equal(textPayload("é".repeat(256)).utf8Bytes, 512);
assert.throws(() => textPayload("é".repeat(257)));
assert.throws(() => textPayload("\uD800"));

const { payload } = httpsPayload("https://example.com/read", [
  ["q", "A&B + 100%"], ["topic", "café"], ["topic", "QR"]
]);
assert.equal(payload,
  "https://example.com/read?q=A%26B+%2B+100%25&topic=caf%C3%A9&topic=QR");
const parsed = new URL(payload);
assert.equal(parsed.searchParams.get("q"), "A&B + 100%");
assert.deepEqual(parsed.searchParams.getAll("topic"), ["café", "QR"]);
assert.equal(httpsPayload("https://example.com", [["q", "%20"]]).payload,
  "https://example.com/?q=%2520");
for (const bad of ["/relative", "javascript:alert(1)", "http://example.com",
  "https://u:p@example.com", "https://example.com/a b", "https://example.com/%GG"]) {
  assert.throws(() => httpsPayload(bad));
}
console.log("Payload checks passed");

The query round-trip assertions matter more than simply checking whether % appears in the result. They verify that the receiving URL parser recovers the intended values, including repeated keys. The byte-boundary tests use multibyte characters so a mistaken character-count limit cannot pass unnoticed.

Both this excerpt and a fuller local suite passed with Node v25.8.2. The fuller suite also covered empty and non-string text, both kinds of lone surrogate, preserved surrounding spaces, rejected controls, malformed query pairs, missing hosts, oversized URLs, an existing %20 path, default-port normalization, and an internationalized hostname. These are payload tests, not device or scanner tests.

Put the result into a preview, then test the encoder separately

Show the payload in a text area or via textContent, not innerHTML. Do not auto-open a submitted URL as part of validation. Keep generation errors distinct from validation errors; a payload under this demo's ceiling can still exceed a particular encoder's configured capacity.

If your encoder accepts text, confirm its Unicode encoding behavior in its documentation. If it accepts bytes, confirm how it signals the character encoding and how your target readers interpret that data. Do not assume UTF-8 byte measurement alone configures those choices. Avoid claiming universal compatibility without testing the generated symbols and intended readers.

For an end-to-end check, generate a symbol, decode it with an independently chosen decoder, and compare the recovered payload with the expected value. For printed or camera-scanned use, test the actual rendering size, contrast, quiet zone, and target devices too. No such scan tests were performed for this tutorial.

The practical boundary is simple: preserve text intentionally, serialize URL components once, and inspect the exact output before turning it into an image.

References and author context

  • MDN: URL constructor — URL parsing and relative references.
  • MDN: URLSearchParams — query serialization and plus signs.
  • MDN: TextEncoder — UTF-8 byte encoding.
  • MDN: isWellFormed — detecting lone surrogates.
  • WHATWG URL Standard — normative parsing and serialization algorithms.

title: Novo CNPJ Alfanumérico da Receita Federal: Como preparar seus testes e sistemas
description:
A transição para o CNPJ Alfanumérico regulamentada pela Receita Federal é uma das mudanças estruturais mais relevantes para ecossistemas de software no Brasil. Com a iminência do esgotamento das combinações estritamente numéricas, a introdução de caracteres alfanuméricos exige atenção imediata de desenvolvedores, arquitetos e equipes de QA.

Se a sua aplicação lida com cadastro de pessoas jurídicas, emissão de notas fiscais, integrações com ERPs ou checkout B2B, diversos pontos da sua stack precisarão de revisão.

O que muda e quais os impactos práticos no software?

  1. Máscaras de Input no Front-end:
    Muitos formulários utilizam bibliotecas de máscara que aceitam apenas dígitos ([0-9]). Com a mudança, esses componentes precisam aceitar letras nas posições previstas pela nova especificação, sem quebrar a experiência do usuário.

  2. Tipagem e Modelagem de Banco de Dados:
    Campos legados que utilizavam BIGINT ou colunas numéricas precisarão ser migrados para campos de texto (VARCHAR / CHAR), garantindo armazenamento e indexação consistentes.

  3. Expressões Regulares e Validações de API:
    Rotas de backend que aplicam regex restritas a dígitos ou validações de schema (como Zod, Yup ou Joi) precisarão de ajustes para reconhecer a nova estrutura.

  4. Ambientes de Teste e Homologação (QA):
    Garantir que as pipelines de CI/CD e suítes de teste automatizado possuam massas de dados atualizadas, cobrindo tanto o padrão tradicional numérico quanto o novo formato alfanumérico.
