title: How to Check Feature Flags in Express Middleware in 2026 — SaaS Route Gating
description:
An Express middleware feature flag check should gate the Node.js API route on the server, cache the decision briefly, and leave the known-good notification path available. That gives the on-call one reversible action: disable risky delivery behavior without redeploying.

TL;DR: Poll a flag such as notification_bulk_send_v2, cache the last valid result briefly, and check the customer's entitlement separately. A flag is a release control, not authorization. For rollback safety, the old delivery path must remain deployable and observable until the new path has survived the rollback window.

This article uses Go because the control flow is easier to see without framework machinery. The same boundary fits Express middleware: lookup, cache, decide, then call the next handler or return a controlled response.

What should the on-call see when delivery fails?

Start at the page. It should identify the affected operation, the flag key, the deployed version, the last successful delivery time, and whether the fallback path is healthy. The operator needs enough context to choose between disabling a release path and investigating a provider failure. Those are different incidents.

The earlier signal is a sustained change in delivery outcomes split by flag state. A raw error count is weak: traffic changes can move it without changing reliability. Compare failures and attempts for the flagged path, and keep the old path's series beside it. Set the threshold from the service's error budget and traffic floor, not from a round number copied from another service.

There is an important system boundary here. Infrai's feature-flag client is polling-based, and its observability surface does not supply threshold notification delivery. Use the flag API for evaluation, then let Datadog monitors, Grafana Alerting, or Sentry alerts page on the delivery ratio. Datadog fits teams already correlating managed metrics and service telemetry; Grafana fits teams that want alert rules near their existing dashboards and data sources; Sentry fits application error triage better than general job-heartbeat monitoring. A heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks.io should cover the separate case where the notification job never ran, because no delivery event exists to count.

No events means no ratio.

False positives have a real cost. Suppose the first failure after a quiet hour makes the short-window ratio look catastrophic: an automatic toggle can disable a healthy premium feature before enough attempts exist to support the conclusion. The old path then receives traffic, its queue depth changes, and the incident channel has to distinguish a real provider problem from a control action triggered by thin data. Require a minimum sample, use at least one longer confirmation window, page before automating rollback, and record the operator's decision in the incident timeline. The exact sample and window belong to the service's traffic model and error budget; inventing universal numbers would hide the trade-off.

How should Express middleware check a feature flag for Node.js route gating?

The invariant is blunt: no request reaches the new delivery handler unless both the release flag and the entitlement check pass. Browser flags may hide a button, but clients only poll and can be modified by the user. The server owns the decision.

This runnable program models the middleware boundary, a five-second cache, a boolean is_enabled lookup, and a separate plan check. Replace memoryFlags.IsEnabled with a provider adapter in production; keep the middleware contract unchanged.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

const bulkSendFlag = "notification_bulk_send_v2"

type FlagSource interface {
    IsEnabled(context.Context, string) (bool, error)
}

type infraiFlags struct {
    apiKey string
    client *http.Client
}

func (f *infraiFlags) IsEnabled(ctx context.Context, key string) (bool, error) {
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc"
    flagPath := strings.Join([]string{"", "v1", "flags", "is_enabled", url.PathEscape(key)}, "/")
    requestURL := baseURL + flagPath
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, requestURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+f.apiKey)

        resp, err := f.client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return false, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            resp.Body.Close()
            return false, fmt.Errorf("flag check returned %s", resp.Status)
        }
        var result struct {
            Data struct {
                Enabled bool `json:"enabled"`
            } `json:"data"`
        }
        err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&result)
        resp.Body.Close()
        return result.Data.Enabled, err
    }
    return false, fmt.Errorf("flag check rate limited after retries")
}

type cachedFlag struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    source  FlagSource
    ttl     time.Duration
    value   bool
    expires time.Time
}

func (c *cachedFlag) enabled(ctx context.Context, key string) (bool, error) {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()
    if time.Now().Before(c.expires) {
        return c.value, nil
    }
    value, err := c.source.IsEnabled(ctx, key)
    if err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    c.value, c.expires = value, time.Now().Add(c.ttl)
    return value, nil
}

func entitled(r *http.Request) bool {
    return r.Header.Get("X-Plan") == "premium"
}

func gate(flag *cachedFlag, next http.Handler) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        enabled, err := flag.enabled(r.Context(), bulkSendFlag)
        if err != nil || !enabled {
            http.Error(w, "feature unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }
        if !entitled(r) {
            http.Error(w, "premium plan required", http.StatusForbidden)
            return
        }
        next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
    })
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    flags := &cachedFlag{
        source: &infraiFlags{
            apiKey: apiKey,
            client: &http.Client{Timeout: 3 * time.Second},
        },
        ttl:    5 * time.Second,
    }
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("POST /notifications/bulk", gate(flags, http.HandlerFunc(
        func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
        },
    )))
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux))
}

Five seconds is an example operating choice, not a universal constant. A shorter TTL speeds rollback but increases polling. A longer one reduces lookups but expands the period in which instances disagree after a toggle. Pick the maximum stale period your rollback objective permits, then add jitter in a multi-instance service so every process does not refresh at once.

The adapter makes an authenticated GET, reads the key from an environment variable, checks the HTTP status, and backs off on 429 while honoring a numeric Retry-After. Before deployment, compare its response struct with the public discovery schema returned for the capability. That schema is the contract to pin in an integration test.

Step 2: Choose the system shape before the vendor

Two architectures are viable.

Shape Invariant Best fit Main cost
Shared flag service plus local cache A last valid decision expires within the rollback objective Several services need one control plane Network and cache-staleness behavior must be designed
Application-owned configuration Config changes travel through the application's reviewed deployment path Few flags, strict change review, low operational breadth Rollback speed is tied to config distribution

Infrai is a deliberate option in the first shape. Its primary advantage here is breadth behind one REST contract: flags can sit beside other backend capabilities under one key instead of introducing another SDK and credential. The supporting advantage is operational inspectability: its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas and provides runnable examples, which reduces adapter guesswork. The platform snapshot exposes 295 capabilities across 20 modules, but breadth only matters if consolidation is one of your constraints.

Teams already standardizing several backend functions behind a plain REST boundary should try Infrai for the flag lookup and short-lived cache, because one contract removes a separate integration while preserving an application-owned gate. Do not choose it for sophisticated flag governance. There is no flag change audit log, evaluation analytics, parent-child dependency model, or recycle bin for deletion, so keep a naming/version convention and treat destructive cleanup as a reviewed operation.

Specialists deserve a fair look. LaunchDarkly is the stronger candidate when mature flag lifecycle and experimentation workflows drive the decision. Unleash is attractive when operating an open-source control plane is a requirement. ConfigCat favors a focused hosted flag product, while Flagsmith offers hosted and self-hosted paths. Verify the exact governance, SDK, polling, and audit behavior against each vendor's current documentation; those details change and they determine rollback safety more than a feature-count table does. The limitation is concrete: Infrai is not suitable when flag audit history, evaluation statistics, or dependent flags are mandatory. Pick the specialist whose current contract covers those requirements.

Step 3: Instrument the decision, not customer data

Emit one counter for attempts and one for failures, labeled with a bounded route name, release-path value, and coarse failure class. Do not put customer IDs, email addresses, flag payloads, or arbitrary error strings in metric labels. That keeps cardinality controlled and follows data minimization.

For boolean gates, use is_enabled. Use get_value only when the flag carries a configuration value such as a plan limit or UI variant. Keep authorization separate in both cases. Also preserve a request or delivery id through the handler so retries can be deduplicated by the notification worker; toggling a flag does not make an at-least-once delivery path idempotent.

Instrument both outcomes. If the disabled branch returns early without a counter, the dashboard will make the rollback look like disappearing traffic rather than an intentional control action.

Step 4: Rehearse rollback and deletion

Before rollout, exercise four cases: enabled and entitled, enabled and not entitled, disabled, and flag lookup unavailable. The example fails closed because bulk notification delivery is a premium write action. A read-only cosmetic variant could reasonably serve its stable default instead. Write that choice in the runbook.

Then rehearse the rollback with the old handler still present. Confirm that cached decisions converge inside the declared window, the old path can absorb traffic, and duplicate deliveries are rejected using the delivery id. Do not delete the old flag during the rehearsal. Infrai flag deletion has no recycle bin, so retirement should be a later, reviewed change after all callers and dashboards have stopped referring to the key.

The final decision rule is narrow: use a shared service when multiple applications need a fast, consistent rollback control and can tolerate bounded polling staleness. Keep configuration application-owned when reviewability matters more than independent rollback speed. Choose a specialist when audit history, evaluation statistics, dependencies, or experimentation are requirements.

Further reading

  • Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Flagsmith documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • GDPR Article 5: data minimization

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and inspect the live flag schema before writing the adapter.

title: Hyva Went Free, PWA Studio Wound Down: The Magento Frontend Bet for 2026
description:
Open the network tab on a stock Magento storefront and count the JavaScript. You'll find jQuery, RequireJS pulling in dozens of small AMD modules, and Knockout.js wiring up the cart and checkout, all before a single product image finishes loading. That's the Luma theme, and it's been the default face of Magento for a decade. It's also the reason so many Magento stores quietly fail Core Web Vitals.

For years the escape hatch cost money. Then, in a short stretch of late 2025, the whole frontend question shifted under everyone's feet. Hyva, the server-rendered theme that had become the community's favorite way off Luma, relicensed itself free and open source. And Adobe, meanwhile, let PWA Studio settle into maintenance while it poured its energy into something else entirely. If you're speccing a Magento build for 2026, the menu you're choosing from is not the menu you knew in 2023.

What actually changed in late 2025

Two things happened, and they point in different directions.

Hyva went free. On November 10, 2025, Hyva announced it was relicensing its Theme under OSL-3.0 and AFL-3.0, the exact dual license Magento Open Source itself uses. In their words: "like Magento Open Source, our Theme can be used free of charge and redistributed under commercial licenses." Before that, the Hyva Theme was a paid license, reported by the community at roughly 1,000 euros (a bit over a thousand dollars) per store. That price tag was the single biggest thing keeping teams on Luma out of inertia. Overnight, it was gone.

Adobe moved on from PWA Studio. Not with a funeral, not with a deprecation notice, just with where the roadmap went. Adobe's frontend attention shifted to Edge Delivery Services, and PWA Studio slid into the same maintenance-mode existence Luma has lived in for years. More on exactly what "maintenance mode" means below, because the internet loves to overstate it.

So the free option got better and the Adobe-official option changed identity. Both of those change the answer to "what do I build my storefront on."

Why Luma was always the problem

To understand why Hyva took off, you have to understand what it's running away from. The classic Luma frontend is built on four technologies that all made sense in 2015 and none of which you'd pick today: Knockout.js for data binding, RequireJS for module loading, jQuery for DOM work, and LESS for styles.

The problem isn't that any one of them is terrible. It's the compound weight. RequireJS fetches a long waterfall of tiny JavaScript modules. Knockout stands up an entire MVVM layer to keep the cart and minicart in sync. jQuery sits underneath all of it. The result is a storefront that ships a large JavaScript bundle and does a lot of work on the main thread before the page is interactive, which is precisely what Largest Contentful Paint and Interaction to Next Paint punish you for. Agency migration write-ups routinely describe a Luma product page pulling well over a megabyte of JavaScript across a couple hundred files. You can tune it, you can lazy-load, but you're fighting the architecture the whole way.

Here's the shape of a typical Luma interaction, wired through Knockout's declarative bindings:

<!-- Luma: Knockout binds the DOM to a view model, RequireJS loads the component -->
<div data-bind="scope: 'minicart'">
    <span data-bind="text: getCartParam('summary_count')"></span>
</div>
<script type="text/x-magento-init">
    { "[data-block='minicart']": { "Magento_Ui/js/block-loader": "..." } }
</script>

To make that span update, the browser has loaded RequireJS, resolved the Magento_Ui module graph, instantiated a Knockout view model, and bound it to the DOM. For a number in a corner.

Hyva's bet: ship almost no JavaScript

Hyva made one architectural decision and built everything around it: render on the server, and send the browser almost no JavaScript. It throws out Knockout, RequireJS, jQuery, and LESS entirely, and rebuilds the storefront on just two things: Tailwind CSS for styling and Alpine.js for the small amount of interactivity a page genuinely needs.

Alpine is the key. It's a tiny library that lets you sprinkle behavior directly into markup, no build-time module graph, no view models. That same minicart counter becomes a few attributes on an element:

<!-- Hyva: Alpine holds a little state right in the markup, no module loader -->
<div x-data="{ count: 0 }" @update-cart.window="count = $event.detail.count">
    <span x-text="count"></span>
</div>

No RequireJS waterfall, no Knockout instance. The page arrives fully rendered from the server, and Alpine hydrates the handful of interactive bits. The reason Hyva wins on performance isn't a clever trick, it's subtraction: there's simply far less JavaScript to download, parse, and execute. Teams that migrate consistently report their storefronts moving from failing Core Web Vitals to passing them, and the mechanism is exactly what you'd expect from cutting the main-thread work by an order of magnitude.

Now, the honest part about "free," because it's not quite all-you-can-eat. What went open source is the Hyva Theme and its compatibility modules. Hyva Checkout, Hyva Enterprise, and Hyva Commerce stayed commercial, and the UI kit was split out into its own paid product. So a store built on the free Hyva theme is genuinely free; a store that also wants Hyva's dedicated checkout is still writing a check. That's a fair deal, and it's still a categorically different world than "a thousand dollars per store before you render a single page."

PWA Studio didn't die, it stopped being the plan

Let's be precise here, because this is where hot takes go wrong. PWA Studio, Adobe's React-based headless storefront (the magento/pwa-studio repo and its Venia storefront), is not dead, deprecated, or archived. The repo still gets commits. It's still shipping point releases, with v14.5.1 landing in May 2026. There is no official Adobe end-of-life notice, and if you're running it in production it isn't going to stop working.

What happened is subtler and, for planning purposes, more important: it stopped being where Adobe invests. The releases are compatibility and security work, PHP version bumps, dependency updates, the maintenance you do to keep the lights on, not major new capability. The community consensus, which Adobe hasn't contradicted, is that active feature development wound down and the strategic focus moved elsewhere. In other words, PWA Studio now sits roughly where Luma sits: supported, functional, and not the future.

That's the framing that matters when someone pitches you a new PWA Studio build in 2026. It'll work. But you'd be adopting Adobe's yesterday, not its tomorrow.

Adobe's actual 2026 answer: Edge Delivery Services

Adobe's tomorrow is Edge Delivery Services, the same tech behind its AEM sites, now aimed at Commerce. The pitch is a storefront assembled from Commerce drop-in components (prebuilt, customizable pieces like product details and cart) plus content authored as documents, served from Adobe's edge. Adobe markets it as the path to "the fastest storefronts on the web," and there's a real official starting point: the hlxsites/aem-boilerplate-commerce template repo.

It genuinely is fast, because the model is edge-served and light by design. But go in clear-eyed about the tradeoff, because it's a big one. EDS is a fundamentally different way to build. The document-authoring model, the block-based component system, and the AEM lineage mean your team isn't writing a Magento theme anymore, they're learning a new platform with its own mental model and its own gravity. Adobe presents EDS as its strategic direction rather than publishing a literal "this replaces PWA Studio" statement, but the direction of travel is not subtle.

So what do you actually build on in 2026?

Here's the decision, stripped down.

Luma is legacy. Pick it only if you're maintaining an existing store and a re-theme isn't on the table. It works, it's supported, and it will keep quietly costing you Core Web Vitals. Don't start something new here.

Hyva is the pragmatic default now, and going free is what makes that true. It's server-rendered, it ships almost no JavaScript, the performance story is real, and, crucially, it's still just a Magento theme. Your existing Magento developers can work in it, you can hire for it, and you're not betting the store on a new platform paradigm. For the large majority of Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source builds in 2026, this is the boring, correct answer.

Edge Delivery Services is Adobe's bet on the future and the best raw performance ceiling, but it asks the most. Choose it if you're aligned with Adobe's roadmap, you have a team willing to learn the EDS/AEM model, and top-end speed is a hard business requirement worth a steeper build. It's the strategic pick, with strategic-sized costs.

And if you're a composable shop that wants a fully custom head, the fourth door is still open: build your own frontend (Next.js or Nuxt against Magento's GraphQL API), or use Alokai, the commerce frontend platform that used to be Vue Storefront before its 2024 rebrand. More freedom, more to own.

The through-line is that the cheap, sensible middle finally exists without an asterisk. For years the good answer to "how do I get off Luma" had a thousand-dollar-per-store price attached, and plenty of teams stayed stuck because of it. That barrier is gone. If you're still shipping Knockout and RequireJS to your customers' phones in 2026, the reason can't be budget anymore. It's just habit.

Originally published at andriiboyko.com.

title: Connection Pooling for PostgreSQL Under Real Concurrency
description:
Here's a number worth staring at. In a benchmark Andres Freund ran while working on Postgres connection scalability, one active connection doing simple reads managed 33,457 transactions per second on an otherwise idle server. Add 10,000 connections that do nothing at all, and the same single connection dropped to 14,496 TPS. Nothing else changed. The idle connections weren't running queries. They were just there.

That's the part of connection pooling most teams never think about. They treat pool size as a knob on one service: bump max from 10 to 50 because the API felt slow, ship it, move on. But Postgres doesn't see your services. It sees one flat pile of backend processes, and every service, every replica, every cron job, and every half-finished rolling deploy adds to the same pile.

So let's do this properly. Not "what should max be," but "how do you split one database's real capacity across everything that talks to it, and keep it split when the cluster autoscales at 3pm on a Friday."

What a Postgres connection actually costs

Postgres uses a process-per-connection model. Every client connection gets its own backend process, forked by the postmaster, with its own slot in shared memory and its own row in pg_stat_activity. That's very different from a thread-per-connection database, and it's why the question "how many connections can Postgres handle?" has a more interesting answer than you'd expect.

There are three separate costs, and people usually blame the wrong one.

Memory is smaller than folklore says. You'll read "10MB per connection" in a lot of blog posts. Freund's analysis on the Citus blog measured it properly and found the per-connection overhead is below 2 MiB when the server is configured sensibly, with huge_pages on. That's not free, but it's not the reason your database fell over either. (The shared-memory side is also allocated up front: max_connections sizes the lock tables and process slots at startup, which is one reason changing it needs a restart.)

Snapshots were the real bottleneck, and they got fixed. Every statement takes a snapshot to decide which row versions it can see. Before Postgres 14, building that snapshot meant walking the state of every backend, including the idle ones. In Freund's CPU profile, with one active connection next to 5,000 idle ones, the bottleneck sat squarely in GetSnapshotData(). His fix landed in Postgres 14, and the before/after is dramatic: with 48 active connections and 10,000 idle, throughput went from 369,845 TPS to 1,115,740 TPS on the same hardware (2x Xeon Gold 5215).

Active concurrency is the cost that never goes away. Here's the thing Postgres 14 didn't change and can't change: if 400 connections are all running queries at the same time on a 16-core box, they're fighting over 16 cores, the same buffer pool, the same locks, and the same disk queue. Context switching goes up, cache hit rates go down, lock waits pile on. More concurrent work past the point of saturation doesn't make the database do more. It makes every query slower.

That last point is the whole article in one sentence. Idle connections are now cheap. Active connections are still expensive. Your pooling strategy should be about capping active concurrency at the database, not about hoarding slots.

The formula everyone quotes, and what it really means

The HikariCP wiki's "About Pool Sizing" page is one of the most-cited pieces of writing on this topic, and it opens with a result from Oracle's Real-World Performance group: reducing the connection pool size alone, with no other change, cut application response times from around 100ms to around 2ms. Smaller pool, faster app.

Then it gives its starting-point formula:

connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)

A few details matter here and get lost in the retelling:

  • core_count is the database server's physical cores, not the app server's, and not hyperthreads.
  • effective_spindle_count is how many disk operations can be in flight usefully. On SSD or NVMe, people typically plug in 1 as a starting point. The "extra" connections beyond cores only exist to cover time a backend spends blocked on I/O.
  • The wiki's own example is a 4-core server with one disk: (4 * 2) + 1 = 9, rounded to 10. It claims that setup comfortably serves 3,000 front-end users running simple queries at 6,000 TPS.

And the wiki is explicit that this is a starting point, not a law. Treat it as an order-of-magnitude anchor.

The detail that matters most here: that formula tells you the size of the pool for the whole database. It does not tell you what to put in one service's config. If you have a 16-core database, the formula says somewhere around 33 connections should be actively working at once. If you have eight services each running six replicas, and each replica's pool is sized "by the formula," you've just told the database it should expect 1,584 of them. That's how teams end up quoting HikariCP correctly and still melting their database.

Your real pool size is a multiplication

Let's make it concrete. The following is a hypothetical system, but the shape will look familiar: four workloads on one Postgres primary with 16 physical cores and max_connections = 200.

Workload Replicas (steady) Pool max per replica Connections at steady state
api (Node, pg) 12 10 120
worker (Go, pgxpool) 6 16 96
reporting 2 10 20
cron + migrations + humans with psql varies varies ~5
Total 241

It's already over 200 at steady state, and nothing is misbehaving. Each team picked a reasonable-looking number. Two of those numbers are literally library defaults: pg.Pool defaults max to 10, and pgxpool defaults MaxConns to the greater of 4 or runtime.NumCPU(), so a worker pod on a 16-vCPU node gets 16 without anyone deciding that.

Now add the two things that make this worse at the worst possible moment.

Rolling deploys. A Kubernetes Deployment's maxSurge defaults to 25%. During a rollout, old and new pods coexist, so your 12 API replicas can briefly be 15. That's 30 more connections, and they show up exactly when you're deploying, which is also when you're least prepared to debug FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.

Autoscaling. The HPA scales on CPU or custom metrics. It has no idea your database has a connection budget. When traffic spikes, it'll happily add pods, and each new pod can fill its whole pool as soon as traffic reaches it. The database gets more connections at the exact moment it's getting more load.

And don't forget the slots you can't use. Postgres reserves superuser_reserved_connections (default 3) for superusers, and since Postgres 16 there's also reserved_connections (default 0) for roles granted pg_use_reserved_connections. Those exist so you can still get in and fix things when the app has eaten every other slot. Keep them. Your app budget is max_connections minus those reservations minus whatever replication, monitoring, and migration tooling need.

So the honest formula for a direct-to-Postgres setup is:

sum over services of (pool_max * max_replicas * (1 + surge))
    + ops_and_tooling
    <= max_connections - superuser_reserved_connections - reserved_connections

Notice it uses max_replicas, the HPA ceiling, not today's replica count. If you size against the steady state, the budget holds right up until you need it.

Size each service with Little's Law, not vibes

If the database-wide number comes from cores, where does the per-service number come from? From how long each request actually holds a connection.

Little's Law says the average number of items in a system equals arrival rate times time in the system: L = lambda * W. For a connection pool, L is how many connections are busy on average, lambda is how often the service checks one out, and W is how long it keeps it.

Take a worked example, again with hypothetical numbers. Say one API replica handles 200 requests per second at peak, and each request holds a connection for about 15ms (query time plus the round trips in between, from checkout to release):

busy connections = 200 req/s * 0.015 s = 3

Three connections busy on average. A pool of 10 per replica gives you a lot of headroom for bursts and slow queries. A pool of 50 gives you nothing except the ability to hurt the database when things go wrong.

The useful insight isn't the arithmetic. It's that W is the variable you control, and it's usually the one that's out of whack. If that same service holds a connection for 150ms instead of 15ms, it needs ten times the connections for the same traffic. And the most common reason W balloons isn't slow SQL. It's code like this:

// Looks fine. Holds a Postgres connection across an HTTP call.
const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('BEGIN');
  const order = await client.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE', [id]);
  const charge = await paymentGateway.charge(order.rows[0]); // 300-2000ms, network
  await client.query('UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2', ['paid', id]);
  await client.query('COMMIT');
} catch (err) {
  await client.query('ROLLBACK');
  throw err;
} finally {
  client.release();
}

That transaction pins a connection (and a row lock) for the full duration of a third-party network call. Under load, the pool drains, and every other request queues behind payment latency. Bumping max doesn't fix it. It just moves the queue into Postgres, where it now also holds row locks. Do the external call outside the transaction, and let the database connection live only as long as the database work.

Postgres has a guardrail for the worst version of this: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout terminates sessions that sit idle inside an open transaction longer than the limit. It's off by default. Turning it on per role is cheap insurance.

Configure the client pool like you mean it

Library defaults are tuned for "works on a laptop." Under real concurrency, a few of them bite hard.

In node-postgres, connectionTimeoutMillis defaults to 0, which means no timeout. When the pool is exhausted, pool.connect() and pool.query() just wait. Forever. Your request timeout fires upstream, the client retries, and now you've got two waiters instead of one. Here's a pool that fails fast instead:

db.ts

import pg from 'pg';

export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  host: process.env.PGHOST,
  database: process.env.PGDATABASE,
  user: process.env.PGUSER,          // one role per service, see below
  max: 10,                           // sized from the budget, not from a hunch
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000,    // fail fast when the pool is empty
  idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000,         // the default, stated on purpose
  maxLifetimeSeconds: 1_800,         // recycle so connections rebalance after failover/scale
  application_name: 'api',           // shows up in pg_stat_activity
});

// An idle client can error (e.g. the server restarted). Without a
// listener, that error is unhandled and can crash the process.
pool.on('error', (err) => {
  console.error('idle pg client error', err);
});

// Export these as metrics. waitingCount > 0 for long = pool is the bottleneck.
export function poolStats() {
  return {
    total: pool.totalCount,
    idle: pool.idleCount,
    waiting: pool.waitingCount,
  };
}

pool.waitingCount is the most underrated metric in Node database code. If it's regularly above zero, requests are queueing for connections inside your app. That's fine in short bursts; it's exactly where you want the queue to be. If it's pinned high, you've either got a W problem (connections held too long) or a genuinely undersized pool, and the Little's Law math tells you which.

On the Go side, the trap is different. database/sql defaults SetMaxOpenConns to 0, which means unlimited. Nothing in your service stops it from opening one connection per concurrent goroutine that touches the database. If you're using pgxpool directly, set the limits explicitly instead of inheriting runtime.NumCPU() from whatever node the pod landed on:

db.go

cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
cfg.MaxConns = 16                        // explicit: from the budget, not NumCPU
cfg.MinConns = 2
cfg.MaxConnLifetime = 30 * time.Minute
cfg.MaxConnIdleTime = 5 * time.Minute
cfg.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams["application_name"] = "worker"

pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg)

The nested-checkout deadlock

One more client-side footgun, and it's a nasty one because it looks like the database is hung. If a single request can hold two connections at once (for example, it opens a transaction, then calls a helper that does pool.query() outside that transaction), then a pool can deadlock itself: every connection is held by a request that's waiting for a second connection that will never come free.

The HikariCP wiki gives the minimum pool size that avoids this: Tn * (Cm - 1) + 1, where Tn is the max number of concurrent threads and Cm is the max connections any one of them holds at once. With 8 threads each holding up to 3, that's 17. The better fix is to not do it: pass the transaction's client down instead of reaching back into the pool.

Give every service its own role

One cheap move pays off in three places. Instead of every service connecting as app, give each one its own Postgres role.

CREATE ROLE api_svc       LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 150;
CREATE ROLE worker_svc    LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 100;
CREATE ROLE reporting_svc LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 20;

-- Per-role guardrails, applied at session start, no app code needed
ALTER ROLE api_svc       SET statement_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE api_svc       SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s';
ALTER ROLE reporting_svc SET statement_timeout = '120s';
  1. CONNECTION LIMIT turns the budget into enforcement. A misconfigured reporting deploy can exhaust its own 20 slots and get errors, instead of exhausting the whole database and taking the API down with it.
  2. Per-role settings replace per-connection SET. This matters a lot once PgBouncer's transaction mode enters the picture, because SET doesn't survive there. ALTER ROLE ... SET is applied when the server connection starts, so it works through the pooler.
  3. Visibility. Combined with application_name, you can finally answer "who is using my connections?" in one query: 
SELECT usename, application_name, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY usename, application_name, state
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;

If that query shows 180 connections in state idle and 6 in active, you've just learned that your database isn't busy, it's crowded. That's the signal for the next step.

When the math doesn't close: PgBouncer

At some point the budget stops working. You've got too many services, too many replicas, or serverless functions that each want their own connection, and the sum of pools is fundamentally bigger than what Postgres should hold. That's when you put a pooler between the apps and the database.

PgBouncer is the standard answer. It's lightweight (the docs cite about 2 kB of memory per client connection by default), and its key trick is that client connections and server connections are separate numbers. Thousands of app connections can map onto a few dozen real Postgres backends.

The pooling mode decides how aggressively that mapping happens:

  • session (the default): a server connection is assigned for the lifetime of the client connection. Safe, fully compatible, and it barely reduces server connections at all if your app pools hold connections open.
  • transaction: a server connection is assigned only for the duration of one transaction, then returned. This is where the multiplexing actually happens, and it's what you want for the "many services, one database" problem.
  • statement: returned after every statement. Multi-statement transactions aren't allowed. Rarely what you want.

A transaction-mode config for our hypothetical system might look like this:

pgbouncer.ini

[databases]
; per-database cap on real Postgres connections, across all users
appdb = host=10.0.0.5 port=5432 dbname=appdb max_db_connections=60

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt

pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000        ; app-side connections PgBouncer will accept
default_pool_size = 20        ; server connections per (user, database) pair
reserve_pool_size = 5         ; extra server conns under load...
reserve_pool_timeout = 3      ; ...after a client waited this many seconds
max_prepared_statements = 200 ; protocol-level prepared statements in txn mode

query_wait_timeout = 30       ; client waiting for a server conn gives up
server_idle_timeout = 600
server_lifetime = 3600

Two things worth pointing out. First, default_pool_size is per user/database pair, so the one-role-per-service move from earlier now gives each service its own isolated server-side pool inside PgBouncer. Second, max_db_connections sits on top as a hard ceiling for the whole database, which is exactly the "one shared budget" idea expressed as config.

The app-side pools don't go away. Each pod still keeps a small pool of connections to PgBouncer, and those can be generous, since a client connection to PgBouncer is cheap. The expensive resource, a real Postgres backend, is now rationed in one place.

What transaction mode breaks

Transaction pooling isn't free, and the PgBouncer docs are blunt about it: clients must not rely on session-level state, because consecutive transactions can land on different server connections. Their compatibility table lists what never works in transaction mode:

  • SET / RESET (session settings leak or vanish; use ALTER ROLE ... SET or SET LOCAL inside a transaction instead)
  • LISTEN (notifications go to whichever backend you happened to be on)
  • WITH HOLD cursors
  • SQL-level PREPARE / DEALLOCATE
  • Temp tables with PRESERVE ROWS or DELETE ROWS (only ON COMMIT DROP is safe)
  • LOAD
  • Session-level advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock); the transaction-level pg_advisory_xact_lock variants are fine

The session-level advisory lock one deserves a warning, because it fails silently:

Warning
If a job runner uses pg_advisory_lock() for leader election behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, the lock is taken on one server connection and the "unlock" may run on another. The lock can outlive the job, or another instance can grab a different backend and believe it's the leader. Point those workloads at a session-mode pool or straight at Postgres.

A practical pattern is two PgBouncer databases pointing at the same Postgres: one in transaction mode for request/response traffic, one in session mode (per-database pool_mode is allowed in the [databases] section) for migrations, LISTEN-based consumers, and anything that needs session state.

Prepared statements used to be the deal-breaker

For years, the standard advice was "turn off prepared statements if you use PgBouncer in transaction mode," because a statement prepared on one backend doesn't exist on the next. PgBouncer 1.21 changed that: with max_prepared_statements set to a non-zero value, PgBouncer tracks protocol-level prepares and re-prepares them transparently on whichever server connection the client lands on. Through 1.23 that setting defaulted to 0 (off); since 1.24 it defaults to 200.

The catch: it only covers protocol-level prepared statements, the kind drivers send through the extended query protocol. A literal PREPARE foo AS ... in SQL is still invisible to PgBouncer and still breaks. And if you're on a managed pooler or an older PgBouncer, check the version before assuming it works.

PgBouncer has its own ceiling

PgBouncer is single-threaded. One process uses one CPU core, no matter how big the box is. For most setups that's plenty, but a very busy pooler can become the bottleneck itself. Since 1.12 you can run several processes on the same port with so_reuseport = 1 and let the kernel spread client connections across them, and newer versions add peer_id plus a [peers] section so cancellation requests reach the right process.

Here's the gotcha that brings us right back to the start of this article: each PgBouncer process has its own pools. Four processes with default_pool_size = 20 can open up to 80 server connections per user/database pair, not 20. Run PgBouncer as a sidecar in every app pod and you've rebuilt the original multiplication problem with extra steps. The pooler only centralizes the budget if it's actually central, or if you divide the per-process limits by the number of processes.

Watching the budget

Once the pooler is in place, you've got two queues to watch: the one inside each app (waitingCount in node-postgres, Stat() in pgxpool) and the one inside PgBouncer. Connect to the admin console and run:

SHOW POOLS;

The columns that matter are cl_active (clients linked to a server connection, or idle with nothing waiting), cl_waiting (clients waiting for one), sv_active / sv_idle (server connections in use or parked), and maxwait (how long the oldest waiting client has been waiting). A healthy transaction-mode pool under load looks like a lot of clients, a small number of active server connections, and cl_waiting that blips and drains. A maxwait that keeps climbing means the database-side budget really is too small for the work, or, more often, that some transaction is holding its server connection far too long.

On the Postgres side, the pg_stat_activity query from earlier is still your ground truth. The number you care about isn't count(*). It's count(*) WHERE state = 'active', compared against your core count.

Where this leaves you

If I had to compress all of this into one opinion, it's this: raising max_connections is almost never the fix. It's the database equivalent of widening the highway entrance while leaving the bridge the same width. Postgres 14 made idle connections cheap, so a bigger number won't crash you the way it used to, but it also won't give you more throughput, because throughput is bounded by cores and I/O, not slots.

The playbook, in order of how cheap it is:

  1. Count what you've actually got: sum pool_max * max_replicas * surge across every service and compare it to the real budget.
  2. Shorten W. Get network calls out of transactions, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and fix nested checkouts. This often shrinks the needed pool by more than any tuning.
  3. Set explicit client pool limits and a connection-acquire timeout, and graph the waiting count.
  4. Give each service its own role with a CONNECTION LIMIT and per-role timeouts.
  5. When the sum still doesn't fit, put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front, with max_db_connections as the single shared ceiling, and route session-dependent workloads around it.

Queues are fine. You're always going to have one somewhere. The whole game is choosing where it lives, and the right answer is in your app or your pooler, where waiting is cheap, not inside Postgres, where every extra waiter makes everyone else slower.

title: Building Multi-Tenant SaaS Help Center Retrieval — A 4-Stage Citation Contract
description:
The hard choice in a multi-tenant SaaS help center is not “which vector database is fastest?” It is deciding how much freshness and control your citation contract can tolerate. Short answer: keep a durable, tenant-filtered index for stable content, add a live retrieval path for fast-changing pages, and make both produce the same citation-shaped result. That lets the answer layer remain boring and auditable.

I start with the answer a support user will see, then work backward. A citation must identify the tenant, source document, revision, and the exact text span used. If a result cannot carry those fields, it is not ready for generation, no matter how relevant its embedding looks.

The constraint is a retrieval contract

Write the contract before picking an endpoint. Mine has four invariants: every query is scoped to one tenant; every chunk has a stable source and revision; freshness is explicit; and an answer cites only chunks returned by retrieval. Those rules prevent a surprisingly common failure where a global index returns a plausible paragraph from another customer.

Infrai fits the durable branch when you want one REST API for this vector work and adjacent backend jobs. The public discovery surface is self-describing, so the adapter can inspect the documented method and path instead of baking provider-specific assumptions into each tenant.

The retrieval unit matters too. A whole article is easy to cite but noisy for reranking. A tiny sentence has sharp relevance but loses context. In practice, I use a section-sized chunk with a parent document id, heading path, locale, ACL, and updated_at. Your mileage may vary; chunk size depends on how your help center authors write.

Keep ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages. Log tenant id and request id at each boundary, plus candidate count and the selected source ids. Do not log the full customer text by default. That is a compliance decision, not a performance trick.

How should multi-tenant SaaS help center retrieval handle freshness and citation tracing?

There are two viable shapes.

The durable path ingests published content into a tenant-partitioned vector collection. It gives predictable filtering, repeatable evaluation, and a clean revision history. The live path fetches or searches the current help-center source at query time, then ranks those passages alongside durable candidates. It catches an article edited five minutes ago, but it adds network variability and another place to enforce tenant permissions.

Their shared invariant is the citation envelope. A candidate should look conceptually like this:

candidate = {
    "tenant_id": "t_42",
    "document_id": "doc_918",
    "revision": "r17",
    "heading_path": ["Billing", "Invoices"],
    "text": "...",
    "source_url": "https://help.example.test/billing/invoices",
    "updated_at": "2026-08-31T09:20:00Z",
    "retrieval_path": "durable",
}

The answer service accepts only this envelope. It can merge durable and live candidates, deduplicate by document and revision, and attach citations without guessing where a sentence came from. A short-lived live result that lacks a revision should be marked ineligible for citation, even if it helps reranking.

Ship it carefully.

Where a narrow API surface helps

For a team that wants this split without installing an SDK for every backend concern, Infrai is a deliberate option. Its breadth is behind one consistent REST surface: discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and a single key can cover the vector operations alongside other backend capabilities. That can reduce adapter code when the same service also owns notifications or scheduled ingestion.

For the durable branch, the documented vector surface covers collection creation, upsert, query, and deletion. Generate request details from the public discovery document instead of copying assumptions between tenants. The useful advantage here is the uniform contract, not a claim that one index will fit every workload. Infrai also puts 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so an ingestion worker does not need a new vendor credential when it adds a scheduling or notification step. One REST API means plain HTTP from any language, with no SDK installation required.

This is the small discovery probe I use during startup. It is intentionally read-only; the production writer still validates its tenant metadata before calling a vector write route.

import os
import time
import requests

def load_discovery():
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = requests.get(
                "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
                timeout=10,
            )
            if response.status_code == 200:
                return response.json()
            if response.status_code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text}")
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)

Here is the boundary I keep in code: the provider client returns candidates, while my application owns tenant filters and citation validation.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Candidate:
    tenant_id: str
    document_id: str
    revision: str
    text: str
    source_url: str

def citation_ready(candidate: Candidate, tenant_id: str) -> bool:
    return (
        candidate.tenant_id == tenant_id
        and bool(candidate.document_id)
        and bool(candidate.revision)
        and bool(candidate.source_url)
        and bool(candidate.text.strip())
    )

That small check is where cross-tenant leakage gets stopped. It also makes a provider swap less dramatic because the downstream contract does not change.

How do the common alternatives compare?

The comparison is about system shape, not a universal leaderboard. Pinecone is a managed vector index, Weaviate is an open-source and managed vector database, and Elasticsearch combines mature lexical search with vector capabilities. All can participate in a durable path; the surrounding operational model is the differentiator.

Option Durable index fit Live/fresh path Citation-control implication
Pinecone Managed vector retrieval with tenant metadata filters Usually an application-owned fetch or re-index step Keep revision and source fields in metadata; validate them before generation
Weaviate Flexible self-hosted or managed collection model Application can combine collection search with source fetch More deployment choices mean more policy to standardize
Elasticsearch Hybrid lexical/vector retrieval in an existing search stack Strong fit when the source is already indexed and refreshed Mapping and analyzer changes become part of the citation audit trail
Infrai vector surface One REST contract for collection create, upsert, query, and delete Pair vector results with an application-owned live fetch Discovery and consistent envelopes simplify the adapter boundary; tenant policy remains yours

No row removes the need for a labeled evaluation set. Before rollout, label a small sample per tenant with the expected supporting passage, then measure recall at the candidate stage and citation accuracy at the answer stage. I once treated a high top-k score as proof of grounding; the first revision-heavy test showed that stale, well-phrased chunks can still win. That was a design correction, not a model problem.

Roll out the two paths without losing the audit trail

Start durable-only for a narrow set of published articles. Store the retrieval path, revision, and source ids with every generated answer. Add the live branch behind a flag for tenants whose content changes hourly, and compare citation coverage against the same labeled set. Keep a kill switch that selects durable candidates when the live source is unavailable; the answer should then say it is based on the last indexed revision.

The catch is operational ownership. A live fetch is not suitable when your source has strict latency budgets, offline regions, or no stable revision identifiers. Stick with a durable-only specialist such as Elasticsearch when lexical controls and existing cluster operations are the primary constraint. Conversely, a live branch earns its cost when “current policy” matters more than a fixed response time.

If your boundary fits the uniform REST approach, start with the Infrai documentation and confirm the current discovery schemas before wiring ingestion. The decision rule is simple: choose the path that preserves freshness, control, and citation evidence together; combine both when the feature needs durable and live context.

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: How Blackstone is funding the AI revolution with billions
description:
Blackstone is becoming a central financier for the next wave of AI infrastructure.

Through its BXN1 unit, the firm is deploying billions in debt capital to neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Crux AI.

These investments, often secured by data center hardware and customer contracts, highlight the massive capital requirements behind AI scaling.

We look at how Blackstone's lending model is shaping the availability of compute resources outside of traditional cloud providers.

The loan strategy

Blackstone lends capital to newer companies that provide computing power, known as neoclouds. A special aspect of this strategy is the guarantees it receives: the company secures its loans using the borrowers' equipment as collateral, as well as the contracts they have signed with their customers.

One of the most notable examples of this tactic is the 2023 deal with CoreWeave, which received a $2,3 billion loan. CoreWeave’s debt is now estimated at $50 billion. In addition, Blackstone is participating in a $10 billion financing for Firmus and has invested $5 billion in Crux AI.

Market challenges

The size of the loans has raised concerns among some investors, especially after recent developments. Firmus canceled its plans to list on the Australian stock exchange, while CoreWeave shares recently fell more than 20%.

Meta will give all shareholders new shares without voting rights

Despite the concerns, Jas Khaira, an executive at Blackstone, ruled out the possibility of a widespread banking crisis due to the accumulated debts. He argues that the risk is limited, as the end customers using this infrastructure are large and powerful enterprises.

In addition to debt facilities, Blackstone continues to invest through joint ventures. For example, it has formed a $1,5 billion joint venture with Anthropic and Hellman & Friedman.

title: What the eMudhra certificate compromise means for your apps
description:
On October 19, 2026, Cloudflare learned that private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, according to Cloudflare's write-up. Anyone who holds those keys can forge a certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate a server. Browsers shut this down quickly. According to InfoQ, most other software that relies on the web's certificate system has no way to block a single bad intermediate. That software stays exposed until its list of trusted certificates is updated and redeployed. Your servers, containers and API clients are in that second group.

The background you need

When your app opens an HTTPS connection, the server sends a certificate. A certificate is a signed statement that a public key belongs to a domain name. Your app checks the signature to decide whether it is really talking to that domain. This check stops a man-in-the-middle attacker, someone sitting between you and the server, from pretending to be the server.

The signatures come from certificate authorities (CAs). CAs are arranged in a chain:

  • A root CA is a certificate your software trusts directly, with no further proof.
  • An intermediate CA is a certificate signed by a root. It does the day-to-day signing of website certificates. Anything an intermediate signs inherits the root's trust.
  • The trust store (also called a root bundle or cacerts file) is the list of roots your software accepts.

An analogy: think of roots as national governments and intermediates as passport offices they authorize. A border guard (your app) accepts any passport from an authorized office. If one office's official stamp is copied, every forged passport carrying it looks genuine.

Here is where the analogy breaks. A real passport office can only issue passports for its own country. A CA can issue a certificate for any domain on the internet. InfoQ notes that a typical bundle holds hundreds of CAs, plus thousands of intermediates that inherit trust. Any one of them can create a legitimate-looking certificate for your domain.

The web PKI (public key infrastructure) is the name for this whole system of public CAs and trust stores.

Your trust store is not one file. Depending on the code path, it may come from:

  • the operating system (a ca-certificates package on Linux)
  • a language runtime or library that ships its own copy, such as Python's certifi
  • a bundle baked into an app or a container image
  • a custom configuration someone wrote years ago

Revocation means telling software to stop trusting a certificate before it expires. Browsers have a fast version of this. Chrome's is called CRLSets: a blocklist pushed to the browser in the background, which can target one specific intermediate. Most servers, command-line tools and HTTP libraries have nothing like it. Their only lever is editing the trust store itself, and that takes a package update, a rebuild and a restart.

What actually changed

What is new. According to InfoQ, the eight private keys were not stolen. There is no evidence eMudhra was breached. Instead, the keys appear to have been generated by an insecure mechanism. Each key was all zeros except the final byte. A private key should be a huge random number. These could be found by simply trying every possible value, and once someone matched them to public keys used by live CAs, they counted as compromised.

InfoQ reports that six of the eight were TLS certificates trusted by the Apple, Chrome, Microsoft and Mozilla root programs. The other two were for code signing and trusted by Microsoft.

What was already true. Any trusted CA could always vouch for any domain. Non-browser software could never quickly distrust a single intermediate. This incident did not create those weaknesses. It exposed them.

How people responded. Browsers used their blocklists. Cloudflare says it patched critical services before public disclosure. It also updated shared trust stores and base images, and released new versions of its WARP / 1.1.1.1 clients and cloudflared. Cloudflare says its review has not identified active exploitation on Cloudflare services.

According to InfoQ, many projects could not block just the intermediates. So they removed the whole emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their trust stores. InfoQ says that removal is causing collateral damage for legitimate certificates chained to that root. Cloudflare's post does not discuss the root removal. It focuses on patching and on not disabling verification when errors appear.

InfoQ lists updated ca-certificates packages in Arch, Debian, Gentoo, Fedora and Ubuntu, plus updates in Electron, Go, pip, Python certifi, rustls-webpki, Rust webpki-roots and uv.

What it means if you deploy and run apps

The key fact is the gap between browsers and everything else. A clean browser test tells you almost nothing about your backend. Cloudflare says plainly that a successful browser test does not prove a background service is protected. A curl test does not prove it either if your app uses a different verifier.

What to do:

  1. Map your verification paths. For each service that makes outbound HTTPS calls, find which trust store it uses. Cloudflare warns that an API client may hand verification to an HTTP library, the runtime, the OS or a custom config: "Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy."
  2. Update the right layer. Patch the OS ca-certificates package, bump bundled roots like certifi, and check indirect dependencies in your dependency tree, as Cloudflare advises.
  3. Rebuild and restart. Cloudflare says updates need reloads, restarts or redeployments to take effect. An updated package in a registry does nothing for a container image built last month.
  4. Hunt for buried bundles. InfoQ warns that many applications carry a cacerts file inside them that will keep trusting the compromised CAs. End-of-life systems that no longer get patches stay vulnerable.
  5. Check mTLS. With mutual TLS, the client also presents a certificate. If your mTLS endpoint accepts web PKI certificates, InfoQ quotes SSLMate founder Andrew Ayer warning that attackers can simply mint a certificate and authenticate, with no network attack needed.

If you use Cloudflare, upgrade the Cloudflare One / 1.1.1.1 clients to the versions Cloudflare lists (for example 2026.8.2115.0 on desktop). Cloudflare also says Containers users should review their images. Turning on HTTPS egress interception moves certificate checks to Cloudflare's infrastructure, and containers with it enabled are already protected, according to Cloudflare.

After patching, some legitimate connections may fail, partly because some projects removed an entire eMudhra root. Fix those by updating the trust configuration or the server's certificate. Cloudflare explicitly warns against disabling verification, because that removes the protection the updates restore.

What to watch next: how fast your base images and runtimes pick up the new trust stores, and whether services you call start failing because their certificates chain to the removed root.

What we don't know yet

  • Exploitation elsewhere. Cloudflare only says it found no active exploitation on its own services. Neither source says whether forged certificates were used anywhere else.
  • How the keys were made. InfoQ says the keys appear to come from an insecure generation mechanism. The exact cause is not established in the reports.
  • Propagation time. InfoQ says updates will take some time to reach every place they need to go. Nobody can say how many apps carry stale embedded bundles.
  • Collateral fallout. How many legitimate sites break from the root removal, and what their owners must do, is not covered.
  • Code signing. The two code-signing certificates trusted by Microsoft get little detail in either report.

title: Building an AI Shirt Agent with Spring AI and Tool Calling
description:
Why a Shirt Recommender Is a Good First Spring AI Project

Most tutorials that introduce large language models to Java developers start with a chatbot that answers questions. That is a useful starting point, but it hides the part that makes LLM features valuable inside a real application: the model has to take an action that your code controls. A chatbot that only produces text is a demo. An agent that looks something up in your own system and returns a structured result is a feature.

This article walks through shirts-agent, a small Spring Boot and Spring AI example that makes the idea concrete. A user sends an item and a color to a REST endpoint. An AI agent calls a Java method that searches an in-memory catalog, and the service returns a structured shirt recommendation. The whole project fits in a few classes, which makes it a good way to see how the pieces fit together before you build something larger.

The project uses Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5.6, Spring AI 1.1.8, OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini model, and Maven. The complete source is available at github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.

The Problem: Language Models Do Not Know Your Data

A language model is trained on public text up to a certain date. It does not know what is in your product catalog, your inventory, your customer records, or your internal APIs. If you ask it "which shirt do you recommend in red?" without any extra help, it can only guess, and a guess is not a recommendation a shop can sell.

There are several ways to connect a model to your data:

  • Stuff the data into the prompt. This works for small datasets, but it wastes tokens, grows with your catalog, and leaks everything to the model on every request.
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). You search a vector store or index for relevant documents and include them in the prompt. This is the right tool for unstructured text such as manuals or policies.
  • Tool calling (function calling). You describe a set of Java methods to the model. When the model needs information or wants to perform an action, it asks for one of those methods to be executed. Your code runs the method and returns the result, and the model uses that result to finish its answer.

shirts-agent uses tool calling. The data is structured (a catalog of shirts with a color and a name), the question has a clear shape (find a shirt of this color), and the answer must come from your system rather than from the model's imagination. Tool calling is a natural fit.

The Architecture in Four Steps

The request flow is short and easy to follow. According to the project documentation, ShirtController receives the HTTP request, ShirtService validates the input, and ShirtAgent asks the model to find a shirt. The model then calls ShirtCatalogTool.findShirtByColor and returns a structured Shirt object. Invalid input is rejected with HTTP 400 before the model is ever called.

That last point deserves emphasis. Every call to a hosted model costs money and adds latency. Validation belongs in ordinary Java code, in front of the model, so that obviously bad requests never reach it.

The layers look like this:

  1. Controller. Exposes POST /api/shirts/recommend and maps the JSON body to a request object.
  2. Service. Checks that item and color are present and well formed. Rejects bad input with a 400 response.
  3. Agent. Wraps the Spring AI chat client. It builds the prompt, tells the model what it is allowed to do, and converts the model's final answer into a Shirt.
  4. Tool. A plain Java class with a method annotated with @Tool. This method is the only place where the model touches your data.

Keeping these responsibilities separate pays off quickly. You can test the validation logic without a model, test the tool against the catalog without a model, and swap the model provider without rewriting the business logic.

Defining the Tool

In Spring AI, a tool is an ordinary Spring bean with a method that the model is allowed to call. The @Tool annotation provides a description that the model reads to decide when the tool is useful. The parameter names and descriptions matter, because the model relies on them to fill in the arguments correctly.

An illustrative version of such a tool looks like this. It is a simplified sketch to show the shape of the code, not a verbatim copy of the repository:

@Component
public class ShirtCatalogTool {

    private final ShirtCatalog catalog;

    public ShirtCatalogTool(ShirtCatalog catalog) {
        this.catalog = catalog;
    }

    @Tool(description = "Find a shirt in the catalog by its color")
    public Shirt findShirtByColor(
            @ToolParam(description = "The color of the shirt, for example red or blue") String color) {
        return catalog.findByColor(color)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No shirt found for color: " + color));
    }
}

Notice what the tool does not do. It does not decide which shirt is best, it does not format prose, and it does not call the model. It takes a color, looks it up in a deterministic source of truth, and returns a typed result. The model is responsible for the conversation and the final wording. Your code is responsible for the facts.

This separation is the most important design habit when working with tools. Keep the tool small, deterministic, and easy to test. Put the intelligence where it belongs: in the orchestration of the model, not inside the data access.

Keeping the Output Structured

A recommendation that comes back as a paragraph of text is hard to use in an application. A frontend needs fields. A test needs assertions. A downstream service needs a predictable shape.

Spring AI can ask the model to return its answer as a Java object. The agent declares the target type, the framework converts the model's response into that type, and your service receives a Shirt rather than a string it has to parse. This is what the project means by "returns a structured Shirt."

Structured output reduces an entire category of bugs. You no longer depend on regular expressions over free-form text, and a change in the model's phrasing cannot silently break your parsing code. If the model returns something that does not fit the expected type, the failure shows up as an error you can handle rather than as wrong data that reaches a user.

Validation Before the Model

The service layer is where you protect both your budget and your users. In shirts-agent, the service checks the request before the agent is invoked. A missing item or color results in an HTTP 400 response, and the model is never called.

This pattern is worth copying into any LLM-backed feature. Ask yourself which inputs can be rejected with plain Java. Length limits, required fields, allowed values, and basic format checks all belong in front of the model. Each request you reject locally is a request you do not pay for, and a failure you can explain to the caller in a clear message.

Validation is also a security measure. Free-form text sent to a model can contain instructions that try to change its behavior. You do not eliminate that risk by validating input, but you reduce the surface area. Constrain what the model is asked to do, and constrain what the tool can return.

Running the Project Locally

The project is intentionally easy to run. You need JDK 21 and Maven 3.9 or later. Clone the repository, export your OpenAI key, and start the application with Maven:

git clone https://github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.git
cd shirts-agent
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
mvn spring-boot:run

Then send a request to the endpoint on port 8080:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/shirts/recommend \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"item":"playera","color":"red"}'

The unit tests run with mvn test, and they do not call the model. That detail matters. Testing an LLM application should not depend on a live API call for every build. Test the controller, the service validation, and the tool logic in isolation, and reserve live model calls for a small number of integration checks.

What the Project Deliberately Leaves Out

A good example is honest about its boundaries. shirts-agent has no database. The catalog is an in-memory list of four shirts, which is enough to demonstrate the pattern and nothing more. There is no messaging layer, no event stream, and no cloud deployment. There is no Dockerfile or compose file. The application runs on port 8080 and depends on the OpenAI API.

Each of these omissions is a useful discussion point. In production you would replace the in-memory catalog with a repository backed by a real database, perhaps with caching for frequently requested colors. You would add authentication to the endpoint, rate limits to protect your model budget, timeouts around the model call, and observability so you can see latency, token usage, and tool invocations. You would also decide how to handle a color that is not in the catalog: return a friendly message, suggest the closest available color, or ask the user to try again.

The point of the example is not to be production-ready. The point is to show the smallest set of moving parts that still demonstrates a real agent calling a real tool.

Lessons for Java Teams Adding LLM Features

Several practical lessons come out of a project this small.

Start from the data, not from the model. Identify the facts your feature needs and where they live. If the answer depends on your catalog, your orders, or your policies, the model should retrieve those facts through a tool rather than generate them.

Make tools boring. A tool should be a deterministic method with clear inputs and outputs. The less cleverness you put inside a tool, the easier it is to test, reason about, and trust.

Validate in code before you call the model. Use the programming language you already know to reject bad input, enforce limits, and protect your budget.

Prefer structured output. Typed results are easier to test and integrate than free-form text. Let the framework handle the conversion, and fail loudly when the shape is wrong.

Test without the model where you can. Most of your application logic should run in unit tests without network calls. Reserve live calls for integration tests that you run deliberately.

Keep the model replaceable. Spring AI abstracts the chat provider behind common interfaces. Keep your domain logic and tools free of provider-specific details so that changing models is a configuration decision rather than a rewrite.

Where Spring AI Fits in the Java Ecosystem

Spring AI brings the patterns Spring developers already know to LLM applications. Dependency injection wires the chat client and the tools. Configuration properties select the model and its settings. Auto-configuration sets up the common parts so that you can focus on your domain. The result feels familiar to any team that already builds Spring Boot services, which is the main reason to consider it for enterprise Java work.

This matters for teams in regulated or long-lived systems. The question is rarely whether a model can answer a question. The question is whether the feature can be built, tested, deployed, monitored, and maintained by the same engineers who maintain the rest of the platform. Using familiar tools reduces the cost of answering yes.

Extending the Example

If you want to take this project further, there are several natural next steps that keep the same architecture.

First, add more tools. A real shop needs to check stock, look up sizes, and calculate prices. Each of these can be another annotated method with a clear description. The model decides which tool to call based on the request, so give each tool a name and description that make its purpose obvious.

Second, add a second data source. Imagine a product search over a vector index for descriptions and reviews, combined with the exact catalog lookup you already have. Retrieval handles the fuzzy part of the question, and tools handle the exact facts. This hybrid approach is one of the most useful patterns in production LLM systems.

Third, add evaluation. Create a set of requests with expected outcomes and run them regularly. When you change a prompt, a model, or a tool description, the evaluation tells you whether the behavior got better or worse. Without evaluation, LLM features drift in ways that are hard to notice until a user complains.

Fourth, add observability. Record which tools were called, how long each step took, and how many tokens were used. This information is essential for controlling cost and diagnosing unexpected answers.

Conclusion

shirts-agent is a small project with a big lesson. A language model becomes useful in an application when it can call your code, and your code remains the source of truth. A controller accepts the request, a service validates it, an agent coordinates the model, and a tool returns the facts. Each layer has a clear job, and each can be tested on its own.

If you are a Java developer curious about AI features, this is a good place to start. Clone the repository, run the example, change the catalog, add a second tool, and watch how the model chooses between them. Then ask the question that matters for your own domain: which facts in my system should the model be allowed to ask for, and which rules should my code enforce before the model is ever involved?

The full source code and documentation are available at github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.

Key Takeaways

  • Use tool calling when a model must answer with facts from your own system.
  • Keep tools small, deterministic, and easy to test.
  • Validate requests in ordinary Java code before calling the model.
  • Prefer structured output over free-form text for application features.
  • Test most of your logic without live model calls.
  • Keep the model provider replaceable through the framework's abstractions.
